Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after he is dropped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:52 UTC
01:40:52 KST

Portugal captain Cristiano Ronaldo on Wednesday announced that he had left the team’s training camp in Denmark after coach Jorge Jesus told reporters that the striker would be dropped for their next match.
Ronaldo had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken stadium in Copenhagen on Wednesday but left abruptly after Jesus’ news conference.
The veteran coach had said that Ronaldo, who spent the entire match on the bench against Norway on Sunday, would not start their UEFA Nations League clash against Denmark either.
Photo: AFP
“Following the national team coach’s press conference, and after having a conversation with the Portuguese Football Federation president, I decided to leave the national team’s training camp,” Ronaldo wrote on Instagram.
“In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated,” he said. “Now is time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception.”
Jesus had earlier said that there was no rift between him and Ronaldo, although the 72-year-old did acknowledge that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in the side’s win over Norway.
The news sparked a wave of memes on social media and furious backlash from Ronaldo’s sister, Elma Aveiro.
“They don’t deserve to have the best of anything,” she said about the Portuguese people on Instagram. “We are envious, scornful, and ignorant, and we deserve to return to the mediocrity that defined us in the pre-CR7 era of football.”
Following the 2-1 victory in Oslo, Ronaldo went straight to the changing rooms without joining his teammates in acknowledging the Portuguese supporters in the stands.
“There was no incident whatsoever,” Jesus told reporters.
“Any player — and I was a player myself ... when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don’t get on ... no one is happy about that,” Jesus said on Wednesday.
The Portuguese coach added that he had told Ronaldo before the match that he would not be in the starting lineup, but that he might bring him on toward the end of the game.
“Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It’s nothing to make a fuss about,” Jesus said.
Jesus had said that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would train as normal on Wednesday. However, despite arriving at the stadium in the team bus, Ronaldo did not join his teammates on the pitch in Copenhagen.
Portuguese media shared a video of him leaving the Parken Stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff just after Jesus’ news conference.
They also said that Ronaldo’s private jet was heading to Copenhagen.
Following Ronaldo’s social media post, the Portuguese federation released a statement confirming that the former Real Madrid, Manchester United and Juventus player had left the squad’s training camp.

16:40:52 UTC
01:40:52 KST

Twenty-one US Democratic senators in a joint statement on Thursday last week urged US President Donald Trump to “immediately deliver congressionally approved defense assistance to Taiwan.”
The statement followed Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Those commitments include US$1.3 billion in funds provided by the US Congress, existing weapons sales and a US$14 billion package of new arms sales approved nine months ago, the joint statement said.
Photo: Screen grab from Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Wang Ting-yu’s Facebook page
“[US] support for Taiwan’s self-defense is non-negotiable and crucial to preventing a cross-strait conflict that would destabilize the region and threaten the global economy,” it said. “The US must stand with Indo-Pacific allies in combating [China’s] economic and military coercion as well as directly confront [its] renewed island-building in the South China Sea and increasing aggression in the East China Sea.”
The joint statement was led by US Senator Jeanne Shaheen, ranking member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, and was signed by other senators, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer; Senate Democratic whip Dick Durbin, ranking member of the Senate Committee on the Judiciary; and Jack Reed, ranking member of the Senate Committee on Armed Services.
The Chinese Communist Party’s repression is worsening across China and expanding beyond its borders, with its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress codifying the forced assimilation of Tibetans and Uighurs, the statement said.
The statement listed people who remain unjustly detained in China, including pro-democracy Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai (黎智英), 78, who is still in prison.
“Human rights cannot be an afterthought in our relationship with China,” it said.
The senators criticized Trump for “roll[ing] out the red carpet for Xi” instead of confronting him on key issues such as “military aggression against our allies.”
Trump had traded “tough diplomacy for a ballroom tour and a lavish dinner with his billionaire friends,” the statement said.
“The American people deserve leaders who fight for their financial security and defend our national interests with purpose and measured strategy, not pageantry,” it said. “We will compete successfully with China only through sustained investment in our own strengths, close coordination with allies and an unwavering defense of our democratic values.”
In related news, the air force yesterday confirmed that the first two of the 66 F-16 Block 70 (F-16V) jets Taiwan purchased from the US are to arrive today at Taitung County’s Chihhang Air Base (志航基地).
The jets left the US on Aug. 17, but remained in Hawaii for an extended period.
Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said the F-16Vs had reached a stage where they were ready for delivery and that the Ministry of National Defense would announce their return flight once the schedule is confirmed.

FDA fines probiotic firm for 7th time this year over kidney disease ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:49 UTC
01:40:49 KST

A probiotic seller has been fined a total of NT$4.02 million (US$125,000) this year for repeated violations over advertisements falsely claiming that the product could "reverse kidney disease," the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said yesterday.
The Huo Hua Sheng (活化勝) probiotic product has been ordered to remove the offending advertisements and fined a cumulative NT$8.9 million since 2024, while its endorser, nephrologist Chiang Shou-shan (江守山), has been referred for disciplinary action.
The FDA said the product and Chiang had appeared frequently in television and other media advertisements promoting purported health benefits and making exaggerated claims that the probiotic could treat or reverse kidney disease.
Photo: Taipei Times
Cheng Wei-chih (鄭維智), head of the FDA’s Planning and Technology Management Division, told reporters that the product mainly contains probiotics and lactic acid bacteria, but the advertisements could lead consumers to believe that the food had therapeutic effects.
Such claims could also cause people to delay seeking medical treatment, Cheng said, adding that the advertisements violated regulations prohibiting food advertisements from making false, exaggerated or misleading claims or claiming medical effects.
The Huo Hua Sheng product has been fined repeatedly over its advertisements. According to FDA data, authorities imposed NT$3.08 million in fines in 2024, followed by NT $1.8 million in 2025.
So far this year, authorities have found seven violations involving the product on four television channels and imposed another NT$4.02 million in fines, bringing the cumulative total to NT$8.9 million.
The FDA has also asked television industry groups to ensure that the offending advertisements are removed from their member channels.
Chiang has been referred to Taipei City Health Bureau for disciplinary action under the Physicians Act (醫師法). Possible penalties include a warning, restrictions on the scope of medical practice or revocation of his medical license, the FDA said.
The FDA reminded consumers, particularly those with kidney disease, that food products are not medicines and cannot replace proper medical treatment or claim to cure diseases.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:48 UTC
01:40:48 KST

World champions India are to face archrivals Pakistan for Asian Games men’s cricket gold after both yesterday won their semi-finals with ease in Japan.
India hammered Sri Lanka by 124 runs after Pakistan beat Bangladesh by six wickets to set up a mouth-watering final tomorrow at the Korogi Athletic Park Stadium in Nagoya.
India posted a testing 169-7 on a sharply turning pitch after being asked to bat.
Photo: AFP
Sri Lanka lost two wickets without a run on the board and crumbled to 45 all out in less than 10 overs of chaos that included three run-outs.
It was Sri Lanka’s lowest total in a men’s T20 international, worse than the 77 they scored against South Africa in New York in 2024.
Sri Lanka opted to field and were given a taste of the power of 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi on his Asian Games debut.
The fearless teenager, who topped the IPL batting charts this year, smoked a whirlwind 38 off 21 balls with six fours and two enormous sixes before falling to a thick edge caught at backward point.
“He is an amazing talent,” Sri Lankan coach Ashan Priyanjan said.
Ishan Kishan was India’s mainstay with a crafted 80 not out, including five sixes.
When Sri Lanka batted, pace bowling great Jasprit Bumrah ripped out two wickets in his first over.
They were 18-5 by the end of the fourth over, with spinner Axar Patel taking two of the wickets.
Nuwanidu Fernando decided he would not wait around for a slow death and smacked two sixes off Washington Sundar only to run himself out for 15 two balls later.
The end came rapidly with the last three wickets falling in three balls.
“We don’t know anything about the final match yet,” Patel said when asked about facing Pakistan. “Especially about which wicket we will be playing on. “But all the three pitches in that square look very similar as they all have a lot of cracks.”
Earlier, Abdul Samad smashed an unbeaten 30 off 15 balls as Pakistan thumped Bangladesh by six wickets with nine balls to spare in a semi-final reduced to 13 overs by a wet outfield.
“To be honest, we don’t really care about who will win and who will reach the final,” said Pakistan batsman Saim Ayub, who scored 21 of his side’s 112-4 after Bangladesh posted 111-7.
“All we care about is winning the final, no matter who we are playing against,” he said of the prospect of facing India.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:47 UTC
01:40:47 KST

DRAM chipmaker Nanya Technology Co (南亞科技) has received approval to build an advanced 3D wafer packaging and testing plant for high-capacity and high-bandwidth memory modules in Pingtung County, the Southern Taiwan Science Park Administration said yesterday.
Nanya Technology is to focus on developing through-silicon vias (TSVs) and wafer stacking technologies, enabling the vertical integration of DRAM chips into compact 3D structures to maximize capacity and bandwidth while minimizing latency, the science park said in a statement.
Nanya Technology did not disclose how much it plans to invest in the new site, as the project is still in its preliminary stage, it added.
Photo: Grace Hung, Taipei Times
Nanya Technology said in July that it provides wafer-to-wafer bonding for customized memory chips and is developing silicon-on-a-chip-attached memory module solutions, extending its core manufacturing business into emerging advanced memory packaging technology.
The move aligns with the company’s strategic expansion into 3D IC and TSV technologies. To scale these new packaging and testing solutions, the company indicated at the time that it was considering building a dedicated manufacturing facility in Taiwan.
The science park administration yesterday also approved Fangsco Co Ltd’s (凡事可) NT$20 million (US$628,101) investment plan to develop surgical power systems and precision components used in dental and orthopedic operations, the statement said.
South Korea’s semiconductor material supplier Hansol Chemical Co also received approval to invest NT$800 million to develop and produce advanced materials in Taiwan, aiming to enhance key semiconductor material supply resilience locally, the statement added.
To date, the science park administration has approved investment projects totaling NT$108.11 billion from 21 companies, it said.

MAC links impersonation, threats to possible Chinese transnational repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) said yesterday that threats made by one or more persons impersonating a Taiwanese documentary distributor who brought a film about alleged forced organ harvesting in China to the country in 2024 appear to be a "new method" of Chinese transnational repression.
Speaking at a regular news briefing in Taipei, MAC Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) said one or more unidentified individuals have contacted and threatened people and organizations on at least three occasions, while claiming to be Kuan Chien-chung (管建忠), who distributed the documentary State Organs in Taiwan.
After the people who were threatened reported the matter, Kuan, head of Lion Movies Culture Co, was questioned by police in connection with the cases, Liang said.
Photo: CNA
"The purpose is to make Mr. Kuan run around exhausted," Liang said.
According to Liang, someone used Kuan’s phone number in November 2025 to threaten a lawyer and demand money, prompting police to summon Kuan for questioning.
A similar incident involving the Kuma Academy -- a Taiwan-based civil defense group -- occurred the following month, while on Sept. 29 this year someone again claiming to be Kuan and using his phone number threatened the Taiwan Falun Dafa Association, a local organization of Falun Gong practitioners.
Liang said that, with MAC’s assistance, Kuan reported the matter to police Thursday, adding that the council will coordinate with the National Police Agency and Ministry of Justice in handling the case.
Asked what led MAC to suspect the involvement of the Chinese authorities, Liang said the incidents did not appear to be simple cases of impersonation and threats, but rather "systematic" operations.
"For now, we are provisionally classifying it as a case of transnational repression," he said, adding that the designation could be reviewed as more information emerges.
Liang also noted that authorities have not identified those behind the threats and the circumstances surrounding the cases remain under investigation by judicial authorities.
State Organs is a Canadian documentary about two families searching for missing relatives and allegations of state-run forced organ harvesting targeting Falun Gong practitioners in China, according to the film’s official website.
In late 2024, cinemas and other organizations involved in screenings of the documentary in Taiwan received dozens of threats, including bomb threats.
Taiwan’s National Security Bureau said at the time that the Criminal Investigation Bureau had traced threatening emails to overseas IP addresses and determined that the senders had used virtual private networks (VPNs).

Navy vice admiral joins CGA top ranks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

Vice Admiral Yuan Sheng-hua (原聖華) yesterday became the first navy officer to be appointed a deputy director-general of the Coast Guard Administration (CGA), tasked with improving coordination between the navy and the agency amid intensifying maritime pressure from China.
No active-duty navy officer had ever served as CGA deputy director-general or director-general, the agency said.
President William Lai (賴清德) presided over Yuan’s promotion from rear admiral to vice admiral and his new position at the CGA at a ceremony at the Presidential Office in Taipei.
Photo: CNA
“I expect Vice Admiral Yuan to draw on his experience to promote coordination between the navy and the coast guard, strengthen maritime intelligence sharing, and ensure that maritime surveillance and reconnaissance, as well as emergency response, are closely coordinated so that we can jointly safeguard the country’s maritime territory,” Lai said.
Recent developments around the world show just how quickly the modern battlefield is evolving, he said.
“Gray zone” operations can unfold alongside cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns, while the growing use of artificial intelligence and uncrewed systems is accelerating tactical shifts and decisionmaking, he said.
These challenges underscore the need for military capabilities that can withstand prolonged periods of attrition, he said, adding that even the most advanced weapons systems are only as effective as the maintenance and sustainment capabilities behind them — and the skilled personnel needed to keep them operational over the long term.
The armed forces and the CGA must work more closely together to respond to the rapidly changing maritime security environment, the president said.
The two sides should share intelligence on maritime activity and ensure stable command and communications under all circumstances, he added.
Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲) said that in the face of China’s “gray zone” activities and complex national security threats, the CGA needed someone familiar with maritime defense operations, and the transition between peacetime and wartime conditions, making Yuan an ideal candidate for the post.
Yuan became the agency’s third deputy director-general — a position created following passage in June of amendments to the Organization Act of the Coast Guard Administration (行政院海岸巡防署組織法).
The CGA said the creation of the new post addresses changes in the maritime situation surrounding Taiwan and the evolving geopolitical landscape.
It is also aimed at advancing a “sea-air integration” strategy, technological transformation and preparations for transitions between peacetime and wartime operations, the agency said.
Yuan previously served as deputy chief of staff of the navy, director of the Strategic Analysis Division under the Ministry of National Defense’s Department of Strategic Planning, commander of the navy’s 192nd Fleet, and director of the navy’s Training and Readiness Division.
Additional reporting by Chen Yun

====================================================================================================

AI has the power to realign politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

Last month, the US showed the world both of its minds about artificial intelligence (AI). The people building the most powerful systems, from Anthropic and OpenAI to Elon Musk, were asked to slow down. The heads of the two leading labs even carried that plea to the UN Security Council. The day before, at the same UN headquarters, US President Donald Trump declared that “whoever wins superintelligence wins” and signaled the US should charge ahead.
Between the builders’ plea and the president’s boast runs a fault line that could remake US politics. Big issues have done this before: slavery gave birth to the Republican Party, and civil rights turned the white South Republican. AI, one of the biggest changes in human history, could do it again, this time through a white-collar revolution.
Demand for AI has no ceiling, and no single company dares slow down alone. So the brakes would come from society. As Pope Leo XIV has said, AI’s challenge is “not technological, but anthropological.”
Nvidia Corp chief executive Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) urges the industry to “run as fast as you can,” and the chips that would train the AI models of 2028 are already leaving Taiwan. Those chips would carry a new kind of intelligence, even a new civilization, that learns, copies itself and coordinates faster than any human society was designed to absorb.
People and institutions move at human speed: a degree takes four years, a career decades, a new social contract a generation. No one can retrain every time a better model ships. The speed and power of AI would upend how we work and live together, and social stability would be among the costs that spill out, onto people and into politics.
The US has lived through this once already. For three decades, globalization shipped factory jobs abroad, while a fiat-money economy of cheap credit inflated the assets of those who already owned them. Factory towns emptied, wages fell behind asset prices and the working class that paid the bill found its champion in Trump. That was the blue-collar revolution.
AI could spark the white-collar one. Globalization’s winners, the lawyers, coders, analysts and graduates who sell knowledge, face a rival that learns faster and costs less every quarter. So do whole economies built on exporting skilled work.
This spring, graduates booed commencement speakers for praising AI. In Festus, Missouri, voters threw out every council member on the ballot after the council approved a giant data center. The people absorbing the costs want a vote on the future they are being handed.
Former White House strategist Steve Bannon now sounds like US Senator Bernie Sanders on AI, and Republican presidential hopefuls are courting the skeptics. A conservative need not change their mind about taxes to decide that their children’s future among the machines matters more.
Meanwhile, at the top of US politics, AI is starting to split along party lines. The Republican president wants to race and leaves the brakes to the builders. Summoned to the White House to talk safety, the industry’s chiefs signed a voluntary pledge to police themselves, which Trump called “morally binding.” Leading Democrats want public brakes. Former US president Barack Obama and former vice president Kamala Harris have embraced a slower pace, and California Governor Gavin Newsom has ordered work on an AI kill switch.
Pope Leo’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, insists that a slower pace is no enemy of progress. Flying home from France, he even took aim at Huang: The man now touting AI “guardrails,” is the same one who wants no limits and no government regulation, he said.
Catholics are part of the US’ great swing vote: They backed the Democrats in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Their Church is drawing young converts, and their pope, who has already opposed Trump over the Iran war, is at odds with him on AI, too.
Voters have yet to decide which party owns the issue, and that is the Democrats’ opening. AI would disrupt society like nothing before it, and the white-collar revolution it sparks would need a champion. Trump rode the blue-collar revolution to power. If they play it right, Democrats could be the Trump of the white-collar one.
Taiwan might be the AI race’s factory floor, but it has reason to watch where this debate is heading. Taiwan relies on the US for its security and has always needed friends on both sides of US politics. If AI proves as disruptive as this writer expects, the voices calling for safety would not stay on the sidelines for long. Taipei would do well to start building bridges.
Taiwan’s values give it a head start. A society that takes universal health insurance for granted, and expects the state to cushion ordinary people through change, already shares the safety camp’s instinct that AI should serve people rather than the other way round. That common ground is also insurance.
“Whoever wins superintelligence wins,” Trump said. The booing graduates and the voters of Festus are asking a prior question: Wins what, and for whom? The party that answers first would stand on the right side of history, and might find a new majority there.
James Lee is senior adviser at the Taiwan External Trade Development Council.
In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

Coast guard’s strategic status is rising: budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) plans to significantly expand its participation in international security cooperative frameworks and its operational capabilities, a budget proposal for next year showed.
The budget indicates a transformation of the CGA from a maritime law enforcement arm into a national defense and intelligence gathering entity capable of tackling larger regional security matters.
The proposal showed that personnel from the coast guard’s Intelligence Division and Special Action Support Center are to participate in high-level national security talks with the US.
Photo: Screen grab from AIT’s Facebook page
As the CGA has dealt with China’s rising “gray zone” threats around Taiwan, it has become a valuable asset to national security agencies. Since establishing a working group with the US Coast Guard in 2021, the agency has developed mutual trust with the US through cooperation on maritime search-and-rescue operations and disrupting the smuggling of advanced chips.
As part of the transition, Navy Vice Admiral Yuan Sheng-hua (原聖華) was yesterday appointed a deputy director-general of the CGA to help prepare the agency for more complex and demanding responsibilities.
The CGA is also allocating funds to organize a “friendship fleet” next year with a large offshore patrol vessel and about 100 personnel and cadets to visit the Philippines for eight days.
It would be the first time for a Taiwanese government ship with paramilitary capabilities to sail to the Philippines on a goodwill mission since the two countries severed diplomatic ties in 1975, marking a breakthrough in bilateral cooperation in maritime security.
The visit and the donation last month of a decommissioned 500-tonne Kinmen-class patrol vessel to the Philippine Coast Guard is expected to elevate Taipei’s relationship with Manila.
Taiwan and the US are jointly building an advanced command-and-control system to coordinate in the region. The Ministry of National defense has allocated nearly NT$500 million (US$15.7 million) to National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology to develop a “common operational picture,” which is expected to be finished by the end of next year, as part of that effort.
The CGA is also planning to integrate its radar systems into the Taiwan Tactical Network being implemented in the nation’s armed forces, and invest NT$1.2 billion to buy US-based Shield AI’s V-BAT vertical takeoff and landing drones.
The V-BAT is a reconnaissance and surveillance uncrewed aerial vehicle with strong resistance to electronic interference and advanced intelligence. The drones are expected to become an important tool for countering Chinese patrol operations near Taiwan.

Dutch test new crop to save peatlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:43 UTC
01:40:43 KST

In a soggy field between Amsterdam and The Hague, farmer Sander Roeleveld plows a small white combine harvester into his crops, gathering a grain never before harvested in the Netherlands: rice.
The surroundings could scarcely be more Dutch. Canals criss-cross polders lying two meters below sea level. Windmills grace the horizon as cows — for centuries the country’s agricultural staple — graze in the nearby grassland.
However, the warming climate is allowing Dutch farmers to produce wine and now even experiment with rice, previously unthinkable in such a wet, temperate country.
Photo: AFP
Researchers behind the scheme hope rice cultivation could help address one of the country’s most pressing environmental challenges: peat soils that are sinking as they dry out, pushing parts of the low-lying Netherlands ever lower.
“It’s extraordinary,” said Philippe Terheggen, chairman of the Land van Ons association that has provided the fields for the rice harvest. “We would never have thought maybe 20 years ago that we would be able to grow rice in the Netherlands.”
For now, the project is a pilot scheme, consisting of just 0.6 hectares, with organizers hoping to produce about 3 tonnes of short-grain rice suitable for sushi or risotto.
The team is working with about 30 different rice cultivars from as far afield as Russia, China, Japan and Uzbekistan, to see which grows best in the Dutch climate.
Roeleveld said he wanted to show other farmers that rice could grow in boggy Dutch soil.
“My goal is to show that more things are possible on wetland than just grass,” he said. “Of course, when you have had cows for 600 years, it’s really hard to imagine that you want to do something else than having milk from your cow.”
“I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future,” he added.
The project is about much more than crop diversification. Researchers believe it could help tackle one of the Netherlands’ most persistent environmental problems.
About one-tenth of the country is peatland, which farmers drain for grass to feed their cattle.
As the peat dries out, it releases millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) while causing the land to subside by up to several centimeters a year in the worst-affected areas.
According to Wageningen University, greenhouse gas emissions from Dutch peat soils account for about 2 to 3 percent of the country’s total emissions.
The only way to resolve this vicious cycle is to keep the fields wet — but then farmers would have nothing to grow there... until now.
“Basically it started with just a crazy idea,” said Wageningen University and Research researcher Julian Helfenstein, who is piloting the project along with colleagues from Leiden University.
It is a rare combination of adapting to climate change and mitigating its effects, he said.
“Rice is an opportunity for this part of the world to adapt to climate change, so to grow something that previously wasn’t possible,” he said. “But also to mitigate climate change because it stops this peat from degrading and emitting all the CO2 because you can keep it wet.”
The peat issue affects not just the Netherlands, but much of northern Europe, including Germany, Belgium, even the Baltic states, he said.
Helfenstein and his team are closely monitoring carbon dioxide and methane emissions from cultivating rice compared with maintaining grassland — to ensure the cure is not worse than the illness.
“So far the results are promising,” he said. “As an environmental scientist, you’re always pointing to the problems. And it can be a bit depressing, like, ‘oh, here’s more climate change, here’s more pollution.’”
“And then here’s an opportunity for science to work also towards a solution. So I find that thrilling,” he added.
Local restaurants have already voiced an interest in offering premium Dutch-sourced rice, said Guusje van der Vossen from the Wij Land association which helps farmers transition to more sustainable production.
The rice being harvested now was a grain from northern Japan, which seems the best adapted to Dutch conditions, she said.
She is one of the few people to have eaten Dutch-grown rice — from an experimental batch grown last year.
“It tasted delicious, to be honest,” she said, adding that the aim was to make sushi with it and maybe sake.

The Kaohsiung branch of the High Prosecutors Office yesterday indicted three former military personnel for allegedly collecting military secrets for China since 2020.
The three were identified by their surnames Chen (陳), Lu (盧) and Mao (毛).
They were charged with violations of the National Security Act (國家安全法), Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例) and Classified National Security Information Protection Act (國家機密保護法), as well as the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces, prosecutors said in a statement.
Photo: Pao Chien-hsin, Taipei Times
Chen, who had retired from the air force, allegedly began receiving instructions and funding from officials at an intelligence agency under a provincial committee of the Chinese Communist Party in late 2020, prosecutors said.
Chen allegedly obtained confidential military information, including tank specifications and details of the Han Kuang military exercises, from Lu, who was still serving in the army at the time, they said.
In 2024, Chen allegedly traveled to Zhuhai, China, with Mao, who had also retired from the military, to attend a banquet with Chinese intelligence officials with whom Chen had been in contact.
Prosecutors said Chen sought to establish an organization for China.
During the banquet, Chen allegedly persuaded Mao to contact serving military personnel and collect confidential military information from them, they said.
In June, the Kaohsiung Military Police, Tainan Military Police, Pingtung County Police Bureau’s Criminal Investigation Corps and the Ministry of National Defense’s Political Warfare Bureau reported the case to the High Prosecutors’ Office, which took charge of the investigation, prosecutors said.
The investigation concluded yesterday after prosecutors collected evidence, conducted digital forensics, examined and verified statements from witnesses and defendants, and reviewed financial transaction records, they said.

Beijing only needs the US’ silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:41 UTC
01:40:41 KST

As Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) plane landed at Joint Base Andrews last week, cameras captured US service members adjusting the red carpet laid out for him while Chinese officials waited. It was the image Beijing desired. US President Donald Trump broke with tradition by greeting Xi himself at the base rather than at the White House.
Xi’s 2015 trip made him the fourth Chinese leader to pay a state visit to the US, and none of his predecessors made a second. Xi now has.
The practical driver was a deadline. As Xi landed, Washington announced that the trade truce, due to expire on Nov. 10, would be extended to Jan. 10 next year. The two sides also agreed to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of goods in each direction and to set up a channel for artificial intelligence (AI)-related incidents. China’s commerce ministry said the extension gives both sides room to evaluate their arrangement. What the summit lacked in substance, Beijing made up for in framing, and on Taiwan, the framing is the substance.
According to Chinese media, Xi told Trump that China hopes Washington will “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwanese independence.’” Washington’s long-standing formulation is that it does not “support” independence, and “oppose” is a tougher position. By asking the US to “adhere” to a position it has never held, Beijing sets up any US silence to be read as confirmation.
In return, Beijing got silence. The White House’s account did not mention Taiwan or the arms package, and Trump said only that Taiwan was raised, but not discussed at length. Taiwan’s foreign ministry accused Beijing of distorting facts. That is true, but it rebuts China’s position, not its record. The only detailed account of what was said about Taiwan is Beijing’s.
This is how China turns summitry into leverage without winning a concession. A Chinese media account that records China’s demand and omits any US response becomes a reference point that Chinese diplomats can invoke later and that third countries would find as the only version on file. Beijing does not need Washington’s agreement if it controls the narrative of what was understood.
The test is the US$14 billion arms package. It has been in abeyance since Trump met Xi in Beijing in May, and Trump has called arms sales to Taiwan a “very good negotiating chip.” Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大?) has urged quick delivery. US Ambassador to China David Perdue said he did not know when the sale would be signed.
The calendar suggests Taipei might be waiting a while. Trump and Xi are to meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and 19 and at the G20 in Miami in December.
US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent has said the truce extension is meant to give the leaders time for those meetings. A White House that treats the package as a bargaining chip has every reason to hold it through two more summits. The likeliest outcome is that it slips into next year, and Beijing would read each week’s delay as confirmation that Xi’s words have landed.
There is a wider cost. Internationally, “no clash over Taiwan” reads as a win for Beijing regardless of what was agreed. When the world’s two largest powers trade tariff cuts and warm words while Taiwan barely features in the US account, observers from Southeast Asia to Europe conclude that Taiwan is an item to be managed between Washington and Beijing, not a democracy with its own voice.
Taipei cannot control what Washington says, but it can control how quickly its own account travels. With two more summits before the year ends, three lessons are urgent to learn.
First, Taiwan should prepare before each summit. Responses to Beijing’s likely formulations should be ready for publication within hours of a readout, in English, Japanese and other key languages.
Second, it should rebut the record, not just the claim. Taipei should point out when the only account of an exchange is Beijing’s, and publicly ask Washington to restate its policy under the Taiwan Relations Act and the “six assurances.”
Third, amplify partners. Statements from Tokyo, Seoul, Canberra and the US Congress opposing coercion should be resurfaced in the same news cycle as Chinese media accounts, so the record carries more than one voice.
Beijing understands that summits are remembered through their images and their readouts. It got both in Washington. Before Shenzhen, Taipei needs to make sure that Beijing is not the only one telling the story.
Aadil Brar is a Taipei-based journalist and geopolitical analyst.

====================================================================================================

One side just overplayed its hand in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:41 UTC
01:40:41 KST

A chance was missed last week to put the standoff between the US and Iran on a path toward settlement rather than escalation: Tehran made an offer and US President Donald Trump refused it. The attempt failed because neither was ready to compromise, and if that is the end of the matter one side will have overplayed its hand. The question is which — and that does not have a simple answer.
The US president is playing hardball with growing confidence. His aides have been briefing media outlets that the US holds all the cards, and Trump himself told Axios that the phased deal Tehran put on the table was one he might have accepted a year ago, but not now. He also said Iran was mistaken if it thought the approach of US midterm elections gave it leverage, because he does not even consider them.
Some of this is clearly untrue. Trump does consider the midterms, or he would not keep saying he might go back to bombing Iran once they are over. He just does not care about them as much as the Iranians — and perhaps some Republican congressional candidates — want him to.
Illustration: Mountain People
It is also inconceivable that the president would have accepted the current Iranian proposal a year ago, before the start of the war. The offer consists of frontloaded concessions to be fulfilled by the US, in exchange for Iran committing to two things: to stop trying to close the Strait of Hormuz to international traffic within seven days and to then begin nuclear talks — or at least talks about what those should cover.
Of course, until the day before the war began about seven months ago, Hormuz was open and the US and Iran were already in nuclear talks. So why on earth would Trump agree to hand over US$12 billion and other gifts just to get what he already had?
But these are just niggles. Much more important is that the Islamic republic and its military successfully turned the war into a contest for control over the strait. For some time, they appeared to have the upper hand. What gives Trump his confidence is that they no longer do?
That is because the US Navy has proved highly effective at closing Hormuz to Iranian oil, while eventually succeeding in the much more difficult task of opening the waterway to non-Iranian traffic. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are trying their best to blow ships up, but the US Navy’s defensive umbrella has caused them to fail.
As my colleague Javier Blas has written, this took time to become apparent because the escorted ships have traveled “dark,” with their transponders switched off and commercial satellite companies cooperating with the US to make it hard for industry analysts to track the tankers. That made it harder for Iran to stop the flow, and also for independent oil analysts to verify US claims about how much oil the navy was getting out.
By now, though, it is clear that Washington’s figures were substantially correct. Flows also surged after drone damage to Saudi Arabia’s East-West backup pipeline forced Riyadh to divert less crude from Hormuz to the Red Sea. As many as 22 million barrels might have passed through the strait in 48 hours over the weekend, compared with about 20 million a day before the war.
Iran has been unable to do the same for its own oil. The US has managed to impose a total blockade on Iran’s maritime crude exports, while at the same time tightening the noose on its wider economic sanctions-busting. That is in part because the Gulf states — which had previously been somewhat leaky — are now motivated to shut evasion channels down, putting an already weak Iranian economy in an increasingly dire situation.
However, that is just one side of the story. From day one of the war, the US administration has failed to grasp the degree to which the Islamic republic sees it as an existential fight, one it has been preparing for since the 1979 revolution. The regime has lived with economic sanctions for most of that time. It built resilience into succession plans not just for Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, but for a host of top military and political positions that it knew to be potential targets.
It is the tragedy of Iran that its leaders do not care about the welfare of its people, on whom the lion’s share of the hardship from sanctions will continue to fall. They care only about the survival of the Islamic republic, which is to say their own. For sure, there are debates among the elite over how best to ensure their security, but the goal is shared. Trump has also proved hardliners correct about US untrustworthiness, tipping the debate away from Iran’s limited willingness to compromise that made the (since abandoned) 2015 nuclear deal possible.
Seen from the perspective of the generals now ascendant in Tehran, the risks to their survival from peace — when they must again face the fury of their own people — are as great as those from continued war. That increases their incentive to hold out for more economic relief than the US wants to give, as well as for the geopolitical leverage and deterrence that control of Hormuz provides, and if need be, to escalate.
So, if the Iranians are overestimating Trump’s political sensitivity ahead of the midterms, Washington is suffering a similar failure of analysis in assessing Iran’s susceptibility to economic pressure. In the meantime, Tehran is threatening to widen the war by asymmetric means, not just in the Gulf, but beyond. Iran has denied responsibility for the five men arrested last weekend for attempting to sabotage a US Air Force base in Fairford, England, and there is as yet no known evidence of a link. Nevertheless, it serves as an example of kind of action the Islamic republic could take.
Something will break, but it is hard to say when, on which side, or after what further unintended consequences have spun off from the conflict. With Qatar still reportedly conducting shuttle diplomacy, a deal could yet emerge from the rejected Iranian offer, which was itself just an abbreviated version of the short-lived memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in June. The one certainty is that neither side actually holds all the cards or can be sure of what happens next should diplomacy fail.
Marc Champion is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Europe, Russia and the Middle East. He was previously Istanbul bureau chief for the Wall Street Journal. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

In ‘Digger’, a ‘Dr. Strangelove’ for the climate change era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:38 UTC
01:40:38 KST

Just as the fate of the world hangs in the balance in Digger, Alejandro G. Inarritu’s over-the-top, climate-disaster satire teeters on the brink.
It’s an audacious plate-spinning act, juggling exaggerated farce, sober anxieties and an oil-mad Tom Cruise. Inarritu, an art-house showman, has always delighted in a grandiosity of vision: the long-take backstage circus of Birdman, the rugged vistas of The Revenant, the metaphysical musings of Bardo. You come to an Inarritu movie for swagger, not subtlety.
And Digger, — a Dr. Strangelove for the climate change era — isn’t trying to mince words. Its desire to make a statement and shake up its audience may be unlikely to find broad critical favor. But there are times to go big. Can you dig it?
Photo: AP
Some, surely, will not. The biggest ding against Digger is that, for a satire, it’s not particularly funny. Cruise is no Peter Sellers and Inarritu is not Stanley Kubrick. Their strenuous efforts to reach a similar black-comedy pitch can fall flat.
But Digger is sharper on the other side of tragicomedy. An impassioned provocation aimed at both politicians and audience members, Digger is by any measure an uncommon major studio release — as urgent as An Inconvenient Truth but a whole lot more operatic. For better or worse, this is an of-the-moment big swing that’s unlikely to come along again anytime soon.
In the movie’s opening moments, Digger Rockwell (Cruise) wakes up in his lavish, wood-paneled home surrounded by antlers, taxidermy and polar bear rugs. With him in bed is his cherished cat, a barely-still-alive creature, portrayed as an animatronic puppet that looks more like Annette than a real feline. The suggestion is not only that Digger, an oil magnate, corrupts nature, but also that something more artificial is going on. The pastoral view outside his window looks more like a natural-history museum diorama than a landscape.
Meanwhile, Digger begins fielding calls from a massive oil drilling platform in Greenland. A glacier crack and methane leak from the seabed are worrying scientists, but Digger charismatically cajoles them with baseball metaphors. He asks instead for some “hustle” in increasing the daily barrels pumped.
Inarritu’s tempo, working from a script by himself and four others, is typically hectic. Cruise launches into the character, a cowboy cartoon, with a torrent of good-ol’-boy dialogue. He proudly brandishes the shovel his granddaddy began the family oil business with. Nearby, a grandfather clock ominously ticks.
Emmanuel Lubezki, the brilliant cinematographer, films these scenes and others from below, giving Digger, a shot in VistaVision, a larger-than-life, carnivalesque quality. Things quickly go off the rails when an ice shelf nicknamed “Judy,” five times the size of Washington, DC, breaks free of Greenland and begins steering toward Europe in what’s predicted to cause catastrophic destruction.
Soon, the not-so-dissimilar US President Compson (John Goodman) and his cabinet are at Digger’s house, needing a plan. Compson pronounces it “a pickle.” The drill-baby-drill brain trust is exclusively male, white and decrepit.
The ensuing drama is more about establishing a narrative rather than saving Europe. Digger vacillates between private scenes with Compson and a scientist named Ganesh (a wonderfully worried Riz Ahmed) whom Digger has, against the odds, taken a liking to. In a showstopper, Digger appears before a UN-like body, all of them outfitted in pistachio-colored clothes and irate at what he’s done to the planet.
It’s a farcical forum in which Digger mounts an emphatic defense of oil, “the mother’s milk of Earth,” he says. Not irrationally, he asks whether the world was really prepared to go without it. With a ringmaster’s flair, he makes a good argument. But the intrusion of reality, in the movie’s apocalyptic second half, has the final say.
There’s a second layer to this, though, running alongside. The movie as we experience it is, in fact, a play being staged, we learn early on. This meta dimension of Digger feels at first like a cop-out, a way of excusing the heightened extremes of the film. With a touch of defensiveness, Inarritu has often tried to preempt criticism of his films with self-reflective digression. Remember how Birdman included a clash with a New York Times theater critic?
But the play-within-a-play structure of Digger opens the movie up to questions about the value of satire and limits of fiction. It also leads the movie to a darkly fateful place, far beyond fossil fuel debate. And it allows Cruise’s full-bodied performance to stretch from caricature to something more poignant. Cruise has always been best in portraying extremes of male ego (Magnolia, Tropic Thunder, Eyes Wide Shut). His Digger will no doubt join those ranks. But, like the film, it’s the quieter, foreboding moments of his performance that stick with you.

Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent.

Nepo baby ‘Backpack’ wins Fat Bear Week contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:37 UTC
01:40:37 KST

The winner of this year’s Fat Bear Week has been crowned after a nail-biting final — and it’s the son of a former champion.
Backpack, a 20-year-old male beloved by rangers in Alaska for his quiet determination, edged out female fellow finalist Dancing Queen in the annual ursine eating competition at Katmai National Park.
More than 2.3 million people voted in the week-long competition that sees bears unwittingly jostle in a series of head-to-head contests to decide which one of them has most impressively piled on the pounds ahead of hibernation.
Photo: Getty Images North America / AFP
Viewers watch a livestream of the enormous animals as they scoop salmon from the Brooks River, while visitors to a dedicated Web site can browse biographies of some of the top contenders, including before-and-after pictures showing how much weight the bears have gained over a summer of feasting.
Backpack’s victory — by a razor-thin margin of just 5,000 votes out of 200,000 cast for the final alone — continues something of a family tradition: his mother Holly is a previous winner.
The animal, known officially by the more prosaic name Bear 89, was nicknamed Backpack by rangers who noted his habit of climbing on his mother’s back when she swam across the river.
He previously suffered a leg injury that left him with a limp and has apparently adapted his lifestyle, preferring to spend his time lazing on a rock, rather than fighting with fellow bears.
“Unlike many large adult male bears, Backpack hasn’t shown much aggression toward his competitors,” his contestant profile says.
Katmai park ranger Sarah Bruce said Backpack weighs about 544kg and is a clear fan favorite.
“He’s one of the bears that we’ve been able to watch on the live cams since the live cams were put in in 2012,” she said.
The bears of Katmai spend summer and early autumn gorging themselves on salmon as they look to bulk up ahead of a long winter of hibernation. For five months, the creatures will not eat or drink, slowing all bodily functions as they shelter away from the harsh Alaskan weather.
While the increasingly popular annual competition is largely for fun, organizers say it is helpful in raising awareness of brown bears and their Alaskan habitats, as well as the risks they face from human activity.

Unknown Publisher

Taipei prosecutors yesterday indicted a man on charges of operating an unregistered office for a Chinese semiconductor firm, seeking an 18- month prison sentence.
Lin Hao-yuan (林浩原), who headed Lontium Semiconductor Corp’s Taipei office, was charged with contravening the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said in a statement.
Article 40-1 of the act states that Chinese companies are prohibited from conducting business in Taiwan unless they have received approval from authorities and have legally established a branch or liaison office here.
Photo: Chien Li-chung, Taipei Times
The company, based in Hefei in China’s Anhui Province had established an office in Taipei’s Neihu District (內湖) in 2012, but its board voted in January 2015 to close it down, prosecutors said. Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs approved the closure later that month.
However, as its business expanded, Lontium chairman Chen Feng (陳峰) allegedly instructed Lin in July 2024 to rent an office in Taipei’s Zhongshan District (中山) to serve as its Taiwan operating base, prosecutors said.
Without prior authorization, the company allegedly recruited high-tech engineers to conduct chip research and development, testing and technical services in Taiwan, they said.
Prosecutors added that they had issued a wanted notice for Chen.
Lontium was among 16 Chinese tech companies investigated by the Ministry of Justice’s Investigation Bureau in August last year for allegedly setting up offices in Taiwan and hiring local staff without authorization.

14 Taipei students fall ill after eating , one under observation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:36 UTC
01:40:36 KST

Fourteen junior high school students at Taipei Huaxing High School were rushed to local hospitals yesterday after eating nuts from tung trees on the school campus during the noon break, with 13 expected to be discharged by the evening and one remaining under observation.
Citing accounts provided by students, school president Tzeng Teng-lung (曾騰瀧) said the students ate the tung nuts out of curiosity because they resembled almonds, according to a Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) report.
One student ate a nut first and the others followed suit. They later began feeling unwell and alerted a teacher, who arranged for them to be taken to two hospitals, he said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Among the students, 13 are boys and one girl, according to the school.
In a press release, Chin Chia-yi (秦家翊), a pediatrician at Shin Kong Wu Ho-Su Memorial Hospital, said the hospital received 10 of the students, most of whom had eaten only a small number of tung nuts, while one had eaten seven.
The students experienced nausea and gastrointestinal discomfort, with one vomiting, but their symptoms have since improved and they are now able to eat, Chin said.
All 10 students were discharged after receiving intravenous fluids, undergoing blood tests and receiving dietary advice, according to the release.
The other four students were taken to Taipei Veterans General Hospital, where one student who ate eight tung nuts was being kept for one to two days of observation, while the other three were expected to return home later yesterday, hospital Vice Superintendent Lee Wui-chiang (李偉強) said.
Huaxing High School said it will launch a campus-wide safety campaign for students and staff, reiterating that plants and fruit on campus should not be picked or eaten, local media reported.
The school said it will step up inspections to prevent similar incidents from happening again.
Toxicity and treatment
Yang Chen-chang (楊振昌), director of the Department of Occupational Medicine and Clinical Toxicology at the hospital, said tung nuts contain tung oil, tung acid and toxic saponins that can cause gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea.
Overall, tung nuts are not considered highly toxic, he said, adding that no life-threatening cases caused by their accidental ingestion have been reported in Taiwan.
Symptoms may begin 30 to 45 minutes after ingestion, with no specific antidote available for tung nut poisoning and treatment focusing mainly on managing symptoms, he said.
Similar cases reported in 2024
Tung trees are common in Taiwan, and Thursday’s poisoning was not the first such incident.
Local media reported two similar cases in 2024, involving five junior high school students in Miaoli in January and four elementary school students in Taoyuan in November.
All the students involved in the two incidents recovered after receiving treatment, with some requiring gastric lavage, according to local media.
After the Taoyuan incident, Taoyuan City Councilor Huang Jean-ping (黃敬平) said he received complaints from parents questioning why the trees were on campus.
The school subsequently put up warning signs beneath the tree to alert students to the potential danger, Public Television Service reported at the time.

Cabinet approves bond, bond ETF tax exemptions extension for 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:33 UTC
01:40:33 KST

The Cabinet yesterday approved a 10-year extension for securities transaction tax exemption for bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and corporate and financial bonds. It would also add active bond ETFs to the exemptions.
The Ministry of Finance said the securities transaction tax on bonds and passive bond ETF beneficiary certificates has been suspended since Jan. 1, 2010, and Jan. 1, 2017, respectively to boost the bond market, help companies raise funds and promote the development of the capital market.
The suspension of the securities transaction tax on corporate bonds, financial bonds and passive bond ETF beneficiary certificates was set to expire at the end of this year, it said.
Photo: CNA
After reviewing the measure, the Financial Supervisory Commission determined that it has helped boost activity and development in the capital market, it added.
Given that active and passive bond ETFs have similar characteristics, the ministry said it decided the two should receive the same tax treatment, and proposed extending the measure to further promote the bond market and support the development of the capital market.
The suspension of the securities transaction tax on bonds and passive bond ETF beneficiary certificates would be extended for 10 years through Dec. 31, 2036, it said.
Beneficiary certificates of active bond ETFs would also be added to the tax exemption from Jan. 1 next year through Dec. 31, 2036.
The amendments to the Securities Transaction Tax Act (證券交易稅條例) have been designated as a priority bill, the ministry said, adding that it would work with the commission and legislative caucuses to complete the changes by the end of this year.
In related news, Taiwan ranked fifth globally in net financial assets per capita last year, averaging 164,470 euros (US$185,785.31), Allianz Research said in its Global Wealth Report.
Taiwan’s ranking remained unchanged from the previous year, trailing behind the US, Switzerland, Denmark and Singapore, the report showed.
Allianz assessed household assets and liabilities in nearly 60 countries, and found that global household wealth reached a record high last year, while the rise of artificial intelligence and market gains made asset ownership increasingly important in determining who benefits from wealth creation.
Global financial assets reached a record 268.4 trillion euros last year, up 8.6 percent from a year earlier, the report showed.
Total financial assets held by Taiwanese households rose 8.7 percent to 4.5 trillion euros at the end of last year, it showed.
The increase was slightly slower than the 9.3 percent growth recorded in 2024 and below the 9.8 percent average for other Asian markets covered in the report — excluding Japan and China — but it remained above the global average of 8.6 percent.
Securities in Taiwan recorded the strongest growth, surging 17.7 percent, compared with 4.9 percent growth in deposits and 2.4 percent in insurance and pension funds, the report showed.
Securities accounted for 34.9 percent of Taiwanese household financial assets, higher than the Asian average of 30.8 percent, but below the global average of 46.9 percent, according to the report.
Taiwan’s financial assets grew 6.9 percent in real terms last year, roughly in line with the 7 percent increase recorded in 2024, the report said.
Since 2019, Taiwan’s financial assets have increased by a cumulative 41.5 percent in real terms, slightly higher than the Asian average of 39.6 percent and significantly above the global average of 22.9 percent, it said.

The government aims to distribute its planned NT$10,000 (US$314) universal cash payments before the Lunar New Year next year, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said yesterday.
The government has allocated NT$235.7 billion for the cash handout program, and relevant ministries have begun preliminary preparations, Lee told a post-Cabinet meeting news conference in Taipei.
Responding to calls from the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus to increase the handout to NT$20,000 per person, Lee said the government’s proposal is based on three principles: First, it must not increase government borrowing; second, it must not crowd out spending on social welfare, national defense, healthcare or education; and third, it must comply with constitutional and legal requirements.
Photo: CNA
Citing Article 70 of the Constitution and Article 91 of the Budget Act (預算法), Lee said the Legislative Yuan is not permitted to propose measures that would increase government expenditures.
The proposed NT$10,000 payment was decided according to strict fiscal calculations and planning, taking into account the nation’s financial capacity, she said.
Lee urged legislators to review and approve the proposal for next year’s central government budget.
The Executive Yuan submitted the central government budget proposal and related spending plans to the legislature at the end of August, with revenue and expenditure budgeted at NT$3.9266 trillion.
Unlike previous universal cash payments, which were funded through special budgets and involved a streamlined administrative process, the latest proposal is included in the annual budget.
The Ministry of Finance has estimated that it would take about five months to complete the necessary system setup and procurement procedures after the budget is passed by the legislature and is promulgated by the president.
The ministry said it has applied to the Executive Yuan for about NT$100 million from the government’s second reserve fund to begin procurement and preparatory work in advance.
The ministry has already initiated procurement procedures in accordance with the Budget Act, Deputy Minister of Finance Chen Yong-sheng (陳勇勝) said.
Separately, KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said that the KMT caucus’ proposal to distribute NT$20,000 would be funded by the excess tax revenue collected this year, not by borrowing.
Chen said current estimates suggest that excess tax revenue could exceed NT$1 trillion this year, providing a substantial source of funding for the proposed NT$20,000 cash payment.
The government collected more from taxpayers than expected, and after accounting for necessary spending and maintaining fiscal discipline, part of that surplus could be returned to the public, he said, adding: “How does that amount to leaving debt for the next generation?”

EDITORIAL: A meeting of contradictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:31 UTC
01:40:31 KST

The second meeting this year between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) in Washington last week was one of grand diplomatic pageantry to showcase the leaders’ supposed personal rapport. However, structural competition and differences persist between the two superpowers.
The 48-hour summit was more symbolic than substantive. The post-summit fact sheets released by the two sides showed that the meeting mostly focused on bilateral trade and tariff agreements, but failed to reach substantive resolutions on many critical issues concerning the global landscape, such as the restrictions on rare earths and advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) risks, and the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Although Beijing intensively deployed cognitive warfare tactics to reiterate that Taiwan is a redline issue ahead of the summit, Taiwan was notably absent from the summit fact sheets. Trump said that the two sides did not spend much time on the nation because Xi was aware of his thoughts and stance, and the US Department of State and US Ambassador to China David Perdue, who also attended the meeting, assured that the US’ Taiwan policy remains unchanged.
The tour of the National Archives Museum also ran into sensitive territory, with the original plan for Xi’s tour to include the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco, an accord that has long been used in support of the argument for Taiwan’s undetermined status, as it only stipulates that “Japan renounces all rights over Taiwan and Penghu” without specifying the disposition of Taiwan. The itinerary reportedly caused complaints from the Chinese delegation, which led to a request for the ad hoc removal of all sensitive documents and shortened Xi’s stay at the museum.
Xi was also showed the US Constitution, Declaration of Independence and Bill of Rights, which should have demonstrated the fundamental difference between the US’ and China’s government systems, individual rights and national sovereignty. Yet, Xi was more concerned with the “Japan issue.”
During the meeting, Xi highlighted the history of the US-China alliance during World War II and said that “the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in a fight against Japanese militarist aggressors,” ignoring the fact that it was the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-led Republic of China (ROC) — not the still-yet-to-be founded Chinese Communist Party-led People’s Republic of China — who had fought alongside the US.
Xi’s distortion of history aimed to erase the historical contribution of the ROC in Taiwan, but it also unveiled his anger with Japan for siding with Taiwan, especially after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s statement last year of Japan’s defense role in a Taiwan contingency. It also highlighted Xi’s anxiety over Japan’s upgrading of defense forces to counter China’s military expansion, with the Xi administration repeatedly stigmatizing the Takaichi government as “neo-militarism.”
Ironically, immediately after Xi’s departure from the US, the White House posted an anti-communist video on social media claiming that “America will never become a communist country, but would defeat communism.”
All of these incidents indicate that, behind the elaborate diplomatic courtesy, the meeting between Trump and Xi was heavy on symbolism and light on major policy breakthroughs.
While Trump faces the upcoming US midterm elections, Xi has prioritized sweeping domestic threats to pave the way for his fourth term and total leadership ahead of the 21st National Congress of the Communist Party of China next year. Last month’s US-China summit was more of a form of “risk management,” depicting the two leaders as seeking “strategic stability,” to prevent miscalculations in escalating US-China competition.
Trump and Xi are to meet twice more — at the APEC leaders’ summit next month and at the G20 summit in December — setting a record of four meetings between the two leaders in one year. A new normal of “high-frequency communication, high-intensity competition” between the US and China is likely to be the trend.
At the same time, pro-China forces will intensify their cognitive warfare, spreading narratives such as “US skepticism” and “Taiwan abandonment” narratives, aiming to divide the US-led democratic alliance and benefit Beijing in acquiring international clout.
For Taiwan, maintaining strategic focus would be of paramount importance.
The nation needs to upgrade its asymmetric defense capabilities and consolidate its position in contributing to global prosperity, such as in high-tech supply chains and First Island Chain security.
Taiwan should also deepen multilateral cooperation with more like-minded countries to develop multilayered regional security networks, and secure international trust as well as the nation’s strategic high ground.

Work to set up migrant return hubs outside the EU is progressing “very well,” Denmark said yesterday as the bloc’s home affairs ministers met in Luxembourg to discuss further ways to boost deportations.
Denmark — along with Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands — has been exploring options to set up such migrant centers.
“When it comes to return hubs it’s progressing very well,” Danish Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bodskov said. “We are moving in the right direction.”
Photo: Reuters
German Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt said there were “preliminary” talks and that more work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits.
“These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term,” he said, adding that he was hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.
The Luxembourg talks come with anti-immigration parties riding high across the bloc, as evidenced by far-right gains in Germany this month.
EU ministers were set to give final approval to tougher new migration rules allowing for the creation of return hubs and granting authorities much broader detention powers. The meeting agenda included discussion on using “enhanced cooperation” with “priority” non-EU countries for returns of people with no right to stay in the bloc.
Proponents said return hubs — which would serve either as the final destination or as transfer centers for those expelled — could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.
However, critics question their effectiveness, pointing to the hurdles faced by similar projects and likening them to “legal black holes” that could see migrants stranded in limbo with little oversight.
The UK abandoned a scheme to deport undocumented migrants to Rwanda, while Italian-run facilities to process migrants in Albania have faced legal challenges and a slow uptake.
Greek Minister for Migration and Asylum Thanos Plevris said his country was aiming to open a center next year in an African country “that we have already agreed on,” but could not yet be named.
Two European lawmakers from the Greens group said officials in Rwanda had told them they were negotiating with the five EU countries.
Dutch lawmakers Anna Strolenberg and Tineke Strik oppose return hubs over human rights and other concerns.
“Most likely the first country that a deal will be struck with is Rwanda,” Strolenberg said.

====================================================================================================

Does avoiding misery make you happy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:21 UTC
01:40:21 KST

In Dr Seuss’s Green Eggs and Ham, the relentlessly upbeat Sam-I-Am spends the entire book badgering a grouchy, nameless narrator into tasting the eponymous dish. He cycles through one inventive but futile pitch after another — in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, on a train, in the rain — until the narrator, caving just to get some peace, tastes the dish and discovers he loves it. When my son was growing up, Green Eggs and Ham was my shorthand for telling him he was avoiding something he’d love if he only tried it.
Of course, not every experience we fear or dread turns out to be a delicious surprise. Misery is an inescapable part of the human condition. We can’t avoid it, yet people try their hardest anyway. We cling to hope even when a situation is hopeless. We push painful thoughts out of mind rather than confront them. We struggle to control things that cannot be changed. And we go to sometimes self-destructive lengths to protect our pride from even the tiniest pinprick. These strategies may sometimes spare us pain in the moment. But while they are intended to promote (or at least preserve) our happiness, over time they have the perverse result of making us much more miserable.
Consider relationships. Declining to chat with the talkative person sitting next to you on a plane avoids one obvious downside — getting stuck in a boring conversation you can’t gracefully exit. But as psychologist Nicholas Epley shows in an extensive body of research, doing this again and again quietly robs us of interactions we might have found genuinely rewarding, though we’ll never know what we missed.
Photo: AFP
The same instinct to protect ourselves can become more destructive in close relationships, when the misery that we fear is rejection. People who are “rejection sensitive” tend to expect the worst and see signs of the coming apocalypse even in ambiguous behavior, like an unanswered text message. When they think they see rejection coming, they try to avoid it by rejecting first — responding with hostility or pulling away from their partner in a self-defeating effort to protect themselves. As a result, behavior that was meant to ward off rejection ends up provoking it.
In my own research, I surveyed a large sample of adults, asking whether they take too many risks, too few, or roughly the right amount — both overall and across key areas such as work, health and relationships. The results were striking. About half felt they took the right amount of risk. But among the rest, the overwhelming majority felt they took too few — and the reason they gave, again and again, was a desire to avoid miserable emotions like fear and regret.
‘COUNTERFACTUAL THINKING’
One of the great engines of misery is “counterfactual thinking”: our mental habit of imagining how things might have gone differently. While we have the capacity to imagine better and worse outcomes, research shows that we are much more likely to dwell on how things could have been better than to consider how they could have been worse. Such “upward counterfactuals” — the job offer we didn’t take, the romantic connection we didn’t pursue — tend to leave us feeling regretful and dissatisfied with the reality we actually have. This asymmetry punishes those who assiduously avoid every opportunity that might result in pain or heartbreak, because such avoidance inevitably creates a stockpile of upward counterfactuals, all the roads not taken. Psychologists distinguish regrets of commission from regrets of omission; it’s the latter – the things we could have done but didn’t – that haunt us longest.
We don’t only avoid misery by avoiding risky behavior; a whole separate category of avoidance happens purely in the mind. We reach for distraction, numbing, and busyness to keep from thinking about what causes us pain. But you cannot anesthetize sadness without anesthetizing everything nearby. Emotional systems don’t come with a dial that turns down grief while leaving joy untouched; suppress one and the whole range tends to flatten.
The practiced avoider often ends up not happy, exactly, but flat — free of acute suffering, perhaps, but also missing the intensity, curiosity, and aliveness that make the good parts of life feel good. This flatness is easy to mistake for equanimity, since it doesn’t announce itself as pain. The protagonist in Stefan Zweig’s story Fantastic Night lives this numbness for years, until one reckless act cracks it open — and what rushes back in isn’t relief but a flood of feeling, the discovery that his calm had been an absence, rather than peace.
Research on physical pain finds, surprisingly, that focusing on pain can diminish its intensity more effectively than trying to distract from it — and there are parallel, if somewhat more mixed, findings for negative emotions generally. One line of inquiry shows that “affect labeling” — simply putting feelings into words — dampens neural reactions to distress. Another set of studies finds that people instructed to accept a negative emotion, rather than suppress it, recover faster, both emotionally and physiologically.
None of this is an argument for deliberately courting misery, or for treating pain as good in itself. But unhappiness-avoidance, adopted as an organizing life principle rather than an occasional and reasonable caution, is self-undermining. It reduces the kinds of experiences available to us, including those of the “Green Eggs and Ham” variety that may prove incredibly meaningful.
My father, born a German Jew, spent part of the second world war in a French prisoner of war camp. He and the small pack of close friends he made there were hungry enough to dig up worms for food and chew on shoe leather. But he once told me that, due to the companionship and challenge of that ordeal, it was the peak experience of his life. Avoidance of misery rests on a false premise about how happiness actually works. The person who spends a life dodging unhappiness does not arrive, in the end, at a life free from misery. Unhappiness avoided is not happiness gained, but more often just misery in disguise.
