UAE probes possible terrorism link to flydubai cockpit incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

The United Arab Emirates has launched an investigation into whether a cockpit altercation aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was linked to “terrorist activity” or involved prior planning or direction.
The country’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi had formed a team of specialised public prosecutors to investigate the incident and establish its circumstances and causes.
The probe follows flydubai's announcement that an altercation occurred in the cockpit during flight FZ1073, requiring crew members to intervene and secure the aircraft.
The investigation will examine all circumstances and motives, “including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction”, the ministry said.
UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, state news agency WAM reported. UAE law therefore applies to crimes committed aboard the aircraft even outside the country's territory, it said.
Emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
Flight FZ1073, carrying 174 passengers, made an emergency landing on Wednesday at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the Saudi city of Tabuk after the cockpit incident was reported.
Flydubai said crew members secured the plane and diverted it safely to Saudi Arabia. Airport officials said the captain and first officer were injured and taken to hospital, while all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for.
Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center said its investigation team had begun work and was coordinating with authorities to establish the circumstances, assess aviation safety aspects and collect evidence.
The UAE foreign ministry thanked Saudi authorities for their cooperation and handling of the incident.
Passengers later departed Tabuk aboard an alternative aircraft provided by flydubai.

U.K. Sanctions Four Georgians Over Occupied Ukraine Visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:27:00 UTC
01:27:00 KST

The U.K. has sanctioned four Georgians—including the brother-in-law of Tbilisi’s mayor—for “legitimising Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory” after they met with the head of a Russian-backed separatist republic.
The designations are part of a broader British sanctions package announced in response to intensifying Russian drone strikes against Ukraine in September. According to a press release Thursday, the wider measures target Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Kremlin propagandists, and individuals allegedly involved in human rights abuses against Ukrainian civilians.
“The U.K. will not flinch in our support for Ukraine,” said Europe Minister Lord Wood of Anfield.
The U.K. sanctions notice states the four men “joined a delegation of Georgian politicians who met with the head of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, and subsequently publicised the visit.” All four now face U.K. asset freezes and travel bans.
The sanctioned delegates include political commentator Paata Abuladze, Mamuka Pipia, leader of the minor Solidarity for Peace party, party member Giorgi Iremadze, and Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, founder of a Georgian Russian-language TV channel.
Separatist leader Denis Pushilin praised the September 2025 meeting on Telegram, referring to the delegation as “likeminded people from Georgia.”
“It was pleasant to hear words of support for our region’s residents from the Georgian guests, who wished for the swift liberation of all the territory of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” he wrote.
According to a video of the meeting, Pipia told Pushilin: “We hope in the very near future the Donetsk People’s Republic will be free.”
Abuladze added: “You won't be able to show me a single country in the world that is such a small country, yet has endured and is doing whatever it takes to restore diplomatic relations.”
Three of the four delegates have so far responded to the U.K. measures, some using profanity and insults.
Mamuka Pipia told the Georgian TV channel Pirveli that he considered the sanctions a “reward” and that he was “very happy.” Mzhavanadze told his Facebook followers that the decision was “shameful,” and said the U.K. was “afraid that the positions expressed by a person will harm their politics.” Iremadze did not respond to Monitori’s request for comment.
Abuladze also took to Facebook following the news of his designation. “Britain sanctioned me… and congratulated me,” he told his followers, “I am grateful to the British for sanctioning me.”
Contacted by Monitori, he added: “So what? Like I won’t go to Donbas now?”
“I have never been to [Britain] in my life,” he said. “It’s just a formality.”
In his Telegram post, Pushilin referred to Abuladze as a “member” of the ruling Georgian Dream party. While Monitori was unable to verify his formal party membership and he holds no elected office, Abuladze has family ties to an influential Georgian Dream figure: he is the brother-in-law of Kakha Kaladze, the Mayor of Tbilisi.
Manana Toqmajishvili, the head of the Tbilisi City Hall Press Service, confirmed to Monitori that Abuladze is Kaladze’s “half-sister’s husband” but that he has “absolutely no connection to Tbilisi City Hall.” She did not comment further.

Journalists decry crackdown after Turkey blocks news site over 'LGBT propaganda'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:23:11 UTC
01:23:11 KST

Journalists decry crackdown after Turkey blocks news site over 'LGBT propaganda'
ANKARA, Oct 1 - A Turkish journalist whose articles were cited among the grounds for blocking independent news portal T24 said the decision effectively treated objective reporting about LGBTQ+ people as a crime, as the outlet prepared to appeal the order on Thursday.
A court ordered access to T24's website and social media accounts blocked after authorities said it had published 118 pieces of content over the past year deemed to constitute "LGBT propaganda".
The decision was taken as part of the "My Family is Safe" investigation, a widening crackdown targeting LGBTQ+ groups which the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and the European Union.
Yildiz Tar, editor-in-chief of LGBTQ+ news outlet Kaos GL, and whose articles published by T24 were among those cited, rejected the authorities' description of the reporting.
"It creates the image that writing about LGBTQI people in an objective way is a crime, because all of the articles I wrote were objective," Tar said in an interview.
"It's not propaganda. It's about basic journalism. It's about reality," he said, adding that the articles covered LGBTQ+ rights, hate killings and the experiences of LGBTQ+ people after the 2023 earthquake in Turkey.
'STATE OF EMERGENCY'
Candan Yildiz, T24's editor in charge, said the decision further expanded restrictions that began last month with operations against LGBTQ+ organisations and activists.
"We are really experiencing a digital state of emergency," she told Reuters. "An authority is telling journalists: you can report these stories, but you cannot report those. This really undermines the foundations of our profession."
T24's lawyers were due to appeal the decision on Thursday, Yildiz said.
"Journalism cannot be shut down. We are doing our jobs," she said.
DETENTIONS
Dozens of people have been jailed pending trial as part of the investigation, and courts have blocked websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, activists and media outlets.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has toughened his anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric in recent years, and last month at the UN General Assembly said a trend of "global gender-neutralisation policies" could be countered by protecting the traditional family.
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe said the arrests, raids and digital restrictions amounted to a coordinated and escalating campaign against LGBT people and rights defenders. It adopted a resolution on Thursday calling on Turkey to immediately release those detained over human rights work and to refrain from adopting anti-LGBT legislation.
The EU has also called on the country to uphold freedom of expression and media freedom.
The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship. REUTERS

This was a visit that has set the course for China-U.S. relations, expanded the scope of cooperation, renewed the bonds of people-to-people friendship, and underscored our shared responsibility to the world, Xie said.
"Under their leadership, our relationship continues to improve and move steadily forward, meeting the hopes of people in both countries and around the world," Xie said.

"If we can get along, then more people can get along," he said.
As the Chinese people celebrate the National Day, Sakolsky said that he was grateful to China for "all the kindness" it had shown him.
Stein, in his remarks, said that the National Day is a great opportunity to recognize and reflect on China's remarkable development over the last 77 years and its extraordinary transformation. "It's also an opportunity to recognize what Americans and Chinese, and what American business and Chinese business have accomplished together," he said.
Responding to those who say American companies are walking away from China, the USCBC president said, "Let me reassure you that American companies continue to hire, innovate and build partnerships in China." ■

Ebola case drop in DRC may mask continued spread: Africa CDC
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:19:21 CST
01:19:21 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned Thursday that a recent decline in reported Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) may reflect disruptions to disease surveillance rather than a sustained reduction in transmission, as the outbreak has claimed nearly 4,000 lives.
Speaking at an online press briefing, Africa CDC official Wessam Mankoula said that the outbreak has spread from three health zones in mid-May to 63 health zones across seven provinces, with 45 health zones still reporting active transmission.
Although the epidemic curve has largely plateaued over the past four to five weeks and reported cases declined in the latest week, the agency cautioned against interpreting the drop as a sign of sustained progress.
"Falling in this curve doesn't mean that the outbreak is totally under control," Mankoula said.
Insecurity and community resistance in multiple areas have hampered surveillance and response activities, raising concerns that some infections may be going undetected.
The warning comes amid growing security concerns in eastern DRC. In Butembo, North Kivu Province, a local ruling-party official was beaten to death following a radio appearance on Sunday, with his party linking the attack to his public support for Ebola prevention efforts. In neighboring Beni territory, an armed attack on a checkpoint also used by Ebola response teams left at least one person dead and several others injured on Saturday, according to local reports.
Meanwhile, in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo Province, a doctor died of Ebola on Sept. 24, raising concerns about infections among healthcare workers. Provincial Health Minister Simon Bokongo said Tuesday that the hospital where the doctor worked had been temporarily closed for 21 days after more than 10 staff members tested positive, with over 123 contacts identified.
The outbreak is also following divergent trends across affected provinces. Over the latest three-week period, reported cases in Ituri Province, the longtime epicenter, declined by about 32 percent compared with the preceding three weeks, while North Kivu Province continued to record an increase.
Contact tracing remains another major weakness. Mankoula said an average of about 14 contacts are now identified per confirmed case, still far below the expected level of around 60. Only about 23 percent of estimated contacts are being followed up, while nearly 80 percent of new cases are detected outside known contact lists.
"This is also one of the reasons... we cannot confidently say the outbreak is under control at this stage," the official said.
The country had recorded 8,224 confirmed cases, including 3,982 deaths, as of Sept. 29, with an overall case fatality rate of 48.4 percent, according to the latest situation report from the DRC's health authorities.
"This outbreak cannot be controlled without building community trust," the official stressed, calling for secure access to affected communities and stronger local engagement to contain transmission. ■

Zhang, competing at her fourth Asian Games, defeated second-seeded Yulia Putintseva of Kazakhstan 6-4, 6-2.
The 37-year-old repeatedly gained the upper hand in long baseline exchanges and converted five of seven break points.
"She is a very tough opponent, and I always find it difficult to beat her. I'm proud of the way I played today," Zhang said.
"Every time, I feel like it might be my last Asian Games. But look, here I am again. So I think you should never put limits on yourself. As long as you have a dream and keep a young heart, it's never too late."
Zhang also spoke of the pride she felt representing China.
"Although tennis is a professional sport, every athlete has a different spark when they talk about events like the Davis Cup, Hopman Cup. There is a different sense of pride that you don't get from tournaments on the tour," she said.
In the other women's singles semifinal, Wang came from a set down to beat Philippine rising star Alexandra Eala 3-6, 6-3, 6-2.
Wang made a slow start and fell 5-0 behind in the opening set. Although she fought back, Eala held on to take it 6-3.
"She was very quick to get into the match and was very calm in dealing with the match. She constantly put me under pressure and didn't give up easy points," Wang said.
"She didn't give me a lot of time to adjust. She had very few unforced errors. That's the pressure that someone ranked in the top 20 puts you under."
Wang reduced her errors in the following two sets to complete the comeback and reach the final.
She said she drew inspiration from compatriot and Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen as she tried to recover from her poor start.
"At the time, I suddenly thought about Zheng Qinwen being down 5-0 before and making that incredible comeback. I wanted to try to do the same," Wang said.
"After all, losing 6-0 would have been a little embarrassing. But I didn't quite pull it off."
Looking ahead to the final, Wang praised Zhang for helping China's younger players.
"Zhang Shuai is a fantastic senior player to me. She has always been generous in sharing her experience with us and encouraging younger players like me, telling us to believe in ourselves," Wang said.
"In the final, I hope I can stay focused on the moment, give it everything I've got and play every point the best I can."
In the men's singles quarterfinals, third-seeded Wu defeated India's Sumit Nagal 6-4, 6-4 to advance to the semifinal.
"The Asian Games have always been unfinished business for me. I missed out on the championship at the Hangzhou Asian Games and before that in Jakarta," Wu said.
"Now I have another chance to step onto the semifinal court, so I have to keep pushing."
Wu will face Japan's Hayato Matsuoka, who rallied to beat second-seeded Alexander Shevchenko of Kazakhstan in three sets in the quarterfinal.
In mixed doubles, China's Jiang Xinyu and Zhang Tianhui beat Chinese Taipei's Chan Hao-ching and Ho Chenjui to advance to the semifinal.
Zhang Tianhui and Jiang Fumin missed out on the men's doubles final, while Zhang Shuai and Guo Hanyu were eliminated in the women's doubles quarterfinal. Wu Yibing and Guo Hanyu also bowed out in the mixed doubles quarterfinal. ■

====================================================================================================

Ditch the dating app. Meet an Irish town's 83-year-old mystical matchmaker.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:12:37 UTC
01:12:37 KST

For hopeful romantics, a small Irish town and its mystical matchmaker are here to help
Lisdoonvarna, Ireland — For nearly two centuries, a small Irish town has lured singletons to a festival every September that sees hopeful romantics seek their one true love.
The monthlong matchmaking festival that started in 1857 has become a global event, attracting over 60,000 visitors annually to the rugged landscape of County Clare, and specifically to the tiny town of Lisdoonvarna.
The festival even broke into American pop culture, featuring several years ago on the sitcom "Schitt's Creek."
In many ways, it's an old-world solution to modern dating. There is no app and no algorithms, just a chance to meet a match organically, through Irish traditional dancing and music, speed dating — or through the matchmaking skills of 83-year-old local legend Willie Daly.
Daly's grandfather helped start the festival, and his family has been pairing couples for three generations. In his father's and grandfather's day, many Irish towns and villages had traditional matchmakers, but Daly is now believed to be among the last, if not the last, keeping the tradition alive.
If prospective suitors wish to find a match through Daly, they meet with him and fill out a form outlining their hobbies, personality traits, and what they're looking for in a partner. Through his somewhat mystical personal intuition, Daly will then find a match and send the pair off on a first date.
"When I'm walking down the street, often I'd meet people … two or three couples said, 'You fixed us up 30 years ago, or 40 years ago,'" Daly told CBS News last month. "We're lucky here. Now this is a wonderful festival, and it's a great provision of opportunity — the opportunity to get married is very consistent in it. Music and dancing all day long, you know, for 30 days."
In a tattered old book, Daly keeps records of the hopeful matches he's arranged over the years, and local legend has it that if you place two hands on the book, you'll be married within six months.
Daly's image is literally etched on the front of a local watering hole — The Matchmaker Bar, where singles gather every year to drink, dance and try to meet their future spouse — in a testament to his stature in Lisdoonvarna.
CBS News attended the festivities at the pub in September and spoke with young attendees about what they were looking for in an ideal partner.
"I suppose a bit of loyalty, a bit of values, but also a bit of craic, you can't beat a bit of craic," said one young woman, using a common Irish phrase that translates roughly to good fun.
"Someone agricultural. I am agricultural myself … we're farming at home, we have a sheep farm at home. That's what I'm looking for at the moment," an Irishman said about his hunt for love.
Another attendee, Erica, told CBS News she had traveled all the way from Colombia for the festival.
"It's the opportunity to meet people the right way, face-to-face," she said. "Those apps, I mean, I'm not saying that people are hiding anything, but right now, just having the contact, just to sit there and talk to people makes [dating] a whole different event."
American Mary Timby from Colorado came to the village last year and ended up going viral, garnering over 2 million views after posting online about how she found love at the matchmaking festival.
She returned this year, and is now an ambassador for the event.
"I first heard about the festival on 'Schitt's Creek.' It was during COVID. I was huddled in a blanket on my couch and I Googled it and I thought, 'Oh, it's a real festival. Wouldn't it be fun if I just went someday?'" she said.
"My partner is from Ennis, here in County Clare, and we met at The Matchmaking Bar," she said. "I loved the Irish accent, and he just, was funny. He made me laugh and we connected right away, so we exchanged information."
But Timby's story shows that even matchmaking with nearly 170 years of proven success can benefit from modern technology.
"He found me on social media the next day," she said of her match. "And the rest is history."

Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

Can anyone broker a new peace between Tigray and Ethiopia?
October 1, 2026
Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks.
Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
But this time, the lay of the land looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.
This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.
Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal
The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.
Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.
Mohammed explained that the ultimate agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF; it ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored harliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace peace as nothing but military defeat.
Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Addis Ababa moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.
"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."
An alliance of former enemies
Mohammed also emphasized the fact that this coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.
It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region — in addition to ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.
Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.
Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."
She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.
Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara, and Afar.
Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.
Could the conflict have been prevented?
Rodrigues also pointed out the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict_
She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.
"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.
Rodrigues also noted that the United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants toward coming to the negotiation table.
The real cost of war
In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.
"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.
Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.
Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."
Limited prospects for mediation
Mohammed also noted that outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers, and Egypt — many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.
However according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."
Rodrigues agrees, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Scientists are decoding elephant rumble calls, including ‘greetings’ and ‘coos’—hear them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:01:32 UTC
01:01:32 KST

In February 2020 behavioral ecologist Mickey Pardo witnessed the aftermath of an elephant birth. In Kenya’s Samburu National Reserve, he watched as a female African elephant named Matisse called to her newborn with repeated “rumbles”—a kind of deep vocalization he describes as like “an idling truck engine.” Pardo watched as another adult elephant, likely Matisse’s sister, rumbled from a distance before the family came together, uniting with another series of rumbles, as if saying hello.
“It was just really ... fascinating to see this whole sequence,” recalls Pardo, a senior scientist at the research organization ElephantVoices. What these calls might mean, exactly, has long been a mystery. But a new study published on Thursday in Scientific Reports helps to shed some light.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In the study, Pardo and a team of scientists used machine learning to analyze hundreds of rumble recordings from a separate population of African elephants in Amboseli National Park, also in Kenya.
The analysis homes in on several kinds of elephant rumbles: “coo” rumbles to calves, “contact” rumbles made from a distance, “let’s-go” rumbles before group movements, “cadenced” rumbles during rest or meals and two different “greeting” rumbles.
In many cases, the recordings captured overlapping calls, a jumble of rumbles the researchers refer to as “choruses.” To be clear, these calls are not at all like elephants’ iconic trumpet sound. They are low and almost like a growl or thunder.
The researchers used the algorithm to predict the elephants’ behavior based on each recording. It wasn’t entirely accurate, but it did predict behaviors better than chance—suggesting that elephant vocalizations during similar situations may have similar acoustic properties.
“It is pretty exciting that we’re able to train a model to look at an entire chorus and have some interpretation of exactly what’s going on,” says Sara Keen, a study co-author and a senior research scientist at the nonprofit Earth Species Project.
In some cases, different rumbles became progressively similar, a pattern the researchers describe as “vocal convergence.” Scientists have observed this phenomenon in other chatty animals, including parrots and dolphins. Humans, too, are known to mirror one another’s language patterns.
Interestingly, converging appeared “only in the situations where they [the elephants] seem to be coordinating group behavior action,” Keen says. It’s possible that this convergence could indicate agreement, but that theory needs further testing to confirm, she adds.
“This study emphasizes how vital it is to pair new computational analyses with real behavioral observations in the wild,” says Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, who was not involved in the study.
Keen hopes scientists may be able to use similar methods to analyze other animal calls, too, such as for orcas and crows. Many other species are known to perform a kind of “chorusing,” she says, which may make good candidates for future research.
“Animals communicate to influence each other’s behavior, and so you can’t just study the sounds in isolation,” Kershenbaum explains. “But when you combine a rich behavioral dataset with powerful machine learning algorithms, that’s when we can start to get answers to questions like ‘What are the animals saying?’”

People found not guilty by reason of insanity show a surprisingly mixed criminal risk profile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:49 UTC
01:00:49 KST

People who experience severe mental health conditions are frequently overrepresented in the criminal justice system, but their psychiatric symptoms alone do not always explain their legal troubles. A recent study found that standard criminal risk factors, such as antisocial attitudes and having friends involved in crime, are strongly linked to whether a psychiatric patient has been involved in the legal system. The research was published in Law and Human Behavior.
In the past, intervention programs aimed at reducing repeat offenses among people with mental illness focused almost entirely on treating psychiatric symptoms. These medical interventions routinely failed to keep people out of jail. Researchers began to realize that most people with mental illness do not commit crimes because of hallucinations or delusions.
Instead, their criminal behavior is closely linked to the same risk factors that drive crime in the general population. In the fields of criminology and psychology, experts often refer to the central eight criminogenic risk factors. These include a history of antisocial behavior, antisocial personality traits, antisocial friends, substance abuse, family or marital problems, school or work difficulties, a lack of positive recreational activities, and criminal attitudes.
Researchers have consistently found that these non-clinical factors outperform traditional mental health variables in predicting criminal behavior. This means that mental illness alone does not necessarily increase an individual’s risk of breaking the law. Instead, some people with mental illness happen to have co-occurring antisocial tendencies that lead to legal trouble.
While this pattern holds true for general psychiatric patients, a unique subset of individuals occupies a gray area between the mental health and legal systems. These are patients who have been found not guilty by reason of insanity. In these specific cases, a court has determined that the person is not legally responsible for a crime because a mental disease or defect impaired their actions at the time of the offense.
Because their crimes are legally attributed to mental illness, one might assume these individuals lack the general criminal risk factors seen in other offenders. To test this idea, psychology researchers Angelea Bolaños, Faith Scanlon, and their colleagues set out to compare different groups of psychiatric patients. They wanted to see how insanity acquittees stacked up against other patients in terms of criminal attitudes, social support, and psychiatric distress.
The researchers gathered data from 349 participants across three distinct groups. The first group consisted of 74 psychiatric patients who had a history of misdemeanor or felony convictions. The second group included 68 psychiatric patients who had no history of criminal involvement. Both of these groups were recruited from a short-term, private inpatient psychiatric hospital in Texas.
The third group was made up of 207 forensic patients residing in the California state hospital system. These individuals had been found not guilty by reason of insanity and were institutionalized for mandatory psychiatric treatment. To compare the groups, the research team administered a series of self-report questionnaires designed to measure attitudes toward crime, social support networks, and current mental health.
One survey assessed general criminal tendencies, conduct problems, and antisocial personality traits. Another measured the participants’ number of criminal friends and their level of agreement with antisocial attitudes, such as feelings of entitlement or the belief that violence is justified. A third questionnaire evaluated how much support the participants felt they received from family, friends, and romantic partners.
Finally, the participants completed an inventory that measured the severity of their current psychiatric symptoms over the previous week. This included looking at markers for anxiety, depression, and paranoia. The researchers then used statistical models to see if the combination of these traits could accurately distinguish the three types of patients from one another based solely on their survey answers.
The team discovered that patients with mental illness and a history of typical criminal involvement scored the highest on almost all indicators of criminal risk. This group reported having the most criminal associates and the strongest antisocial attitudes. They also reported the lowest levels of perceived positive social support from their families and friends.
The patients found not guilty by reason of insanity presented a more mixed profile. They showed some shared criminal risk factors with the traditional criminal group, scoring higher on general criminal tendencies than the patients with no legal history. However, they did not display the same elevated levels of antisocial attitudes as the group with typical legal involvement.
When it came to social networks, the insanity acquittees actually resembled the patients with no criminal history. Both of these groups reported feeling a comparable level of social support. The researchers suggest that friends and family might remain more supportive of someone whose crime is attributed to a mental health crisis, compared to someone who engages in standard criminal behavior.
In an unexpected twist regarding psychiatric symptoms, the insanity acquittees reported the lowest severity of current mental health distress among all three groups. The researchers suspect this is due to the nature of their hospitalizations. The Texas patients were in a short-term, acute crisis facility, while the California forensic patients had likely been living in a stable, long-term therapeutic environment for an extended period, allowing their symptoms to subside.
Overall, the data showed that criminal risk factors and social support metrics successfully sorted roughly two thirds to three quarters of the participants into their correct legal categories. This predictive accuracy reinforces the idea that criminal attitudes and social environments are defining features of justice-involved populations. The results highlight the need for treatment programs to target these specific criminal risk factors alongside standard psychiatric care.
For example, specialized rehabilitation programs exist to address the concurrent mental health and criminal needs of people in the justice system. Providing this kind of dual-focused therapy could assist forensic patients in developing necessary life skills to optimize their recovery. Preparing these patients for eventual release requires treating the whole person, rather than viewing them solely through a psychiatric lens.
While the study offers a detailed look at forensic and non-forensic patients, the research design relies on data collected at a single point in time. This cross-sectional approach prevents researchers from determining exactly how a person’s mental illness and criminal behavior evolved over time. It is impossible to know whether a patient’s antisocial attitudes developed before or after their psychiatric symptoms began.
The reliance on self-reported questionnaires also introduces the possibility of response bias. Participants might have underreported their antisocial attitudes or exaggerated their mental health symptoms based on what they thought the researchers wanted to hear. Corroborating these self-reports with official legal records or clinician observations in future studies could yield a more comprehensive picture of their behavior.
The sample composition limits how broadly the results can be applied to the general population. The patients from the Texas hospital lacked demographic diversity, being predominantly White and male. Comparing patients across two different states also introduces variations in how different legal systems define and handle insanity acquittals, meaning a patient in California might be treated differently than one in Texas.
A final complication is that 85 percent of the forensic patients in the California sample had additional criminal convictions on top of the charges that led to their insanity acquittals. This high rate of prior criminal behavior blurs the boundary between the strictly psychiatric and the strictly criminal groups. Future investigations could separate insanity acquittees based on their past criminal histories to better understand this unique population.
The study, “Psychiatric Symptoms and Criminogenic Risk in People With Mental Illness: Comparing Patients Across Forensic and Nonforensic Settings,” was authored by Angelea D. Bolaños, Faith Scanlon, Robert D. Morgan, Sean M. Mitchell, and Darci Delgado.

Hong Kong invests billions to accelerate innovation of impactful solutions as an AI-powered future comes into focus
•    The HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme aims to accelerate the transformation of AI R&D projects into impactful practical solutions.
•    Over 30 projects have been approved, backed by a total of HK$1.7 billion.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Artificial intelligence has rapidly evolved from an emerging technology into a cornerstone of Hong Kong's economic transformation strategy. Under the Government's AI+ initiative, further reinforced by the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the HKSAR (2026-2030), the city is stepping up efforts to integrate AI across industries, public services, scientific research, healthcare, finance and smart-city development, with the ambition of becoming a leading innovation hub in the Greater Bay Area and beyond.
At the heart of this strategy is the HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme (AISS), a three-year programme that supports universities, research institutions, enterprises and government departments in harnessing the immense computing power of Cyberport's Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre, the city's largest AI computing facility and a key piece of digital infrastructure. Hong Kong's total computing capacity has now surpassed 5,000 petaFLOPS.
The scheme marks a strategic shift from supporting AI research alone to accelerating real-world applications capable of generating tangible economic and social benefits. .
Against this backdrop, a new generation of researchers, scientists and innovators is translating cutting-edge breakthroughs into practical solutions.
Since the launch of AISS in 2024, more than 50 applications have been received and over 30 projects approved, spanning local universities, R&D centres, government departments, technology companies and start-ups. Total subsidies granted have exceeded HK$1.7 billion.
Speaking at a sharing session featuring approved AISS projects, Daniel Cheung, Acting Commissioner for Digital Policy, highlighted the scheme's role in supporting Hong Kong's broader development goals. "The AISS closely aligns with the National 15th Five-Year Plan by advancing ‘industries for AI’ and ‘AI for industries,’ promoting the transformation and upgrading of traditional sectors such as finance and healthcare. Since its launch, the AISS has received enthusiastic responses, with subsidised projects demonstrating immense potential in technological innovation and industrial application," he said.
 
Echoing this view, Hendrick Sin, Chairperson of the Committee of AISS, said: "The approved projects not only showcase scientific breakthroughs but are steadily being transformed into practical applications that benefit society and industry, enhancing citizens' quality of life and exemplifying the power of collaborative innovation among government, industry, academia and research."
One of the highlights of the sharing session was a multimodal large language model for medical diagnosis and surgery developed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR) under the Hong Kong Institute of Science & Innovation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Focused on advancing innovation at the intersection of AI and life and health sciences, CAIR has built a comprehensive medical AI ecosystem centred on CARES 3.0, a multimodal medical model equipped with continual learning and trustworthy decision-making capabilities. The platform pioneers a new "copilot" approach to intelligent healthcare.
Among its innovations is EchoCare, an ultrasound foundation model trained on four million ultrasound datasets. Adaptable across a wide range of clinical applications, the model can accurately identify lesions in more than 50 organs. CAIR's technological advances have helped overcome critical technical bottlenecks.
Financial innovation
AI is also reshaping Hong Kong's financial sector. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Cyberport launched the first and second cohorts of the GenA.I. Sandbox in 2024 and 2025 respectively, focusing on use cases in anti-fraud operations, risk management and customer experience enhancement.
Trial results demonstrated significant operational gains across the banking sector. Participating institutions recorded a 30 to 80 percent reduction in preparation time for suspicious transaction reports, while document processing times were cut from one day to approximately five minutes. The technology also reduced risk assessment report production time by 60 percent, enabled more comprehensive risk analysis workflows, and resulted in more than 70 percent of GenAI-generated credit assessments being regarded as useful references by adopting institutions.
Building on this momentum, the HKMA joined forces with Cyberport, the Securities and Futures Commission, the Insurance Authority and the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority to launch GenA.I. Sandbox++ in March 2026, with a strong emphasis on exploring Agentic AI applications.
Moving beyond content generation, selected use cases under Sandbox++ are examining how AI systems can responsibly take on greater autonomy across end-to-end processes, including customer onboarding, payments, insurance claims and customer interactions.
Collaborative Generative AI Platform
Another project demonstrating the breadth of Hong Kong's AI ambitions comes from InfiX.ai, which has independently developed the Collaborative Generative AI (Co-GenAI) Platform. It enables enterprises, research institutions and industry partners to train domain-specific AI models using their own datasets at significantly lower computing costs. By avoiding the centralisation of proprietary data while safeguarding privacy and intellectual property, Co-GenAI allows specialised intelligence distributed across organisations and devices to be connected and integrated into a continuously evolving collaborative intelligence network.
This approach enables AI technologies to be co-created, co-developed and shared among participating organisations. Supported by high-efficiency computing resources, model engineering, knowledge bases and application workflows, the platform offers capabilities ranging from local deployment and model fine-tuning to evaluation, inference services and multi-model collaboration.
Designed as a scalable, secure and controllable AI infrastructure, the platform has applications across sectors including manufacturing, public administration, finance, healthcare and education, helping drive digital transformation and strengthen the broader AI ecosystem.
These three projects illustrate how government support, world-class computing infrastructure and research excellence are converging to address pressing challenges, unlock new opportunities and demonstrate the transformative potential of artificial intelligence for Hong Kong's future.
The city's ambitions are set to grow further with the planned commissioning of the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster in the Northern Metropolis by 2032. Once fully operational, the facility is expected to propel Hong Kong into the ranks of the world's leading centres for computing capacity, strengthening its position as a regional and global AI powerhouse.

Tim Heidecker Is Bringing His Joe Rogan Parody Show to The Onion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

As satirical news outlet The Onion continued to wage a legal battle to acquire the assets of Infowars out of bankruptcy this summer, it launched a streaming program that spoofed the brand and its bellowing conspiracist ringleader, Alex Jones.
Comedian Tim Heidecker took the reins of the operation, adopting Jones’ guttural and paranoid bluster as he investigated, among other unconfirmed reports, whether Jones himself had exploded in his car after eating too much Whataburger.
But Heidecker wasn’t about to stop there in his quest to transform the Infowars brand into a gonzo comedy network along the lines of Adult Swim. Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.
A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.
Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. (The pair have essentially perfected the art of fake celebrity web content and once even got Justin Theroux in on the joke for a mock Hollywood Reporter-style actors roundtable.)
“What is essentially happening is, in place of Christianity, we have the 10 commandments of woke,” Levick says during a discussion of DEI policies on the first episode of The Tim Heidecker Podcast. The chat veers into concerns that bearded men are dressing as princesses to visit Disneyland. Heidecker then abruptly informs the boys that he’s planned a weekend trip to Glasgow “for Scotch wrestling.”
In 2026, it’s more difficult than ever to exaggerate the absurdities of the right-wing media ecosystem, with its fact-free moral panics and bizarre alternative medicines. Though if anyone is up to the task, it’s the endlessly inventive Heidecker—who will have no shortage of grifters and lunatics to go after once he’s done with his run as a Rogan type. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

France Has Begun Training Ukrainian Rafale Pilots

France has begun preparations to train Ukrainian pilots to fly Rafale fighter jets.
This was announced by Benjamin Haddad, France’s Minister Delegate for European Affairs, in an interview with franceinfo.
“We are currently discussing with the Ukrainians the issue of deploying Rafale fighter jets, piloted not by French but by Ukrainian pilots, in Ukrainian airspace. That is why we have also begun work on training these pilots,” said Benjamin Haddad.
Earlier, France and Ukraine agreed on the delivery of a batch of 16 Rafale fighter jets.
Ukraine is expected to receive its first French fighter jets as early as 2028–2029.
Overall, it has been reported that 100 French Rafale fighter jets are planned to be ordered to strengthen the Ukrainian Air Force.
In July, Volodymyr Zelensky stated that training for Ukrainian pilots and mechanics to operate the Rafale is set to begin in France this year. Upon completion of the training, the first four Rafale aircraft are to be transferred to Ukraine’s arsenal.
Currently, France has specialized GROB G-120TP training aircraft at its disposal to conduct the basic and advanced stages of training.
France also operates Dornier Alpha Jet advanced jet trainer-combat aircraft.
These aircraft enable pilots to acquire the necessary skills in flying, navigation, and performing aerial combat maneuvers before transitioning to combat fighters.

A protest by French secondary school students over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities deepened on Thursday, with fires set outside schools and blockades in several cities.
More than 160 schools were shut down on Thursday, while university students joined the protests in Paris and Marseille. The movement in the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France, has seen hundreds detained.

dune-inspired promenade brings sand and vegetation into comillas’ waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:45:11 UTC
00:45:11 KST

dune-inspired promenade brings sand and vegetation into comillas’ waterfront
hector navarro + arkhitekton rework the seafront of comillas, spain, using sand, vegetation, permeable surfaces, and limestone.
Sand Becomes Part of Comillas’ Seafront Landscape
Located on Spain’s northern coast, Comillas is a small Cantabrian town with a rich architectural heritage, including El Capricho, one of Antoni Gaudí’s few buildings outside Catalonia. Against this historic backdrop, the transformation of the town’s seafront by Hector Navarro + arkhitekton addresses its changing relationship with the Cantabrian Sea. Instead of treating sand as something to be removed, the intervention incorporates it into the everyday functioning of the promenade. Carried inland by wind and beachgoers, sand settles within planted areas and permeable paving, becoming part of the public space.
Dune-Inspired Landscape Connects Town and Coast
Through this strategy, the design team extends into a new landscape inspired by the dune ecosystems of the Cantabrian coast. The promenade creates a transition between the built fabric of Comillas and the beach, using vegetation, permeable surfaces, and mineral materials to accommodate the changing conditions of the coastline. Limestone riprap reinforces the connection with the rocky coastal landscape, while permeable surfaces allow water and sand to remain part of the ground.
Benches and Open Space Reframe Comillas’ Waterfront
Individual benches are distributed along the promenade, providing places to stop and look toward the sea without creating a continuous line of conventional street furniture. By reducing the presence of cars and expanding pedestrian areas, the intervention gives greater space to everyday public use. Rather than introducing an autonomous object on the coastline, the project works with processes already present on the site: wind, sand, vegetation, water, and movement, to shape a new public landscape for Comillas.
project info:
name: Comillas Waterfront Promenade
 architect: Hector Navarro | @hectornavarro + arkhitekton
location: Comillas, Spain
landscape designers: Héctor Navarro, Diego Jardinería (Diego Cuartas & Adolfo Vila)
photographer: Imagen Subliminal (Miguel de Guzmán + Rocío Romero) | @imagensubliminal
designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. See more project submissions from our readers here.

vollebak turns thousands of tiny slate tiles into a flexible rock jacket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:39:40 UTC
00:39:40 KST

vollebak turns thousands of tiny slate tiles into a flexible rock jacket
the rock jacket uses thousands of 5mm slate tiles, neoprene and cordura to turn geological time into flexible outerwear: somewhere between material experiment and a harrington built from the earth’s crust.
VOLLEBAK ROCK JACKET TURNS SLATE INTO FLEXIBLE OUTERWEAR
Vollebak takes its material experiments underground with the Rock Jacket, a one-off garment built from thousands of tiny pieces of slate. The British clothing brand has previously worked with copper, wood, aerogel and electromagnetic shielding, but its latest prototype goes considerably further back in the material timeline: stone. Rather than treating it as a rigid shell, the project sets out to make rock behave more like fabric.
Each 5mm x 5mm slate tile sits on a neoprene backing, forming a gridded surface that can twist and bend while retaining the uneven texture of natural stone. From a distance, the jacket reads almost like pixelated armor; up close, its fragmented surface reveals the layers and variations of the slate itself. The result lands somewhere between geological sample, digital texture and something a particularly well-dressed space miner might keep by the door.
STEVEN LEPRIZÉ ADAPTS WOOWOOD MARQUETRY TO STONE
The material was developed with French designer, material technologist and experimental cabinetmaker Steven Leprizé, whom Vollebak initially approached to explore a more wearable version of its earlier Wooden Jacket prototype. Leprizé adapted WooWood, his elastic marquetry technique that bonds hundreds of small wooden tiles onto a flexible rubber membrane, replacing timber with thin squares of slate.
Producing the new surface is a precision-heavy exercise. The slate arrives in sheets measuring 100 x 50cm and just 0.5mm thick before being cut into clean-edged squares half a centimeter wide. According to Leprizé, making the material involves around 50 individual steps, with the cutting process determining whether the final grid can move cleanly without losing the visual character of the stone.
SLATE TILES AND CORDURA SHAPE VOLLEBAK’S CROPPED HARRINGTON
Vollebak turns the flexible sheets into a cropped, minimalist Harrington jacket with a deliberately stripped-back silhouette. The slate panels are laser cut and joined with visibly taped seams, while Cordura pockets and a conventional zipper bring a few recognizably garment-like details back into the equation. The contrast is part of the appeal: an everyday jacket typology, except its surface happens to be made from rock.
The Rock Jacket currently exists as a one-of-one piece, with Vollebak positioning it as the beginning of a longer investigation rather than a finished material system. Co-founder Nick Tidball suggests that rock could eventually be explored as a construction material for clothing in much the same way it has long been used in architecture. Whether stone ever becomes wardrobe staple is another question, but a jacket made from a fragment of the Earth’s crust certainly makes the usual seasonal turnover feel rather hurried.
project info:
name: Rock Jacket
 designer: Steven Leprizé for Vollebak | @vollebak
 location: London, UK

IDF names 170 slain Gaza ‘journalists’ it says served in Hamas, Islamic Jihad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:37:58 UTC
00:37:58 KST

The IDF on Thursday published the names of 170 Palestinians killed in Gaza during the war who were presented internationally as journalists or media workers but who the military says also served as members of terrorist organizations, primarily Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad.
The move comes after the IDF said it had identified a recurring pattern in recent months in which Hamas and Islamic Jihad themselves published information after the deaths of some media workers acknowledging that they had also served in the organizations’ military wings.
“Following an extensive research effort, the IDF is now revealing that 170 Gazans who were killed during the war and presented as journalists and media personnel actually served as terrorists in terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, primarily Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad,” the IDF said.
The military said it was publishing what it described as verified evidence, including images and documents produced by the terrorist organizations, some of which were recovered in Gaza, that it says demonstrate the individuals’ affiliations and roles.
The IDF said 118 of the 170 were members of Hamas’ military wing, 49 belonged to Palestinian Islamic Jihad, one was affiliated with Adonei HaShmama and two with the Popular Resistance Committees.
According to the military, 17 of those on the list participated in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. The IDF said more than 40 of the deaths on the list prompted condemnations of Israel from the United Nations.
Some of those named had also worked for major international media organizations, according to the IDF, including Reuters, CNN, ABC News, The Associated Press, Agence France-Presse, the BBC, Le Monde and Australia’s ABC.
The military said the disclosures were intended to challenge accusations that Israel has deliberately and systematically targeted journalists during the Gaza war.
“Throughout the war, various media organizations in the international community repeatedly accused the State of Israel and the IDF, without presenting verified findings, of deliberately harming journalists,” the military said.
It added that in some cases, “the terrorist organizations themselves presented those individuals as terrorists in their ranks and even claimed them as their own.”
The military said the material illustrates what it describes as a gap between how some of the dead were portrayed internationally and their alleged roles on the ground.
“The information now being revealed illustrates the gap between the picture presented around the world and the reality on the ground, and provides additional conclusive evidence that the IDF does not deliberately and systematically operate against journalists, but against terrorist organizations and their members, in accordance with international law,” the military said.
International media outlets, human rights organizations and international institutions have repeatedly cited the number of journalists and media workers killed in Gaza while criticizing Israel’s conduct during the war. The IDF argues that such figures often fail to distinguish between journalists carrying out media work and people who were simultaneously serving in terrorist organizations.
Among the cases highlighted by the military was Amro Nahid Abdel Rahman Abu Odeh, who worked for Reuters and Turkey’s Anadolu Agency.
According to the IDF, Abu Odeh was also a team commander in the photography unit of Hamas’ military wing. The military published images showing him both carrying a camera and holding a Kalashnikov rifle.
Another man named by the IDF, Hassan Majdi Ibrahim Abu Warda, worked for the Barq Gaza news agency but was also, according to the military, a sniper in Palestinian Islamic Jihad’s Northern Gaza Brigade.
The IDF said its new website was created to make the underlying material publicly accessible, including the individuals’ alleged organizational affiliations and military positions as well as evidence that the military says can be released publicly.
The military also addressed controversy surrounding the documentary NAZA, after IDF representatives viewed the film.
“The film presents a distorted, misleading and unrealistic picture,” the IDF said. “We never planned, approved or carried out a strike in which 500 civilians were expected to be killed.”

NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Thursday took a swipe at the ongoing turmoil in the Congress state unit and said that even the new state president will not be able to unite the party leaders.Mann said that the Congress has fewer party workers but more leaders who aspire to become chief minister.“A new president will be appointed, but even the new president will not be able to unite the Congress leaders. After the new president comes, the fight amongst them will further intensify,” Mann said.“The Congress has fewer 'karyakartas' but more leaders who aspire to become CM, not for the well-being of the people but for satisfying their lust for power,” he added.This comes after the Congress high command replaced Amrinder Singh Raja Warring as the Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) chief ahead of the Punjab assembly polls.Although Warring declined to comment on the development, he confirmed it by changing his X bio to “former Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee President”.The move comes after months of infighting within the Punjab Congress, which intensified after the party high command decided on July 1 to retain Warring as the state unit chief.
A section of leaders led by former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi had opposed Warring’s continuation and sought his removal. Here’s how brain-eating amoebas may infect people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

Some deadly amoebas may be primed to invade the brain.
Naegleria fowleri, known widely as the brain-eating amoeba, typically dine on bacteria in ponds. But the amoeba’s meal-seeking skills might make it uniquely suited to crawling up people’s noses and into their brains.
Naegleria amoebas are intrepid explorers, probing nooks and crannies in the lab — and they’re persistent, too. When creeping down narrow passageways, the amoebas charge relentlessly forward, almost never turning back, researchers report September 10 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. “They’re like robots,” says Lillian Fritz-Laylin, a cell biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. “They just go and go and go.”
Such persistence might help these tiny, single-celled creatures make the marathon journey from the nostrils all the way to the brain. Fritz-Laylin’s work helps flesh out a largely skeletal picture of Naegleria behavior. “We know almost nothing about the basic biology of these organisms,” she says.
N. fowleri amoebas don’t routinely harm humans. They usually dwell in warm bodies of fresh water, where they squirm through sediment and mind their own business. But on rare occasions, the creatures can be washed up a swimmer’s nose. As the amoebas migrate through the nasal cavity and into the brain, they destroy and eat tissue. Then they begin to reproduce, usually with lethal consequences. The United States typically sees fewer than 10 Naegleria infections each year, often at summer swimming spots, but nearly every one is fatal.
In the lab, Fritz-Laylin’s team tested Naegleria amoebas’ ability to move through different environments. They focused on N. gruberi, a harmless species that shares behaviors with its brain-eating relative. “It’s a lot safer to work with something that can’t kill you,” Fritz-Laylin says.
The researchers placed the amoebas on glass-bottom dishes containing narrow microchannels and watched them move under a microscope. They squeezed through channels smaller than themselves and seemed to be interested in exploring. When the amoebas encountered a channel opening, they very rarely left it, Fritz-Laylin says. Confinement sometimes sped them up, too. Inside the largest channels tested, the amoebas still zipped along twice as fast as cells on the outside.
Naegleria’s persistence and need for speed may make it unique. The team didn’t observe the same behaviors in a different type of amoeba tested. Such attributes probably make Naegleria well-adapted to hunting bacteria in pond sediments, says Fritz-Laylin, who is also a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator. But those innocent behaviors could also explain N. fowleri’s dark side. Put one at “the wrong place at the wrong time,” she says, “and it can cause devastating infection.”

MANILA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Inflation in the Philippines may have accelerated again in September, reaching its fastest pace in over three years, according to the country's central bank on Wednesday.
The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) said it estimated consumer prices rose between 6.4 percent and 7.4 percent in September year on year. At the upper end of the forecast, inflation might reach its highest level since March 2023, when consumer prices rose 7.6 percent, further above the BSP's 3-percent target.

BEIRUT, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Chinese companies are seeking opportunities in Lebanon's reconstruction market, with 16 firms showcasing steel structures, expandable houses, security systems, and building materials at Project Lebanon 2026 in Beirut.
The four-day exhibition, running through Friday, has drawn Chinese suppliers seeking customers, distributors, and local partners as Lebanon gears up for reconstruction.
"We are preparing for the reconstruction phase, so the participation of Chinese companies and others shows that they see Lebanon as a market where they can invest in the future," Jessica Bou Samra, marketing manager at organizer IFP Group, told Xinhua.
Samra said residential construction, particularly in southern Lebanon, is a key opportunity for Chinese companies.
"We are highly interested in projects in Beirut and in southern Lebanon, where a lot of people lost their houses," said Jiang Zhiyun, regional product marketing manager for the Middle East at Chinese technology company Hikvision.
The company provides CCTV, access control, intercom, and parking security systems, and has completed projects in Lebanon via local partners.
Jiang said the firm seeks to expand cooperation, adding that Lebanon also offered a gateway to the Syrian market.
At the booth of Shenheng Steel, visitors showed strong interest in expandable houses priced between 4,000 and 30,000 U.S. dollars.
"There is a great potential here," said sales manager Jay Zhang. "The clients here are asking for quantities of expandable houses, perhaps because of the situation in south Lebanon and because they cannot pay a lot to reconstruct their previous houses."
The company already serves several Lebanese customers and is exploring deeper cooperation with local construction firms.
Door manufacturer Real-Best WPC Door is participating the exhibition for the first time, seeking clients, dealers, and engineers.
"The reconstruction projects in southern Lebanon are an opportunity to market our doors," said marketing representative Judy Liao, adding that the company may open a warehouse in Lebanon.
Some Chinese firms are already established in Lebanon. Vicy Chen of Haowang Group, which makes wall paint, PVC ceilings, and decorative materials, said the company has served Lebanese customers for about a decade.
"The Lebanese now appreciate Chinese products more generally," Chen said, adding that reconstruction could increase demand.
Lebanese visitors also cited growing interest in Chinese products.
Raafat Mehio, a tile store owner who attended the fair to explore construction products and suppliers, said Lebanese buyers are increasingly turning to Chinese products, though price, quality, and reliability remain key factors. ■

PURSAT, Cambodia, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Preap Sineath, a local grocer based along National Road 10 here in western Cambodia, has witnessed a significant rise in sales as a growing traffic flow of passengers, tourists, and freight transport has filled the area since the China-funded highway was developed.
For the 35-year-old mother of three residing in Veal Veng district, the newly built corridor has completely transformed local livelihoods. The asphalt highway replaces what was once a narrow, muddy, and challenging trail.
Officially inaugurated on Thursday, the 198.5-kilometer highway connects Battambang province to Koh Kong province, passing directly through Pursat province. The project was constructed by the China Road and Bridge Corporation.
"National Road 10 is crucial for local travel and goods transportation. It significantly saves travel time and reduces transport costs," Sineath told Xinhua on the sidelines of the inauguration ceremony. "It has made it much easier for farmers to transport their agricultural products. Traffic volumes have increased substantially compared to the past, thanks to the smooth road conditions."
She noted that her business is thriving because of the surge in passenger and tourist traffic, which has altered her household's livelihood for the better.
Om Sareth, a 65-year-old farmer in Veal Veng district, shared similar relief, saying that before this arterial route was established, moving goods across the rugged terrain was extremely difficult.
"Now, local growers can transport cash crops like cassava and corn smoothly to regional markets," she told Xinhua.
The mother of four expressed her excitement, noting that because the majority of households in the district depend heavily on farming, National Road 10 provides long-awaited, reliable access to the rest of the country.
"This road has greatly benefited our farmers, who can now transport produce like cassava and corn without worrying about their vehicles getting bogged down like before -- it is bringing happiness and progress to our district," she said.
The arterial corridor also features the Techo Santepheap Russei Chrum Bridge, officially recognized as the tallest bridge in Cambodia. Towering up to 80 meters high and stretching 530 meters long across the Stung Russei Chrum River valley in Veal Veng district, the bridge includes built-in viewing platforms. It has quickly become a prominent landmark, prompting commuters and tourists to halt their journeys to capture photographs of the panoramic, mist-covered mountain scenery.
"Since National Road 10 was so beautifully built, tourists have traveled to our community non-stop," Sareth said, adding that the infrastructure has completely transformed the livelihoods of her family and the broader local population.
"I am deeply grateful to China for helping develop Cambodia, and I wish China even greater development in the future," she added.
Similarly, Duong Thon, a 58-year-old cassava farmer and father of four in Pursat province, emphasized that the highway delivers substantial, compounding economic benefits by enabling seamless regional logistics.
"The key advantages are that farmers can now transport their products from agricultural fields directly to commercial markets much more quickly, while saving significantly on fuel costs," he told Xinhua. "National Road 10 is very beautiful. I used to live in a remote area plagued by many hardships, so seeing this modern road completed makes me absolutely thrilled."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said the highway marks a monumental leap forward for Cambodia, stitching together regional connectivity while transforming daily life across Battambang, Pursat, and Koh Kong.
"By linking agricultural hubs directly to seaport logistics, this strategic corridor empowers rural communities with faster market access, while seamless border-to-port transport enhances our trade competitiveness," he told Xinhua.
"Supported by our partnership with China under the Belt and Road Initiative, National Road 10 stands as a practical deliverable of the 'Diamond Hexagon Cooperation,' translating bilateral friendship into tangible, sustainable economic growth for the Cambodian people," Mengdavid said. ■

Ex-Hungarian Minister Detained in $53 Million Graft Probe
Unknown

2026-10-01

00:25:00 KST

Reported by
Black-masked law enforcement officers escorted Balázs Hankó, a former Hungarian culture minister, into a district court on Thursday, where a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention over allegations that he masterminded the widespread misappropriation of state funds to benefit the party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
Hankó was taken into custody after Hungary's Parliament voted 139 to 0 on Monday to strip his legislative immunity. Before surrendering to prosecutors later that evening, he spent the day inside the Parliament building surrounded by his family, framing his pending arrest as political persecution.
"My conscience is clear; this is a political show trial," Hankó said in a video broadcast live on Orbán’s Facebook page before walking out alongside relatives and lawmakers from Fidesz, Orbán's right-wing party, which is now in opposition.
Prosecutors allege that Hankó misused 17.3 billion forints (about $53 million) during his concurrent tenure as president of the National Cultural Fund. According to the prosecutor’s office, between September 2025 and March 2026, Hankó and his associates established a "dual decision-making system" that bypassed legal evaluation procedures to distribute public grants across 1,079 separate instances along electoral and political lines.
The investigation was launched after whistleblowers alleged that the cultural fund was secretly channeling state grants to artists and organizations loyal to Fidesz. In one instance, public money was allegedly used to book a circus for a Fidesz campaign rally, which officials registered as a cultural event. Police previously raided offices housing Fidesz’s internet servers in July as part of the inquiry.
The court order marks one of the most high-profile moves yet in a sweeping anti-graft drive led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose administration took power after defeating Orbán and ending his 16 years in office. Magyar has estimated that systemic corruption under the prior government cost Hungary 8 to 10 percent of its gross domestic product. Writing on social media, Magyar declared that "millions of Hungarians had experienced for the first time what true regime change and equality before the law mean."
Fidesz leaders have fiercely denounced the proceedings, accusing Magyar’s government of authoritarian overreach. János Bóka, the leader of the Fidesz parliamentary group, pledged that the party would hold anyone involved in the prosecution answerable "in court, in politics, and in their finances."
The anti-graft inquiry has expanded beyond Hankó. On Monday, authorities also detained Miklós Seszták, who served as national development minister under Orbán from 2014 to 2018, in connection with a separate bribery investigation. Seszták has denied any wrongdoing.
Prosecutors have not formally charged Hankó beyond the initial suspicion of misappropriation, and he has not been convicted of a crime.
Lawmakers also voted to strip Prime Minister Péter Magyar of his immunity in an unrelated case that predates his time in office.

New footage shows the stabbed Indian pilot receiving treatment, while the attacking pilot is seen restrained:
Later Thursday, Hayun met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the second time. Netanyahu hosted several of the flight’s other rescuers at his office, including Dr. Shota Musaev, who treated the wounded Indian captain, Musaev’s wife Sigalit and Or Pradilov. “The whole world is seeing Israeli heroism,” Netanyahu told them.
