No porn, no doomscrolling, no processed foods: Meet Israel's spermmaxxers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:55:39 UTC
21:55:39 KST

"I want my sperm to be high-quality, strong and healthy," says Itamar, a 37-year-old car mechanic from Mishmar Ayalon in central Israel. He recently changed his diet and started exercising, partly with that goal in mind.
"I make sure to eat a lot of meat," he says, "lift weights, rarely turn on the Wi-Fi at home and don't carry my cellphone in my pocket. I mostly wear cotton clothes, buy shampoo and cleaning products only from health food stores, and don't use sunscreen or perfume – except for important events – to avoid hormone-disrupters."
Itamar got most of his information from health-related YouTube content, and podcasts, and a year ago, he participated in Israeli bio-hacker Ram Shechter's "Testosterone Challenge," which teaches participants how to raise their testosterone levels through lifestyle changes.
Itamar is currently in a relationship and hopes to start a family soon, but his interest in fertility began a few years ago, while he was still single. "I've known for a long time that I want to be a father, and it's important to me to rise to the occasion in the best and most fertile physical condition I can," he explains.
Tal Levi, a school caretaker and multidisciplinary artist, has also adopted new habits in recent months in an effort to boost his fertility. The 30-year-old Tel Aviv resident concocts his own hygiene products and creams out of natural ingredients, and avoids passing through metal detectors or placing his laptop on his body. Levy is single, but in his view, the issue can't wait. "Modern life is harming our health and, as a result, our fertility. If I want children in the future, I have to take active steps to increase the chances of that actually happening."
Up until recently, only women were expected to prepare their bodies for pregnancy and support fertility through lifestyle changes such as taking supplements, quitting smoking and looking after their general health. But as of late, signs of change have been budding in Israel, with men adopting new lifestyle habits to support fertility.
Overseas, this phenomenon already has a name: "spermmaxxing" – a wellness trend in which men try to optimize their sperm. Health influencers teach their followers how to boost fertility by "detoxing" metals from the body, avoiding processed foods and regulating dopamine levels by abstaining from pornography and late-night doomcrolling on social media. Thousands of men swap tips in online forums, some of which are backed by research and some less so – from testicle icing with ice cubes and replacing espresso with decaf to taking supplements such as ashwagandha, zinc, selenium and copper.
"Men should have to spend nine months getting into the best physical shape of their lives before having a baby," says one TikTok creator in a video that received 2.5 million likes. He claims that "50 to 60 percent of the baby's epigenetic makeup is because of the man." Another creator shared his fertility-boosting routine – which includes squats, ice baths and protein-rich meals – under the caption: "Just a regular 33-year-old improving his health and fertility one day at a time."
The wellness industry has also started promoting sperm health as part of a general health routine. In recent years, the male fertility market, which generates millions annually, has become saturated with products, supplements and apps designed to help users optimize their reproductive health. The subject has also become increasingly popular in cultural discourse through podcasts, documentaries and television shows. Last year, longevity guru Bryan Johnson proudly boasted his sperm metrics to his two million followers on X, discussing the correlation between sperm health, testosterone levels and life expectancy.
Optimization as compensation
To some extent, the current obsession with the topic is a response to the growing alarm over the male fertility crisis. Israeli epidemiologist Hagai Levine led a major 2017 study that found sperm counts among Western countries had fallen by about 50 percent between 1973 and 2011, and that one in 20 men are currently facing reduced fertility – a statistic that received media resonance and was even dubbed "spermaggedon." A subsequent study published in 2022 found that the decline extended globally.
The studies did not examine the causes of the crisis, but research literature links poor sperm metrics to poor diet, low physical fitness, smoking, alcohol, use of radiation-emitting devices (though evidence on their effects remains mixed), exposure to toxins like phthalates, obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and metabolic syndrome.
Last year, the World Health Organization published its first global guideline on infertility, noting that male infertility can be caused by unhealthy habits, and in 2024, the U.S. National Library of Medicine published a review examining the effects of lifestyle factors on sperm quality. The Israeli Ministry of Health has not published specific guidelines regarding sperm health, but local fertility clinics provide recommendations on their websites for improving sperm count through lifestyle changes.
There is also growing body of evidence that a father's health affects not only sperm quality, but also pregnancy outcomes and the health of his offspring. For example, cigarette smoking during the pre-conception period increases the risk factor for pregnancy loss, while experiments in mice have shown that paternal alcohol consumption affects normal placental development, can alter the baby's facial symmetry and increases the risk of liver cancer during its lifetime.
Despite the new focus on sperm quality, male involvement in fertility treatments remains ambivalent. Prof. Itai Gat, director of Assuta Superm, one of the largest specialized sperm banks in Israel, says that while he has noticed a certain change, it's partial. "We see more men coming for fertility counseling than before, showing more willingness to undergo testing or openness to discussing the issue, but it's not widespread and depends on the population.
"There is also a difference in the role a man assumes in the process based on his sperm test results. Sometimes a man who discovers his sperm is normal deduces that that he is not responsible for his and his partner's difficulties and becomes a kind of support person in the process, rather than an active participant."
Roni Baltuch, a social worker who accompanies fertility patients at Assuta Ramat Hahayal Hospital, says that "in contrast to women, men show a disconnect when it comes to reproductive system issues and their potential implications for fertility and fatherhood. Medicine socializes women for reproduction by treating gynecological checkups as an integral part of general health, while for most men, the first examination they have is during their military draft intake – and often, the only one they'll ever have.
"Even if a finding comes up that requires further medical investigation, men usually won't connect it with the need to protect their fertility later on. They arrive for fertility treatments years later and are surprised to discover they have a fertility problem."
This year, Israel decided to eliminate the testicular examination during the first military draft order appearance, on the grounds that its results rarely affect a recruit's medical profile – which could push the issue even further aside.
Baltuch attributes men's detachment to another factor. "Fertility treatments focus on women, because even when the problem is with the sperm, medical interventions for men are specific and performed in the beginning of the process – while the rest of the interventions are performed on the woman's body."
According to Gat, male fertility problems are primarily treated by diagnosing their source. "A sperm disorder can stem from a variety of causes, each with a targeted treatment. For example, there may be a hormonal disorder requiring hormonal treatment; abnormal dilation of the veins in the scrotum, known as varicocele, which can be corrected through surgery or catheterization; or a genetic disorder requiring genetic testing of the embryo during in vitro fertilization. There are also cases where the source of the problem is unknown, and then we recommend lifestyle changes to prevent deterioration. But usually, treatment for men is specific."
What is the connection between testosterone levels, sperm quality and the ability to conceive?
"The testicles have a dual role: one is sperm cell production, and the other role is testosterone production. Testosterone is essential for a man's general health, and there is an interplay between it and sperm. Men with functioning testicles will have normal sperm production and testosterone production. Men with impaired sperm production will have a higher risk of testosterone disorder. These factors ultimately affect the ability to impregnate a woman; a healthy man with normal testicular function will have a higher ability to impregnate a woman than someone with impaired function."
So, which habits can improve sperm?
Gat explains that "healthy habits such as a good diet, physical activity, quitting smoking and maintaining a healthy weight have been scientifically proven to improve both general health and fertility. However, adopting a healthy lifestyle will not turn a man with a severe fertility disorder into a sperm donor. It can, however, prevent an existing condition from getting worse and can also lead to improvement.
"As for trends like ice baths and so on, there is currently insufficient scientific evidence that they work. Regarding avoiding radiation – the global decline in sperm quality began in the 1970s, before we all had cellphones in our pockets. The decline has also been recorded in different countries around the world, so it goes beyond technology."
As for supplements, he adds, "It's difficult to say scientifically how much they help, because each company produces supplements in different concentrations and combinations, and there can even be variation between capsules. Supplements like zinc and Coenzyme Q10 can certainly benefit a man with a fertility disorder, and we do recommend them. But should healthy men take them? I doubt it would make a difference."
Baltuch notes that "until five years ago, it felt like men weren't part of the equation, and some doctors wouldn't even send them for testing, even though statistically, male factor issues contribute to roughly 40 percent of all couple infertility cases. This has recently changed, and now usually both partners are now sent for testing. In some cases, there is also a greater willingness on the man's part to be involved in the treatment. But I still hear from many women that when they ask their partner to cooperate – for example, by taking vitamins, quitting smoking or giving up a harmful habit – they are met with resistance."
Another factor is gender roles in Israeli society. "Gender roles in the context of reproduction are based on models that could be called prehistoric, or survivalist," says Baltuch. "The man's role is to impregnate and the woman's role is to conceive. While difficulty having children can create a sense of failure in both sexes, for men it's not necessarily linked to the idea of starting a family, but primarily to their masculinity and their perception of themselves as men."
She continues: "For male patients who discover that the fertility problem stems from them, it can feel like a subject too painful to touch, like we have to walk on eggshells. Men also feel they have no right to complain about the emotional difficulty, because their partners are usually the ones who have to undergo the grueling physical treatments. In many cases, men express their difficulty through a desire to ease their partner's burden as much as possible, as a kind of compensation."
Sharing the burden
Nadav (not his real name), a 33-year-old software developer from Tel Aviv, has in recent months begun preparing his body for fatherhood – out of a desire to support his partner. "Until recently, I would smoke a small joint at the end of the day," he says, "but I read studies linking cannabis use to poorer sperm quality, so I stopped. I also discovered that saunas and hot baths – something I really love to do – can harm fertility, so I'm avoiding them now."
Nadav learned about the subject through conversations with his friends who are parents and even consulted ChatGPT about it. He says he is only at the beginning of his journey and wants to educate himself and change other habits that could support fertility. He even intends to make additional sacrifices during his partner's pregnancy, such as abstaining from alcohol – so that the burden is more equal. "I'm doing it out of solidarity with my partner, because she will have to sacrifice quite a lot for the pregnancy and for building our family, so why shouldn't I do everything I can on my end to contribute to the effort?"
"In our society, which is also a militaristic society, gender roles steer men to go to battle and women to stay behind in supporting roles," Baltuch says. "In this context, pregnancy creates a role reversal: Women are on the frontlines, the action is happening to them, while men are in supporting roles. For many couples I meet, this reversal creates emotional distress in men who feel they need to do everything they can to be part of the 'battle.' So changing habits can stem not necessarily from concern about fertility, but from a desire to be involved. In other cases, the male desire to take action over fertility can align with perfectionism. Statements such as 'I want strong sperm' express a desire to excel at masculinity."
Sharon Carmi, a 35-year-old physiotherapist from Beit Herut and the father of a 14-month-old daughter, has also decided to devote the coming year to improving his fertility for his future children. "Before the first pregnancy, I stopped smoking cannabis on my wife's advice," he says. "But now I want to get into the best shape I've ever been in, because I know it's important that the children be conceived with strong, high-quality sperm."
Carmi adheres to an organic diet, has stopped smoking cigarettes, makes a point of wearing natural fabrics such as cotton and linen and uses natural hygiene and cleaning products to avoid chemicals. "I also want to run a marathon," he adds, "because I want to be at my peak. I think it can help us conceive more easily, and I also want to be a healthy and strong father, so I can support my wife and children. It's great motivation to make positive changes in my life."
Prof. Danny Kaplan, head of the Gender Studies program and founder of the Masculinity Studies track at Bar-Ilan University, says that "the body is a central element in the traditional perception of masculinity, a tool meant to achieve and perform. In the post-industrial era, where there is almost no physical difference between men and women in the worlds of work, military or sports, and now in the digital age, where there is almost no need for the body, this poses a threat to what it means to be a man."
According to Kaplan, there is a perception that masculinity today must be proven through a continuous series of tests. "The idea is that in the modern era, masculinity is something that needs to be proven. Physical optimization, longevity and the 'maxxing' trend fit this approach, because the potential for improvement is infinite. There is also a competitive dimension here – whether against others or against yourself. The only place where the male body is almost irreplaceable is reproduction – and now even that is being challenged by technologies such as IVF, sperm donation and so on. This brings the desire to excel and maximize the body down to ever smaller dimensions of medical metrics. Sperm seemingly becomes the ultimate test of masculinity."
The pressure on "sperm value" that Kaplan describes is also reflected in the new sport of sperm racing, in which fresh ejaculate is analyzed under a microscope to see which sperm cell crosses the finish line first. A few months ago, the "Sperm Racing World Cup 2026" was announced, with organizers announcing that "athletes" from 128 countries will compete for a $100,000 prize.
Gat notes that studies have shown that male fertility disorders are associated with an increased risk of long-term morbidity such as testicular cancer and cardiovascular diseases at an earlier age than in the general population. "Today we understand that fertility is a kind of window into general health, and sperm metrics can be seen as a biomarker that predicts future health," he says.
"We need to look at things from a broad perspective: The goal isn't just to impregnate, but to build a family – usually with more than one child. Awareness of the link between lifestyle and fertility and men's willingness to support fertility are extremely important because of their impact on several critical areas – quality of life, the success of their partner's pregnancy and the health of future generations."
Men need to be part of the fertility conversation. But the path there does not necessarily lie in an obsession with metrics. It begins with a medical examination when needed, a healthy lifestyle, giving up smoking and excessive alcohol consumption, and especially in understanding that fertility is a matter for couples and families, not another masculinity test.

====================================================================================================

Iran War Highlights 2 Challenges for Japan in a Taiwan Contingency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. Despite ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran at the time, Israel and the U.S. launched a barrage of attacks, and Iran retaliated across a wide area, including Israel and the Gulf region. In the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on commercial vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, traffic control measures, and a U.S. maritime blockade of Iran combined to impose severe constraints on shipping routes that are vital to global energy transportation. Even in late September, traffic through the strait had not returned to prewar levels, and the crisis had yet to be fully resolved.
Against this backdrop, Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan. The Iran war has raised many issues, but two are especially important for Japan. The first is how to evacuate Japanese nationals and travelers when a crisis begins sooner than expected and civilian transportation networks suddenly cease to function. The second is how Japan can help ensure the safety of maritime traffic while avoiding becoming a direct party to the conflict. Both expose gaps in the institutional arrangements Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.
Evacuating People from a Sudden Crisis
The first lesson of the Iran war is that the traditional approach of waiting until a crisis escalates before evacuating people is no longer sufficient. Even before the outbreak of hostilities, the Japanese government had warned of the deteriorating situation in Iran and encouraged Japanese nationals to leave early. Once the fighting began, however, it became necessary to confirm the safety of Japanese nationals and assist with their departure not only in Iran but also across neighboring areas, including Israel, Qatar, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates.
In March, the Japanese government supported multiple overland evacuations from Tehran to Azerbaijan and also assisted Japanese nationals in Gulf countries with their return home. Importantly, these evacuations were not carried out solely by Self-Defense Forces aircraft or charter flights; they relied on a combination of overland routes, commercial aviation, and transit through third countries.
An even larger problem was the temporary degradation of airports and airspace across the Gulf, including major hubs such as Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Doha. Dubai is not simply one airport in the Middle East; it is one of the world’s leading aviation hubs linking Asia with Europe and Africa. Disruption there complicated movement not only for people evacuating Iran and Israel but also for travelers and foreign residents throughout the Gulf. The experience demonstrated once again that a crisis may not remain confined within the borders of one country and can quickly engulf regional transportation hubs.
This lesson applies directly to a Taiwan contingency. In peacetime, large numbers of Japanese nationals are in Taiwan for tourism, business, study, and long-term assignments. Once hostilities begin, not only Taiwan’s airports and ports but also the surrounding airspace and waters could become dangerous. Transportation in Hong Kong, coastal China, Okinawa, and the Sakishima Islands could also be affected. In other words, a plan designed only to move Japanese nationals out of Taiwan would be insufficient. Japan must prepare for a scenario in which multiple transportation nodes across East Asia become unavailable at the same time.
Within Japan, civil protection plans to evacuate residents and tourists from the Sakishima Islands to Kyushu and Yamaguchi have become increasingly concrete, with field exercises scheduled for fiscal year 2026. This is an important development. Yet civil protection planning primarily concerns the evacuation of people inside Japan. By contrast, the evacuation of Japanese nationals from Taiwan, Hong Kong, coastal China, and other overseas locations spans several frameworks, including consular assistance by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, transportation under the Self-Defense Forces Act, and the securing of civilian transportation. If domestic evacuation and overseas evacuation occur simultaneously, Japan would still face the unresolved question of how to allocate aircraft, ships, airports, and ports between the two missions.
The lesson from the Iran War is not simply that Japan should increase the transport capacity of the Self-Defense Forces. Moving tens of thousands of people within a short period ultimately depends on cooperation with commercial airlines, shipping companies, airports and ports, and third countries. Japan therefore needs, in peacetime, to identify which civilian services could be maintained during a crisis, which third countries could serve as evacuation hubs, and which ports could be used if air routes were closed.
Plans must also address how to provide shelter, food, communications, and medical care for those who cannot be evacuated immediately. An evacuation plan cannot consist only of a plan for getting people out; it must also include a plan for keeping them safe until evacuation becomes possible.
Ensuring Safe Navigation Without Becoming a Party to the Conflict
The second challenge is how to ensure the safety of maritime traffic. During the Iran War, the Strait of Hormuz was not completely closed, but normal commercial navigation became extremely difficult because of the risk of attacks on and seizures of merchant vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, Iranian traffic control measures, and the U.S. blockade of Iran.
In June, the United States and Iran reached a memorandum of understanding that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the Japanese government also called for the early restoration of free and safe navigation. Yet even in late September, traffic through the strait remained well below prewar levels.
On September 22, Iran indicated that it was prepared to reopen the strait quickly if the United States eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. This, in turn, shows that as of late September, the restoration of safe navigation remained a matter of diplomatic and military negotiation.
This raised a further question: who should be responsible for ensuring safe navigation? If the United States, as a party to the conflict, leads convoy escorts or other maritime operations, participating states are more likely to be perceived as having been militarily incorporated into the U.S. side. Yet civilian shipping cannot simply be left exposed in dangerous waters.
European states have therefore sought arrangements that would protect freedom of navigation while maintaining a degree of distance from U.S.-led operations. In September, France was reported to be considering a United Nations Security Council resolution for an international mission to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Such an approach can be understood as an attempt to distinguish, as far as possible, alliance military operations from the protection of maritime traffic as an international public good.
A similar dilemma would arise in a Taiwan contingency. If the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters became dangerous, maintaining maritime traffic would be a major economic and security concern for Japan. Yet the threshold for participation would be extremely high if measures to protect shipping could immediately lead to armed conflict with China. What is needed is an institutional distinction, to the greatest extent possible, between joining combat operations and supporting the safe navigation of civilian vessels. Japan should therefore clarify in advance options that are not integrated into the use of force, including post-ceasefire mine clearance, information sharing, sea-lane monitoring, rescue of vessels in distress, and cooperation with escort frameworks led by third countries.
This issue is also related to the limits of Japan’s 2015 Legislation for Peace and Security. The legislation permits the minimum necessary use of force only when the so-called three new conditions are satisfied, including cases in which an armed attack on a foreign country that is in a close relationship with Japan poses a clear threat to Japan’s survival and to the fundamental rights of its people. It is important to note that, as a matter of law, U.S. participation in a conflict is not itself a requirement for recognizing a situation that threatens Japan’s survival. The Japanese government has also stated with regard to a Taiwan contingency that whether a particular situation constitutes such a threat must be determined comprehensively in light of the specific circumstances actually arising. It is therefore inaccurate to frame the issue as one in which Japan can do nothing unless the United States participates.
However, what is legally possible and what can actually be recognized in practice are different questions. A situation threatening Japan’s survival can be recognized only when there is a clear danger to Japan’s existence and to the rights of its people, and when no other appropriate means are available. Disruption to maritime traffic or higher resource prices alone would not automatically meet that threshold.
Moreover, when Japan seeks to secure safe navigation in a manner that is not directly connected to combat with the opposing state, the framework of a situation threatening Japan’s survival may in some cases be too weighty. In March 2026, views were expressed within the Japanese government that minesweeping in the Strait of Hormuz after a ceasefire could be considered as one option. This is one example of the importance of maritime security measures that are institutionally separated from direct participation in combat.
The same perspective should guide discussion of a Taiwan contingency. The debate should not be reduced to a binary question of whether Japan would exercise the right of collective self-defense. Japan instead needs to strengthen the legal and institutional arrangements that apply before that threshold is reached and in adjacent areas. Specifically, it should clarify the legal basis and timing for measures such as the evacuation of Japanese nationals, maritime security, mine clearance, information sharing, warnings to civilian vessels, coordination with third countries and international organizations, and the alternative use of ports and airports. A U.N. resolution or an international framework led by third countries could be one option. Yet because China is a permanent member of the Security Council and possesses a veto, it would be unrealistic to rely solely on a U.N. resolution. Japan therefore needs multiple legal and diplomatic pathways.
What Should Japan Learn From the Iran War?
The Iran-U.S. war became a major crisis that simultaneously challenged the protection of Japanese nationals and the security of maritime transportation. It demonstrated that preparing for contingencies cannot be reduced to the question of how far the Self-Defense Forces can be used. In the initial phase of a crisis, airport closures and airspace restrictions may halt civilian transportation, while the population requiring evacuation may rapidly expand from the belligerent state to neighboring countries. At sea, Japan may be called upon to help ensure safe navigation even without participating in hostilities, while still facing the risk that such activity could be interpreted as support for one of the parties to the conflict.
The same problems could arise in a Taiwan contingency. The central issue is not to reduce a Taiwan crisis immediately to the questions of a situation threatening Japan’s survival or the exercise of collective self-defense. Rather, Japan needs to institutionalize and operationalize the measures that would become necessary before such a determination: the evacuation of Japanese nationals, the evacuation of residents, the maintenance of air and maritime transportation, protection of sea lanes, and cooperation with third countries. The Iran war has revealed a new “intermediate domain” within the legal and institutional framework Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.
Diplomatic efforts to prevent a Taiwan contingency must of course continue. Yet considering what should be done if deterrence fails is also part of security policy. The most important lesson Japan should draw from the Iran War is that the issue should not be framed as a binary choice between participation and non-participation in war. Instead, the many practical tasks that lie between those two poles must be institutionalized in advance.

Central Asia’s Diplomatic Balancing Act on Display from Bishkek to New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

The general debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly closed this week, and the Central Asian speeches put the region’s balancing act on full display. As the world moves toward multipolarity, the five Central Asian states find themselves in a tight spot. They must manage relations with the two leading global powers, the United States and China, while preserving their ties with Russia, with which they share deep historical, economic, and political bonds.
Three weeks before the debate opened, Kyrgyzstan hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s (SCO) 25th-anniversary summit on August 31 and September 1. Four of the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – are SCO members, while neutral Turkmenistan remains formally out, although it occasionally participates as a guest. The SCO is widely seen as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to limit Washington’s footprint in Eurasia, and the 2026 summit’s Bishkek Declaration gave the United States plenty to dislike, from a firm condemnation of military strikes on Iran to opposition to “unilateral coercive measures.”
Taken together, the two gatherings reveal a clear division of labor in Central Asian diplomacy. The region’s governments echo Beijing’s and Moscow’s grievances in regional group settings like the SCO, court Washington with concrete deals via bilateral channels, and use the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) podium to say as little as possible that might offend any of the three.
The balancing starts with who showed up. Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Emomali Rahmon, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, and Sadyr Japarov all attended the SCO summit in person, alongside China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi. Three weeks later, only Japarov traveled to New York, after making a stop in the U.S. state of Utah. All five Central Asian countries had sent their heads of state last year for the U.N.’s 80th anniversary. Xi and Modi also skipped this year’s session, though Xi was in Washington on a state visit around the same time.
This does not mean, however, that Central Asia has abandoned Washington for its rivals. Kazakhstan, for one, backed Security Council Resolution 2803, the November 2025 measure endorsing Trump’s Gaza peace plan and his Board of Peace, even though Russia and China abstained. Tokayev sits on that board. Kazakhstan, which announced it would join the Abraham Accords last November, also took part in its first accords meeting in New York on September 24. Japarov, for his part, carried the SCO’s complaint about Western sanctions to the UNGA podium, yet he also thanked Trump for cutting U.S. funding to foreign NGOs.
These are low-cost gestures aimed at a transactional White House, and they come bundled with commerce. In mid-October, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will lead a delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand for a C5+1 ministerial meeting, his first trip to the region. With the United States and China racing to secure critical minerals, Central Asian capitals have something Washington wants.
Beijing, meanwhile, offers trade on a scale Washington cannot match. Xi paired the Bishkek summit with a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and pledged an SCO center for AI cooperation and 100 joint technology projects over three years. He arrived as the region’s largest trading partner, after China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record $106 billion last year. In Bishkek, all four Central Asian members also reaffirmed their support for China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Competition between the two powers lets Central Asian capitals bargain with both.
Central Asia is also building influence inside the U.N. system, and the great power scramble for its mineral wealth may give it more leverage to raise its global profile. Kyrgyzstan joins the Security Council in January, having been elected with 142 votes in June. Tajikistan used its UNGA address to announce its first-ever U.N. Security Council bid, for 2028-2029. Uzbekistan declared its candidacy for 2035-2036 and will chair the Non-Aligned Movement next year, while Turkmenistan will chair the group of landlocked developing countries.
Uzbekistan’s statement, delivered by the president’s daughter and head of the presidential administration Saida Mirziyoyeva, captured the balancing act neatly. Observing that countries are being asked which side they choose, Mirziyoyeva answered with “human dignity” rather than a camp, echoing the Bishkek Declaration’s own rejection of “bloc-based and confrontational” approaches. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev sat beside Xi and Putin in Bishkek; next month, Samarkand hosts Rubio.
Central Asia’s multivector strategy has not disappeared, but it has changed form. The region now aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations. As great power rivalry intensifies, the open questions are how long Central Asian governments can hold this position and how much they can gain from it.

New EU Airline Baggage Rules: What Changes and When They Take Effect

Bulgaria Moves From Low-Cost to Quality Tourism
Bulgaria is moving toward a tourism model focused on quality rather than low prices, Tourism Minister Ilin Dimitrov said, citing positive signals from several important markets
Air passengers flying within the European Union may soon be entitled to more free hand luggage. In June, the European Parliament and EU member states reached a provisional agreement on new air passenger rights, marking the first major overhaul of EU aviation legislation since 2004.
Under the proposed regulations, a standard airline ticket within the EU will automatically include two free pieces of hand luggage:
Personal Item: One small item (e.g., handbag, small backpack, or laptop bag) that fits beneath the seat in front.
Cabin Bag: One larger piece of hand luggage weighing up to 7 kg with maximum combined dimensions of 100 cm.
The rules aim to eliminate extra hand-luggage fees currently imposed by many carriers. However, the European Parliament has noted that airlines will still be permitted to offer discounted fares for passengers traveling without a cabin bag.
The new rules are expected to take effect no earlier than October 2027, pending final approval through the remaining stages of the EU legislative process. The baggage revision forms part of a broader review of air passenger rights, covering delays, flight cancellations, and compensation.
Due to Brexit, the EU mandate will not automatically apply to UK-based carriers (such as easyJet UK, British Airways, and Jet2):
Flights Departing the UK: Passengers taking off from UK airports will not receive free cabin baggage under the EU regulation.
Return Flights from the EU: According to easyJet, the EU rules will apply to UK travelers solely on return flights originating from an EU member state.
Major UK airlines are currently reviewing their baggage policies ahead of the EU legislation taking effect./Novinite.bg

Wizz Air launched its new direct Sofia-Berlin route on September 20, the airline said, with flights operating year-round four times a week

This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:26:47 UTC
21:26:47 KST

This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
Following the MIND diet may help slow brain shrinkage and delay some signs of brain aging by years.
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- BMJ Group
- Summary:
- People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.
- Share:
A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating plan designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.
Greater adherence to the MIND diet was linked to less brain tissue loss over time, particularly in grey matter, which plays an important role in memory, learning, decision making, and information processing. It was also associated with less enlargement of the brain's ventricles, fluid filled spaces that tend to grow as brain tissue shrinks.
What Is the MIND Diet?
The Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay diet, or MIND for short, has previously been associated with better cognitive health, according to the researchers.
The eating pattern emphasizes green leafy vegetables; other vegetables; berries; nuts; whole grains; fish; beans; olive oil; and poultry, along with moderate wine consumption. It also recommends limiting butter/margarine, cheese, red meat, pastries/sweets, and fried fast foods.
Although previous research has connected the MIND diet with cognitive benefits, its relationship with age related changes in brain structure has remained less clear. Those structural changes are also relevant to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
Researchers Tracked Brain Changes for Years
To investigate, researchers studied 1647 middle aged and older adults (average age 60 at the start of the study) from the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort (FOS).
Participants underwent regular health evaluations every 4-8 years. Starting in 1999, they also received MRI brain scans every 2-6 years.
Diet was assessed through at least 1 food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) completed during check ups between 1991-5, 1995-8, and/or 1998-2001. Each participant also had at least 2 brain MRI scan assessments between 1999 and 2019 and showed no evidence of stroke or dementia at the time of their first MRI scan.
The average MIND diet score was just under 7 out of a possible 15, with 15 representing the strongest adherence.
People in the highest third for MIND diet adherence were more likely to be women and college educated. They were also less likely to smoke or have obesity.
They were also less likely to have conditions that can affect brain health, including type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease.
Higher MIND Scores Linked to Slower Grey Matter Loss
Over an average follow up period of 12 years, MRI scans showed the expected age related changes across the group. These included decreases in total brain, grey matter, white matter, and hippocampal volumes.
At the same time, cerebrospinal fluid and ventricular volumes increased, as did white matter hyperintensities, which appear as bright spots on MRI scans and can indicate tissue damage.
However, people with higher MIND diet scores experienced slower loss of grey matter.
Each 3 point increase in MIND diet score was associated with slower grey matter loss of (0.279 cm³/year). According to the researchers, that corresponded to 20% less age related decline and the equivalent of 2.5 years of delayed brain aging.
A similar pattern appeared in ventricular enlargement. Each 3-point rise in MIND diet score was associated with slower expansion of total ventricular volume by −0.071 cm³/year, equivalent to 8% less tissue loss and about 1 year of delayed brain aging.
Berries and Poultry Stand Out
Some foods appeared to contribute more strongly to the favorable associations.
Higher berry intake was linked to slower increases in ventricular volume. Poultry was also associated with slower ventricular enlargement, along with a slower decline in grey matter.
In contrast, higher consumption of sweets was associated with faster ventricular enlargement and greater hippocampal atrophy. Fried fast foods were also linked to a larger decline in hippocampal volume.
"MIND-recommended foods rich in antioxidants, such as berries, and high-quality protein sources like poultry may reduce oxidative stress and mitigate neuronal damage," suggest the researchers. "Conversely, fried fast foods, often high in unhealthy fats, trans fats, and advanced glycation end-products, may contribute to inflammation and vascular damage," they add.
Some Findings Were Unexpected
Not every food produced the expected pattern.
Higher whole grain intake was associated with several unfavorable structural changes, including faster losses of grey matter and hippocampal volume, as well as faster ventricular enlargement.
Cheese showed the opposite pattern. Greater cheese intake was associated with slower declines in grey matter and hippocampal volume, less ventricular enlargement, and fewer white matter hyperintensities.
Benefits Appeared Stronger in Older Adults
The overall associations remained consistent across several additional analyses and were stronger among older participants.
The researchers say this may suggest that the MIND diet could be especially relevant for people at greater risk of faster brain aging or those who show more variation in the pace of brain atrophy.
Stronger associations were also seen among participants who were more physically active and among those who were not overweight or obese.
That pattern raises the possibility that combining a brain healthy diet with other healthy lifestyle habits could help reduce the risk of neurodegenerative disease, the researchers say.
The Study Cannot Prove Cause and Effect
The findings come from an observational study, so they cannot establish that the MIND diet directly caused the slower brain changes.
The researchers also note that food frequency questionnaires rely on participants accurately remembering what they ate, which can introduce recall bias.
They were also unable to rule out mild cognitive impairment at the time of the first MRI scan, changes in diet over time, or the influence of genetic risk factors.
Because the participants were predominantly White, the findings may not apply equally to people from other ethnic backgrounds.
Still, the researchers conclude: "These findings reinforce the potential of the MIND diet as a brain-healthy dietary pattern and support its role in strategies aimed at slowing neurodegeneration in aging populations."
Story Source:
Materials provided by BMJ Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hui Chen, Gulisiya Hailili, Lu-sha Tong, Leqi Fei, Yaying Cao, Xin Xu, Xue Li, Debora Melo van Lent, Changzheng Yuan. Adherence to the MIND diet and longitudinal brain structural changes over a decade: evidence from the Framingham heart study offspring cohort. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, 2026; 97 (6): 505 DOI: 10.1136/jnnp-2025-336957

Officials Detained as Kazakhstan Mourns Soldiers Perished at Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:26:00 UTC
21:26:00 KST

Kazakhstan is mourning the deaths of 14 servicemen who were lost during a military drill. The tragedy took place on September 24 during the 2026 Caspian Defense exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan. The episode has led to the dismissal of the defense minister, while five officials are being investigated for negligence in relation to the case.
According to the Kazakh Ministry of Defense, a total of 17 servicemen were swept out to sea during one of the naval exercises due to a sudden deterioration in weather in the area, including strong winds. While rescue teams did manage to save three servicemen, the remainder were lost, their bodies recovered over the following days.
While President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared a day of mourning out of respect for the soldiers who passed away, criticism has hit the authorities hard, both regarding the accident and the subsequent approach by the authorities to the relatives of the deceased.
The accidental deaths prompted criticism at all levels of authority, not least in regards to how the tragedy was communicated to the relatives who were left behind. As news about the September 24 accident spread, relatives of servicemen involved in the exercise started to gather outside the Aktau morgue located close to the scene of the accident. There they sought answers regarding who was lost, demanding the names of those who had been identified.
Separated by a fence surrounding the morgue, military personnel later that day read out the names of the identified servicemen, most of whom were under the age of 25. The scene, which was captured on video and shared on social media, quickly gained attention for its impersonal and monotonous tone, with both activists and journalists calling out the authorities for handling the announcement in a way that was “Shocking [and] heartless.”
In the week following the accident, disciplinary actions were rolled out, with five officials from the Ministry of Defense being detained and put under investigation for their role in the accident. Among those detained were the chief of staff working with the naval forces, two military unit commanders, and a naval infantry company commander connected to the incident. The men are allegedly to blame for the accident due to negligence of service and violation of navigation rules, according to Kazakh police.
The incident did also force consequences at the highest levels of governance. Initially, Tokayev gave his condolences to the affected families and declared a day of mourning, to be observed on September 25. Days later, he sacked the minister of defense, Dauren Kosanov, who had been in the post just over 15 months. In his place, the now former commander of special operation forces, Aidos Myrzakhmetov, was appointed.
This is not the first accident of its kind. Four servicemen died as strong winds hit a military exercise in the same area of southwestern Kazakhstan in 2015. While this time the investigation and reshuffling of people connected to the Ministry of Defense might help prevent the recurrence of such accidents, military analyst Yermek Seitbattalov, whom the outlet Kaztag spoke to, still sees multiple shortcomings that the military has not fixed. The retired colonel, among other things, mentioned flaws in combat training and the preparation of officers, specifically in relation to the safety of servicemen during exercises. He said this issue was one of the most important matters of attention for the new defense minister.
The Kazakh authorities have shown themselves unequipped not only to properly communicate the passing of soldiers to their loved ones, but also to ensure the safety of those participating in military exercises. While Kazakhstan still mourns the tragedy, the test will be what the military learns from it.

Russian Drones Attack Kyiv’s Pivdennyi Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:18:59 UTC
21:18:59 KST

Two Russian drones struck near the supporting structure of the Pivdennyi Bridge in Kyiv, after which traffic across the bridge was halted.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klychko reported the incident.
Following the strikes, metro trains and surface public transport were temporarily suspended from using the Pivdennyi Bridge.
Specialists from the municipal enterprise Kyivavtoshliakhmist kp have begun inspecting the bridge’s structures to determine the extent of possible damage following the strikes.
According to Channel 5, citing passengers, one of the drones struck the bridge at the moment a metro train was passing over it.
Eyewitnesses reported a powerful explosion and a flash, after which smoke appeared inside the carriage and ash began falling from the ventilation system. According to their accounts, no passengers were injured.
The metro train managed to reach the Vydubychi station, where all passengers were evacuated. It is not yet known whether the train was damaged by the explosion.
Traffic across the Pivdennyi Bridge has been completely suspended while engineers inspect the structure for possible damage.
The Pivdennyi Bridge is part of Kyiv’s Syretsko-Pecherska metro line and connects the city’s right and left banks. The upper level carries road traffic, while a metro line runs between the bridge’s structural elements.

A few weeks ago, I got an interesting email from Jean Charconnet, referencing a 9/10/2026 LLOG post, noting general issues about the logic of analogies and metaphors, and offering to submit a guest post on the topic.
I agreed, and couple of days later he sent me a fascinating document, which starts by citing his doctoral dissertation on analogy, later published in 2003 as « Analogie et logique naturelle », and its roots in earlier work by Jean-Blaise Grize.
I immediately ran aground trying to locate copies of those references, and/or other ways to learn about the intellectual world they come from. And my life over the past couple of weeks has been dominated by the need to wade through through various "AI HR" swamps*, so I haven't been able to get back to the search.
To avoid further delay, I've formatted Jean's guest post as an HTML document, more suitable to its style than LLOG's antique WordPress theme, and here it is. Enjoy!

2 Driverless Cars Crashed Going 155 mph. That Could Be a Good Thing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

The grandstands erupted with shock as engineers clutched their heads in the paddock. One driverless race car, produced by the company PoliMove, slammed into Unimore’s slowing vehicle in an event held by the Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL).
At the famous racing track in Imola, Italy, Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari, both cars crashed in an area called Rivazza. This is the circuit’s final sequence, made up of corners that are notoriously difficult to navigate. Formula 1 champions have met a similar fate here. But this time, the impact posed no danger to the drivers because there weren’t any.
Launched in 2024, A2RL sought to introduce self-driving cars to the motorsport to test the boundaries of their current capabilities. And this year’s race at Imola revealed those edges, demonstrating the gap between the computational abilities of autonomous vehicles and their capacity to respond when something goes wrong.
Only two of the five cars in the final completed the race. The UAE’s Kinetiz finished first, followed by Germany’s Constructor Racing. PoliMove clocked in at third place, though its battered entrant had to be replaced for the podium ceremony. Two-time winner TUM withdrew its car after it developed a brake problem during the formation lap.
Participating teams had just nine days of physical testing before the race, in conditions that included rain and hail. This also happened to be the league’s first international competition away from its usual testing ground at Abu Dhabi’s Yas Marina Circuit.
So why choose one of motorsport’s most unforgiving tracks?
“Because everybody can do ‘easy’, right?” says Nicola Palarchi, engineering director at Aspire, the company that founded A2RL. “We have to show we go where it matters.”
Palarchi made it abundantly clear that autonomous racing did not intend to compete with human racing, which would remain its own motorsport. It could even support the latter.
Because autonomous racing is pitched as more than spectacle: It’s a laboratory with guardrails. Its proponents describe it as a way to test perception, prediction, and vehicle control at extreme speeds without endangering a human driver. These are all factors in the safety of driverless cars in the real world, and so measuring the limits at which these vehicles succeed—or perhaps more importantly fail—can inform future improvements in the technology.
The first hurdle is perception. The vehicle’s sensors identify its location and surroundings, informing planning software that then chooses a trajectory. Finally, the control system translates that decision into steering, acceleration, and braking. Racing makes each of these stages more challenging, since at high speeds, vehicles have less time to interpret incomplete information, predict another car’s movements, and execute an evasive maneuver.
“The car will be blind for a certain point because the track drops off,” Alexander Winkler, A2RL’s head of sporting, said before the final. If one vehicle stopped beyond that drop, he explained, the car behind could have less than a second to react.
That warning proved prescient.
Unimore said its car, Gianna, initiated a safety stop after losing all data from its lidar and radar sensors. GPS alone could not locate the car accurately enough to continue racing at speed. The team said future systems could use cameras and an inertial measurement unit to continue at a slower pace until precise localization returned. In other words, the car stopped because it lacked a reliable fallback.
PoliMove’s vehicle, Eva, detected Gianna ahead, according to the team, but could not avoid hitting it. Gianna had braked with a force of approximately 1 g, with Eva just 1.5 seconds behind it.
PoliMove said its system identified the danger and began an evasive maneuver. But perception, decisionmaking, trajectory replanning, actuator response, and vehicle dynamics all introduce delays. Once Gianna braked that severely mid-corner, the team said, a collision was physically impossible to avoid.
Even F1 legends like Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz have crashed at this part of the track. However, the A2RL teams’ explanation exposes a problem that faster processors alone cannot solve: An autonomous vehicle may recognize a hazard and still be unable to respond before physics takes over.
TUM’s failure was less algorithmic but equally instructive. The team said its car, Hailey, retired after the rear-left brake became stuck at low-to-medium pressure during the formation lap. Even sophisticated autonomous software cannot compensate for mechanical faults.
Kinetiz’s car, Sparkz, took the lead all the way to a first-place podium finish with Constructor AI’s vehicle as the runner-up. But almost any result can be considered progress when the failures produce useful edge cases: sensor loss, compromised localization, sudden braking, limited visibility, and interaction between autonomous systems making separate decisions.
Beyond crash data, Palarchi says these motorsport environments provide the opportunity to develop more resilient hardware. Temperatures in cockpits can get near 170 degrees F, and—while hopefully your robotaxi is not that hot—radars and lidars that can withstand high heat can be useful in our warming cities.
Chee Kiong Ong, deputy team principal at Kinetiz, also observes that predictive algorithms developed on the track could eventually help civilian vehicles respond to emergencies. “You could probably apply it to make the car stop itself in a safer manner or control it at the limits so that you can save lives,” he says.
One caveat is that, unlike other lab testing, the companies aren’t required to share the precise data collected from their vehicles. The data from A2RL’s EAV 25, the racing car developed by the league based on modified Dallara SF23 cars, currently stays within the competition.
The next A2RL race returns to Yas Marina, where teams have spent years developing their software. Organizers are already considering making the competition harder by shortening testing periods, increasing the grid to eight cars, or restricting access to GPS.
Those changes could reveal whether the systems are becoming more adaptable. In the meantime, we’ll wait to see how this information transfers into real-life scenarios.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

U.S. President Donald Trump said he does not believe reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received warnings in the days before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack, while declining to publicly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s elections this month.
In an interview with Time magazine published Thursday, Trump said he had heard about the reports for the first time that day.
“I can't imagine this,” Trump said. “I heard that today for the first time.”
Asked about reports that Netanyahu had been warned before the attack, Trump said he did not think that was the case.
“I think, you know, I think if he would have known, he would have done something about it,” Trump said. “Certainly, he would have had people at least alert.”
Trump, however, stopped short of endorsing Netanyahu for another term ahead of Israel’s elections this month.
Asked whether he believed Israelis should elect Netanyahu to another term, Trump replied: “Well, I can only say that I'm not involved in politics anymore.”
Trump was also asked specifically about Gadi Eisenkot and the possibility that the Yashar party chairman could win the election. Asked whether the United States might be able to work better with Eisenkot than with Netanyahu, Trump said he did not know.
“I don't hear bad things about him,” Trump said. “Well, people have written off Bibi many, many times, just like they've written off me many, many times. I wouldn't underestimate Bibi,” he added, using the prime minister's nickname.

Kindness isn’t always what it seems: The psychology of women’s competitive altruism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:37 UTC
21:00:37 KST

New research suggests that some women report using kindness and generosity strategically to gain an edge over rivals, a tendency linked to manipulative personality traits and lower agreeableness. These findings, published in Frontiers in Psychology, provide evidence that cooperation can sometimes serve as a subtle tool for interpersonal competition.
The research, led by Maryanne Fisher, a Santamarian Research Chair in the Faculty of Science at Saint Mary’s University’s Department of Psychology, builds on the concept of competitive altruism. The study grew out of a Faculty Mobility for Partnership Building Program grant from the Government of Canada, which allowed Fisher to spend a month at the Universidad del Desarrollo in Santiago, Chile, with additional funding from Chile’s ANID Fondecyt program. “I relocated there for a month and it was amazing,” Fisher told PsyPost.
In evolutionary psychology, competitive altruism refers to the idea that people give away resources or help others in ways that boost their own reputation and social standing. A 2006 experiment showed that people can gain higher status and social influence by making showy, generous sacrifices, as observers tend to prefer these cooperative individuals as future partners.
Initially, scientists viewed competitive altruism as a predominantly male tactic for winning status and attracting mates. For example, a 2012 experiment indicated that men eagerly competed to endure pain and inconvenience to secure status within a group, while women held back from this overt display. Because of findings like this, visible generosity was often treated as a public broadcast of quality aimed at a large audience.
“There was absolutely a research gap we tried to address,” Fisher said. “Most research on competitive altruism (the idea that people compete to be seen as the most generous or kind) has focused on men. It also often centered around men’s conspicuous public displays, such as men becoming more generous in the presence of a potential mate.”
However, research into female social dynamics provides a different perspective. A 2020 review highlighted that women tend to seek social status through subtle, low-risk strategies rather than the overt, public contests that men often favor.
“Past studies that included women produced highly mixed results, and we thought it might be because researchers were looking in the wrong place,” Fisher explained. “A long line of work shows that women’s rivalry tends to involve minimal risk and rely on indirect means, for example, carried out through gossip, exclusion, and the management of reputation rather than open confrontation.”
This pattern of indirect competition raised the question of whether women might weaponize kindness and giving as a subtle way to outcompete others. Fisher and her colleagues suspected that some women use generosity not as a flashy public contest, but as a quiet, low-risk way to win allies and reputation while remaining deniable as competition.
“Given this is how women often compete, kindness seemed like an ideal competitive tool because it wins allies and social standing while being very difficult to call out as competition,” Fisher noted. “The everyday expression ‘kill them with kindness’ captures that thought. We went one step further, though, and tried to actually measure its occurrence, which meant we had to create the Competitive Altruism Survey.”
To investigate this, the scientists developed the survey and recruited 103 heterosexual cisgender women, aged 18 to 45, primarily from the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada, through an online research platform. The participants rated 15 statements describing the strategic use of kindness, such as offering help to gain an advantage or behaving generously to look better than a rival.
Participants rated these statements twice: once based on how they behave toward other women, and once based on how they behave toward men. They also completed several established psychological questionnaires. These included a measure of Machiavellianism, which is a personality trait characterized by treating social life as something to be manipulated for personal gain. Other questionnaires measured general personality traits, such as agreeableness, as well as the participants’ tendencies to give socially desirable answers or claim implausibly virtuous behaviors.
The results indicated a strong positive association between competitive altruism and Machiavellianism. Women who reported higher levels of strategic kindness were also more likely to possess a manipulative, self-interested approach to social interactions. In contrast, competitive altruism was negatively associated with agreeableness, which is the personality trait linked to genuine warmth, trust, and cooperative sincerity.
Some predictions were not borne out: competitive altruism was unrelated to extraversion and conscientiousness. As expected, neuroticism was linked not to strategic kindness itself but to the anxiety and frustration that can accompany it, such as worrying that one’s kindness will seem insincere or feeling upset when it goes unnoticed.
“The biggest finding is that kindness and competition are not opposites, because some prosocial behavior can serve a competitive purpose,” Fisher told PsyPost. “This is not to say we are totally aware that our kindness or generosity might have this motive attached to it, or that all ‘nice’ acts are for competition, but to say they are opposite is incorrect.”
“The real point to consider though is that the average score on the survey was below the neutral midpoint of the scale, meaning that, on average, women leaned towards disagreeing with the strategic statements,” she added. “The study tells us which women report the behavior and how it relates to personality. It does not tell us how common strategic kindness is in women’s daily life, or whether it works. Those need follow up studies.”
The overall average competitive altruism score was 2.51 on a scale of 1 to 5. The audience of the behavior mattered. The participants reported slightly but reliably higher levels of competitive altruism directed toward other women (an average score of 2.58) than toward men (2.43). This aligns with the idea that women’s reputational management and social rivalry frequently occur within female peer groups.
Unexpectedly, the study found a negative relationship between competitive altruism and impression management. The researchers had anticipated that women who use kindness strategically might also try to present themselves as perfectly virtuous on the survey. Instead, women who endorsed strategic kindness appeared relatively open about their manipulative intent and tended to score lower on a measure of the need for social approval.
“What was really unexpected was that women were so open,” Fisher said. “We expected women who use kindness strategically to be the most concerned with presenting themselves favorably but the opposite emerged.”
“It might be that women who endorse strategic kindness are simply more candid about it and less invested in being liked by everyone; this is a very real possibility,” she explained.
When asked to rate their own traits compared to peers, these women described themselves as more manipulative, deceptive, and fake, less honest, and more popular than other women their age, but not as kinder or more generous.
At the end of the survey, 101 participants provided open-ended descriptions of times they had witnessed other women using kindness strategically. The most common themes included offering gifts or favors to create a sense of obligation, performing warmth in public that contradicted private unkindness, and directing exaggerated helpfulness toward superiors or men in romantic contexts.
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which investigated concern-framed gossip rather than self-reported generosity. That study similarly found that women use seemingly benevolent behaviors to gain social advantages in competition, successfully knocking down rivals while appearing trustworthy to observers.
“This research offers a new way to think about how people, in this case women, can use kindness in a strategic way and how this relates to other similar measures,” said Daniel Farrelly, a principal lecturer in psychology at the University of Worcester who was not involved in the research. “The authors have found that their newly-created measure of competitive altruism (which is altruistic acts that aim to improve the actor’s reputation compared to others) correlates with some existing personality measures, and that when asked about it women often describe how and when they see such acts being used.”
“There is good evidence that women do compete with one another, but unlike men this competition often involves indirect acts (such as gossip, reputation challenges etc),” Farrelly told PsyPost. “This study further supports the indirect nature of women’s competition, showing that competing to be seen to be cooperative is just another example of this.”
There are a few details to keep in mind when interpreting the current study. Because the data relies entirely on self-reporting, it might underestimate how often this behavior occurs. Women who are deeply invested in maintaining a kind reputation might be unwilling to admit their manipulative motives on a survey, meaning the results only capture the behavior of women willing to be honest about their deception.
Fisher noted another possibility: “women who are strategically kind but unwilling to admit it would score low, which means a self-report survey probably underestimates the behavior among the women most invested in appearing kind.”
“It’s important to note, as the authors rightly do as well, that competitive altruism doesn’t cover all types of altruism,” Farrelly noted. “In this case it is only a very strategic display that is used in particular circumstances, and how much an individual uses competitive altruism is unlikely to have a clear relationship with how kind/altruistic they are overall.”
“We do not want readers to walk away thinking that all kindness is fake,” Fisher emphasized. “We also have not compared how it occurs relative to men, and our findings are really preliminary.”
“There are some clear findings here, but not all hypotheses are supported so as the authors state there is more to find out about this potential effect,” Farrelly said. “One thing I did feel was missing was a comparison with men’s competitive altruism. As this study only used female participants we don’t yet know if the same effects might occur in men’s behavior.”
It is also unknown whether this strategy actually works in practice. The survey measures the intent and the self-reported behavior, but it does not test whether the targets of this strategic kindness actually extend greater cooperation, status, or alliances in return. Future research using observational methods could help determine if competitive altruism successfully tricks observers into granting social rewards.
“The most important question is whether strategic kindness works,” Fisher told PsyPost. “We have a qualitative study underway to start to address this question. We would like to use designs that observe both the person being kind and the people receiving that kindness, such as economic games in which generosity is made more or less visible, partner-choice tasks, and observation of real groups, with the sex of the audience varied.”
“It would be good to see examples of competitive altruism being used in women’s intrasexual competition, this is something that could be explored in future experiments,” Farrelly added. “I would also like to see this study replicated in male participants so we can see if/how the behaviors the authors describe in this study are unique to women.”
Finally, the sample was modest in size and consisted of heterosexual cisgender women from predominantly Western, English-speaking countries. Because cultural norms dictate how competition and self-presentation are expressed, the findings might not apply to populations with different social expectations.
The study, “Kill them with kindness: preliminary evidence for women’s competitive altruism,” was authored by Maryanne L. Fisher, Oriana Figueroa, Nohelia Valenzuela, Ferity Thorne, Pablo Polo, José Antonio Muñoz-Reyes, Nerea Aldunate, and Simón Ramirez.

A video of a humpback whale and her dead calf reveals the animals’ bond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Scientists had a rare view of what could be humpback whale mourning when they spotted a female attending the body of a dead calf.
The sighting suggests that baleen whales may experience grief, marine biologist Olaf Meynecke and rescue boat captain Andrew Mulville report September 16 in Discover Animals.
Some toothed whales, such as orcas, have been seen spending long periods with dead calves, occasionally carrying them at the surface for days. Such demonstrations of apparent grief are rarely seen in baleen whales. This may be because newborn baleen whales are born without the fat stores that would cause a whale corpse to float. If mothers spend time with dead calves on the seafloor, there’s a very low chance humans would see the interaction. The authors believe this is the first detailed documentation of a humpback attending to a calf after its death.
In July 2025, Mulville, who works for the Australian marine animal rescue group Sea World Foundation, saw two adult humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) in the water off Palm Beach in Queensland, Australia, and went to check on them. As he approached, he saw some tissue floating on the surface that looked like amniotic membrane — the placental lining that whales shed into the water at birth.
On the seafloor, he could see a small newborn calf, less than four meters long. The female “ended up diving down, making eye contact and actually putting her pectoral fin — her arm — over the stillborn and resting next to it,” says Meynecke, from Griffith University in Brisbane, Australia.
Two adult whales, which the researchers believe were the calf’s mother and her male escort, were seen in the same area for two more days. “We can’t prove it, but I’m very certain they were the same whales, which also suggests that this is a prolonged change of behavior … something that we might call mourning or a form of grieving,” he says.
“It was pretty emotional to observe,” says Meynecke, but he warns against anthropomorphizing and drawing parallels to humans. Remember that “the whale is experiencing their world in a completely different form and shape,” he says. “They have different ways of understanding their environment.”
