20:14:24 KST

Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.
Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.
"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.
Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.
"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.
Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.
"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.
"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.
At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.
 "We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.
 
"Terrible ending"
The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release, which included images of the rescue.
French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.
"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.
Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.
The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.
Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.
In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.
The New Zealand military released dramatic drone video of the yacht plunging below the water's surface and the crew ultimately being rescued.
A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.
Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.
But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.
"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."
Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.
"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."
Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.
The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board. Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

United States air forces are engaged in combat operations today, and not all the aircraft are modern stealthy platforms like the B-2, F-22, or F-35. The venerable Lockheed Martin F-16 Fighting Falcon remains the backbone of the U.S. Air Force fighter fleet and will be in service for two more decades, yet combat operations in Operation Urgent Fury prove it needs electromagnetic warfare (EW) upgrades to survive in modern threat environments.
Our knowledge of the frequencies and waveform characteristics across the Electromagnetic Spectrum (EMS) and our ability to manipulate them with hardware and software have grown tremendously. We harness our knowledge and capabilities continuously for tracking, intelligence, communication, jamming, radar, and many other applications. Unfortunately, so do our adversaries.
To survive and accomplish combat missions, F-16 pilots need to first detect enemy threat systems, like surface-to-air missiles or air-to-air radars, via a Radar Warning Receiver (RWR) and then counter the threat with Electronic Countermeasures (ECM) that manipulate radio signals to jam guidance systems outright or deceive them in such a way that makes them ineffective. If it were only that easy.

Acknowledging the EMS’s asymmetric impact, both Russia and China created separate branches of service and senior commands specifically focused on electromagnetic warfare.

This foreign investment is funding development, lab testing, flight testing, and current production of operational Viper Shield systems, which presents the U.S. Air Force with a massive savings opportunity to avoid those upfront costs.

Furthermore, the pod version of Viper Shield offers maximum flexibility to rotate systems across deploying squadrons, share them among operational units during training periods, and maintain them without taking an aircraft off the flying schedule.
F-16 pilots today – and for the next 20+ years – deserve the capability an EW pod like Viper Shield brings to the fight.

His insights are based on that experience and from his efforts to champion EMS capabilities as the U.S. European Command J3 and Deputy Chair of the NATO Military Committee.

Turkish defense manufacturer Otokar has signed a $1.47 billion contract to export wheeled armored vehicles and logistics support to a customer it has not named, though the deal will not take effect until government approvals are in place and the buyer pays an advance.
The contract, worth exactly $1,472,080,360, covers the supply of several types of wheeled armored vehicles and integrated logistics support services for them, Otokar said in a disclosure filed on Oct. 1 with Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform, the country’s stock market disclosure system. The filing did not identify the buyer, the vehicle models or the number of vehicles.
The contract will enter into force once the required approvals from official authorities are obtained, the letters of guarantee are completed and the customer makes an advance payment, according to the filing. Otokar will provide the customer with letters of guarantee totaling $441,624,108 to cover its obligations under the deal and the advance it will receive.
Once the contract is in force, vehicle deliveries are planned to start in 2027 and be completed in batches over three years. The contract will remain in effect for seven years, which leaves time for logistics support after the last vehicles are handed over.
The deal is larger than Otokar’s previous headline export, a 2024 contract with Romania for 1,059 Cobra II 4×4 armored vehicles worth roughly $1 billion. Under that contract, the first 278 vehicles are being built at Otokar’s plant in Sakarya, in northwest Türkiye, and the rest in Romania through a joint venture, with the first vehicles delivered in June 2025.
The filing’s reference to “wheeled armored vehicles” narrows the possible models. Otokar’s wheeled range includes the Cobra and Cobra II 4×4 tactical vehicles, the Arma 6×6 and 8×8 armored personnel carriers and infantry fighting vehicles, and armored internal security vehicles, while its Tulpar tracked infantry fighting vehicle falls outside that description.
Otokar, part of Türkiye’s Koç Group, sells military vehicles to customers in Europe, Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. Estonia ordered about 230 armored personnel carriers, roughly half of them Arma 6x6s, in 2023, and Cobra vehicles serve with armies including those of Nigeria, Ghana and Rwanda. Kazakhstan has been reported to be buying Arma 8x8s, though that order has never been officially confirmed.

How climate change is altering petrichor, the glorious smell after it rains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:03:20 UTC
20:03:20 KST

The distinct, earthy smell that fills the air after rain following a long dry spell can trigger some serious nostalgia. This scent, petrichor, goes right to our brain’s memory and emotional centers for reasons that may be to do with our very evolution. But as climate change alters Earth’s weather and environment, petrichor is going to transform, too.
First, it helps to know why petrichor even happens. During dry periods, soil-dwelling bacteria produce a compound called geosmin that deters insects such as fruit flies. The chemical signals to the flies that the plant material the bacteria grow on isn’t appetizing and that it might be toxic. Geosmin also attracts spore-spreading animals, such as springtails, which help disperse the compound even more widely.
“Humans are extremely sensitive to geosmin,” says Johan Lundström, a psychologist specializing in olfactory perception at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden. “If there was one drop of geosmin stirred up into an Olympic-sized swimming pool, we’d still smell it.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
READ MORE: Weird Weather: How to Tell a Williwaw from a Haboob
While bacteria in soil produce geosmin, plants discharge aromatic oils during a drought to create a shield to protect against harsh heat and minimize water loss. When raindrops hit dry ground and plants, the impact creates microscopic bubbles filled with geosmin and oils that rise into the air, pop and scatter into tiny particles that can then fill human nostrils.
Exactly how petrichor changes will depend on where you are as the effects of rising global temperatures on weather and climate patterns will vary from place to place and year to year. Overall, parts of the world that get more rainfall will experience less petrichor, whereas areas that have droughts will experience more, says Jeppe Lund Nielsen, a professor of microbial physiology at Aalborg University in Denmark.
Droughts cause geosmin to build up, and when they occur with hotter temperatures, bacteria produce even more geosmin as heat speeds up chemical reactions inside the microbes. “If you get a higher temperature, you also get a higher production of the compounds,” Nielsen says. So when it finally does rain, more geosmin is released. But if soils get too dry, “the geosmin will dry up and not be released,” Lundström says.
Where rain falls more frequently, there will be less petrichor because the aromatic compounds won’t have enough time to accumulate. And heavy downpours—which are increasing as the planet warms—are too forceful to trap the tiny air bubbles required to launch the scent into the air. Instead the compounds are diluted, pushed underground or mixed in surface floodwaters.
Soil degradation—which has also increased as a result of higher temperatures and heavier downpours—plays a role, too, because it means fewer geosmin-producing bacteria can grow.
Any changes to geosmin won’t stop at what humans smell. Insects that react to petrichor will also have to adjust their behavior, Nielsen says. For example, areas with large amounts of petrichor will likely see an increase in mosquitoes, because the smell indicates to these insects that the dry ground is now a moist fertile environment in which to lay their eggs.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini Review: A Fitbit for Your Cat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Cats are finally getting the dog treatment. This smart cat collar features GPS location, activity, and sleep tracking, plus all-new heart and respiratory rate monitoring.
Advanced health monitoring with heart and respiratory rates. Weekly AI-powered health summaries. New visual health history timeline.
TIRED
Battery dies in about four days. Collar clasp and adjustments are tricky. Proprietary charger. Location data isn’t very granular. Needs a subscription to use.
As the pet tech industry expands rapidly, pet owners are more eager to adopt technology that tracks health metrics, similar to human wearable devices like smart rings, smartwatches, and fitness trackers.
I've been testing smart collars for the better part of the year, previously testing the Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker on my cat Basil, which monitored his location, movement, and sleep.
The Tractive Cat 6 Mini was released this spring, and I tested it on Basil for a month, comparing how this new-and-improved smart collar made specifically for cats with improved health features, like heart and respiratory rate, stacked up against other models.
This new model had surprisingly accurate health and activity stats that helped me understand Basil's routine and baseline a bit more than the previous models I've tested. I think these new health features would be especially helpful for people with aging cats or cats in poor health. (If you have an outdoor cat that roams, I'd go with the Fi Mini because it's more compact with a longer battery life.)
I valued the Cat 6 Mini's new AI-powered weekly reports and comparisons to similar cats to know if Basil is healthy. However, the collar itself died quickly, was a pain to charge, and GPS location accuracy could be hit-or-miss. Whether this smart cat collar is the right fit for you largely depends on your and your cat's needs.
Photograph: Molly Higgins
Feline Features
The Tractive Cat 6 Mini cat tracker is available in three colors: black, brown, and lavender. Unlike the previous Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker models I tested, which used an attachment that fits on the cat's existing collar, this device is the collar itself, and the entire thing needs to be taken off the cat to charge on its proprietary magnetic charger. (It takes about three hours to fully charge.) To set it up, all you need to do is download the Tractive app, choose a subscription plan, and set up your pet's profile.
For the 6 Mini model, there is one plan, but you can choose between one-, two-, and five-year contracts. One year is $10 per month, or $120 annually; two years is $7 per month, or $168 annually; and five years is $5 per month, or $300 every five years. The smart collar also has a two-year manufacturer's warranty. All plans include a 30-day money-back guarantee as well as family sharing, LTE cellular coverage, 365-day location history, and GPS data export.
The tracker weighs only 1.1 ounces and is suitable for cats weighing 6.6 to 17.6 pounds, to ensure the breakaway collar opens when it should. Basil is 17 pounds, and the Cat 6 Mini fits him well with room to spare. This smart collar fits necks between 7.5 and 9 inches, whereas the previous Tracker Mini model could fit virtually any neck size because it attached to your existing collar.
Tractive claims the collar's charge lasts up to seven days for indoor cats and that it needs to be charged nearly daily if your pet roams outside. When I tested the smart collar on my indoor-only cat Basil, the battery needed to be charged by the fourth day of use.
Because the device itself is the entire collar, I felt like I was taking Basil's collar off more often than I'd like in order to charge—I didn't like that he was collarless while it charged. My anxiety told me that in this brief moment of his nakedness, he would escape. Also, because charge time took several hours, there were a few times I forgot to put it back on him until the next day.
Another gripe I had was that it was very difficult for me to remove the collar and adjust its diameter. I'm physically disabled and have reduced grip strength and fine-motor function. The collar has a simple looped clasp, but the thick material was difficult to slide under the plastic buckle; it often fell too long or too short, and I couldn't take off the collar without pulling it to trigger the breakaway feature, which was stressful for Basil—especially since the collar needed to be charged every four days.
I would've preferred the clasp to open by easily squeezing the top and bottom to release. Again, this would probably not be as big of an issue if I were able-bodied, but it is a potential issue for other pet owners who may have reduced motor function.
Photograph: Molly Higgins
Once you've picked a coverage plan, you'll create your pet's profile, set your home's location so the device enters power-saving mode when at home, and set up a virtual fence so you'll be alerted if the pet leaves the safe area. Using the stats I provided, Tractive compared Basil to cats of similar age and weight to set a personalized daily activity goal and compared his health stats to those of similar cats.
Putting It to the Test
The Tractive app lets you track activity daily (by the hour) and over time, recording minutes to compare your cat's activity and sleep patterns. Each week, the app provides an AI summary of the previous week's activity and health stats. This pretty much always said Basil slept and relaxed a lot, but noted that he is more active than cats of similar age and breed. There's also average activity per day, which was around four hours for Basil, and average calories burned per day, which was helpful for knowing how much Basil should be eating.
Tractive estimates the cat’s daily calories burned by factoring in your pet's biometric info like weight, size, age, and spay/neuter status to create a baseline. The device contains a three-axis accelerometer that “continuously records the orientation and intensity of your cat’s physical movements,” while algorithms filter out minor movements like stretching to try to prevent false stat inflation. When the sensor detects physical acceleration, like running or playing, it logs these as the “active” minutes and converts them into daily activity time.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
Sleep metrics break down the data by day and week and classify sleep into night sleep, day sleep, and “calm” time (when a cat is awake but not active). Each day's stats are compared to the average, which helped me track Basil's habits throughout the week. Similarly to how the device tracks activity, the built-in accelerometer motion sensor tracks when the cat is still and translates that into sleep and calm time, respectively, based on micro-movements.
You can opt out of Tractive using your cat's data for their anonymized global database and leaderboard comparison features. The device continuously syncs health metrics to the app via cellular networks, but you can request a full copy of what data has been gathered or request the permanent erasure of your data.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
This model's new health metrics for cats include heart and respiratory rates. Basil's resting heart rate was consistently lower than that of cats of similar age and weight. On one day, it was 92 bpm, compared with the normal range of 105 to 168, according to the app. This was a bit alarming to me, and I plan to bring this data up the next time we visit the vet. The app also listed “potential reasons” for the low heart rate, including “fitness and conditioning” and “cold temperatures."
As with the heart rate, the app tracked respiratory rate over time by day and compared it with Basil's historical stats and those of similar cats. His daily average was 20 breaths per minute, which was within the normal range of 15 to 30. This number closely aligned with my personal tests using visual evidence and a timer on my phone.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
Live and historical location services weren't as useful for Basil since he's indoor-only. Like the earlier Tractive model, the 6 Mini features a built-in SIM card, similar to what’s on your phone, which uses nearby mobile networks for location updates. You can set up to five virtual fences through the app, which will notify you when your pet enters or leaves these zones. However, similar to the previous model, the default virtual fence was too small around my apartment, so I had to expand it to cover my entire complex. This is concerning because if Basil escapes but stays near my building, I wouldn't receive an alert.
Since my cat is indoor-only, I ran some experiments to track location accuracy. I had my roommates take the collar with them when they left to run errands, and I timed how long it took to receive an alert that Basil had left the “safe zone." I also took the tracker with me along with my phone, and tracked how long it took to receive a notification via Bluetooth.
When I took the tracker outside the safe zone with my phone, I was alerted via a notification on my home screen that Basil had left the “safe zone” almost immediately after exiting it. It provides an approximate location rather than pinpointing the exact spot on the street where he'd be, but it is still more helpful than randomly searching in the event he did get out. If I were to engage it in lost mode, the battery usually dies within four hours, so there is also a bit of a time limit in the event he did escape.
The alerts when the tracker was away from my phone were less precise. I tested it three times—once I was notified within a minute, the next time took about eight minutes, and the last time it took about five and a half minutes to alert after exiting the allotted safe zone. I should note that I get very poor cell phone service near my home, which could affect tracking and notification timing. Tractive also falsely alerted me that Basil had left the “safe zone” about once a week (during one week of testing, it alerted me four times). Each time, he was sitting in my home with the smart collar still on. I noticed it tended to send me false notifications more often when the battery was low or while it was on the charging dock.

I just wish the battery didn't die so damn fast and that the collar had a universal design that was more accessible.

Sleep disruption increases preference for artificial intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:34 UTC
20:00:34 KST

When a person’s biological sleep cycle falls out of sync with their daily schedule, the resulting fatigue can trigger feelings of social anxiety. To avoid the pressure of human judgment in this anxious state, people often prefer to be evaluated by artificial intelligence instead. These findings were recently published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior.
The human body operates on an internal biological clock that regulates sleep and wakefulness. Often, the demands of work, school, or socializing clash with this natural rhythm. Social jetlag happens when a person’s biological sleep cycle falls out of sync with these external time constraints.
A common example is staying up late on Friday and Saturday, sleeping in on Sunday, and then forcing oneself awake early on Monday morning. The resulting fatigue feels similar to traveling across time zones. This temporal misalignment does more than just cause daytime sleepiness. It can disrupt emotional regulation and make people hyper-sensitive to how others perceive them.
Researchers Xiaoyu Zhou, Yuxuan Chu, Liwei Zhang, and Jianping Liang of Sun Yat-Sen University wanted to know how this specific type of fatigue influences human behavior in the digital age. They hypothesized that social jetlag induces social anxiety, which is an intense worry about being negatively judged by others.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly stepping into evaluative roles across many industries. According to industry reports cited by the researchers, the vast majority of companies have integrated algorithmic tools into their hiring processes, and several dating applications claim to use AI to evaluate user profiles.
Because these algorithms are widely viewed as consistent, objective machines, being evaluated by an AI might feel less threatening than facing the subjective judgment of a human being. The research team suspected that people suffering from social jetlag might actively seek out these automated evaluations to cope with their anxiety.
To test this idea, the researchers conducted four interrelated experiments. In the first study, they recruited 250 participants and assessed their natural chronotype, determining whether they were biologically wired to be morning or evening people. The participants were then randomly assigned to complete a second survey at either 8:00 a.m. or 8:00 p.m. the following day.
If a natural evening person was forced to complete the morning survey, the mismatch between their biological clock and the required time served as an experimental induction of social jetlag. In the second survey, participants read a scenario about registering for a dating application. They were told the platform would evaluate their attractiveness to recommend potential partners.
The participants then had to choose whether they wanted this evaluation to be conducted by a human staff member or an AI system. The researchers found that participants experiencing social jetlag were substantially more likely to choose the AI evaluation. By contrast, those who completed the survey at a time that aligned with their natural clock showed no strong preference between the human and the AI.
The second study explored the underlying psychological mechanism by measuring social anxiety. The research team recruited 226 participants and calculated their real-world social jetlag by comparing the middle point of their sleep cycles on workdays versus free days. The participants then imagined passing a resume screening for a job and had to choose between being interviewed by a human recruiter or an AI recruitment system.
After making their choice, the participants filled out a questionnaire designed to measure their current levels of social anxiety. The results mirrored the first experiment: participants with greater social jetlag were more likely to choose the AI interviewer. The data also revealed that social anxiety acted as a statistical bridge between the two variables. Greater social jetlag was associated with more anxiety about being judged, which in turn was associated with a preference for the AI system.
For the third study, the team wanted to ensure that people were actually fleeing human judgment, rather than just acting out of laziness or a general distaste for social interaction. They recruited 240 participants on a Monday morning, a time when weekend-induced social jetlag is especially common. The setup was similar to the dating app scenario used in the first experiment.
This time, however, the researchers provided no descriptive information about how the AI or human evaluators operated, forcing a purely intuitive choice. Alongside social anxiety, the researchers measured the participants’ desire to avoid interpersonal contact and their motivation to complete tasks efficiently.
Once again, social jetlag predicted a strong preference for the AI evaluator, with 80 percent of the participants choosing the algorithm. The statistical analysis showed that social anxiety was the sole psychological driver of this choice. Neither a general desire to avoid people nor a need to be efficient explained the preference for AI.
The final study examined whether this preference depends on how people fundamentally view artificial intelligence. The researchers recruited 218 participants and presented a scenario involving an AI-based virtual app that evaluates a user’s clothing choices. The participants were split into two groups and given different descriptions of the technology.
One group was told the AI evaluated outfits objectively based on standardized data, while the other group was told the AI had learned subjective aesthetic biases and evaluated outfits emotionally. When the AI was framed as an objective and unbiased tool, participants with greater social jetlag reported a stronger intention to adopt its evaluations.
However, when the AI was described as subjective and capable of emotional bias, the effect vanished. The socially jetlagged participants no longer showed a greater intention to adopt the AI’s evaluations, suggesting that they were specifically seeking an escape from subjective judgment.
While the experiments demonstrate a consistent pattern, the researchers note a few limitations to their work. The studies relied on self-reported measures of sleep schedules and hypothetical scenarios. These methods may not perfectly capture how people behave in high-stakes, real-world situations.
Real-life evaluations often involve power dynamics that a survey cannot fully replicate. A real job interview, for instance, carries financial consequences that might alter how an anxious person weighs the benefits of an algorithmic assessment against a human one. Future studies could track actual user behavior on digital platforms to see if social jetlag predictably shifts real-world choices.
Researchers might also explore how other factors, such as a person’s baseline technical literacy or their general distrust of opaque algorithms, interact with their social anxiety. The current findings focus specifically on short-term sleep disruptions. This leaves room to investigate how chronic social jetlag, such as the fatigue experienced by permanent night-shift workers, influences decision-making over time.
The study, “Too tired to be judged by humans: Social jetlag increases preference for AI through social anxiety,” was authored by Xiaoyu Zhou, Yuxuan Chu, Liwei Zhang, and Jianping Liang.

What Trump Has Built
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

Donald Trump struts onto the new White House helipad, an 80,000-sq.-ft. expanse of carved granite on the South Lawn. “Can you believe this?” he says, taking in the scene, the Washington Monument rising in the distance. The President lingers over the details of the project with obvious pleasure, pointing out the gray stone imported from Italy and describing how five separate sections were fitted together, with measurements he says are precise to an eighth of an inch.
Behind him rises a bigger renovation project: the new White House ballroom, its concrete skeleton consuming the former East Wing. Lawsuits have followed the endeavor, alleging that Trump demolished the historic structure and began building its replacement without congressional authorization or the required federal reviews. He kept building anyway. Trump points to the walls, calling them “nuclear concrete” (the sort, he says, used in nuclear facilities), and describes a military complex beneath the ballroom that will plunge six stories underground. There will be five separate floors, he says, with one side made entirely of glass, 6 or 8 in. thick. He holds his hands apart to demonstrate. “The steel goes up next week.” 
As we walk toward the Oval Office, Trump stops several times to inspect his handiwork. There are freshly painted doors, new gold doorknobs, the Rose Garden lawn ripped out and replaced with a Mar-a-Lago-style patio, where he now presides over dinners at what he calls the Rose Garden Club. “People say, why do you spend so much time on this?” he says. “But I find it relaxing.” Later, he returns to the subject again. “It’s what I do best,” he muses aloud. “I say, am I a better builder or a politician?”
One can understand Trump’s fixation on his construction projects. At one of the lowest points of his presidency, he is absorbed with the physical details of a world he can remake to his liking. There is something revealing in the contrast. Here, he can still point to a wall and say how thick it should be, decide where the grass ends and the stone begins, make demands and have them fulfilled. With his presidency seemingly spinning off course, Trump has busied himself with things he can control.
Outside these gates, events have become increasingly resistant to Trump’s will. The war in Iran, launched without congressional authorization and initially described by Trump as a four-to-six-week undertaking, is seven months old when we meet, with no end in sight. It has sent oil and gasoline prices soaring and convulsed the global economy. Inflationary pressures compounded by Trump’s tariffs have pushed the Federal Reserve—now led by his handpicked chairman—to raise interest rates over his objections, with another hike possible before year’s end. Mortgage rates have climbed to 7.5%, worsening an already punishing housing market.
The political coalition that returned Trump to power has frayed, with signs of discontent among independents, rural voters, and parts of the Latino electorate, even as his GOP base remains substantially loyal. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in September put his approval at 32%, the lowest of his political career; a recent Wall Street Journal survey recorded the lowest ratings of any President heading into midterm elections since 1990. Republican candidates have distanced themselves from his military actions and his deportation campaign. Voters have recoiled at his laissez-faire approach to the artificial intelligence industry and his accumulation of wealth while in office through crypto deals, thousands of disclosed stock trades, and an expanding empire of Trump-branded developments stretching from Saudi Arabia and Qatar to India and Vietnam.
Inside the Administration, senior advisers increasingly recognize that he has passed the apogee of his second-term power. Across the Republican Party, officials are preparing for the likelihood of losing the House—and perhaps the Senate—in the midterms. After two years spent almost entirely on offense, Trump may soon be forced onto defense. Democratic control of Congress would bring investigations and subpoenas, hearings, and potentially a third round of impeachment proceedings. Cabinet officials could be hauled before Congress. Trump describes the prospect in characteristic terms. “They’ll probably go after me,” he says, “and I’ll go after them.”
Yet with so much at stake—for the country and the world, for his party and his own power—Trump can seem curiously preoccupied. During a 75-minute Oval Office interview with TIME, he was discursive and grievance-fueled, veering from the crises of his presidency to resentments old and emerging. He said he regretted appointing Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, after they ruled against him on tariffs, mail ballots, and birthright citizenship. “I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.” On his expectation of fealty, he was unapologetic: “I do like loyalty, yeah.” Again and again, he returned to the condition of the White House itself, complaining that his predecessors had left the building in disrepair and deriding Barack Obama as someone who “doesn’t know if something’s dirty or clean.”
Trump dismissed widespread opposition to the rapid build-out of data centers, including among his own base, as a prescription for a poorer America. When pressed on the limits of his power, Trump left himself ample room: He would not rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms, nor promise to refrain from bringing wrecking balls to the Kennedy Center without congressional approval. “I’m not committing to anything,” he says. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”
In Trump’s telling, he is simply doing what has to be done, even when that means breaking foundational promises to his voters. He campaigned as a president of peace, but is now waging a war he says was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He points to Venezuela, where his removal of Nicolás Maduro and the elevation of Delcy Rodríguez have brought the country into Washington’s orbit, as proof that his projection of U.S. power can produce results. He touts most-favored-nation drug pricing and restricting institutional investors from buying single-family homes as measures that will lower costs for Americans. New GDP and inflation figures suggest the economy remains strong.
When asked why he remains consumed with construction projects so removed from the country’s concerns, Trump offers a rationale: “The White House is a very special symbol. It’s a symbol of America. It’s a symbol of our greatness.” He speaks of his building projects in the language of legacy—monuments meant to endure long after he is gone. But while Trump obsesses over stonework and fixtures, gold and glass, the more important parts of his legacy are being built too—in the decisions he makes from inside these walls, and the consequences unfolding far beyond them. 
In late April, the President summoned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a retinue of military and national security officials to the Oval Office. By Trump’s own timeline, the war with Iran was supposed to be over already, with a new regime in place and a nuclear program throttled. But the Islamic Republic had proved resilient and resourceful, choking off oil through the Strait of Hormuz and sending tremors through the global economy.
Now there was another problem. Trump had learned from a New York Times report that the U.S. military was running low on certain munitions after firing more than 1,200 Patriot missile interceptors. To replenish the losses, the Pentagon was drawing on assets stationed in Asia and Europe, potentially weakening American defenses in other theaters. “What the f-ck is this?” Trump said to Hegseth, according to two officials familiar with the exchange, handing him a printout of the story.
According to those officials, Hegseth borrowed one of Trump’s favorite terms of derision, telling the President it was “fake news.” The Secretary of Defense insisted that the reporters had taken the facts out of context and exaggerated them to make the Administration look bad. But the reporting emerged from an official DOD inspector general’s assessment. (A spokesperson for Hegseth denied the exchange.)
Trump’s frustration went beyond munition stores. The war was polling miserably. At the time, 13 U.S. service members had been killed and nearly 400 wounded. (Those numbers would increase to 19 killed and more than 800 wounded by the end of September.) Gasoline prices had risen more than 40% since the opening attacks on Feb. 28. The conflict had already cost more than $25 billion, and the consequences were beginning to bleed into the midterm campaign. The President found himself without an exit ramp. That dynamic appears to hold true: Instead of concluding the war, Trump tells TIME, he may ramp up the bombing after the midterms if they can’t reach a satisfactory deal. “Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world,” he says. “With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”
In recent months, Trump’s relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has grown more acrimonious, according to a senior Administration official. Netanyahu urged Trump toward war with Tehran but has since complicated Trump’s efforts to end it, including by striking Hezbollah targets in Lebanon after Trump told him not to, multiple U.S. officials tell TIME. Trump says he does not believe reports that Netanyahu was warned by Egypt and the UAE ahead of the Oct. 7 attacks, but stops short of endorsing him for re-election as Israelis prepare to vote in late October for the first time since the worst security failure in the country’s history. Asked whether he might work better with Netanyahu’s leading challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, Trump leaves the possibility open. “Well, I don’t know,” he says. “I don’t hear bad things about him.”
The decision to attack Iran was a hinge point in Trump’s second term. His first year back in power had unfolded as a frenetic exercise in presidential will, a barrage of executive actions and dismantled guardrails that had largely gone according to plan. Then his second year opened with the raid on Caracas and capture of Maduro, a daring operation that reinforced Trump’s conviction that audacity could succeed where caution had failed. The subsequent attack on Tehran would test the limits of that conviction—and reveal how quickly confidence born of success could lead to overreach.
A cascade of crises followed. Though Trump has dismissed the pain of rising gas prices, he concedes the war has depleted a subset of U.S. munitions. “Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms,” he says. Trump says he has struck deals with leading defense manufacturers, including Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, to replenish the arsenal and expand production. “They’re building four, five, six plants,” he says, citing Patriot and THAAD anti-ballistic-missile facilities. “They’re building tremendous amounts of capability.”
When asked what this will cost American taxpayers, Trump offers a curious metric: less, he says, than America makes in a single month from Venezuelan oil. Yet Americans have so far felt little benefit from that arrangement. Major U.S. oil companies have returned to Venezuela and begun extracting from the world’s largest proven crude reserves, but gas prices remain at record highs for September. Meanwhile, Trump’s tariff regime strained America’s global relationships and reverberated through the economy. 
Trump points to low unemployment, robust consumer spending, and a stock market at record highs as evidence that his economic program is working. By those measures, the economy has remained strong. But they coexist with a harsher reality: the cost of everyday life remains painfully high.
By summer, Trump was growing angrier with U.S. allies that had refused to come to America’s aid against Iran—from the European powers and South Korea to Canada. Trump has directed much of his ire over the issue at America’s neighbor to the north, according to a close aide. “He doesn’t like the fact that we essentially protect them because of their proximity to our military might, and doesn’t think they give us enough in return,” says a Trump senior adviser. On July 20, Trump invoked a 1930 statute to impose a 50% tariff on Canadian goods. The trade war with America’s second largest trading partner hit steel, aluminum, and lumber especially hard, disrupting supply chains and raising the cost of materials that went into everything from factories to new homes. 
Borrowing costs were becoming their own problem. For Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, preventing a sell-off in the bond market from becoming a broader crisis was an increasingly urgent task. By late September, only 25% of Americans believed Trump’s policies had improved the economy, according to a Wall Street Journal poll, while 60% said they had worsened it. Trump had returned to office promising cheaper energy, lower prices, and an economic boom. Instead, voters were finding the opposite. “It’s not lost on any of us,” a Trump adviser tells TIME. “When voters aren’t happy with the economy, they tend to vote against the party in charge.”
Since returning to office, Trump has marveled at AI’s capabilities. He is increasingly in thrall to the tech executives courting him. In December 2025, Elon Musk returned to the Oval Office for a clandestine meeting. Trump spent hours asking Grok, Musk’s AI chatbot, questions about his presidency and legacy, according to an official present. At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes against Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the U.S. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured Maduro. According to the official present, the chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall. After Trump ordered the mission to seize Maduro, the following month, celebrations broke out in the streets. Trump, according to officials, came away thinking Grok was ingenious.
Along with his fascination with the technology came two related concerns. One was economic: that enthusiasm for AI’s potential was propping up the stock market. The other was geopolitical, reinforced in conversations with industry titans such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: that China could gain a decisive advantage over the U.S. if it developed more powerful AI first. Trump was committed to giving American companies the freedom to build faster than their foreign competitors. That meant embracing the unprecedented infrastructure build-out required to support the industry’s computing needs. After watching a cable news segment about the backlash, Trump fired off a Truth Social post. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote Aug. 31. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” 
Days later, aides showed Trump surveys from his longtime pollster, Tony Fabrizio, showing pervasive anxiety about AI: fears of lost jobs, rising costs, and technology eventually escaping human control. Fellow Republicans facing voters in November were increasingly eager to put distance between themselves and the issue. Trump “really just didn’t seem to care,” one aide says. “He wants to do what he wants to do. He’s used to generating outrage and then watching everyone eventually crawl back to him. It’s hard to convince him to do anything at this point.”
Trump was unfazed by the burgeoning bipartisan calls for new AI regulations. “I don’t have to destroy the industry,” he says. “We’re making a lot of money with that industry. That industry is the Industrial Revolution, but bigger. It’s the internet, but much bigger.” The details don’t appear to concern him. When TIME asks about OpenAI agents’ meddling with federal government websites, Trump responds: “Who breached it? They’re not allowed to do that.”
Trump’s contribution to the debate about AI safeguards has been to announce the formation of an “AI Force,” which he now wants to rename the “SI Force”—part of his effort to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” Asked what the group will do, Trump responds: “It’s going to be super intelligent.” Pressed further, he explains that it will consist of industry leaders advising him on government policy. On Sept. 29, he met with AI leaders at the White House, where the President and top executives from six leading tech companies signed a “constitution” to police themselves—a covenant of self-regulation in lieu of government oversight. An Administration official present said they left with a “no surprises if something happens” understanding between the White House and the industry. 
It was an example of how Trump has surrounded himself with industry leaders, seeking their advice, favor, and political donations. A recent CNN poll found 75% of Americans viewed artificial intelligence with more fear and concern than excitement, with broad bipartisan support for greater federal oversight. But Trump waves away AI fears, placing them in a familiar catalogue of what he considers manufactured panics. “They said that our country was going to burn down because of global warming,” he says. “Then they changed the name to climate change because global warming turned out to be a hoax. Russia, Russia, Russia was a hoax.” Asked who, exactly, is perpetrating the supposed hoax of AI concern, Trump throws his hands in the air. “The whole country is based on fake stuff,” he says, “because these people have Trump derangement syndrome.”
Inside the Oval Office, Trump’s redesign is impossible to miss. There is gold everywhere, from the decorative plasterwork to the inscriptions on the ceiling and the gilded frames crowding the walls. The room is so dazzling you practically need sunglasses. Trumpian tchotchkes are scattered about: a FIFA “World Peace Prize” sits next to the Resolute Desk, where the President keeps a commendation given to his uncle during his years as an MIT professor. 
At times, Trump’s train of thought was difficult to keep up with, his conversation moving in streams and eddies before circling back to familiar obsessions. He recounted conversations that sometimes sounded improbable. At one point, Trump claimed the Secret Service had wanted to tear down the Oval Office and rebuild it, only for him to intervene. “I said, ‘My ass, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place.’”
Whatever happens in November, people close to Trump expect him to devote more of his remaining presidency to foreign affairs, as second-term Presidents often do, with particular attention to the western hemisphere, where ideologically sympathetic governments have given him opportunities to expand American influence. At home, they expect another emphasis altogether: Trump’s campaign against what he calls “lawfare” and his effort to reshape cultural institutions, including the nation’s museums, in his battle against what he calls “woke” ideology.
Looking ahead to the midterms, Trump dismisses unfavorable polls as fake and insists Republicans can prevail. “I think we’ll do OK if I campaign, and I intend to,” he says. So far, he has done little beyond a two-day midterm convention and a few fundraisers, but top advisers say the President is preparing a campaign sprint to help Republicans stave off disaster in the midterms: visiting 32 competitive districts in the next month, with the MAGA-style rallies that powered his political rise.
Inside the White House, advisers are already contemplating what a divided Washington would mean. “I think if the worst happens in the midterms, we’ll be forced to think more bipartisan,” one top official says. “I would hope that if we win, we can still do that, because for two years we’ve run a completely partisan play. When you’re looking back on your time, I don’t think that’s what you should be proud of, even if it was successful.”
Trump’s political operation boasts a $400 million war chest, but he has only recently begun opening his checkbook. Aides say he has been reluctant to spend because he wants to preserve cash for future elections as a means of keeping his grip on his party. “He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now,” a Trump aide told TIME this fall. “He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities.”
Aides are bracing for turnover after the midterms as Trump sheds officials who have frustrated him. A source close to the President says he has openly mused about firing the FBI Director Kash Patel and has expressed frustration with Hegseth. Trump says he intends to protect those who remain. When TIME asks whether he plans to issue pre-emptive pardons to aides and associates before Democrats—or a future Administration—can pursue them, he suggests he will, offering a familiar justification: “Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody.”
As the conversation moves between war and peace, his own grip on power, and the possibility of impeachment, Trump keeps returning to the trappings of the office. He asks Natalie Harp, his ever present aide, to bring in photographs of earlier White House construction projects, including renovations from the 1930s and the Truman-era reconstruction. He studies the pictures as evidence for his case, lamenting the judges and injunctions now complicating his own efforts. Holding up a photograph of work being performed on the State Dining Room in 1950, Trump complains about a judge he says accused him of destroying the White House. “It’s the sh-t I have to go through,” he says. 
Toward the end of our interview, I ask what he will miss most when his presidency is over. This time there is no digression, no grievance, no story. Trump does not need a moment to think: “This beautiful room.” 
—With reporting by Leslie Dickstein, Simmone Shah, and Olivia B. Waxman

How Richard Nixon Reshaped the Relationship Between the President and the Press
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

Berating reporters, revoking credentials, suing news organizations—hardly a week goes by without Donald Trump’s attacking the press. An experienced commander of headlines and inveterate consumer of media, he cajoles journalists one day and harangues them the next. But the man who preceded Trump as the President to appear most often on the cover of TIME reigned supreme in media manipulation too. Well before Trump railed against fake news, Richard Nixon waged a sustained campaign to intimidate and punish those who covered him.
The relationship between Presidents and the press is inherently adversarial. Since the emergence of a modern mass media and a professional White House press corps in the early 20th century, Presidents have sought to use journalists to disseminate their ideas, goals, and achievements—and have treated coverage that deviates from their spin as misleading, hostile, or malicious. Reporters, on the other hand, while recognizing their duty to relay what the President says and does, believe that they can offer a fuller, more accurate account of events than the White House does—by adding context, checking facts, and airing dissenting views. In that difference of perspective lies a recipe for conflict.
Every President has warred with journalists. Theodore Roosevelt sued Joseph Pulitzer’s New York World for alleging corruption in the purchase of the Panama Canal. (He lost.) Franklin Roosevelt instructed an impertinent correspondent to don a dunce cap and stand in the corner. Dwight Eisenhower baldly lied to the press after the Soviet Union shot down an American spy plane. Barack Obama tried to exclude Fox News from an interview with the other TV networks and used the Espionage Act to pursue leakers. The list goes on.
But, at least until Trump, no other President had a more contentious relationship with the media than Nixon. By the time he took office in 1969, the White House–press relationship had grown sharply combative, thanks to the Vietnam War, Lyndon Johnson’s “credibility gap,” and the cultural upheavals and suspicion of authority that marked the 1960s. Journalists took it for granted that Nixon, with his long history of resenting the press, had nefarious designs on neutering the Fourth Estate. The venerated CBS anchorman Walter Cronkite labeled Nixon’s antipress campaign “a grand conspiracy.” Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee charged that “the First Amendment is in greater danger than any time I’ve seen it.” A National Press Club report found Nixon guilty of “an unprecedented, government-wide effort to control, restrict and conceal information” and “discredit the press.” And all of this happened before impeachment proceedings even began.
The relationship was not exclusively hostile. As with all administrations, there were ups and downs. At times, even as they distrusted him personally, reporters showered Nixon with admiring coverage, such as during the summer of 1972 when détente was easing tensions with the Soviet Union and after Nixon made his breakthrough trip to communist China. That summer, according to press critic Ben Bagdikian’s count, of more than 2,200 Washington correspondents, only about a dozen pursued the emerging Watergate story. Nixon coasted to re-election.
Yet these bouts of positive coverage did little to appease Nixon, whose antipress campaign continued unabated. Some of the President’s men later owned up to zealotry. “We used to watch the news broadcasts and go up the walls at what we thought was unfair coverage of Nixon,” recalled Chuck Colson, who in the fall of 1972 bullied CBS executives into shortening the second part of a Watergate exposé. Speechwriter Ray Price said flatly, “We did often lie, mislead, deceive, try to use [the press], and to con them.” William Safire, another speechwriter, recalled Nixon insisting that “the press is the enemy ... to be hated and beaten”—an attitude Safire called “neither justifiable nor defensible” and yet deeply held.
The particular skirmishes in Nixon’s war on journalists would fill not only a ledger but a shelf of books. (In writing my own book about Nixon, I consumed at least a dozen books on the subject, with titles like The Chilling Effect in TV News: Intimidation by the Nixon White House and The Engineering of Restraint: The Nixon Administration and the Press.) Some of the Administration’s offenses appear in retrospect fairly routine or mild, like the maddening evasiveness of press secretary Ron Ziegler, or even Vice President Spiro Agnew’s baroque diatribes in which he lashed out at the power of the TV networks and major newspapers. But others were genuinely disturbing assaults on the independence of the press corps, waged by a man loath to acknowledge any constraints on his power.
One of the earliest of these was Nixon’s plan, hatched with National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger, to stop leaks by wiretapping the homes and phones of journalists who reported critically on the Administration’s actions, starting with the 1969 bombing of North Vietnamese sanctuaries in Cambodia, which the White House had hoped to keep secret. At the Georgetown home of syndicated columnist Joseph Kraft, another targeted newsman, White House hireling John J. Ragan, wearing a repairman’s uniform, climbed up a nearby telephone pole to install a battery-operated transmitter that would convey every conversation on the Kraft family phone to a tape recorder in the trunk of a car parked close by. The wiretaps on Kraft and other reporters, installed without any warrant, wouldn’t be exposed until just before the 1973 Watergate hearings, but they were later found to be unconstitutional infringements on the journalists’ rights.
The wiretapping scheme grew out of Nixon and Kissinger’s mania for clamping down on leaks that might damage the Administration’s standing. That mania resurfaced in 1971, after the New York Times published the Pentagon Papers, a Defense Department study of American involvement in the Vietnam War. Told by Kissinger that he would be seen as a “weakling” if he didn’t respond, the President had his Attorney General sue the Times to force it to stop publishing the classified documents. No previous Administration had ever tried to impose “prior restraint”—government censorship prohibiting the publication of material before it appears. Eventually, in a landmark First Amendment case, the Supreme Court rejected Nixon’s claim that national security justified the suppression of the information. But the Pentagon Papers leak had other consequences too: it spurred the White House to create the so-called Plumbers unit—plumbers, after all, fix leaks—that would soon engage in a battery of illegal activities, including the break-ins at the Democratic headquarters at the Watergate complex in 1972.
Nixon also used the power of the Executive Branch to punish news outlets he considered unfriendly. The Washington Post Co. at the time owned two Florida television stations, WJXT in Jacksonville and WPLG in Miami, whose licenses were regulated by the Federal Communications Commission. Furious that the Post was digging into Watergate, Nixon fumed to his aides H.R. Haldeman and John Dean in September 1972, “The Post is going to have damnable, damnable problems out of this one. They have a television station ... and they’re going to have to get it renewed ... the game has to be played awfully rough.” Soon thereafter, allies of Nixon challenged the Post’s ownership of those licenses—challenges that failed but that hurt the company’s stock price and cost it huge legal fees.
Individuals, too, faced retribution. White House correspondent Martin Schram of Newsday, who had reported on Nixon’s dubious financial entanglements with his shady friend Bebe Rebozo, was excluded from the President’s historic 1972 China trip. CBS News’ Daniel Schorr endured an FBI investigation after a negative piece about Nixon’s pledge to help Catholic parochial schools. Nixon often told aides to have the IRS audit his journalistic detractors; some of these enemies were audited, although direct links to the President’s instructions were hard to prove. Nixon and his confidants also discussed taking revenge on syndicated journalist Jack Anderson, a regular thorn in the Administration’s side. G. Gordon Liddy, the resident wild man of Nixon’s re-election team, at one point plotted in all seriousness to have the columnist assassinated, even enlisting a CIA poison expert to help with the planning. Saner heads quashed the plan.
Nixon’s war on the media ultimately failed. The courts rebuffed his attempt to censor the Pentagon Papers. Congress exposed many of his illegal and covert operations. Watergate showed the value of investigative journalism in holding a lawless President accountable. But Watergate also heightened journalists’ propensity to distrust power and embrace a confrontational posture, sometimes manifested in productive reporting but as often evident in a reflexively snide, captious tone. Presidents, meanwhile, if not matching Nixon in their sheer hostility toward the media, followed him in viewing reporters as adversaries to be monitored, punished, and discredited. In that sense, Donald Trump simply inherited a playbook bequeathed by Nixon.

Donald Trump Has Appeared on the Cover of TIME More Than Anyone Else
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

It was 35 days before the midterm elections and President Donald Trump wanted to talk about dirt.
Standing on the White House lawn, outside the Residence, he told us about the poor conditions his predecessors had left in the world’s most famous home office. Dirty walls. The dirt that visitors, especially those in high heels, confronted when they visited the Rose Garden, before his installation of a patio. Most pressing of all, the dirt that Marine One had to land in before he completed his newest addition to the complex, a 100-ft.-wide helipad. “The happiest people were the pilots,” he said of the change. “They would land in the mud.”
The night before, Trump had been greeted at the helipad by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his wife Cami Clark, who joined the President for a late-night dinner. It was part of another whirlwind week that included a speech before the U.N. General Assembly and hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping and his delegation at the White House—name cards for leading attendees were still on the walk outside the Oval Office when we visited—as well as an Air Force One flyover of the Texas-Tennessee football game, a visit to the Presidents Cup golf tournament outside Chicago, the announcement of a new steel mill in Iowa, and a controversy over the release of taxpayer-funded political ads.
As the midterms near, the President is touting successes: low unemployment, economic growth, oil exports rebounding in the Middle East, business opportunities created in Venezuela. But for the moment, Trump seemed stuck in the mud. The costs of housing, health care, and gasoline are increasing at significant rates. His polls are at career lows (he dismissed these numbers as “fake”), Democrats are salivating over the possibility of taking over the House and maybe the Senate, and Trump’s approach to ending an unpopular war with Iran is unfolding as trial and error. The day we met with the President marked seven months since the beginning of the Iran conflict, an engagement he repeatedly told Americans would last only a matter of weeks. Our interview also followed a week in which he had attempted to bar some of our colleagues from reporting on him from the White House and as part of the President’s traveling press corps, a move we have joined our colleagues in objecting to. With Eric Cortellessa's cover story, as part of our commitment to transparency, we are publishing a full transcript of our interview with the President along with a fact-check of his remarks on Time.com.
This cover marks a milestone for this magazine and for the President: with 56 appearances, Trump has now been on the cover of TIME more often than any other individual, surpassing President Richard Nixon, who held the title for more than half a century, repeatedly breaking his own record as the Watergate scandal progressed. Trump’s first TIME cover came in 1989, when he appeared to personify that moment’s collective aspiration for luxury. His voice in that story remains familiar to us now: “I have an absolute strategy, but it’s an innate strategy and not definable,” he said. “When you start studying yourself too deeply, you start seeing things that maybe you don’t want to see.” (This cover has hung above a urinal in a men’s room at Mar-a-Lago.) It should come as little surprise that American Presidents (and Jesus) rank among the most regular occupants of TIME’s red border. Eight of the 10 most frequent TIME cover subjects over the past century have been Commanders in Chief. More than 20 different artists and photographers, including Dan Winters, who photographed the President at his helipad for this issue, have contributed Trump covers over the years.
We focus on leadership and influence at TIME, and so Trump has been a constant subject since 2015. Our covers capture his improbable 2016 campaign and first election, his impeachments and legal battles, the disgrace of Jan. 6, his return to power, his foreign policy wins, and all that has come in between. This moment—with Trump tested by a war many counseled against, facing voters who will soon take their first measure of his second presidency—marks another milestone for a man who may be the most consequential leader of this century so far.
Trump has not been shy about his interest in being on the cover of this magazine. During a 2025 visit to Israel he was presented with a framed compilation of his previous TIME covers. “Wow, I love it,” he said. “I want to make sure it comes back with us.” On the first day of his first term in office, he stood in front of national-security officials and reflected on the frequency of his cover appearances. “I have been on their cover like 14 or 15 times,” he said. “I think we have the all-time record in the history of TIME magazine. If Tom Brady is on the cover, it’s one time because you won the Super Bowl or something, right? I’ve been on the cover 15 times this year. I don’t think that’s a record that could ever be broken.” (By Jan. 20, 2017, he had appeared 11 times, including eight in 2016.) Fake TIME covers featuring Trump were once a feature of his private clubs. When he celebrated an effort to stop New York City’s congestion pricing in 2025, he circulated another counterfeit cover. And another TIME cover was transfigured and transformed into a favorite meme.
While the President covets being on the cover of TIME, he makes it clear he is not always happy with the result, and he has been keeping score: he told us this week that of the 55 previous covers, he has liked 17 of them.
Trump is unbounded by history, norm, or custom. For more than a decade now, he has maintained the ability to surprise. To his critics, this leads to shock. To his supporters, delight. He is intent on leaving his imprint on the presidency. That preoccupation with his legacy has been a factor in the burst of renovation and construction projects at the White House and across Washington. He says this work is a form of relaxation. If he cannot control the events of the world, he can control what happens in his own backyard.
There is one thing he’d like to leave untouched. Someone from the Secret Service told him they should knock down the Oval Office, he said, and build a new one. “My ass, you can’t build a new one,” he said he responded. “This is a special place.”
He also told us he wasn’t sure whether he was a better builder or a better politician. “This whole place was a disgusting mess,” he said of the White House as we left, “and now it’s perfect.”

Exclusive: Neurable’s First Brain-Scanning Headphones Want to Fine-Tune Your Focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Neurable unveiled its very own pair of brain-scanning headphones on Thursday, the Neurable One. The company claims that wearing them helps you concentrate on whatever you’re doing—working, studying, or playing a video game.
When I spoke to Neurable earlier this year, the company said it planned to license its brain-scanning technology to power a flood of gadgets that were ready to enter the market. But it decided to launch its own hardware first.
“We wanted to take the product in-house,” Ramses Alcaide, Neurable’s cofounder and CEO, tells WIRED. “There were a lot of areas where we wanted to improve the product, and we wanted to move at a much faster rate. It also puts a little more capability for us to be able to show off what’s possible with the technology.”
The Boston company has until now relied on other brands to showcase its brain-scanning technology in their products, all of which promise to help people improve focus and provide data about your brain activity in a companion app. It began a few years ago by building its tech into some Master & Dynamic headphones. At the start of this year, Neurable showed off a gaming headset with HP's HyperX featuring two electroencephalography (EEG) sensors built in.
Like the original M&D MW75 Neuro headphones, the Neurable One features 12 EEG sensors in the nylon earpads that are used to monitor brain waves. The headphones cost $499 and will be available in October from Neurable’s website.
Alongside the new headphones is a new app (the old app will continue to exist for now for older hardware), which Alcaide says tracks eight brain metrics:
- Brain Age: Tracks your brain’s perceived age against your real age.
- Brain Battery: What you have left in reserve.
- Speed: How quickly you process information.
- Focus: How well your attention is holding.
- Load: How much effort you spend doing the task.
- Stress: How much tension you have doing the task.
- Sleepiness: How far you are drifting toward sleep.
- Alpha Peak Frequency: Your strongest resting rhythm, which Neurable claims is like the brain's heart rate variability.
The biggest hardware and software change with the Neurable One is that you no longer have to start a session in the app to capture brain activity. Instead, the Neurable One passively monitors your brain as soon as you put the headphones on—Alcaide likens it to wearing a Fitbit.
At that point, the sensors begin monitoring your brain activity to measure your focus. When it detects that you’re getting distracted, the headphones play a ping to get you back on track. If it thinks you're burning out instead, it’ll recommend a break so you can come back later fully recharged.
The headphone-app combo works similarly to help you fall asleep and to meditate. For example, with meditation, you can follow a guided session, and when the headphones detect you’re in the flow, the guide will stop talking so you stay in that zone. If it detects you’re drifting away, it’ll start guiding you back again. For sleep—designed for naps rather than proper bedtime—it can, over time, lower the headset volume of guided naps or soundscapes as it detects you falling asleep. (You can also turn off the EEG sensors and just use them as regular headphones if you want.)
Alcaide says when the app tells him his brain battery is low for the day, he’ll go to the sauna and go to bed early to help him recover. It can tell him when his peak brain speed hours are, allowing him to rejigger his schedule so he does his hardest work during those times. There’s also a check-in system called Cognitive Snapshot; when you trigger it, the app shows your current brain state and offers recommendations to improve it. That could be a guided meditation or small games to exercise those parts of your brain. The app also provides weekly or monthly reports to track your brain activity over time.
Neurable doesn’t have any new research or data to share that can speak to the effectiveness of its latest headphones. That research is in the works, but it will take time. So Neurable still points to previous research with the Mayo Clinic, which showed a 30 percent increase in focus in individuals using Neurable's headset versus people using Pomodoro techniques or other types of focus-sustaining systems. The study also saw a drop of about 10 percent in end-of-day burnout and an increase in end-of-day happiness.
The product isn’t categorized as a medical device, and Neurable says it isn’t designed to diagnose, treat, or monitor any conditions. The company also promises not to sell any of the data it collects about your brain—which could become very valuable in the future—and says it doesn't use that data for advertising. Alcaide says enterprise customers buy its headsets in bulk to help employees focus, but they’re not buying the headsets to monitor the workforce.
“It's because we know we're going to get higher productivity per employee; they're going to be happier, they're going to feel less burned out, it's a win-win for everybody,” he says. “It's like how sometimes companies get gym memberships for their employees.” He stresses that each user’s data stays with them.
Alcaide says the company partnered with an audio brand to help with the non-brain-scanning bits of the hardware, though he wouldn’t share the name. These cans have the “same premium sound” as the earlier M&D collaboration, with 40-mm beryllium drivers, six microphones, active noise cancellation, a transparency mode, and 22 hours of run time—12 if you have those EEG sensors running. It supports Bluetooth 5.2, and both AAC and aptX codecs. Neurable’s app is available on both Android and iOS.
