Fact-Checking What Donald Trump Said in His Latest Interview With TIME
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

On Sept. 28, about five weeks before Election Day, President Donald Trump sat down for an interview with TIME in the White House.
TIME has published the transcript of that conversation. Below is a review of some of Trump’s statements from the interview.
What Trump Said: “I won all seven swing states. They said if you won three swing states, I won all seven. I won the counties. It's very important, 86% popular vote.”
The Facts: Trump did win the popular vote in the 2024 presidential election, and he did win all seven swing states, but he’s conflating two figures. He won the popular vote by receiving 49.8% of the vote to Kamala Harris' 48.3%. He won the electoral college by 86 votes, 312 to Harris’s 226. He did not win all of the counties in the seven swing states, but he surprised many pundits by winning counties in the Detroit, Milwaukee and Philadelphia metro areas.
What Trump Said: “Their economy is gone. Their inflation is at 300% or something like that.”
The Facts: At the end of September, Iran’s Central Bank reported inflation at 83.8%, a slight decline from the month prior. The price of food in the country has skyrocketed, and Iran’s currency hit a record low, tumbling to 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar. At the end of 2025, the exchange rate was 1.2 million rials to the dollar.
What Trump Said: “I think the press fed it to them.”
The Facts: Trump was responding to being asked why many thought the war in Iran would be over in four to six weeks. Operation Epic Fury launched Feb. 28. In early March interviews, the President said the action would last four to five weeks.
What Trump Said: “We had more barrels of oil come through last night than at any time in the history of the Strait.”
The Facts: Various reports show about 20 million barrels of oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz daily before the war. On Sept. 26, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Fox News that there was a day last week “where over 20 million barrels of oil, more than pre-conflict levels, flowed out of the straits. The running average today is almost 13 million barrels a day.”
According to Oil & Gas Mideast, oil is flowing at about 13 million barrels per day, about 77% of pre-war levels.
What Trump Said: “They killed 75,000 people in the last number of months. Protesters…”
The Facts: Trump is referring to the killing of civilians by the Iranian regime during protests that began at the end of December 2025 and lasted until mid-January.
The protests began in Tehran after the country’s currency collapsed, and morphed into a widespread anti-regime movement that expanded across the country—until reaching its deadliest peak on Jan 8th and 9th. Iranian authorities responded to the protests by cutting off the internet and embarking on what is now considered the deadliest government crackdown by the Government of Iran since the 1979 Revolution.
The death toll was likely lower than Trump alleges—and the crackdown is believed to have reached its deadliest point earlier this year. Iran’s state run media has put the death toll at 3,117, while human rights organizations estimate it to be in the tens of thousands. At the end of January, two senior officials from Iran’s Ministry of Health told TIME that as many as 30,000 protesters could have been killed on Jan. 8th and 9th alone.
What Trump Said: “We're popular [in Israel], like 99%”
The Facts: A poll showing a 99% approval rating for Trump among Israelis does not exist, but he has polled well in Israel in the past. A 2026 Pew Research Center survey found “66% have confidence in Trump, while only a third or fewer have confidence in the other leaders.” A 2026 survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute found 73% of Israelis think of Trump as a better-than-average U.S. president for Israel’s interests, and 49% described him as one of the best U.S. presidents for Israel. However, the poll was sharply divided on party lines, with 92% of the Israeli right calling Trump an above-average president, but only 34% of the Israeli left had a positive view of Trump.
What Trump Said: “He [Biden] allowed 25 million people that shouldn't have been here.”
The Facts: There is no U.S. Customs and Border Protection data to back up this 25 million number, and there is a lack of definitive data on unauthorized immigrant numbers. The agency tracks encounters at ports of entry, instances of people being detained for trying to enter illegally or who were seeking legal entry but deemed ineligible. Between the start of the 2021 fiscal year through late 2024, the agency reported 10.8 million of these encounters. Pew Research Center has been publishing its own estimates of unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. for the last two decades and reported in 2025 that there were 14 million unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. in 2023—an all-time high.
What Trump said: “Look at the poverty numbers. The lowest we've had in…ever.”
The Facts: This is correct. According to the Census Bureau’s annual poverty report, the official poverty rate fell to 10.2%—the lowest on record since the agency began tracking in 1959. However, the bureau also publishes a supplementary poverty measure (SPM), created in 2009, which accounts for government benefits, like food stamps and housing subsidies, and has a more expansive view of poverty that considers whether a household has the resources for basic needs—like food, housing, clothes, and utilities. The SPM was at 13.1% in 2025, several percentage points above its all-time low of 7.7% in 2021.The Census Bureau’s report also relies on data from a survey conducted in March 2025—just three months into Trump’s presidency.
What Trump Said: “When I took over, I inherited the greatest inflation in history.”
The Facts: The Federal Reserve’s official inflation target for the U.S. economy is 2%. Towards the end of Trump’s first term, in Jan. 2020, the inflation rate was 2.5%. By the time his term ended that Dec., it was at 1.4%. Under Joe Biden, inflation reached a peak of 8% in 2022, the highest inflation the country had seen since 1980, when it hit 13.5%. However, by the end of Biden’s term, inflation dropped to 2.9%.
What Trump Said: “Look, we're building more automobile plants in the United States, and bigger ones, than we've ever built before.”
The Facts: Instead of building new factories, automakers appear to be largely adapting current ones.
General Motors has also announced plans to convert a number of internal combustion engine plants—located in Michigan, Tennessee, Ohio, and Kansas— to EV production as it moves to end the sale of gas-powered vehicles by 2035.
Hyundai announced that it will invest $5.8 billion in a steel plant in Louisiana to produce steel that will be used by Hyundai’s two existing U.S. auto plants.
Nissan has a target to reduce imports from Japan, aiming to produce 80% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. domestically by 2030. However, the company has no plans to open a new plant.
What Trump Said: “We did a convention that had 107 million views, and it stupidly was put opposite the NFL opening, and we got more views, they got 25 million, we got 107 [million].”
The Facts: The ratings tell a different story. Nielsen data showed that Trump’s approximately two-hour speech at the GOP midterm convention on Sep. 9 in Dallas averaged 2.5 million viewers on Fox News, the only major cable network to carry the speech in full. NBC said the Patriots-Seahawks NFL kickoff game averaged 25.1 million views.
What Trump Said: “We got more manufacturing jobs coming online than at any time in the history of our country.”
Manufacturing employment peaked in 1979 with 19.6 million jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. While 16,000 manufacturing jobs were added in August, the total number is 12.6 million, well below the 1979 peak.

Pentagon wants a hypersonic cruise missile for jets, ships and bombers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:56:30 UTC
19:56:30 KST

- DARPA issued a request for information on Sept. 30 for a Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile demonstrator, with responses now due Nov. 6.
- The agency wants an air-breathing missile that leaps ahead in range, speed or altitude and can be built affordably at high rates.
The Pentagon’s research agency DARPA is asking industry how to build a new hypersonic cruise missile that would fly much farther, faster or higher than current designs and could still be produced cheaply in large numbers.
DARPA’s Tactical Technology Office posted a request for information for the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile on Sept. 30 and later pushed the response deadline back a month, from Oct. 6 to Nov. 6. The agency says the answers will shape the requirements and acquisition plan for a possible competitive program whose goal is to design, build and flight-test a complete hypersonic cruise missile demonstrator. The notice is not a solicitation, and DARPA has not said how much the program could cost or when a first flight might take place.
A hypersonic cruise missile flies at more than five times the speed of sound using an air-breathing engine, usually a scramjet, that draws oxygen from the atmosphere instead of carrying it on board. DARPA says earlier demonstration programs have already proven that scramjet-powered flight works, but that existing concepts deliver only incremental gains and that legacy manufacturing makes them too expensive and complex to build at the scale a war with a major power would demand.
The agency wants a “revolutionary leap” in at least one of three areas, range, cruise speed or altitude, so the missile can strike targets defended by advanced air defense networks. It also wants the design built for easy manufacturing and assembly from the start, with a realistic path from a demonstrator to affordable, high-rate production.
DARPA is open to very different sizes of missile. The notice lists four broad classes: a weapon carried inside or under a fighter jet for quick response, one sized for a bomber’s internal bay, cargo-aircraft pallets or a ship’s vertical launch tubes, a larger missile carried under a heavy bomber, and a large ground-launched version for strategic missions that would make the most of an air-breathing engine’s range at bigger scales.
The request covers three areas for industry. One asks for overall missile concepts and a fast plan for reaching a first flight. Another seeks high-risk technologies such as new engines, high-energy fuels, boosters, heat-resistant materials and cooling systems, and DARPA says it is not interested in modernization or incremental improvements. A third asks for new ways to test hypersonic weapons, which is one of the slowest and most expensive parts of any program. DARPA is running its own studies on the missile’s operational use in parallel.
The testing section stands out. DARPA wants flight test methods that can cover distances of 250 to 2,000 nautical miles (460 to 3,700 km), reduce reliance on traditional test ranges so programs can test on demand, and give off fewer signs that a test is about to happen. It asks for autonomous telemetry, tracking and data systems that could be based on the surface, underwater, in the air or in space.
DARPA is encouraging companies outside the traditional defense industry to respond, particularly on the technology and testing questions, and to form teams with established contractors. The agency’s earlier Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept program flight-tested scramjet-powered designs from Raytheon, Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin and fed into the U.S. Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile program.

The left-wing Die Linke party, which won Berlin’s election about two weeks ago, is facing growing scrutiny over its ties to figures linked to Arab crime families in the German capital, as well as antisemitic and anti-Israel activists. Now, questions are also being raised about Elif Eralp, the party’s candidate for mayor, and her involvement in a group that Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has described as one of the country’s most important far-left organizations.
Warning signs emerged on election night, when Issa Remmo, head of Berlin’s largest crime clan, attended the party’s victory celebration in the immigrant-heavy district of Neukölln. Remmo said the party had finally given him a sense of political belonging. Ibrahim Ibrahim, a representative of an umbrella organization linked to Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine in Germany, was also present.
The party sought to distance itself from the two men, but the Remmo clan later publicly released messages between its members and Die Linke lawmakers who had asked the family to distribute campaign material on their behalf.
It has now emerged that until a year ago, Eralp was a member of the organization Red Aid, whose motto is “the end justifies the means.” The group provides legal and financial support to offenders as long as their crimes were committed in pursuit of left-wing political causes.
Many Germans had already raised concerns over the party’s ties to crime clans and its calls to reduce police funding and presence. Some voters are now questioning whether Eralp’s past in an organization seen as supporting violence, or turning a blind eye to violations of the law in pursuit of its goals, could undermine her ability to serve as Berlin’s democratic, law-abiding leader.
While a left-wing coalition involving the Greens, Die Linke and the Social Democrats is beginning to take shape in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a similar coalition in Berlin, though mathematically possible, appears increasingly remote. Many Social Democrats and Greens have warned against opening coalition talks with Die Linke.
Once again, the party is giving potential coalition partners reasons to keep their distance.
It was revealed this week that representatives of the Barbak clan were also present at Die Linke’s victory party in Neukölln, where the party won 31% of the vote, compared with 25.7% citywide.
The clan arrived in Berlin from Khan Younis in recent years and now numbers more than 130 family members, most of them living in Neukölln.
Unlike the Remmo clan, the Barbak family is not considered heavily involved in conventional criminal activity. Its members are primarily involved in organizing anti-Israel demonstrations, supporting Hamas and its military wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, disseminating inflammatory messages, spray-painting red triangles associated with Hamas on walls across the city and sharing extremist Islamist content on social media.
According to police, the family’s activities, violence by some of its members against officers, calls for Israel’s destruction and attacks on Jews, as well as efforts directed against Germany’s constitution and democratic order, have led intelligence agencies to place many of its members under surveillance.
Despite this, two representatives of the family not only attended Die Linke’s victory celebration but also interviewed senior party officials and filmed them on video.
“We express full solidarity with the Barbak family,” wrote the Palestine Solidarity group, which is affiliated with the party.
The group also wrote on its Instagram account that “the Palestinian resistance will not stop until Tel Aviv is Palestinian. Solidarity with Palestine is not a crime.”
Meanwhile, Jewish and Israeli activists in Germany are continuing efforts to provide Eralp with a degree of public legitimacy in response to warnings from numerous Jewish institutions and public figures against including her in a coalition because of manifestations of antisemitism within the party.
After 150 Israeli and Jewish artists and cultural figures signed a letter supporting the party, Eralp visited a solidarity sukkah organized by the group Israelis for Peace on Monday.
She delivered remarks there with sukkah decorations behind her bearing slogans including “Israelis against genocide” and “Germany, impose sanctions on Israel now.”

Surviving the execution chamber: Five US cases before Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:33:11 UTC
19:33:11 KST

Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, has survived an execution attempt after receiving two injections of a lethal drug.
Her lawyers said on Thursday that she was being treated in hospital, while Governor Bill Lee suspended executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review.
Pike’s case is not the first in which a prisoner has left the execution chamber alive in the United States. Previous failed attempts have ended with prisoners later executed, sometimes using a different method, or dying in custody before another attempt.
Surviving an execution attempt does not automatically overturn a death sentence. US courts have permitted authorities to try again, including in a 2016 Ohio Supreme Court ruling that a second attempt was not inherently barred by the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
Here are five earlier cases and what followed.
Tony Carruthers: Two failed executions, one doctor
Tennessee halted its attempt to execute Tony Carruthers on May 21 2026, after staff were unable to establish the intravenous access required by the state’s lethal injection protocol.
The physician involved was Dr Mark Fowler, who was later selected to oversee Pike’s execution and administer her lethal injection, according to NPR. Tennessee-based broadcaster WVLT subsequently reported that the same doctor administered the injection that Pike survived.
In Carruthers’ case, officials said medical personnel secured a primary IV line but could not establish a backup. An attempt to insert a central line also failed.
Carruthers, sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of three people in 1994, was returned to his cell after officials spent more than an hour attempting the procedure, according to Reuters report.
Governor Bill Lee then granted him a one-year reprieve, postponing his execution without commuting his death sentence.
Kenneth Eugene Smith: Executed with nitrogen after surviving lethal injection
Alabama’s first attempt to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith in 2022 was abandoned after officials were unable to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
Smith spent about four hours strapped to a gurney as legal challenges played out and staff repeatedly tried to access his veins, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
His lawyers later argued that a second execution attempt would violate the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment, but the US Supreme Court declined to stop it.
On January 25 2024, Alabama executed Smith, this time using nitrogen gas. Smith, 58, became the first person executed using the method, breathing pure nitrogen through a mask that deprived him of oxygen.
The execution lasted about 22 minutes, and Smith appeared to remain conscious for several minutes.
Alan Eugene Miller: A second attempt using a different method
Alabama’s attempt to execute Alan Eugene Miller by lethal injection in September 2022 failed after difficulties accessing his veins. A federal judge subsequently ordered the state to preserve evidence relating to the aborted procedure.
On September 26 2024, Alabama executed him using nitrogen gas, making him the second person put to death by that method.
Witnesses reported that he shook, pulled against his restraints and gasped for several minutes. Alabama’s corrections commissioner said the movements were involuntary and that the execution had proceeded as planned.
Miller had been sentenced to death for killing three men in workplace shootings in 1999.
Doyle Lee Hamm: A bloodied execution chamber and a deal preventing another attempt
Alabama abandoned its attempt to execute Doyle Lee Hamm in February 2018, after about two and a half hours of unsuccessful efforts to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
The procedure left Hamm, then 61, with at least 12 puncture wounds and the execution chamber bloodied, his lawyer, Columbia Law School professor Bernard Harcourt, said, according to a 2018 Reuters report. Medical personnel had tried to access veins in his groin and lower legs.
His lawyers had warned that terminal cancer and a history of intravenous drug use had severely compromised his veins. Alabama maintained that it could carry out the procedure, but stopped when officials determined the difficulties could not be resolved before the death warrant expired at midnight.
A federal judge subsequently ordered the state to preserve evidence, including Hamm’s clothing.
In March 2018, Hamm and Alabama reached a confidential settlement preventing further execution attempts, according to Harcourt.
Hamm remained on death row and died in November 2021 after suffering from cancer. It was the agreement, rather than an automatic legal exemption for surviving the first attempt, that prevented another execution attempt.
Romell Broom: Courts allowed another attempt, but he died before it could take place
Ohio stopped Romell Broom’s execution on September 15 2009, after staff spent about two hours trying unsuccessfully to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
Broom challenged the state’s right to try again, arguing that another attempt would violate constitutional protections against being punished twice for the same crime and against cruel and unusual punishment.
In 2016, the Ohio Supreme Court rejected his challenge in a 4–3 decision, noting that no lethal drugs had been administered during the first attempt.
His execution was eventually rescheduled for March 2022 after a shortage of execution drugs forced another postponement.
But Broom died in custody on December 28 2020, aged 64, before another attempt could take place. Prison authorities said he was suspected to have died from complications of COVID-19, pending confirmation.

Bolivia arrests attorney general accused by U.S. of drug cartel ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:31:46 UTC
19:31:46 KST

Bolivian attorney general blacklisted by U.S. is arrested for alleged money laundering and drug trafficking
Bolivia's attorney general arrested for alleged money laundering and drug trafficking
U.S.-sanctioned Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca has been arrested on suspicion of money laundering and drug trafficking, with police finding bundles of cash smuggled out of his house, the government said Thursday.
Mariaca was arrested on Wednesday night in the eastern city of Santa Cruz, two days after the United States revoked his visa due to his alleged links to drug trafficking.
"A criminal organization entrenched in the justice system has been dismantled," Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo told a press conference.
Oviedo said that in the early hours of Thursday, four people were caught trying to remove bundles of cash from Mariaca's house aboard an ambulance.
A video released by the interior ministry showed police removing wads of cash from the ambulance's panels.
Oviedo said that the Attorney General's Office, "headed by Roger Mariaca, became a criminal organization dedicated to protecting, encouraging, and safeguarding narco-terrorism."
According to the Reuters news agency, a prosecutor's office official reported the "abduction" of Mariaca during a live broadcast. Local media said Mariaca had been detained at Viru Viru International Airport, Reuters reported.
The U.S. State Department said Monday that Mariaca received "bribes to facilitate drug trafficking and help violent criminals evade justice." Mariaca has denied the allegations.
Oviedo said that Mariaca's arrest took place with the "cooperation of the U.S. government" as part of the "fight against terrorism."
In total, four prosecutors, six employees of the public prosecutor's office and the four people found aboard the ambulance were arrested.
The raids come as Bolivia's center-right President Rodrigo Paz, who took office in November 2025, seeks to strengthen ties with the United States after two decades of socialist rule marked by mutual enmity.
On Monday, the U.S. revoked the visas of 12 Bolivian officials and nine other Bolivian nationals who do not currently have visas were rendered ineligible to receive them.
 In March, Paz took Bolivia into the "Shield of the Americas," a U.S.-led alliance of right-wing Latin American governments to combat transnational organized crime.
 
"Mariaca is my friend"
Mariaca was appointed attorney general in October 2024.
The Attorney General's Office stated in a press release that, given Mariaca's "definitive absence," the next most senior public prosecutor, Luis Montano Morales, would replace him on an interim basis.
Mariaca's lawyer Romel Ipamo told local media that his client would "cooperate fully" with the investigation.
During Mariaca's tenure, Bolivian police captured Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastian Marset earlier this year. Marset, who was on the U.S.' most-wanted fugitives list, was passed to agents of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration at the Santa Cruz airport, then put on a U.S. airplane, state TV showed. In March, he made his first appearance in a federal court in Virginia.
Local media on Wednesday broadcast a video purporting to show Marset on the day of his arrest declaring: "Mariaca is my friend."
AFP has been unable to verify the authenticity of the video.
Police also raided the headquarters of the public prosecutor's office in the southern city of Sucre, according to footage shared by the police on social media.
Surrounded by hooded police officers, Claudia Pardo, head of communications for the prosecutor's office, denounced the raid as "illegal."
She told AFP later that she was under arrest.
 The public prosecutor's offices in Santa Cruz and La Paz were also targeted in the nationwide raids, according to images broadcast by local media.

'We didn’t think for even a second about our own lives': Flydubai heroes adjust to new reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:31:42 UTC
19:31:42 KST

Dr. Shota Musaev, the dentist who treated the wounded Indian captain aboard the Flydubai flight targeted in an attempted hijacking, said Thursday that his medical instincts — and the example set by his late parents — guided him as passengers fought to save the aircraft.
“I come from a family of doctors. My late father was a cardiologist and my late mother was a biologist, so I knew what to do when I was faced with the injured pilot,” Musaev, 47, said at his home in Rishon Lezion, south of Tel Aviv.
Musaev was among a group of Israeli passengers who intervened during Wednesday’s dramatic flight to Tel Aviv after the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to crash the aircraft. He said he saw three Israelis — Yaniv Hayun, Zvika Manes and Assaf Rajuan — rush the co-pilot and realized he had to help.
“My wife initially tried to stop me, but I saw there were heroes there and I joined them,” Musaev said. “At that moment, we didn’t think for even a second about our own lives or what might happen to us. We thought about how to save the entire plane.”
Musaev, who owns a dental clinic in Holon and was born in Georgia, helped restrain the suspected attacker before turning his attention to the wounded captain, Smit Machchhar.
“The captain told me he wanted to live and didn’t want to die there,” Musaev said. “There were moments when I thought we wouldn’t manage to land in time because he was bleeding heavily, but after we stopped the bleeding, his condition stabilized.”
Musaev said a series of chance events played a role in preventing a disaster, including a child going to the bathroom at a critical moment, the passengers who rushed the cockpit and additional pilots who happened to be aboard.
He said he now considers Hayun, Manes and Rajuan members of his family.
“I wrote in the WhatsApp group we created after the incident that all of us were born again yesterday,” he said. “We went through a historic event and even landed in Saudi Arabia.”
Passengers praise treatment in Saudi Arabia
The aircraft made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where Musaev said passengers were treated well.
“There was some chaos after landing because the children were under a lot of stress,” he said. “Even very senior officials came and spoke with us, and they assigned doctors to us who made sure everything was OK.”
The Israeli passengers then faced another difficult decision: whether to board another Flydubai aircraft for the trip home to Ben Gurion Airport.
Musaev favored returning on the airline despite what had happened.
“I spoke with a very senior official and with the manager of the local airport,” he said. “I was on the side that said we should get on the flight, mainly because you can’t fly only on Israeli airlines. Despite the serious incident we experienced with Flydubai, you can’t simply rule them out.”
He said passengers ultimately made the decision together after learning that an Israeli aircraft would not be allowed to land there.
“I told everyone we needed to get on,” he said. “We told the parents with children that they would decide what we did, and in the end, when they said they wouldn’t allow an Israeli plane to land there, we made the decision together and boarded.”
Musaev said he took several girls into the cockpit to meet the pilots before the flight home.
Back with his wife and children Thursday, he said the enormity of what happened was only beginning to sink in.
“We’re emotional to be with them again and are starting to understand more deeply that we’re alive,” he said.
Musaev stressed that saving the plane had been a collective effort.
“The act of heroism was something we did together,” he said. “I tied up the terrorist pilot and then treated the other pilot. But the other three were the ones who entered the cockpit and neutralized the terrorist. Others took care of the children on the plane. We did everything together, hand in hand.”
‘I’m an upgraded plumber’
Hayun, 38, of Ness Ziona, helped stabilize the aircraft as the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to disable the instrument panel.
On Thursday, Hayun responded to remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump, who described him as an Israeli plumber who had never flown a plane and rarely traveled by air but saw what was happening and intervened.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun joked. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with stinking pipes, and he was right. I wasn’t offended.”
Hayun said he never imagined the U.S. president would talk about him.
“I never dreamed Trump would talk about me and what I did. I actually like his sense of humor,” he said. “It was amusing how he described it. I’m not exactly Bruce Lee. But I did manage to overpower the terrorist with a few other Israelis and pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Hayun said he had not slept since the ordeal.
“I just want to get back to my routine now, to work, to my truck,” he said. “I’m getting so much love and I thank everyone — everyone who was on that flight, who worked hand in hand and helped us get our lives back because they were hanging by a thread. I hope it doesn’t come back to me in my dreams.”
Herzog recommends civilian bravery awards
President Isaac Herzog spoke with the passengers who intervened and said he would recommend that Musaev, Hayun, Manes and Rajuan receive the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism, Israel’s highest civilian bravery award.
“At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness and extraordinary mutual responsibility,” Herzog told them. “You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster.”
“Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society,” he added. “I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”
Herzog said he would bring their actions before the advisory committee responsible for the award and recommend that they receive the honor.
The president also praised the Indian captain, who fought the co-pilot and opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene.
Herzog later recommended Tali Manes, Zvika Manes’ wife, for the same civilian bravery award after further accounts indicated she played a crucial role in alerting passengers to the danger.
According to the President’s Residence, Manes heard violence and commotion coming from the cockpit and was the first to alert other passengers and call for help, prompting those who ultimately rushed in and subdued the suspected attacker.
After he was restrained, she continued to act, calling pilots who were traveling in the rear of the aircraft to come forward and help restore control of the plane.
“Tali, the more we learn about what happened in those dramatic moments, the clearer it becomes how significant a part you played in saving the lives of the passengers,” Herzog told her.
“You heard that something terrible was happening, immediately understood the scale of the danger, raised the alarm, called for help, and did not stop acting even after the attacker had been subdued,” he said. “The resourcefulness, responsibility, and composure you showed in moments of mortal danger are civilian heroism in the fullest sense of the word. You are a hero, Tali, and I am proud of you and thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”

Why the U.S. Must Simultaneously Compete—and Cooperate—With China on AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:30:03 UTC
19:30:03 KST

Last week, President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. It's their second meeting this year, following the May summit in Beijing. This visit, the stakes were even higher.
We have learned about security incidents from nearly every major AI company, American and Chinese, built on both open and closed models. The leading AI labs are openly debating whether to pace their frontier model development, and the government is working out what role it plays in that decision.
I spent four years as Secretary of Commerce focused intently on America’s economic, technological, and security competition with China—instituting first-of-its-kind export controls on the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China to protect our national security, and leading implementation of the CHIPS Act to onshore chip manufacturing. I also created the AI Safety Institute so we could accelerate our AI development responsibly and safely. I have sat across the table from China, and I have an understanding of how they think about AI.
I believe AI companies are right to want to pace the frontier. But we need to stay ahead of China while we pace, because a world where China leads the global AI competition threatens America’s interests.
The challenge is this: We need to outcompete China on the technology itself, while also working with China on addressing the risks posed by AI. Competition and cooperation are often in tension, but the stakes are too high in this case to pick only one.
How we cooperate—while staying ahead
China has its own reasons to take AI safety seriously. The Chinese Minister of State Security recently said publicly that the greatest risk advanced AI poses to China is the risk it poses to the stability of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Beijing is no more interested in powerful AI systems wreaking socio-political havoc than Washington is; both countries have incentives to align on certain safety standards or even just a shared understanding of AI risks. It is in neither country’s interest for companies to lose control of their AI systems or for AI to be used to create bioweapons by rogue actors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement of a possible AI dialogue with Chinese counterparts after his meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng is a tangible sign that China sees at least some space for cooperation here.
I would argue that now is the moment to fully establish that dialogue and keep the momentum going. We should do this by convening experts from both countries. I’m well aware that we’d be foolish to trust People's Republic of China (PRC) leaders. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t try. It just means we need to develop verification mechanisms to ensure agreements work even in the absence of trust.
Even if we don’t reach agreement on a shared set of standards, starting a dialogue and opening those lines of communication are critical—just as we did in 2008 during the financial crisis, when it was in our mutual benefit to coordinate. And we spent decades during the Cold War in careful, ongoing dialogue with the Soviet Union about nuclear arms control because the risks to both countries were enormous. During that time we developed zero-trust methods to verify arms control agreements even while locked in an adversarial relationship.
None of that changes the need to vigilantly and continuously update our controls as technology changes so China can’t access our most sophisticated compute in ways that threaten our national security. That includes continuously updating our export controls on leading-edge chips, addressing the risks of China accessing controlled compute remotely in data centers around the world, and cracking down on diversion of technology that is controlled.
We also need to tighten remaining gaps in our semiconductor manufacturing equipment controls so China can less capably obtain tools to manufacture powerful chips at scale and service their pre-existing equipment. That work has to happen with our Dutch, Japanese, and German allies and partners who manufacture and service this chipmaking equipment.
American AI
Finally, the U.S. government should put a greater burden on the AI companies to take adversarial distillation much more seriously. Distillation—coordinated, industrial-scale efforts by AI labs to train their weaker models on the outputs of frontier models—has become a significant issue in the past year. Anthropic has attributed more than 16 million Claude exchanges to distillation campaigns, and has estimated that over 3 million of these distillation campaigns can be traced back to China’s Moonshot AI (the company behind China’s version of ChatGPT, Kimi) along with other Chinese AI labs like Alibaba and DeepSeek. Moonshot, for instance, was later caught forwarding user prompts to Claude to answer and feeding those answers back through Kimi.
China has certainly indigenized much of its AI stack, something Xi publicly made a priority in his Made in China 2025 plan, many years before the U.S. government was talking openly about chips or models. And China has made progress on this plan. But it is clear to many that China’s most competitive models, to some degree, are ripping off American ones. American AI labs should be allocating even greater amounts of their money and compute towards finding and exposing this kind of activity so that policymakers—and the public—can adapt accordingly.
The risks and benefits of AI are enormous, something more and more Americans have come to realize as AI advances more quickly than we previously thought possible. There is much to do on AI safety at home, to ensure our society and economy are resilient to the dramatic changes AI will bring. But I also know that safe deployment of AI is only possible if we successfully manage our relationship with China—both by maintaining our technological lead and working towards collaboration.

19:30:00 KST

Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for New York governor, promised last November to erect a wall of spy gear, license plate readers, and biometric surveillance between the city and the suburbs. He has since received millions of dollars in donations from the family and businesses of James Dolan, the owner of Madison Square Garden, where a network of cameras capture the faces of (nearly) every patron who walks in the arena and corporate security forces hunt for critics of the boss.
Dolan’s support of Blakeman, the executive of suburban Nassau County, could be seen as something of a counterintuitive move in a state long run by Democrats, and in a year when political surveys are picking up indications of a blue wave. He’s down by nine points or more in most polls.
Blakeman, however, backs data centers, AI deepfakes, Flock surveillance, ICE, private militias, and president Donald Trump. All of which makes him at least somewhat simpatico with Dolan, the Trump-allied magnate operating the sports world’s best-known surveillance state. Dolan has long been a mercurial presence in the political game, and in fact, as Politico notes, he supported Blakeman’s opponent, Governor Kathy Hochul, during the last election. Dolan’s sheer amount of spending in the race could also benefit him, even if his preferred candidate loses.
Long an outsized force in sports and entertainment, Dolan now has a chance at a major political role, too.
“Dolan can step into the breach and become the biggest player in [New York’s] Republican politics, donor-wise, and I'm sure his people are smart enough to know that,” one veteran strategist tells WIRED.
James Dolan has given heavily before, including nearly a million dollars to Trump’s reelection campaign and the Republican National Committee in the 2020 election cycle. But the New York governor’s race represents another level, a review of city, state, and federal databases shows.
The Dolan family has given $108,000 to Blakeman’s campaign directly and another $970,000 to the local Nassau County Republican party, which in turn has become Blakeman’s single-largest contributor. But that’s just for starters. MSG entities have contributed another $2 million to a political action committee supporting Blakeman’s run. That super PAC, Strong and Safe New York Inc., which lists Madison Square Garden’s top government relations executive as an officer, has raised $5.3 million overall. That helped make up for a 9-to-1 cash advantage that the governor’s campaign reported over her challenger’s at the last filing deadline in July.
Dolan and MSG’s bankrolling of Blakeman could come with risks, however. Opposition to Dolan’s use of facial recognition has hit a new peak locally, where a majority of the City Council are now in favor of a bill to rein in biometric surveillance. State lawmakers introduced a bill to end the property tax break that has been worth over a billion dollars to Madison Square Garden. The federal government has agreed to take over the $8 billion renovation of the train station below Madison Square Garden—a project that could pay Dolan’s company $500 million or more. But multiple sources note that state and local authorities will likely continue to have a say.
Meanwhile, the New York attorney general’s investigation into MSG’s deployment of facial recognition continues to progress, a source familiar with the matter tells WIRED. And while mayor Zohran Mamdani’s critiques of Dolan’s security practices have been muted, so far, there are signs that may be changing. One of his commissioners said last month that “this kind of mass surveillance opens the door to abuse and discrimination.”
(Madison Square Garden, which did not respond to a request to comment for this story, filed a defamation suit in July against WIRED and this reporter over our coverage of its operations.)
Dolan’s friction with state and local officials is coming at what should be a peak moment for the mogul: the long-suffering basketball team he owns, the New York Knicks, recently won their first title in 53 years. And yet, during the Knicks’ run in the NBA Finals, his organization fought with the mayor and the police commissioner over security procedures around the Garden. In the days leading up to the championship parade down Broadway, a source with knowledge of the preparations tells WIRED, Dolan’s team tussled with the governor’s and the mayor’s for control over the event, particularly over who got to be on stage and in the audience as the players were presented with keys to the city at City Hall.
“Dolan micromanaged the Knicks parade like it was his own sweet sixteen,” the source tells WIRED.
Dolan and Blakeman, on the other hand, have in recent years demonstrated a host of common interests, common enemies, and one extremely prominent mutual friend. In June, Trump came to the Garden for game three of the Finals; Blakeman joined the president of the United States and the team’s owner in the luxury box. Two months later, in mid-August, Strong and Safe New York released an ad calling on Hochul to stop blaming the state’s problems on Trump. (Strong and Safe, which is also supporting James’ opponent in the attorney general’s race this year, recently sent $83,400 to her former employers, the Republican law firm behind Kanye West’s presidential bid in 2020.)
Blakeman has been one of the state’s most enthusiastic implementers of Trump’s mass deportation machine, ordering local detectives to work with ICE and opening up the county’s jails for those caught up in the crackdown. (Less than 5 percent of the immigrants jailed had violent criminal records, a Newsday investigation found.) He recruited dozens of armed “special deputies,” which looked a whole lot like a personal militia to critics. And when Mamdani won his New York mayoral election last November, Blakeman promised to erect a wall of surveillance along the city line to keep suburban residents safe. “We are installing technology along the border of New York City that will read license plates, that will have facial recognition, that will have video cameras,” he told Fox News. Since then, drivers in Nassau County have become some of the most surveilled in the nation, with a Flock Safety camera for every 9.5 miles of road, according to the DeFlock activist group.
Dolan has been aggressive in his deployment of surveillance at his venues, which include the Sphere in Las Vegas and Radio City Music Hall in Manhattan. Arrays of surveillance security cameras tied to a video management system running a facial recognition program are a major reason why MSG “is the most secure venue in the country,” Dolan has previously said.
“They’re in the same mindset that surveillance is good for business,” Brad Hoylman-Sigal, the Manhattan borough president, says of Blakeman and Dolan. “And I don’t know how that's a winning political issue.”
For the majority of more than three decades in politics, Blakeman presented himself as a moderate as he launched unsuccessful bids for state comptroller, US House and Senate seats, and even New York City mayor. Then in 2021, Blakeman went full MAGA, and won his Nassau County Executive race by 2,000 votes. He’s been tied to Trump and the Trumpists ever since, starting with an all-out push behind MAGA megadonor Miriam Adelson’s multibillion plan to build a casino on the site of the Nassau Coliseum. The bid was ultimately withdrawn.
Hochul’s recent political journey has gone in something like the opposite direction. Once considered a conservative Democrat, she’s become a vocal Trump critic; passed a law banning local cops from cooperating with ICE (a move Blakeman said was “written with the blood of the victims of illegal migrants,” before reluctantly complying with it; and put in place the country’s first statewide data center moratorium (Blakeman called that “crazy,” while using AI to lampoon Hochul in his TV spots).
Dolan largely stayed out of last year’s mayor’s race. But an MSG political action committee, the Coalition to Restore New York, dumped more than $400,000 into 11 local City Council races. Seven of them won, and all but one lined up to support Julie Menin as City Council president, who was seen as a check on Mamdani’s power.
Menin now holds the power to bring the Council’s bill curbing facial recognition to a vote—or to let it die without one. Menin, who returned a Dolan donation in 2023, is currently undecided on how to proceed, the veteran strategist tells me. “She doesn't want to ban facial recognition”—and to be clear, the bill in the Council doesn’t aim to do that. “She thinks that it should be reformed, and that there should be guardrails and parameters,” the strategist says. (A Menin spokesperson did not reply to a request for comment.)
One longtime outside counsel for MSG has filed a flurry of lawsuits against the Mamdani administration, while a second former outside attorney has raised a million dollars for a political organization to counter the mayor’s agenda. John Catsimatidis, a billionaire Republican donor, indicated to Politico that Dolan’s backing of Blakeman could be seen as a move against Mamdani, of sorts. “Everybody believes the governor has oversight of the mayor,” he said. (Representatives for both the Hochul and Blakeman campaigns did not respond to requests to comment for this story. Neither did a City Hall spokesperson. But Mamdani did say on Monday that a candidate "who embraces ICE and has gone so far as to create, effectively, a private militia in Nassau County” is “in many ways the antithesis” of what New Yorkers want.)
The governor is not without her own well-funded allies, however. That includes Blakeman’s ex-wife Nancy Shevell, who’s now married to Paul McCartney. She donated $18,000 to Hochul. The Pegula family, which owns the NFL’s Buffalo Bills, has given her and the state Democratic Party nearly $175,000. (A small sum to pay, considering Hochul helped steer $600 million in state money into her hometown team’s new stadium.) Uber spent more than $12 million in a six-month period to a PAC supporting Hochul, who has proposed auto insurance reforms that the ride-share giant likes.
That’s way more than Dolan has devoted to his candidate so far. But what he has given appears to be the most money a Dolan-backed business has devoted to a political cause since it spent an estimated $30 million in 2004 to stop a football stadium from being built on Manhattan’s west side, a signature project by the mayor at the time, Michael Bloomberg. Dolan’s push was so effective, it caused the mayor to sputter in public. “You’d think,” the mayor fumed on his radio program, that “a company on corporate welfare would be less selfish to the city that has been so good to it.”
For that campaign, Dolan’s firm funded an outfit called the “New York Association for Better Choices,” which took out full-page ads in every city newspaper, ran anti-stadium commercials on local TV, and counted the lobbying firm of a former US senator as one of its many advocates. For this election, Dolan’s chosen candidate is relying heavily on AI. Blakeman’s ads featuring ersatz Hochuls hiding behind dumpsters, getting clowned by Mamdani, and producing BS. One recent anti-Hochul spot lifted footage from a comedian’s bit—shot in 2011 and criticizing the Republican leader of Wisconsin at the time. “Bruce Blakeman,” the progressive local news outlet Hell Gate proclaimed, “is the governor of slop.”

Czechia to Reduce Troop Presence on NATO’s Eastern Flank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:25:31 UTC
19:25:31 KST

The Czech Senate has approved a lower cap on the number of troops the country can deploy to defend NATO’s eastern flank in 2027–2028.
According to a Czech Senate document, the new limit will be 1,600 troops – 400 fewer than the current limit.
Czech Defence Minister Jaromír Zůna said the reduction was driven by cost savings and the fact that Czechia had not previously used the full troop limit.
According to government data, 427 Czech troops were deployed in Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Slovakia in May 2026.
The new plan would allow Czech troops to be deployed not only to Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Slovakia, but also to Estonia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Finland.
Their deployment will depend on NATO’s needs.
Overall, the Czech Republic plans to reduce the maximum number of troops it can deploy on overseas missions from 2,571 in 2026 to 2,091 in 2027 and 2,066 in 2028.
Meanwhile, the government emphasizes that the number of Czech troops assigned to NATO forces will increase.
The Senate’s decision still needs to be approved by the Chamber of Deputies. The new mandate will take effect on January 1, 2027, and remain in force until the end of 2028.
Militarnyi previously reported that Czech AH-1Z attack helicopters had been deployed to patrol the airspace near the Polish-Belarusian border.
The deployment of the new Czech helicopters to Poland was announced in March 2026, when the Czech government approved sending UH-1Y utility helicopters there.

Archeologists unearth a ‘major’ early Christian monastery in Scotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:14:34 UTC
19:14:34 KST

The earliest days of Christianity are hazy—relatively few written records survive from this era, and religious artifacts are rare archaeological finds. Still, a newly discovered early Christian monastery, dating to just six centuries after the religion got its start, could offer clues to how the faith spread across the world.
In a new study published this week in the journal Antiquity, researchers describe how a group of historians helped discover the early medieval monastery in a stroke of good luck.
The site is situated on the island of Lismore and is believed to have been founded by Saint Mo Luóc, an early Christian saint also known as Moluag. Researchers had long suspected Mo Luóc’s monastery was there but hadn’t been able to prove it until the local Lismore Historical Society led an excavation in the area, which also holds the ruins of a 13th-century cathedral.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
With the help of professional archaeologists, the historians uncovered ancient grave sites, buildings, pieces of sculpture and extensive evidence of craft workshops at the site.
Gordon Noble, the paper’s senior author and an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen in Scotland, says that the evidence of craftworking is particularly exciting. The team found hundreds of clay molds and crucibles used for working bronze, silver and gold—a somewhat “unusual” find for a monastery, Noble says.
“It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he says.
Overall, the size of the monastery suggests Lismore, which lies on Loch Linnhe on Scotland’s west coast, was likely more important to medieval Christian society than previously realized, he says.
Other sites are known to have played a major role. For example, the island of Iona, to the southwest of Lismore in Scotland, is known for being the “Cradle of Christianity.” But the new findings suggest Lismore was “a very significant mover and shaker” in the spread of the early religion, Noble says.
Noble and his colleagues plan to keep investigating the site, including an analysis of the monastery’s “vallum,” or outer boundary, often indicated by a wall or bank.
The entire monastery appears to have been “huge,” Noble says. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”

UK Suspects Iran of Involvement in Planned Terror Attack Near Fairford Air Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:02:28 UTC
19:02:28 KST

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are indications of Iranian involvement in the suspected preparation of a terrorist attack near RAF Fairford air base.
He made the remarks to Sky News while commenting on the investigation into five men detained near the base in Gloucestershire.
The Prime Minister also said he chaired a COBRAgovernment committee meeting on Monday over the incident. According to him, there is currently no need to urgently recall Parliament, but he is prepared to do so if the situation requires it.
“This remains a complex and very serious police investigation, so at this stage I cannot say anything more,” Burnham said.
As Militarnyi previously reported, on September 27, British police detained five men aged between 23 and 25 after receiving a report about three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford.
All five men are British citizens and residents of London. They were arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
Following questioning, all five were released on bail. However, they remain under investigation and are subject to restrictions on their movements and contacts.
Initially, bomb disposal experts worked near the vehicles, and around 85 households in the area were evacuated due to the potential danger. Later, after a detailed examination of the three vans, police clarified that no improvised explosive devices were found, although a quantity of petrol was discovered.
Even before the Prime Minister’s statement, counter-terrorism police said they were considering several lines of inquiry, including the possibility that the detainees may have acted as intermediaries or proxies on behalf of a foreign state, either knowingly or unknowingly. At the time, no specific country was officially named.
The Iranian Embassy in the UK rejected reports of possible Tehran involvement, calling them baseless. Following Burnham’s statement, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied the allegations.
RAF Fairford is one of the key air bases in the UK and is also used by U.S. military aircraft, including those that have been involved in strikes on Iranian territory.
Amid the investigation, U.S. Ambassador to the UK Warren Stephens separately highlighted the cooperation between U.S. and British authorities in the case.

Green tree ants are famous in the tropics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

Green tree ants (Oecophylla smaragdina) are plentiful in tropical forests from India to northern Australia. And, as this short from the science documentary series Deep Look details, their dominance has spawned quite a few imitators. With close-up looks at four of these copycats – one insect and three spiders – the video explores how each has evolved to resemble the ants in appearance, behaviour and even smell. Some leverage the ants’ reputation as fierce fighters to avoid being eaten themselves; others use their disguise to get close enough to make a meal of the ants and their young. While some disguises are more convincing than others, each is good enough to provide an evolutionary advantage that allows these creatures to reap the benefits of the green tree ant’s success.

Lower cognitive ability is linked to stronger Christian nationalist views, even after accounting for education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

A new study indicates that Americans with lower scores on a vocabulary test commonly used to measure cognitive ability are more likely to endorse Christian nationalist beliefs, even when accounting for their overall level of education. The findings suggest that the appeal of this political and religious ideology relates to underlying cognitive resources rather than just differences in schooling. The research was published in Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion.
The research, conducted by Samuel L. Perry, the Sam K. Viersen Presidential Professor of Sociology at the University of Oklahoma and currently a visiting scholar at the Russell Sage Foundation, explores the individual characteristics associated with Christian nationalism. Christian nationalism is a set of beliefs asserting that the United States has conservative Christian foundations. The ideology promotes the idea that the government should institutionalize Christian dominance in American society, often merging religious identity with civic belonging.
“One of the most consistent predictors that Americans adhere to Christian nationalism is that they have lower education,” Perry told PsyPost. “But there have also been a number of studies that find that persons who subscribe to Christian nationalist views (even after accounting for level of education) exhibit significant knowledge gaps across a variety of different domains.”
For example, people who strongly endorse the ideology tend to score poorly on tests about “American history or scientific knowledge,” Perry noted. “They are also more likely to hold factually incorrect beliefs about vaccines,” he said, referencing a 2021 study he co-authored, which was covered by PsyPost. “And related to that last point, they are also more likely to affirm ridiculous conspiracy theories related to COVID-19, January 6th, or QAnon.”
“The dominant explanations for these substantial knowledge deficits and the apparent credulity of Christian nationalist adults have been motivated reasoning and siloed information sources,” Perry explained. “Both of those theories are no doubt true. But we have yet to consider whether there may be evidence of a gap in cognitive resources, one that can’t be explained solely by educational background or other relevant factors.”
Perry sought to see if general cognitive ability also plays a role in explaining these patterns. Cognitive ability refers to a person’s capacity to learn, apply new information, and engage in the complex reasoning required for critical thinking. A study covered by PsyPost in 2017 provides evidence that an intuitive thinking style tends to predict higher religious belief, while lower cognitive ability predicts higher social conservatism.
“A large number of studies have already documented an association between lower cognitive ability and greater religious fundamentalism, political authoritarianism, or otherwise right-wing views,” Perry said. Based on this prior research, he anticipated that cognitive ability might similarly predict support for Christian nationalism, viewing the study as a “necessary next step to empirically connect all the dots.”
To test this, Perry analyzed data from the General Social Survey, a long-running and nationally representative survey of American adults. The researcher measured cognitive ability using a vocabulary exercise where respondents identify the closest synonym for ten different words. This test is a common proxy for crystallized intelligence, which reflects the knowledge and reasoning skills a person has accumulated over time.
The study examined two specific measures of Christian nationalist ideology. The first asked respondents how important it is to be a Christian to be “truly American,” using data from survey waves in 1996, 2014, and 2024 with a sample of 1,659 adults. The second measure asked if respondents disapproved of the Supreme Court’s decision to ban mandatory Christian prayers and Bible reading in public schools. This second question included data from 17 survey waves between 1989 and 2024, creating a sample of 18,700 adults.
The researcher accounted for a wide range of variables to ensure the vocabulary scores were not just standing in for other demographic factors. These included educational attainment, such as whether a person completed high school or earned a college degree. The models also adjusted for religious affiliation, fundamentalist beliefs (such as viewing the Bible as the literal word of God), worship attendance, and political ideology. Additional demographic controls included age, race, sex, household income, and geographic region. The results remained consistent even when further controlling for parents’ education and family income at age 16.
For both outcomes, higher vocabulary scores were consistently and negatively associated with Christian nationalist views. As vocabulary scores increased, people were less likely to say being Christian was highly important for being truly American. They were also less likely to disapprove of the Supreme Court ban on school prayer. These negative associations persisted even when comparing people with the same level of education and similar religious habits.
The negative association between cognitive ability and Christian nationalism held steady across different demographic subgroups and was consistent across all survey years for the “truly American” question. For the school-prayer question, the link was always negative but reached statistical significance in only 11 of 17 survey years (and 7 of the 8 years since 2008).
The only exception was among the least educated Americans, specifically those who did not finish high school. For this specific group, vocabulary scores did not change their likelihood of supporting Christian nationalism. Notably, the effect was just as strong for high school graduates as for those with college degrees, indicating the pattern is not simply a result of college education. Perry suggests there may be a basic level of schooling, reached sometime during middle or high school, below which cognitive ability does not incline people to reject Christian nationalist views.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, also authored by Perry, which found that higher support for Christian nationalism was linked to lower factual knowledge about the role of religion in American political history. Both studies link the ideology to lower test performance, though factual knowledge and general cognitive ability are different things.
“To the extent that belief systems like Christian nationalism appeal to those Americans who for whatever reason tend to be less adept at thinking carefully and effectively, it suggests Christian nationalism (like religious fundamentalism or right-wing authoritarianism) is not the result of more sophisticated and complex ruminations on politics, religious ethics, and pluralism,” Perry said. Instead, he argued, it “appeals to more basic impulses for control and binary distinctions.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. “Readers shouldn’t read further into this finding than what the evidence warrants,” Perry cautioned. “I cannot make any claims about where cognitive ability comes from here.”
The data is cross-sectional, meaning all the information was collected at a single point in time for each respondent. “I actually show in one of my appendix tables that Christian nationalist views also predict wordsum scores,” Perry said. “So the correlation could theoretically go either way.”
“While I think the causal arrow almost certainly goes in the direction of cognitive ability shaping adherence to Christian nationalism, the cross-sectional nature of the data prevents me from making that definitive claim.”
It is possible that adopting a fundamentalist religious and political worldview alters the way people engage with educational material and language. In addition, despite robust statistical controls, “I cannot demonstrate definitively that lower scores on the wordsum vocabulary exercise are not the result of some childhood exposure or socialization that might also help explain the Christian nationalism connection,” he noted.
Another detail to note is the measurement of cognitive ability. The vocabulary test is a brief exercise, not a comprehensive intelligence test. However, Perry found that two other measures available in the General Social Survey, an abstract reasoning test and a numeracy item, also correlated with Christian nationalism in the same direction. Future studies could use more robust, multi-part intelligence tests that assess mathematical ability and problem-solving. Tracking individuals over time would also help clarify whether cognitive ability shapes political ideologies, or if the ideologies influence intellectual development.
In this study, the link between cognitive ability and Christian nationalism did not depend on people’s political ideology or party. But Perry has several other studies under peer review suggesting that ideology does shape how cognitive ability relates to other social attitudes. “There is a sense in which cognitive ability inclines us toward particular social or political views,” he said. “But there is also evidence that cognitive ability simply helps us discern and defend the ideological commitments of our in-groups.”
“This would be consistent with the theory that our higher reasoning abilities help us solve social problems of status rather than guide us toward certain ‘enlightened’ moral views,” Perry concluded. “And sure enough, I find in several of these studies that more cognitively sophisticated liberals hold liberal views more strongly, while cognitively sophisticated conservatives hold conservative views more strongly.”
The study, “Cognitive Ability and Christian Nationalism,” was authored by Samuel L. Perry, author or co-author of Taking America Back for God, The Flag and the Cross, and Religion for Realists.

future-proof design relies on a chain of sustainable decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:09 UTC
19:00:09 KST

future-proof design relies on a chain of sustainable decisions
the iF design award 2026 highlights how intentional design decisions drive circular systems, material innovation, and resilient communities.
iF DESIGN EMBEDS SUSTAINABILITY INTO GLOBAL DESIGN STANDARDS
The term sustainable design has too often been reduced to a marketing label, diluted by superficial claims of recycled content or carbon offsets that mask short product lifespans. But true sustainability cannot be stamped onto a surface, it is woven into the entire process. A design is genuinely sustainable only when its creators can offer clear, responsible answers to fundamental questions across its entire lifecycle: Does this product solve a genuine problem, or does its quick path to replacement expose a design failure? Are materials selected for enduring quality and minimal extraction impact, or only to satisfy eco-branding trends? What is the object’s path after its primary function ends? Can it be repaired, remanufactured, or cleanly returned to the natural cycle? Addressing these questions requires designers to combine creative vision with rigorous, long-term strategic foresight.
This holistic approach is precisely what the iF DESIGN Award prioritizes during evaluation. Across 93 categories, environmental impact carries equal weight alongside traditional factors like function and style, setting a global benchmark. See how winning projects from the iF Design Award 2026 demonstrate how designers resolve fundamental challenges by identifying true functional needs, selecting responsible materials, and planning for post-use recycling.
INTENTIONAL DESIGN FOSTERS REGENERATIVE ECONOMY
Since 1953, the institution’s Design Award has made sustainability central to its judging framework. Covering diverse categories, environmental and social impact stands as one of five fundamental criteria evaluated by the jury. This system highlights how intentional design decisions, from micro-level material selections to macro-level architectural strategies, actively foster a circular economy and lasting environmental care.
CIRCULAR SYSTEMS, MATERIAL INNOVATION AND RESILIENT COMMUNITIES
While materials determine how a product looks, feels, and performs, they also define its environmental impact, from raw extraction and labor practices to transport, energy use, and eventual disassembly. Because industrially produced products and packaging compound their environmental impact through volume, the iF Design Award emphasizes that sustainable design must move beyond high-minded ideals to deliver intuitive, everyday utility.
Illustrating this principle, the Taiwan Textile Research Institute developed its Gold Ratio Fibrous Resin Material, a circular thermoplastic composite crafted entirely from recycled carbon fibers and plastics. Engineered for infinite repairability, the material can be reshaped repeatedly, extending product lifespans without sacrificing durability.
Grounding material innovation in local ecosystems, DesertBoard® PSB® upcycles palm fronds into a formaldehyde-free and termite-resistant building material. Converting a regional waste stream into a durable, deforestation-free resource, it establishes a circular baseline for healthier construction.
As winning projects from the iF Design Award demonstrate, circular design works at a systems level, managing what happens to materials before and after a product is used. In the UK, Geopak replaces throwaway lighting boxes with reusable, trackable containers designed for specific building sites.
Beyond individual products, circular design operates as a broader system for managing material lifecycles. In Taiwan, TRASH+ LAB collects leftover event materials in Taitung to create an online rental system for designers.
Nearby in Taichung, CyclePath Lab’s HomeWork Circular Living Project integrates zero-waste retail, material transparency, workshops, consulting, and local pilot projects under one roof. This hybrid retail and community network renders circularity accessible, actionable, and collectively practiced.
When applied to technology and infrastructure, these circular decisions transform broader urban and rural grids. PHL Reduction in Kenya deploys solar-powered cold rooms across supply chains to reduce agricultural loss and stabilize farmer incomes, while Portugal’s Galp Energy retrofits existing municipal streetlights with electric vehicle chargers to expand EV infrastructure without adding to the urban footprint.
At an architectural scale, design sets long-term physical conditions for land use and coastal resilience. Takenaka Corporation scaled circular material principles into temporary architecture for Expo 2025 Osaka-Kansai, utilizing 3D-printed biodegradable wood and handmade seed paper designed to return cleanly to nature post-event.
Demonstrating this large scale urban strategy in New York, the Financial District and Seaport Climate Resilience Master Plan for Lower Manhattan, engineered by ONE Architecture, SCAPE, NYC EDC, and Arcadis, integrates flood protection, waterfront design, and traffic systems along one mile of vulnerable shoreline. The plan connects resilience with urban planning, balancing storm protection with future public space. In South Korea, BIG and SAMOO developed OCEANIX Busan, a floating urban prototype powered by solar energy, circular water systems, and local food production. Meanwhile, Row House Zurich in Switzerland demonstrates circularity by renovating an 1890 structural frame rather than tearing it down.
Design reaches its fullest purpose when it empowers communities and protects the future. The iF Design Student Award shines a light on forward-thinking concepts, like LiliPur’s water-regenerating lagoon systems in Italy and TextileRefuge’s Limetex bricks in Ghana, which turn discarded clothing into building materials and jobs. Concurrently, the iF Social Impact Prize recognizes tangible community solutions: Malaysia’s EPIC Bamboo Home and MaxLife’s three-dollar pump part, which keeps clean water flowing for 15 million people in Malawi by making pumps last six times longer.
