The Secrets of the US Spyware King
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Spyware maker Paragon Solutions has long positioned itself as the good guy in an industry seemingly filled with bad ones, vowing to never sell its mobile spyware to authoritarian regimes or ones with poor human rights records. It also promises to cut off any customer caught misusing its products against journalists, dissidents, or other non-legitimate targets.
Yet weeks after Paragon, then Israeli-owned, was acquired by the US equity firm AE Industrial Partners in December 2024 and merged with REDLattice—an American offensive cyber firm owned by AE that this week announced plans to go public—WhatsApp alleged that Paragon’s Graphite spyware was used to infect the phones of more than 60 individuals in more than 20 countries, including journalists and activists. Most of the targets were not identified, but the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab named two journalists and two activists in Italy.
Italian authorities denied misuse. Paragon and its new US owners, despite their zero-tolerance policy for customer abuse of their software, initially declined to comment on the allegations, and reportedly was exploring potential legal action against WhatsApp after the company sent a cease-and-desist letter to Paragon. Within a week, however, Paragon had canceled the two contracts it had with Italy’s domestic and foreign intelligence agencies.
From the outside, it seemed Paragon must have conducted an investigation and verified the allegations before canceling the contracts. But Paragon and RedLattice’s new CEO, Andrew Boyd, now says in an exclusive and surprisingly candid interview with WIRED that the company simply “fired” Italy because it “just was not worth it, from a risk perspective, to maintain the relationship” following the allegations.
In other words, there was no Paragon investigation and no interest in conducting one to determine if the allegations were true—Italian government investigators concluded they were not. Paragon didn’t even follow up with WhatsApp or Citizen Lab to obtain details about the alleged abuse and determine if any contracts in the other countries named by WhatsApp should be canceled as well. More damning, according to critics, is what Boyd revealed next: Paragon has no technical way to know if customers misuse its software, because it can’t see who customers target or the data they extract from targeted devices. It can only learn about misuse if customers admit to it or third parties uncover it. He says WhatsApp and Citizen Lab did the company a great service when they exposed the alleged misuse last year.
Paragon also doesn’t have a “kill switch” to disable customers when misuse occurs. All they can do is halt customers’ 24-hour support and system “updates.” But Boyd says the updates, the nature of which he won’t specify, are frequent and essential to using the spyware, and without them the system is rendered ineffective in about 12 hours.
“Things start falling apart quite quickly,” he says.
Boyd’s comments mark the first time a Paragon executive has spoken in detail about the secretive company or its handling of the Italian affair. He agreed to speak with WIRED now because he says more public discussion is needed about the offensive cyber industry and what it means for a US company to operate responsibly in this space. Prior to the interview, REDLattice founder John Ayers wrote in an email that they were “not looking for a favorable write-up.”
“If the honest assessment is still damning, that's a conversation we're prepared to have,” he wrote.
But Boyd’s admissions reveal that despite priding itself on being better than competitors, Paragon/RedLattice has less oversight and accountability than its most significant one—NSO Group, the Pegasus spyware maker, which has been excoriated for selling its tool to Saudi Arabia and other countries with poor human rights records. According to NSO’s transparency reports, which the company began publishing in recent years in response to criticism, it sets up infrastructure and portals that customers use to infect targets and, like Paragon, can’t see who customers target or detect misuse. But it claims it does have a kill switch to disable a customer’s access to the spyware if allegations of misuse arise, and NSO says its systems keep “tamper-proof” logs to record user activity. Customers are contractually obligated to provide these to NSO if allegations of misuse occur or else face “immediate suspension.”
By contrast, Boyd says Paragon customers can enable logging on some systems if they opt to, but Paragon has no access to the logs, nor does it want access. Instead, he says, government oversight bodies can use the logs to investigate allegations of misuse among their agencies, as an Italian parliamentary committee did last year in the case of the Citizen Lab allegations. However, this raises the possibility that a government investigator could lie about misuse if they uncover it in logs.
Rather than see Paragon’s lack of access to logs as an accountability problem, however, Boyd describes it as a selling point: No one would buy their products if the company could see a customer’s sensitive targeting information or logs that contain it.
“There's a balancing act between privacy and security and being able to ensure that our customers are using these things correctly,” Boyd says. “And I think we've landed on the best balance.”
That balance is achieved mostly through careful vetting of customers, he says, and rejecting any country that might be prone to abusing the spyware.
John Scott-Railton, senior researcher at Citizen Lab, which has tracked government misuse of commercial spyware for years, calls the revelations astonishing and the lack of mandatory logging “reckless.”
“What Paragon is saying in several substantial ways means [it has] less oversight, less transparency, less contractual protection against abuses than NSO Group,” he says. “It’s exactly the opposite of the picture that Paragon has painted for itself for years. The CEO admitting that his customers won’t tolerate oversight is refreshing honesty: Accountability is bad for business. And it signals to lawmakers and regulators that the spyware industry cannot be trusted to self-regulate."
Scott-Railton also finds it ironic that Paragon relies on Citizen Lab and others to uncover customer misuse when Paragon actively works to hide its spyware on infected devices and prevent discovery—which inherently includes potential misuse.
“We only find a very, very, very small subset [of infections], and the total numbers are always larger,” Scott-Railton says. “These companies spend millions trying to hide from us.”
US senator Ron Wyden tells WIRED that surveillance tools that lack oversight and transparency are “inevitably abused.”
“It’s easy to claim your powerful hacking tool isn’t being misused if you go out of your way to ensure you don’t know how customers use it,” Wyden says. “The fact that Paragon refuses to audit use of its tool, or even attempt to match the work of a small team of researchers at the Citizen Lab is a massive red flag.”
Israeli Intelligence Roots
Paragon was launched in 2019 by Israeli Brigadier General Ehud Schneorson, former commander of the Israeli military’s signals intelligence group, Unit 8200. He cofounded it with three other 8200 veterans and former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak. Two years later, the company reportedly had no customers but was developing Graphite and hoping to conquer the lucrative US market. But then the US government began cracking down on foreign spyware companies after NSO’s Pegasus and Candiru’s DevilsTongue tools were misused by their customers against government workers, journalists, dissidents, activists, and academics.
The US Commerce Department sanctioned both companies in 2021, and the Israeli government drastically cut the number of countries to which Israeli firms could sell spyware—from 102 countries to 37, excluding Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Morocco, and Mexico. Over a year later, the Biden administration and Congress imposed guardrails making it difficult for the US government to purchase foreign-made commercial spyware if it posed a national security risk or could be misused by foreign governments.
By then, Paragon reportedly already had a contract with the Drug Enforcement Agency to combat drug traffickers outside the US, but it otherwise could not “make any substantial headway” in the US, Boyd says. So the company began looking for a US buyer to overcome its foreign-ownership handicap. In December 2024, AE acquired it for $900 million. The result is a company that is now American on paper, but is still effectively Israeli. Paragon is a RedLattice company—though Paragon has no working website, and the RedLattice website currently doesn’t mention Paragon—but, according to Boyd, it retains its name and offices in Israel, where it has more than 600 employees. Any Paragon-built products still require licensing approval from the Israeli government to sell abroad, while RedLattice-made products sold to non-US customers are governed by US International Traffic in Arms Regulations.
Nonetheless, the US acquisition has served as an end-run around foreign-ownership guardrails. Once the AE deal closed, Boyd says, “everybody started talking” to them about Paragon products, and Paragon began looking to hire 150 new workers to handle its expected new business.
Ayers, the REDLattice founder, told WIRED in an email that prior to acquisition, REDLattice and AE spent more than two years in discussion with US and allied governments and “didn't move without their buy-in.” But asked whether the government pushed back on the acquisition, Boyd says there were no objections, and no one imposed conditions or governance requirements on them either.
“The US government in any form [was] never going to formally say … we approve this acquisition,” he says. “But they didn't have any discomfort with it … If the [National Security Council] said, ‘This would be a colossally bad idea,’ we probably wouldn't have gone through with it.”
Less than a year after Paragon merged with REDLattice, NSO Group and Candiru copied their savvy acquisition move. A US investment group acquired controlling ownership of NSO and appointed David Friedman, former US ambassador to Israel under President Donald Trump, as executive chairman. Candiru was acquired by the US-based Integrity Partners. Now all three companies are vying for US contracts.
Boyd, who became CEO of RedLattice and Paragon eight months after the acquisition, gives the companies an edge in the US market. As a former military intelligence officer, State Department diplomat, and director of the CIA’s Center for Cyber Intelligence until retiring in 2023, he has many US government, military, and intelligence community connections to help secure contracts.
During the interview, Boyd was open with many of WIRED’s questions, but also inexplicably opaque with others. He wouldn’t even, for example, confirm that Graphite is the name of a product the company sells or say how many products the combined companies possess. He says only that before the acquisition, Paragon had fewer than five products, and together they now have between five and 10. Some of these do “over-the-horizon” data collection (by hacking devices and systems remotely), while others require physical access to targeted devices. He bristles at calling the tools “spyware,” though. He considers them “defensive” tools since, broadly speaking, they help defend against national security and criminal threats. But in truth, they are designed for surveillance, espionage, and possibly even disruptive cyber operations.
Graphite, the only product ever publicly identified, extracts communications from chat applications, particularly encrypted messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Signal. This contrasts with NSO Group’s Pegasus, which can spy on all aspects of a mobile phone, including surreptitiously activating its microphone and camera to spy on targets. Reportedly, Graphite’s capabilities can be expanded through modules, though its full feature set is not publicly known.
WhatsApp and Citizen Lab have reported that Graphite uses a powerful zero-click zero-day exploit to infect phones without user awareness. Boyd won’t say if the companies hunt for zero-day vulnerabilities and develop their own exploits or purchase them from others, but says both Paragon and RedLattice have “substantial” research and development teams. RedLattice’s website says the company has more than 200 “vulnerability research experts.”
In addition to their products, Paragon and RedLattice build bespoke solutions for some customers, and some contracts provide customers with personnel who possess “appropriate clearances” to do a “variety” of tasks. Boyd won’t elaborate on the tasks but says his company doesn’t do offensive operations for customers; it just provides hardware and software. But after the Trump administration recently announced plans to contract with select private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against cybercriminal groups, he says RedLattice will pursue these contracts.
Customer Vetting
Without the ability to monitor customer activity and detect misuse, Paragon relies on its governance model to prevent abuse. This involves customer vetting and contractual deterrence. Customers, and the countries in which they reside, are vetted by an internal risk committee that Boyd and other board members chair using various criteria to determine if a prospective country or customer might have a negative business or reputational impact on the company.
“We don't want our products to be involved in things that they weren't intended to be used for,” he says.
Boyd wouldn’t provide a full list of the country-assessment criteria but mentioned several during the interview: political and government stability, human rights record, corruption-index ratings, strength of a country’s legal system, and whether a potential customer has a track record of adhering to its national laws. He says they lean more toward rejecting countries than approving them. They currently have between 20 and 30 countries on their approved list, and have more than 100 customers in 23 countries.
“I think there's some people that would argue that we're too conservative [about who we’ll sell to],” he says, but notes that “it's better to take a hit on revenue” than sell to countries that could prove detrimental in the long run. (Boyd says, for example, that canceling Italy’s two contracts cost the company “seven figures” in revenue. He would not specify the exact value, but Israeli media have estimated the contracts were worth “tens of millions of dollars.”) In the year since he became CEO, he says a “handful” of countries have been rejected as potential customers but won’t say which ones.
Paragon sells only to the US and select US allies (whether democratic or not), and only to national entities, not state or local governments and police forces. But being a US ally doesn’t guarantee a sale. They won’t sell to Saudi Arabia, even though it’s an ally. After the Saudi government reportedly used NSO’s Pegasus to spy on the fiancé and close associates of Washington Post opinion writer Jamal Khashoggi, who was murdered by Saudi government agents, the Israeli government reportedly asked Paragon to take over the Saudi Arabia contract from NSO Group, but Paragon reportedly refused. Boyd says they still won’t sell to Saudi Arabia, and also says the company has no commercial relationships with any country in the Middle East.
“I think there's very important national security reasons why [the US] would want a close relationship with the Saudis from a nation-state to nation-state level,” he says. But that “does not translate into … this private-sector company having a business relationship with them … I don't need to get into the why’s, because you probably know the why’s.”
They also won’t sell to Venezuela, even with President Nicolas Maduro gone. “There's too much chaos,” Boyd says, “and it wouldn't fit our risk calculus for other variables.”
Yet the company reportedly signed a lucrative contract in Singapore in 2023 worth tens of millions of dollars. Though an electoral democracy, Singapore imposes significant restrictions on free speech, media independence, and human rights.
The customer vetting, Boyd says, “usually works 99 out of 100 times” to eliminate those who might misuse their tools—the assumption being that if they choose only reputable customers, the customers they choose will act only reputably. For the remaining 1 in 100, the customer contracts and zero-tolerance policy are meant to deter misuse. These prohibit using the tools against journalists, civil society members, opposition politicians, and anyone else who is not the target of a legitimate intelligence or criminal investigation. Also embedded in any system sold to non-US customers is a block that prevents targeting of any person in the US—that is, any number that requires the US +1 country code to dial. US law enforcement agencies who have a warrant can get the block disabled, he says.
What if a US customer let a non-approved country use Graphite to spy on targets? During the first Trump administration, the CIA reportedly purchased NSO Group's Pegasus to give to an East African country to use. Boyd insists they would know if this occurred.
“We know where the system is, because we [help customers] install it and train [them on it] … And so we would know if it was not installed in the place where they intended it to be,” he insists.
Would they also know if a customer used the tool on their own infrastructure but to spy on behalf of another non-approved country? He says they would, because the majority of customers have similar intelligence, military, or law enforcement backgrounds to RedLattice and Paragon employees, and they have robust relationships with customers. They would have a “sixth sense” if something were “fishy” about a customer, he says.
Boyd insists that the fact that there has been only one allegation of misuse so far is evidence that the company’s vetting and governance model is effective. This, however, ignores the fact that the odds of someone uncovering misuse are low, especially because the company takes care to ensure its spyware won’t be easily detected on infected systems.
All of this, of course, leads to questions about US customers. Based on Paragon’s vetting criteria, some might wonder how the current Trump administration would meet them. Given reports of corruption, disregard for the rule of law, and Trump’s unveiled threats to use government power against political opponents, fears of misuse by US agencies are not irrational. Asked what the company would do if there were allegations of misuse by a US customer, Boyd said an inspector general or legislative committee would likely investigate the matter, and if they found concrete evidence of misuse, Congress or the company would likely take action.
A year after the acquisition, however, it’s unclear how much US sales have expanded. Shortly before the 2024 acquisition, Paragon signed a $2 million contract with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, to help dismantle foreign terrorist operations and disrupt fentanyl traffickers. And RedLattice has had long-standing contracts with the US Air Force. But no other government contracts for the companies show up in a search of public databases, though classified contracts likely would not appear. Boyd won’t identify customers but indicates the company is particularly interested in Pentagon and CIA contracts.
“There are offices across the national security enterprise that don't even know they need our product yet,” he says. “And I consider that an unaddressed market.”

'It's coming for everything': Eddie Perfect on AI and his new satire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Eddie Perfect turns Molière satire Tartuffe into a black comedy about AI
Eddie Perfect doesn't want his teenage daughters talking to AI chatbots.
"We have a rule in our house that no one talks to the machines," he says.
He sees the technology as outsourcing thinking and cognition, which he reckons is particularly harmful to young people.
"Maybe everyone should have access to AI once they turn 25, and that would be perfect," he says.
"I really hate it because I think it's coming for everything."
It's something Perfect has been thinking about a lot as he works on his latest show, a new adaptation of 17th-century French playwright Molière's Tartuffe for Melbourne's Malthouse Theatre.
The original play, otherwise known as The Impostor, or The Hypocrite, is a satire about a charlatan, posing as a religious man, Tartuffe, who manipulates his way into foolish Orgon's home and family.
Perfect's answer to a quasi-religious figure for a modern audience? A hairdressing AI robot.
"I can't write anything but what I know, so what's been really fun is to meet Tartuffe where I am in my life," he says.
"And I love a good sci-fi. I love synthetic humans and the idea of robots and machines and our relationship with them into the future.
"So, it just felt right to make Tartuffe a robot."
Perfect's The Tartuffe, in which he will also star as Orgon, is one of eight plays in Malthouse's 2027 season, the first from artistic director Dean Bryant
The season is notable for being all-Australian, with seven plays making their world premiere, including an adaptation of Charlotte Wood's Booker-shortlisted novel Stone Yard Devotional and the second play from Logie-winning actor Thomas Weatherall.
It reflects Bryant's approach to the top job, which he took over from now-Adelaide Festival director Matthew Lutton in October 2025.
"We want to have new experiences," Bryant says. "We want to see things we haven't seen on stage before."
While it's thrilling for Bryant to have a season made up of new Australian work, it also feels scary.
"New work is the hardest work to make," he says.
"It's dealing with the unknown … But when it comes off, there's nothing like a new play."
Creativity and AI
The announcement of Perfect's The Tartuffe arrives as the federal government considers a proposal to water down copyright protections in an effort to lure AI companies to Australia, angering local artists and creatives.
Perfect is impressed by the ways AI can be used in areas like translation and learning new skills but is frustrated by how it came about — being trained for free on human creativity — and that it is now being deployed to replace that creative process.
"The game of creativity is who can sit in the discomfort of not knowing what to do the longest," he says.
"If you know there's AI there that can give you an answer, any answer, to stop the discomfort of not having anything on the page, then I think you've lost the game.
"You've got to go to the fire for creativity."
For Bryant, there's also something interesting about taking a story about a family trying and failing to connect with each other through technology and putting that into a theatre, a space that can't be replicated by AI.
"[Theatre] is a communal experience where we still voluntarily put our phones away," he says.
"It's such a beautiful kind of metaphor to go, you've all come here to have the human experience of this, and we're telling you a cautionary tale about where not to find connection."
While The Tartuffe may have a serious message, Perfect stresses it's a "front-footed black comedy", which might entice new audiences to the theatre.
"I know that I and people like Dean are always looking for new ways to connect with new audiences and to engender a greater sense of ownership or belonging from people for theatre," he says.
"It's not a big shiny gold edifice with fancy carpets you're always worried about getting dirty.
"It's a place of welcome where you should be able to go and see an Australian take on a classic or a new Australian story and have a conversation about what it is to be Australian and alive right now."
Adaptations that explode expectations
The Tartuffe is one of four adaptations in Malthouse's 2027 season, alongside Stone Yard Devotional; Henry James's The Turn of the Screw; and Gone with the Wind, from theatre collective Bloomshed.
Bryant says the appeal of adaptation is about more than familiarity.
"You get a whiff of a context of the evening, a sense of what you're going to see," he says.
"Our job is to then explode that."
Artist Tamara Dean will collaborate with director Sarah Goodes and adaptor Joanna Murray-Smith on Stone Yard Devotional to help create the visual world of the novel, which follows a woman who leaves her home and marriage in the city to live in an enclosed religious community on the Monaro plains in regional NSW.
It will star Lisa McCune as the unnamed protagonist, alongside Catherine McClements as a celebrity nun who visits the community.
"There's so much about atmosphere and the plains and the way the nunnery feels [in the novel]," Bryant explains.
"[Goodes] wants it to feel like [the show] crosses over with art installation, and for the sound design to be as immersive and important in the dramaturgy as the text … That will give the kind of transcendent feeling of the book."
Meanwhile. The Turn of the Screw has been turned into a one-woman show, starring AACTA winner Tuuli Narkle (ABC TV's Mystery Road: Origin).
Bryant emphasises Narkle will be doing more than playing all the characters in the Victorian gothic novel about a governess looking after two children in a country house.
"She's creating an incredibly chilling atmosphere," he says.
"It's a really big ask to be a solo performer taking us into a world where there may or not be ghosts."
Bryant stresses the technical skill and artistry needed to build a world entirely on your own.
"It's the ultimate challenge for an actor to be given a one-person show," he says.
Building capacity in the sector
The collaboration with Bloomshed is part of Malthouse's commitment to developing the local theatre sector.
"We scour the independent scene for makers that have developed a unique voice, and we are actively putting at least one of those companies in our seasons each year," Bryant says.
"[That's] to either elevate a piece they've put on in an independent venue and scale it up for the main stage, or to build with them a new piece for the main stage."
This year, Bloomshed brought their new take on Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, which took aim at the housing crisis and replaced Mr Bennet with a pot plant, to Malthouse, after it premiered in 2025 as part of Darebin Arts Speakeasy.
Next year, Malthouse will be helping the collective to create from scratch its version of Gone with the Wind, which will look at the relationship between resource ownership and power.
"Melbourne has always had a really interesting independent scene, and they fizzle out if they don't get more of a spotlight on them," Bryant says. "It's our job to give them that lens."
But it's about more than simply shining a light on the talent that already exists in Melbourne.
Instead, it's about building capacity within the sector.
"By moving into a company that's set up to create this kind of work, they upskill really quickly," Bryant explains.
"It elevates their practice as well, which makes them better inclined to have longevity."
Capacity-building at Malthouse in 2027 also means giving opportunities to young writers to debut new work, including Yve Blake (Fangirls) and Thomas Weatherall (Blue).
Blake's play Jackpot is about intergenerational inequality, while Weatherall's play Lucy is an intimate relationship drama.
"They both think very deeply about where we find ourselves and yet write from the age they actually are," Bryant says.
"They understand the generation they're in."

U.S. Army Selects Five Winners in Humanoid Robot Competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:28:10 UTC
18:28:10 KST

The U.S. Army has selected the winners of the xTechHumanoid competition, focused on developing humanoid robots and technologies for their military applications.
Army FUZE reported this.
The competition received 103 applications from developers of humanoid platforms and individual components. Ten companies reached the finals, nine of which demonstrated their technologies at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on September 9–10.
Following the trials, five companies were selected as winners: ACEs Group, Florida Institute for Human and Machine Cognition, Hydroplane, RAS Labs, and Velocity Explorations. The competition covered not only complete robots, but also technologies required for their operation, including power sources, tactile sensors, and control software.
The Florida Institute for Human and Machine Cognition presented the most complete humanoid platform. Its Alex robot features impact-resilient actuators, ballistic protection elements, and a hybrid control system combining AI-based autonomy with operator control.
The other winners focused on solving specific technological challenges. ACEs Group proposed a scalable energy storage system, Hydroplane — a compact long-duration power source, RAS Labs – highly sensitive tactile sensors for robotic fingers, and Velocity Explorations – a software for translating operator commands into specific machine actions.
The U.S. military views humanoid systems as part of a broader effort to develop robotics and autonomous capabilities. They could potentially be used for physically demanding or dangerous tasks to reduce risks to servicemembers. At the same time, the competition was primarily intended to assess the commercial technologies’ development level.
Ukraine already has practical experience testing similar systems. In February 2026, U.S. company Foundation Future Industries delivered two Phantom MK-1 humanoid robots to Ukraine, which were used primarily for logistics tasks in hazardous areas during field trials.
However, the trials demonstrated significant limitations of current humanoid robots. The Phantom MK-1 can carry around 20 kg of cargo, lacks sufficient water protection, and has limited battery life, while its complex mechanics make the platform vulnerable to breakdowns and loss of balance. The cost of one such robot was estimated at around $150,000.
Other challenges include power consumption, actuator reliability, communications stability, and the ability of artificial intelligence to correctly assess situations. The U.S. Army identifies power supply and endurance as one of the areas for further research following the xTechHumanoid competition.
At the same time, Ukraine also plans to develop its own humanoid systems. In July, Brave1 announced plans for a separate grant competition to develop humanoid robots for the Defense Forces. The stated goal is to maximize the use of robotic systems on the front line and reduce risks to servicemembers.
Thus, Ukraine is effectively pursuing a path parallel to that of the U.S.: moving from testing ready-made foreign platforms toward developing its own solutions that can be adapted directly to the conditions of the modern battlefield.
Japan is also exploring a similar approach. In September, it became known that the Japanese government plans to study the use of humanoid robots with physical AI in the Japan Self-Defense Forces amid a personnel shortage.
Initially, they are expected to be used primarily for non-combat tasks, including base security, logistics, reconnaissance, and rescue operations. Japan also plans to hold its own competition among companies and universities to assess the capabilities of existing platforms under real-world operating conditions.
Thus, the U.S., Ukraine, and Japan are moving from experiments with humanoid robots toward programs to select and develop such systems. At the same time, the current level of technology suggests that in the near term, these systems will primarily perform logistics, engineering, and other support tasks rather than directly replace servicemembers in combat.

wood-framed family home in osaka revolves around flexible open sports space

wood-framed family home in osaka revolves around flexible open sports space
the free space accommodates sports, play, and everyday activities, and can be quickly reconfigured.
Flexible ‘free space’ adapts to sports, play, and family life
Osaka House by SHIOYA DESIGN is a two-generation residence in Japan organized around a large, flexible open space known as the ‘free space.’ Initially conceived as a dedicated judo area, the space developed during the design process into a gymnasium-like room that can accommodate multiple sports, play, and everyday family activities.
Rather than assigning a fixed function, the free space can be adapted to changing needs and interests. Judo, basketball, golf, bouldering, and other activities take place within the generous volume, with ceiling heights calibrated to different sports. A retractable golf net, basketball hoop and court markings, and bouldering wall are integrated into the room. Loose-laid tatami mats can be rearranged, allowing the space to be reconfigured in around 15 minutes.
‘free space’ connects Osaka House’s interior and exterior
The open volume also forms a visual and spatial connection with the surrounding living areas. A shared kitchen and dining space brings the two generations together, while a second-floor living room and rooftop terrace overlook the free space below. Gardens and additional outdoor areas extend the house beyond its enclosed rooms, while planting around the perimeter provides privacy without fully separating the residence from its surroundings.
Completed in 2025, Osaka House by SHIOYA DESIGN Studio is a wood-framed residence of approximately 183 sqm. Its undefined central space provides a flexible framework for movement, exercise, play, and shared activities, allowing the domestic layout to change over time.

 architect: SHIOYA DESIGN – Taichi Shioya | @shioya_design

Pentagon Does Not Invite Britain, France or Baltic States to NATO Future Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:09:20 UTC
18:09:20 KST

The United States plans to hold a meeting in Poland on the future of NATO without the participation of several European allies, including the United Kingdom, France, and the Baltic states.
Politico reports this, citing six diplomats familiar with the planning of the meeting.
The meeting is being organized by the Pentagon, with the initiative being pushed by Elbridge Colby, the U.S. Defense Department’s top policy official.
The meeting is expected to focus on the future of NATO and possible changes to how the alliance operates.
Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany, and the Netherlands have been invited to the meeting.
Meanwhile, the lack of invitations for the United Kingdom, France, and the Baltic states has raised questions among diplomats.
These countries have significant defense budgets and play an important role in NATO. One representative of an uninvited country said that his government was trying to understand the criteria used to select participants for the meeting.
The emergence of this format comes amid demands from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration for allies to increase defense spending and support U.S. policy.
In June, following the first meeting in Bergen, Colby said that the format included allies that were quickly implementing agreements on defense spending, had sufficient military capabilities, and were ready to move on to practical work.
In June 2025, NATO countries agreed to increase defense spending and security-related expenditures to 5% of GDP by 2035.
Of this, at least 3.5% is to be allocated directly to defense needs, while up to 1.5% will be spent on infrastructure, cybersecurity, civilian resilience, and other related areas.
Militarnyi previously reported that Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen called on NATO member states to increase defense spending.

U.S. Orders 22 Additional F-15EX Eagle II Fighter Jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:58:02 UTC
17:58:02 KST

The U.S. Air Force has awarded Boeing a $2.3 billion contract to procure 22 additional F-15EX Eagle II fighter jets.
This was reported by the Air & Space Forces Magazine of the Air & Space Forces Association.
The order, which is part of the seventh production lot, brings the total number of F-15EX aircraft ordered to 120.
The agreement was signed ahead of the end of the fiscal year to ensure the allocated funds could be used in time.
The average cost per fighter under the new contract is approximately $108 million, excluding the engines, which are purchased separately from GE Aerospace.
The F-15EX Eagle II is a heavily upgraded version of the Gen 4 F-15 base fighter, often classified as a Gen 4.5 aircraft.
The aircraft features a digital fly-by-wire flight control system and a fully ‘glass’ cockpit with touchscreen displays.
The fighter is equipped with a new APG-82 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar.
The aircraft’s protection is provided by the advanced EPAWSS (Eagle Passive Active Warning Survivability System) electronic warfare suite.
Boeing is currently delivering aircraft from the third production lot and plans to increase production to two F-15EX fighter jets per month.
In April, the U.S. Air Force approved increasing the total planned F-15EX procurement from 129 to 269 aircraft.
Earlier, an Iranian missile strike on a U.S. base in Jordan damaged eight U.S. F-15 fighter jets.

Romania Aims to Adopt the Euro by 2035
The country must exit the EU’s excessive deficit procedure by 2030 to meet its eurozone target, Finance Minister Alexandru Nazare says
Bulgaria’s consolidated fiscal programme recorded a deficit of €3.0755 billion by the end of August 2026, equivalent to 2.4% of projected GDP, according to data from the Ministry of Finance.
Total revenue, grants and donations reached €30.1178 billion, or 60.7% of the amount projected for the full year. Compared with the same period in 2025, revenue increased by 11.9%, or €3.1923 billion.
The increase was driven mainly by tax and social-security revenue, which rose by 10%, or €2.2127 billion, as well as by grants and donations, which were €1.51 billion higher than a year earlier.
Non-tax revenue, however, fell by €530.4 million year-on-year. The Finance Ministry attributes the decline primarily to lower dividend payments from state-owned enterprises. In 2025, an interim dividend for the 2025 financial year had been paid, reducing dividend revenue recorded in 2026.
Tax revenue, including social-security contributions, amounted to €24.2607 billion, representing 63.1% of the annual target and accounting for 80.6% of total revenue under the consolidated fiscal programme.
Expenditure under the consolidated fiscal programme, including Bulgaria’s contribution to the EU budget, reached €33.1932 billion by the end of August, or 58.4% of the annual projection. This compares with €29.5918 billion during the same period of 2025.
The main increases were recorded in social and health-insurance spending, including pensions, as well as personnel costs and capital expenditure.
The rise in spending reflects, among other factors, pension increases under the so-called Swiss rule in July 2025 and July 2026, the increase in the minimum wage from January 2026, and higher wages reflecting accumulated inflation for 2025.
Capital expenditure also increased significantly, driven by the implementation of investments and projects under Bulgaria’s Recovery and Resilience Plan and the Municipal Investment Programme.
Non-interest expenditure amounted to €31.7757 billion, representing 58.6% of the amount planned for 2026 and an 11.4% increase, or €3.2447 billion, compared with August 2025.
Current non-interest expenditure stood at €27.6797 billion, while capital expenditure, including the net increase in the state reserve, reached €4.0734 billion. Current and capital transfers abroad amounted to €22.7 million. Interest payments totalled €661.3 million, or 62.4% of the annual plan and €271.5 million more than during the same period last year.
The Finance Ministry said the deterioration in the monthly budget balance in August was mainly due to the concentration of significant investment payments under the Recovery and Resilience Plan.
Spending under the plan is expected to continue putting pressure on the consolidated fiscal programme’s cash deficit until Bulgaria receives its fifth payment from the European Commission.
As of August 31, 2026, Bulgaria’s fiscal reserve stood at €7.7808 billion. Of that amount, €7.5321 billion was held as deposits with the Bulgarian National Bank and commercial banks, while €248.7 million represented receivables from EU funds for certified expenditure, advances and other payments.
The Finance Ministry has published the data on the execution of the consolidated fiscal programme as of August 31 on its website, together with an information bulletin containing an overview of the implementation of the state budget and the main consolidated fiscal indicators.

The Bulgarian government has set a target of keeping the budget deficit at no more than 3% by 2027, alongside restoring a sustainable financial system and maintaining predictable tax policy

Britain’s retired Hercules head to Türkiye in December
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:52:12 UTC
17:52:12 KST

- Türkiye's Defense Ministry said the first two of 12 former Royal Air Force C-130J transports will arrive in December after maintenance in the UK.
- Six pilots and six technicians are training in the United States, and 29 maintenance personnel are training in the UK.
Türkiye will receive the first two of 12 C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft it is buying from the UK in December, once maintenance on them is finished in Britain, the Turkish Defense Ministry said on Oct. 1, with the rest of the former Royal Air Force aircraft to follow in stages.
The ministry also said crews are already training to fly and maintain them. Six pilots and six technicians are training in the United States, and 29 maintenance personnel are training in the UK. It did not give a schedule for the remaining 10 aircraft or say where the first two will be based.
The aircraft are stretched C-130J-30 models that the Royal Air Force retired in June 2023, when the UK decided to rely on the larger Airbus A400M for its tactical airlift. Türkiye confirmed the purchase in October 2025, and the 12 aircraft were handed over to Marshall Aerospace in Cambridge, England, for overhaul and modernization before delivery. Turkish officials have said Türkiye plans to take over routine maintenance of the fleet itself once its personnel complete type training.
The UK government said in December 2025 that the sale and related work were worth more than £550 million ($727 million) to the British defense sector and Marshall Aerospace and would support about 1,400 skilled jobs in Cambridge, Turkish Minute reported.
The C-130Js will fill a gap in Türkiye’s airlift fleet. The Turkish Air Force operates about 10 A400Ms and a fleet of older C-130B and C-130E Hercules, many of them decades old. Those older C-130s were grounded after an accident in November 2025 near the border between Georgia and Azerbaijan, leaving the air force dependent on its A400Ms for heavy airlift, Aviation Week reported.
The C-130J is the latest version of Lockheed Martin’s long-serving four-engine turboprop transport, with a two-pilot glass cockpit, digital flight controls and more efficient Rolls-Royce engines than earlier Hercules models. The stretched -30 version has a longer cargo hold, letting it carry more troops, pallets or vehicles than the standard aircraft.
Türkiye is not the only buyer of the RAF’s surplus Super Hercules fleet. The UK has previously sold former RAF C-130Js to Bangladesh and Bahrain.

Gunvor publicly condemned Russia’s war but continued to do business with Russian energy firms, records show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:48:52 UTC
17:48:52 KST

CHINA CAPITAL
Gunvor publicly condemned Russia’s war but continued to do business with Russian energy firms, records show
Even as the trading giant publicly claimed to be winding down its Russia business, Gunvor privately acknowledged the deals to its bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, saying they complied with sanctions laws.
Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, several major trading firms pledged to stop or reduce new dealings with Russian businesses, joining global efforts to weaken Vladimir Putin’s military machine.
One of them was Gunvor Group, a company co-founded by a Swedish businessman and a Russian oligarch close to the Kremlin. In 2014, a U.S. Treasury Department report said that Putin himself had investments in the energy trading firm and may have had access to its funds. Since then, Gunvor’s co-founders have exited, and the company, now valued at about $5 billion, has over the last decade sought to shake its image as a Putin investment tool.
Gunvor has publicly condemned Russia’s war in Ukraine, and in 2023 corporate filings stated that it had “largely wound-down the trade of Russian oil and products.”
Now, confidential records reviewed by Swedish daily Göteborgs-Posten and the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists show how, despite its public pledges, the trader, using some of its subsidiaries, continued doing business with sanctioned Russian oil and gas producers.
The records come from the archives of the U.K. operations of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the world’s largest bank by asset size and one of Gunvor’s lenders.
While likely not violating sanction laws, the deals found in the ICBC records are at odds with the trading giant’s public posturing following the start of the war. The dealings also go against a private reassurance Gunvor made in a 2022 email to ICBC saying that it had stopped new sales to Russian entities, the investigation found.
ICBC’s records were examined as part of China Capital, an ICIJ-led investigation that exposed the inner workings of the Chinese state-owned bank and its maneuvers to advance Beijing’s geopolitical goals. The project showed how ICBC’s London units routinely financed companies with opaque financial flows and murky corporate ownership, justifying the deals as part of its support for the Chinese government’s top priorities.
China Capital found, for example, that ICBC London provided loans to Norilsk Nickel, a Russian mining company partly owned by sanctioned oligarchs close to Putin, in breach of an internal branch policy forbidding dealings with clients linked to sanctioned people or entities. ICBC’s other branches also provided foreign exchange, deposits and cash management services to Norilsk Nickel, a key supplier to China’s booming electric vehicle and battery industries.
Justin Ko, a researcher at the University of Macau who studied China’s state banks, described China’s relationship to Russia as “opportunistic.” As mounting war sanctions have forced Western traders to stop dealing with Russian counterparts, Beijing has emerged as Moscow’s steadiest ally. “In that sense,” Ko told ICIJ, “there is going to be more business, more trade, and it’s only natural that ICBC and Bank of China, as [China’s] two leading international banks, will be leading the way for that.”
To be sure, ICBC London officers made an effort to ensure the bank complied with sanctions restrictions imposed following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, the records show.
But the bank’s continued dealings with Gunvor shows how ICBC chose to serve clients considered strategic by Beijing even when they did business with sanctioned Russian entities.
For ICBC, Gunvor was a special client. An internal memo dated 2016 said that a “China rationale” for financing the company was its ongoing expansion within China: “Gunvor is expanding its reach into the Chinese domestic market : by sealing supply contracts with new independent (teapot) refineries and supplying [specialty] ores.”
Confidential records provided by Gunvor to ICBC show that between 2022 and 2024 the company based in Geneva continued to deal with sanctioned Russian parties, using licenses and other forms of authorization.
In 2024, during an ICBC “client review” as part of a prospective $594 million credit line to support Gunvor’s “trade finance needs,” some bank officers raised concerns about the trader’s Russia dealings.
In a report marked “strictly confidential,” Gunvor had acknowledged to ICBC London that, through its subsidiaries, the “Group had dealings with Russian counterparties target of Sanctions,” including buying and selling oil, gas and other products to and from “entities part of Gazprom, Rosneft, Lukoil and Novatek groups.” But those transactions, the Gunvor report said, represented only 0.69% of the group’s revenue in the first quarter of 2024 — or about $234 million, according to Göteborgs-Posten’s estimates.
In an internal meeting, an analyst from ICBC’s Zurich office told his London colleagues that the Swiss branch found “Gunvor trading a bit more aggressive than other traders” and had chosen not to do business with the trader.
Still, ICBC London ultimately decided to keep serving its long-time client, classifying it as “high risk.” “The group remains vital part of ICBC London relationship,” a bank officer noted in an internal memo.
In response to reporters’ questions, Gunvor’s corporate affairs director, Seth Pietras, acknowledged that in 2024 the company “did undertake some limited sanctions-compliant trading of Russian commodities” and said that those activities are “disclosed transparently to our financial institutions and to relevant national competent authorities.” In his emailed statement to Göteborgs-Posten, Pietras added that all of Gunvor’s trading activity is performed in strict compliance with U.S., U.K., the European Union and other countries’ sanctions laws.
“Gunvor fully stands by its public statements relating to its decrease in trading and activities in Russia,” he said.
ICBC did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment.
Göteborgs-Posten’s Tobias Andersson Åkerblom and ICIJ’s Denise Ajiri contributed reporting for this article.

Ukraine spots “whiskered” Shahed aimed at power lines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:42:35 UTC
17:42:35 KST

- Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko published video of a jet-powered Shahed fitted with whisker-like contacts, likely to detonate on power lines.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Russia appears to have used a jet drone carrying a 40-kg cutting warhead built for pylons and bridges.
A previously unseen version of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drone has appeared in Ukraine fitted with whisker-like rods on its nose, a modification that Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko says is designed to detonate the warhead on contact with high-voltage power lines.
Sternenko, a Ukrainian volunteer and activist who runs one of the country’s largest drone fundraising efforts, published video of the drone on X, saying the “whiskers” are most likely there to close an electrical contact and set off the charge when the drone strikes something as thin as a power cable. A similar modification has been seen at another location, though Sternenko did not say where either drone was found or whether it was intact.
“And this is a whiskered Shahed with a specialized warhead for attacks on high-voltage power lines. Most likely the whiskers were added to close a contact and initiate the warhead when hitting small targets such as power lines,” Sternenko wrote.
A standard impact fuse needs a solid surface to trigger, so a drone that clips a cable or the open lattice of a transmission tower may fly through or fall without exploding. Rods sticking out ahead of the airframe would let the drone detonate as soon as they touch a wire.
A second development points in the same direction. Serhii Beskrestnov, known as “Flash,” a specialist in drones and electronic warfare who serves as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s adviser on defense technology, said Russia appeared to use a special warhead on a jet-powered drone for the first time on Sept. 30. He identified it as a shaped-charge cutting payload, known by its Russian initials KRSN, designed specifically to destroy high-voltage transmission towers and steel bridge structures.
According to Beskrestnov, the KRSN consists of a 40-kg (88-pound) main charge and four additional strike modules. A cutting charge focuses its blast along a line to slice through metal, which makes it suited to severing the legs of a steel pylon or the girders of a bridge rather than causing broad blast damage. Beskrestnov did not say where the drone carrying it struck or what damage it caused.
Russia has attacked Ukraine’s power system throughout the war, mainly with missiles and Iranian-designed Shahed drones aimed at power plants and substations. Ukraine’s long transmission lines, which run across open country and are hard to defend, have been less frequent targets because individual towers and cables are small and difficult for a drone to hit and destroy. The jet-powered Shahed variants, which fly much faster than the original propeller-driven model, also give Ukrainian air defenses less time to react.

Could US sanction Netanyahu? Democrats push anti-settlement bill in House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:41:57 UTC
17:41:57 KST

Six Democratic members of the U.S. House are introducing legislation Thursday that would impose sanctions on foreign individuals and entities involved in building or expanding Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, a proposal that could potentially apply to senior Israeli government officials.
The Stop the Settlements Act is being introduced by Reps. Joaquin Castro of Texas, Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania, Don Beyer of Virginia, Greg Casar of Texas, Sara Jacobs of California and Veronica Escobar of Texas. More than 30 other House Democrats have signed on as original co-sponsors, including several longtime members of the party.
The bill would require sanctions against foreign individuals or entities involved in establishing new Israeli settlements or outposts in the West Bank or Gaza, including through infrastructure development, construction in the area known as E1 or facilitating the movement of Israeli civilians into settlements. It would also authorize measures targeting those involved in maintaining or expanding certain existing settlements and outposts.
E1 is a strategically sensitive tract of land east of Jerusalem between the city and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim. Settlement construction there has long drawn international opposition because critics say it would make a contiguous Palestinian state more difficult to establish.
Potential penalties under the legislation include blocking assets and denying or revoking U.S. visas. The measure would also prohibit imports into the United States of goods produced wholly or partly in Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, moving beyond product-labeling requirements to an import ban.
Because the legislation applies broadly to foreign individuals and entities involved in settlement activity, Israeli government officials could potentially fall within its scope. U.S. citizens would be exempt from the sanctions provisions, including Israeli settlers who also hold American citizenship.
The proposal does not itself provide a comprehensive list of locations considered settlements, leaving implementation and sanctions designations to the executive branch.
The bill represents a broader approach than previous U.S. sanctions targeting individuals accused of violence or destabilizing activity in the West Bank. Its sponsors say they are seeking to use economic pressure against settlement construction and expansion itself.
Castro said the legislation was intended to give individuals and companies a choice between participating in settlement activity and maintaining access to the U.S. economy. He said he plans to continue pressing the issue “in the coming months and in the next Congress.”
Supporters of the legislation argue that settlement expansion displaces Palestinians and undermines the prospects for a negotiated Israeli-Palestinian settlement. Several sponsors also characterize Israeli settlements as violations of international law. Israel disputes some international legal characterizations of the settlements and has historically argued that the status of the territories should be resolved through negotiations.
The proposal comes amid growing criticism among congressional Democrats of Israeli settlement policy. J Street, a U.S. organization that describes itself as pro-Israel and pro-peace, endorsed the legislation, saying economic consequences were needed after decades of international opposition to settlement expansion.
The legislation faces significant obstacles in the current Republican-controlled House and under President Donald Trump, making enactment in the current Congress unlikely. Its sponsors, however, are framing it partly as groundwork for a future Congress.
A senior Democratic official said the prospects for such legislation would also be affected by the outcome of Israel’s elections and whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current governing coalition remains in power. The official said senior Democrats’ ability to block such measures “depends entirely on whether the current coalition continues. If it does, these laws will pass.” That assessment represents the official’s political judgment rather than a certainty about future congressional action.

U.S. Air Force taps BAE for pulsed laser research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:33:42 UTC
17:33:42 KST

- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded BAE Systems a contract worth up to $19.7 million for pulsed and solid-state laser research.
- Work will take place at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, through September 2031, with $1 million obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has hired BAE Systems to work out how pulsed lasers could be used for military missions and how to pair solid-state lasers with beam control systems the U.S. Air Force already has, under a contract worth up to $19.7 million.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, for a program called Laser Utilization for Military Innovation and Novel Applications, went to BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Broomfield, Colorado. The laboratory obligated $1 million in fiscal 2026 research funds at the time of award, and the work runs through Sept. 29, 2031. Six companies bid for it.
The contract notice describes two goals: finding ways to use the advantages of pulsed lasers, and integrating solid-state laser technology with existing beam control systems. A pulsed laser releases its energy in very short, intense bursts, while a continuous-wave laser, the type used in most laser weapons fielded so far, delivers a steady beam. Beam control is the set of optics, sensors and tracking equipment that points a laser, keeps it locked on a moving target and corrects for distortion in the air, and it is often the hardest part of making a laser weapon work.
The notice does not say what military applications the U.S. Air Force has in mind, whether the work is aimed at weapons, sensing, communications or something else, or what kind of targets or platforms are involved.
All of the work will take place at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, home to the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Directed Energy Directorate, which leads the service’s research on high-energy lasers and high-power microwaves.
BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems is the former Ball Aerospace, which BAE Systems bought in 2024. The Colorado unit builds spacecraft, satellite instruments and optical and sensor systems for the U.S. military and NASA.
As a cost-plus contract with a maximum ceiling, the deal reimburses BAE Systems for its costs plus a fixed fee, and the U.S. Air Force is not obligated to spend the full $19.7 million.

design museum gent reopens with new wing built from locally made waste bricks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:30:02 UTC
17:30:02 KST

design museum gent reopens with new wing built from locally made waste bricks
carmody groarke and ATAMA lead the new extension, while RE-ST restores the historic buildings as part of a wider transformation that rethinks the museum’s collection, exhibitions and public spaces.
Design Museum Gent opens its collection to new perspectives
Design Museum Gent in Ghent, Belgium, reopens on October 3rd, 2026, following a four-year renovation and expansion led by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, with the historic buildings restored by RE-ST. The project repositions the museum as an open civic space where design is used to examine how objects, cities and social systems are shaped. The new 2,200-square-meter wing completes the fragmented museum complex around its historic courtyard and introduces freely accessible spaces for exhibitions, workshops, lectures, events and community activity. The extension uses timber and white brick, with a facade made from Gent Waste Brick (find designboom’s previous coverage here), a lime-cured brick produced from locally sourced municipal waste. More than 82,000 bricks were produced locally at Het Arsenaal in Ghent, hardened through a low-energy lime-curing process.
Its new exhibition, Collection. Models from the Past for the Future, places around 500 objects from the museum’s 24,000-piece collection into contemporary themes including copy, comfort, migration, folds and connections, asking what earlier design ideas can still offer and what now needs to be reconsidered. Meanwhile, Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy treats democratic systems themselves as designed structures, while projects such as the AI-powered Searcher and the collaborative CO-LAB extend the role of the institution from displaying design to testing how it can operate as a tool for participation, debate and change.
completing a fragmented museum in ghent, belgium
The architectural project brings together a complex collection of buildings dating from the 16th to the 20th century, working to connect the existing parts into a more coherent whole. The new wing occupies a previously underused southern passage and an unused plot at the center of the site. Its addition allows the historic courtyard of Hotel de Coninck to become a garden and a central point of orientation, with views toward it running through the building and helping visitors understand the relationship between the different parts of the museum.
The building is organized around six zones: the basement art-handling area, the Stadskamer reception and shop, the Forum lecture space, the Atelier workshops, the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions, and the Loft, an event space on the fourth floor with views over Ghent. The Stadskamer, conceived as a freely accessible ‘city room,’ is intended as a place where local communities and neighborhoods can meet and present their own creations.
The white color of the new wing relates to the historic houses along Drabstraat, while the scale and rhythm of the facade draw from Ghent’s guild and merchant houses. Deep window reveals and pronounced copings give the contemporary building a civic presence without attempting to imitate its historic neighbors. Historic interiors have been restored, while later additions have been adapted to create additional space and improve climatic conditions. Materials are reused where possible, positioning the renovation as an exercise in working with what already exists.
looking at the collection differently
The renewed architectural framework of the Design Museum Gent is matched by a change in how its collection is presented. Collection. Models from the Past for the Future, curated by Evelien Bracke, returns to the institution’s origins as a ‘model museum.’ Founded in 1903, Design Museum Gent originally collected exemplary objects intended to inform and inspire craftspeople and visitors. The new display takes that premise and turns it into a contemporary question. Around 500 objects are organized around five themes, copy, comfort, migration, folds and connections, rather than being presented primarily through individual designers or chronological development. The curatorial goal is to make historical design less about established canon and more about changing interpretation. Objects once regarded as exemplary can now be reconsidered through contemporary concerns, while historical techniques and approaches can offer unexpected models for the future. Contemporary designers including Kana Arioka, OpenStructures and Victor Verhelst respond to objects and themes from the collection, bringing them into conversation with new work and showing how the archive can continue to inform contemporary practice.
The scenography of the exhibition by Nord + Laura Muyldermans also stages a conversation between different forms of making. Traditional clay-plastered walls are combined with the Belgian circular steel construction system Skellet, placing artisanal and industrial approaches alongside one another.
from objects to democratic systems
The museum’s most direct expansion of its design remit comes through Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy, the opening exhibition curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti. The premise is straightforward but consequential: democratic systems are designed. Ballot papers, parliamentary buildings and voting procedures are visible manifestations of that design, but so are the less tangible structures that determine who participates, who is represented and who is heard.
The exhibition considers questions of accessibility, including how people experiencing homelessness or visual impairments interact with electoral systems, alongside histories of women’s suffrage, civil rights and protest. Its Democracy Fitness Trail extends the exhibition into an interactive format. Visitors are invited to practice skills such as active listening, compromise and constructive conflict, treating democratic participation as something that can be exercised.
The approach grew partly from DE40, a citizens’ panel in which 40 residents of Ghent discussed how the museum could make design more accessible and relevant to people regardless of their background or prior knowledge. Their input was used as a framework for the museum’s transformation.
an institution that experiments with its own tools
 Technology becomes another way for Design Museum Gent to question how collections are accessed.
 Searcher, developed by Jon Stam, Valentin Vogelman and Boris Smeenk, uses AI to allow visitors to explore the collection of the museum through similarities in form, color and text. A museum archive can easily become a fixed narrative, organized around established classifications and historical hierarchies. Searcher presents it as a network that can be navigated through association and discovery.
The museum is also using its physical spaces as a platform for collaborative production. CO-LAB, curated by Siegrid Demyttenaere, brings Belgian and international designers, researchers and local communities together across eight historic period rooms in Hotel de Coninck. The projects address subjects including sustainable energy, queer archives, designing with nature and open-source tools.

 opening: October 3rd, 2026
 new wing area: 2,200 sqm

'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' documentary in detailed response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:29:32 UTC
17:29:32 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- 'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' film in detailed response
'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' film in detailed response
In a detailed rebuttal to the documentary "NAZA," the IDF said the film relies on anonymous, uncorroborated testimony from junior intelligence personnel to mischaracterize the IDF's strike process
The IDF published a formal response to the documentary "NAZA," saying it presents "a distorted, misleading, and disingenuous picture" of the military's target planning and strike process. The IDF said the film's narrative relies on testimony from anonymous individuals who generally describe only the initial, intelligence-gathering stages of a much longer targeting process, resulting in what it called "an incorrect and highly misleading description of reality."
The military noted that "NAZA" is the Hebrew acronym for "collateral damage," a standard term used by law-abiding militaries worldwide. It points out that the film paradoxically presents the IDF's detailed civilian harm estimation process as evidence of indifference to civilian life, when such assessments are in fact required under international law.
The IDF said the filmmakers did not submit their allegations for examination before publication and declined to provide the IDF a copy of the film after a public screening, despite the military's request. As a result, the IDF said it based its response on an account from a representative who attended a public screening, along with other public reporting and statements from the filmmakers themselves.
The IDF argued that the anonymous interviewees spoke about matters beyond their knowledge and competence, and testimony confined to preliminary stages does not establish the final assessments on which commanders relied. For example, an interviewee may recall a general, preliminary estimate of civilians present in an area around a military objective, but did not account for precautions decided later in the process.
Suggested articles
Additionally, the IDF claimed that besides the anonymous accounts, the film did not cite any military directives, contemporaneous records, or other corroborating evidence. The film's accounts of alleged strikes include no specific targets, dates, locations, or casualty figures, making the claims "general and unverifiable," the IDF claims.
Among the specific claims addressed, the IDF denied that artificial intelligence autonomously generated tens of thousands of human targets that were then struck, stating flatly that "in the IDF, artificial intelligence does not determine whether an object or a person is designated as a target, nor whether a target is struck." The military said human analysts identify targets under defined procedures, with decisions ultimately made by operational commanders.
Regarding allegations that soldiers fired on civilians near humanitarian aid distribution sites, the IDF said rules of engagement permitted fire only against armed operatives or suspects posing an immediate threat.
The IDF strongly rejected the film's suggestion that an interviewee's personal view constituted evidence of genocide, calling the allegation "outrageous and unfounded." It noted that genocide under international law requires specific intent to destroy a group, which it said, "never existed."
The military said its objectives in Gaza were to dismantle Hamas's military and governing capabilities and secure the return of hostages, not to harm Palestinian civilians. The IDF pointed to its warnings, strike cancellations, and facilitation of humanitarian aid, including more than 3.9 million metric tons of food delivered into Gaza since October 2023, as evidence against the claim.
The IDF said the film omits essential context necessary to understand its conduct during the war, including the October 7 massacre and Hamas's systematic embedding of military infrastructure within civilian areas such as hospitals, schools and mosques. It said the film's narrative is reinforced through "manipulative editing of interviews" and omits the professionals, including legal advisers and commanders, responsible for mitigating civilian harm throughout the targeting process.
"The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts," the IDF said, adding that "the IDF has acted and continues to act humanely, even if the filmmakers have done everything they can to conceal that fact."

Casio’s Crystal G-Shock Is the Most Expensive Ever Made
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:59 UTC
17:25:59 KST

At Madison Square Garden in New York City on November 9, 2017, at the G-Shock 35th Anniversary Celebration, G-Shock creator Kikuo Ibe showed off three sapphire-crystal prototype watches: one clear, one ruby, and one sapphire blue. Because machining sapphire was so difficult at the time, each watch took over a month to produce.
These were built with, for the time, high-end Casio features such as Tough Solar power and Multiband 6 radio-controlled timekeeping—but as they didn’t meet the G-Shock shock-resistance standards, the trio was never intended for sale. They were primarily a symbol of innovation for the Japanese brand, which started in 1983 specializing in super-tough performance timepieces.
Now, nine years later, in what Casio is calling the culmination of an “eight-year project” (so presumably the ball started rolling soon after the excited reception Ibe’s crystal concepts got on stage at MSG), G-Shock is launching a three-watch collection using blue sapphire as an expression of what happens when G-Shock toughness meets Japanese engineering. The flagship model, and by far the most expensive, is the $80,000 MRG-D5000, the first-ever retail G-Shock with an outer case and bezel hewn entirely from blue sapphire crystal.
The collection is called the “Blue Rose Project” because the blue rose is viewed as a symbol of making the impossible possible since it doesn’t exist in nature. It sees the super-expensive MRG-D5000 released alongside the $9,500 MRG-B5000SA-2, and the GMW-B5000SB-1A for $850.
Only 20 of the $80,000 MRG-D5000 full-sapphire G-Shocks will be made, putting these rugged “luxury” timepieces somewhat implausibly in the same price bracket as a Patek Philippe or Porsche Macan. This is quite the flex from a company that also sells its watches for less than $90.
The 2017 concept watches required metal bracing to hold the crystal sections together, which is partly why they couldn’t pass G-Shock’s rigorous toughness tests. The new MRG-D5000, however, is a fully functional G-Shock, taking construction lessons from the MR-G engineering team who found that dividing the outer case into multiple interacting components could disperse impact more effectively than a conventional single-piece construction.
G-Shock fans will have already seen this technique employed in the titanium MRG-B5000 from 2022, but this “Multi-Guard Structure” has now been reengineered specifically for sapphire crystal, with Casio claiming the construction takes inspiration from traditional Japanese timber-frame techniques, using interlocking pieces rather than placing stress around screw holes or other details that could result in cracking.
While the MRG-D5000’s bezel and outer case are entirely machined from blue sapphire crystal ingots grown over several months, sadly—unlike the 2017 concepts—the strap isn’t matching sapphire but instead a rubber strap that repeats the brick pattern seen on the watch face in raised detail. To round off the luxe makeover, the MRG-D5000’s MR-G mark, “Shock Resist,” and other lettering on the face are in 24-carat gold.
The G-Shock development team responsible for the new collection tells WIRED the fundamental challenge was building a “near-unbreakable” watch using an inherently brittle material. Making watch cases from sapphire is not new in the high-end watch world, and many distinguished makers, including Richard Mille and Hublot, have released pieces made of the crystal.
To make the sapphire case work for a G-Shock, however, Casio had to develop a brand-new, dedicated shock-resistant structure, with the Multi-Guard construction using virtually invisible seams, alongside a completely screwless assembly method to hit the required shock performance. To do this, the outer case assembly required the development of completely new, dedicated jigs and fixtures, a process apparently so demanding that only one person at Yamagata Casio (the primary “mother factory” for Casio) can currently perform it.
All three new watches, along with the proper G-Shock resistance to knocks and drops, are water-resistant to 200 meters, solar-powered, and feature radio-controlled timekeeping, world time, stopwatch, countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full-auto LED backlight.
If the $80K G-Shock is too steep an investment, the MRG-B5000SA-2 with two two-carat facet-cut blue sapphires and a grade-5 titanium exterior is limited to 500 pieces. The cheapest GMW-B5000SB-1A2 marries a full-metal black exterior with four round brilliant-cut blue sapphires.

U.S. Navy buys more 30mm guns to shoot down drones
Unknown
