- The U.S. Navy awarded MSI Defence Systems US a $197 million sole-source contract for MK88 MOD4 30 mm gun mounts and MK48 MOD2 sights.
- Most of the work will be done in Norfolk, England, with deliveries due by January 2031.
The U.S. Navy has awarded British-owned MSI Defence Systems a $197 million contract for 30mm deck gun mounts and the electro-optical sights that aim them, the weapons the service is fitting to its warships to shoot down small drones and fast attack boats.
The firm-fixed-price contract, issued by Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland, covers MK88 MOD4 gun mounts, MK48 MOD2 electro-optical sights, related hardware and spares. The Department of War did not say how many systems it buys. Deliveries are due to finish by January 2031.
Together with an operator console, the gun mount and sight make up the MK 38 MOD 4 gun weapon system, which replaces the 25 mm MK 38 MOD 3 on U.S. Navy ships. The U.S. Navy has said the older system fell short of its requirements for countering drones, and the new version adds a larger 30 mm MK44 Bushmaster II cannon, with an optional coaxial .50-caliber machine gun. The mount holds 400 rounds in two separate ammunition bins, letting the crew switch between ammunition types.
Unlike earlier versions, the MOD 4 places its camera sight away from the gun rather than on the mount itself, so the system can track a target independently and pass aiming data to the gun. The design is based on MSI’s Seahawk DS30M A2 mount, a family of guns already used by the Royal Navy and other fleets.
The destroyer USS Mustin (DDG 89) became the first U.S. Navy warship to receive the system, with two mounts installed during a maintenance period in San Diego, Naval News reported in April 2024. The U.S. Navy plans to replace the 25 mm guns on its Arleigh Burke-class destroyers with the new system, and the U.S. Coast Guard also uses it.
The new contract is far larger than earlier orders. MSI received about $23.5 million in September 2023 for 15 gun mounts in low-rate production and about $34.5 million in late 2025 for 18 more, along with separate deals for the sight system. The company first delivered eight prototype systems for testing.
The U.S. Navy awarded the contract without competition under a legal exception for production that follows prototypes successfully completed under an other transaction agreement, a faster contracting route used for experimental work.
Most of the work, 73%, will take place at MSI’s facilities in Norfolk, England, with 19% at its U.S. subsidiary in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and the rest in Bozeman, Montana, and Eagleville, Pennsylvania. MSI Defence Systems is part of British company MS International.
The U.S. Navy obligated about $61.3 million at the time of award, drawing on weapons procurement and shipbuilding funds from fiscal 2023 through 2026, including money from accounts used to build new ships.

U.S. Marine Corps orders 32 ACV-R armored recovery vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:17:35 UTC
17:17:35 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps awarded BAE Systems a $230.1 million contract modification for 32 full-rate production ACV recovery variants.
- Work will be performed mainly in York, Pennsylvania, with completion expected in November 2028.
The U.S. Marine Corps has ordered 32 recovery versions of its Amphibious Combat Vehicle from BAE Systems, the armored repair-and-tow vehicles that will haul broken-down or damaged ACVs off the battlefield and fix them in the field.
Marine Corps Systems Command awarded BAE Systems a $230.1 million firm-fixed-price modification on Oct. 1 to exercise options for the 32 full-rate production vehicles, along with production, fielding and support costs and spare parts. That works out to about $7.2 million per vehicle, though the figure includes support and spares as well as the vehicles themselves. The work is due to finish in November 2028.
The recovery variant, known as ACV-R, is the fourth and final member of the ACV family, which is replacing the U.S. Marine Corps’ decades-old Assault Amphibious Vehicles. It is designed to give field-level maintenance and towing support to other ACVs, and it replaces the AAV recovery variant, the AAVR7A1, which Marines have kept using while the new vehicle was developed.
The U.S. Marine Corps started paying for the recovery variant in March 2022 with a $34.9 million contract for its design and development, and BAE Systems was due to deliver production-representative test vehicles in 2025. The service said in 2023 that the ACV-R would not reach initial operational capability until early fiscal 2028, Defense News reported, meaning the first units could field it about a year before this order is due to be completed.
The rest of the ACV family is already in service or production. The basic personnel carrier, ACV-P, carries three crew and 13 Marines and has been in full-rate production since December 2020, followed by the ACV-C command and control version. A third variant, the ACV-30, carries a remotely operated 30 mm cannon. BAE Systems builds the eight-wheeled vehicle with Italian partner Iveco Defence Vehicles, whose design it is based on.
Most of the new work, 60%, will take place at BAE Systems’ plant in York, Pennsylvania, with 15% each in Aiken, South Carolina, and San Jose, California, and 5% each in Sterling Heights, Michigan, and Stafford, Virginia. The full order is paid for with fiscal 2026 U.S. Marine Corps procurement funds.
The underlying ACV contract is worth up to $4.1 billion if all options are exercised.

Nearly month after controversy, IDF hits back at ‘NAZA’ film over ‘manipulative misrepresentations’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:15:53 UTC
17:15:53 KST

“The film 'NAZA' presents a distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process. The film's narrative is based on substantial factual errors stemming from manipulative misrepresentations of reality,” the military said Thursday morning, responding to the film by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Shor nearly a month after it sparked controversy.
The IDF then listed several points that it said contradicted claims made in the film.
In the first, the military said: “Binding IDF directives explicitly, comprehensively and clearly distinguish between military operatives and uninvolved civilians in Gaza. IDF targeting processes are fundamentally based on this distinction, prohibit intentionally directing strikes against civilians, and require mitigating the possibility of harm to them to the greatest extent feasible.”
In its second point, the IDF said: “The IDF has never planned, approved or carried out any strike in Gaza in which 500 civilians or anything close to that number were expected to be killed. Nor has anyone seriously alleged that an IDF strike caused deaths on that scale or anything close to it.”
“Artificial intelligence has never independently selected targets to strike in the IDF,” the military said in its third point. “The identification of targets to strike is done only by authorized intelligence officers, strikes are planned by relevant professionals, and the decision whether to strike is made by operational commanders.”
According to the fourth point, “Binding IDF directives have never granted automatic authorization for strikes against targets placing a fixed number of civilians at risk (such as 20 in a strike against a junior operative or 200 in a strike against a senior commander, as a person in the film claims).”
In its fifth point, the military said that “‘Lavender’ is not a database of targets approved to strike, but a database that assists intelligence analysts.”
“Binding IDF directives do not permit an evacuation warning for an area to be treated as authorization to carry out strikes there while disregarding civilians who remain,” the military said in its sixth point.
Finally, in its seventh point, the IDF said: “The IDF does not ignore the aftermath of its strikes but acts to assess them, including with regard to unintended civilian harm, contrary to the claim in the film. These assessments have prompted reviews of hundreds of incidents during the hostilities and provide a basis for lessons learned.”
‘Distortion of reality through manipulative editing of interviews’
The IDF Spokesperson’s Unit later said in a statement: “Had the filmmakers conducted adequate verification and corroboration of facts in good faith, as professional standards require, they could have identified the substantial errors presented in the film. The end result shows that they did not.”
“Many errors arise because the interviewees, described as having served in IDF intelligence roles, usually refer to only limited, initial stages dealing with intelligence, rather than the much broader process of planning and approving strikes. That process is not the responsibility of intelligence, but of operational bodies that manage and carry out targeting processes.
“Accordingly, it is apparent that in various cases interviewees raise speculation and assumptions without a factual basis.
“The filmmakers chose not to show many of the other individuals involved in the full targeting process – those responsible for planning that mitigates civilian harm, legal advisers who review proposed strikes, and commanders responsible for approving or rejecting them. The result, as noted, is an incorrect and highly misleading portrayal of reality.
“To fit the narrative the film seeks to promote, the filmmakers also omit context essential to understanding the war in Gaza and the IDF’s conduct during it.
“The film does not give due weight to Israel’s security reasons for operating in Gaza and the October 7th Massacre; to Hamas’ deliberate strategy of embedding itself within the civilian population, which is the root cause of harm to civilians; or the countless actions and methods the IDF employed to mitigate civilian harm, including warnings before strikes, selection of munitions and appropriate strike planning, facilitating humanitarian aid and more.
“The processes and decisions the film omits show what the IDF’s effort to protect civilians meant in practice – additional required intelligence, plans changed, strikes cancelled and military opportunities forgone. These decisions restricted the use of force solely because of assessed risks to civilians.
“Particularly troubling is the film's further distortion of reality through manipulative editing of interviews, irresponsible allusions to historical atrocities, and its false and baseless attribution of malicious intentions to the IDF.
“Even the film’s title inverts reality. “NAZA” is an acronym of the Hebrew term “Nezek Agavi”, which means “collateral damage” in English. This is a professional term used by every law-abiding military worldwide to describe incidental harm to civilians resulting from a strike on a military objective, which serves commanders to assess the lawfulness of the strike and adopt measures to mitigate harm to civilians to the greatest extent feasible.
“Paradoxically, the film portrays the exceptional effort and detail the IDF devotes to estimating civilian harm in strikes as indifference to civilian lives.
“In reality, assessing expected harm to civilians in strikes is a requirement under international law. The IDF conducts this assessment so commanders can determine whether a strike is lawful, direct additional precautions, modify the strike plan or cancel the strike, all to mitigate the possibility of harm to civilians to the greatest extent feasible, as IDF commanders did many times during the war.
“The IDF is open to hearing genuine criticism of its conduct and attaches importance to learning from substantiated allegations and continually improving its practices. It is bound by and committed to international humanitarian law, its operational procedures are designed to implement those legal obligations, and it operates dedicated units and mechanisms to mitigate civilian harm.
“The IDF does not disavow deficiencies and errors that occurred during the war; they do occur in complex combat situations. Suspected violations of the law or IDF directives are examined and, where warranted, addressed through disciplinary action, criminal investigation or other measures.
“Contrary to accepted practice, the filmmakers did not submit their allegations to the IDF for examination and response before publication, nor did they provide a copy of the film after its screening, although the IDF requested it. Therefore, in assessing the film’s contents, the IDF relied on a detailed account from a representative who attended a public screening, as well as other public accounts.”
The film “NAZA” presents what it describes as troubling testimony from 24 soldiers, allegedly from Unit 8200, the IDF's elite signals intelligence and cyber unit, about IDF operations during the war in Gaza.
The film, which was shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv during the war, includes interviewees who claim they were involved in “war crimes and genocide” and describe policies relating to collateral damage, bombardments and targeted killings.
One of the film’s central themes is the use of artificial intelligence, which interviewees claim was used, among other things, to recommend targets for assassination based on intercepted phone communications, including in cases in which a strike was expected to kill family members of targeted individuals.

Iliyan Filipov was a businessman from Plovdiv and the owner of PIMK, a major Bulgarian transport and construction company with interests including rail transport and real estate. He also owned Botev Plovdiv football club.
Born in Plovdiv on March 31, 1973, Filipov was one of the two co-founders and owners of PIMK. The company operates through numerous subsidiaries involved in construction, freight forwarding, rail transport, concrete production and quarrying.

U.S. Air Force buys 40 electronic warfare kits for F-15EX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:09:09 UTC
17:09:09 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded BAE Systems a $146.7 million sole-source contract for 40 EPAWSS hardware sets for F-15EX Lots 7 and 8.
- Work will take place in Nashua, New Hampshire, through August 2030, with $58.8 million obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded BAE Systems a $146.7 million contract for 40 sets of the electronic warfare suite that protects the F-15EX Eagle II, covering jets in the fighter’s seventh and eighth production lots.
The sole-source contract, announced by the Department of War, buys 40 production hardware sets of the Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System, known as EPAWSS, along with magazines and retainers for the jet’s countermeasure dispensers. BAE Systems will do the work in Nashua, New Hampshire, and expects to finish by Aug. 31, 2030. The U.S. Air Force obligated $58.8 million in fiscal 2025 and 2026 procurement funds at the time of award, and the full value works out to roughly $3.7 million per set.
EPAWSS is the F-15’s built-in self-protection system. It warns the crew when enemy radars are tracking the jet, works out where those radars are, jams them, and controls the release of chaff and flares to decoy incoming missiles. Every F-15EX is built with EPAWSS installed at Boeing’s St. Louis factory, and the U.S. Air Force is also retrofitting the system into part of its older F-15E Strike Eagle fleet, where it replaces an analog electronic warfare suite in use since the 1980s.
The award follows a U.S. Air Force move to add a capability EPAWSS does not cover. On Sept. 29, the F-15 program office asked industry for an already-qualified missile warning system that could be fitted into six sensor locations built into the F-15EX for that purpose, The Defence Blog reported. EPAWSS focuses on radar threats, while a dedicated missile warning system looks for the heat or light of an incoming missile’s motor, including heat-seeking missiles that give off no radar signal.
The F-15EX is a two-seat, heavily modernized version of the F-15 that the U.S. Air Force is buying mainly to replace its aging F-15C and F-15D fighters. The order for Lot 7 and Lot 8 hardware means EPAWSS supply is being lined up for jets that will be built over the next several years, and the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request asked for 24 more F-15EX aircraft.
EPAWSS cleared full-rate production in early 2025, and the U.S. Air Force has since opened a dedicated installation line at Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex in Georgia to speed upgrades of F-15Es outside their regular depot maintenance.

A New Lens on Modern Heritage: ArchDaily Partners with World Monuments Fund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

What makes a building worth preserving? Age is the most common answer, but not always the best one. A building from the 1950s or 70s may carry as much historical significance as a medieval cathedral; it simply demands a different framework, one that weighs political context, cultural meaning, and architectural innovation over the mere passage of time. This is especially true for modernist architecture across the so-called Global South, where the movement took on unique forms of expression.
It is precisely this conversation that ArchDaily and World Monuments Fund are now opening together. WMF brings on-the-ground conservation expertise across the world, and ArchDaily brings the editorial capacity to contextualize that work and connect it to a global audience. The goal is to do both at once: preserve places and tell their stories, shaping how modernist heritage is understood far beyond the field of preservation itself.
To mark the start of this collaboration, we spoke with Javier Ors Ausín, Director of Thematic Programs at World Monuments Fund, and Christele Harrouk, Editor-in-Chief of ArchDaily. Read the full conversation below.
Related Article
United Nations’ Africa Hall Restoration in Ethiopia Receives 2026 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize
Romullo Baratto [Managing Editor]: What does this partnership mean to World Monuments Fund and ArchDaily? Javier, would you like to begin?
Javier Ors Ausín: This is a new partnership for World Monuments Fund, and we are genuinely exploring what it means as it unfolds. But what strikes me as particularly special is how complementary our roles are. At WMF, we engage directly with sites, implementing conservation projects, advocacy initiatives, and documentation of heritage preservation work. We work with governments, communities, local NGOs, and professionals in the field. Having ArchDaily as a partner — a platform that communicates architecture to an international audience through a broad network — means we can both engage with sites and preserve them, while also explaining why this work matters and why these places are globally relevant. The ability to pursue preservation and narration in parallel is very valuable.
Christele Harrouk: I really like what Javier said about this complementarity. We represent two complementary forms of responsibility toward architecture. WMF works with communities, places, and physical conservation. We work on narration, giving the world access to these stories. What makes this collaboration so meaningful is that it brings both capacities together and makes the work accessible to a global audience, while also contributing to safeguarding it.
 Because talking about something, documenting it, is itself a form of conservation. For ArchDaily, this partnership is particularly significant because we see ourselves as active participants in architectural culture. This collaboration gives us a chance to reflect that — to help shape what conservation is, what heritage is, and how people understand and engage with it.
JOA: Exactly. By doing the editorial and communication work, you are making communication itself part of the conservation process. In the conservation field, we sometimes limit ourselves to before-and-after photographs. But communicating the work from beginning to end is also conservation; it builds visibility, awareness, and ultimately support for the initiatives and field projects we undertake.
RB: Christele, why World Monuments Fund, and why now?
CH: ArchDaily has been around for 18 years. Almost two decades documenting and doing more than what a platform typically does. Our role goes beyond documentation and narration: we contextualize, connect information, make knowledge available, and we explain why it matters. Over those years, heritage has been a recurring thread. So when WMF came along, the timing felt exactly right — we had, in some sense, built everything toward it. They brought conservation knowledge, on-the-ground expertise, and active projects. We brought our editorial team, our global audience, and our archive. It was the best timing.
JOA: When I joined World Monuments Fund as an architect, almost ten years ago, I realized how segregated our field was. A lot of experts working in heritage preservation were not really part of the broader architectural conversations and discourses. Partnering with ArchDaily is a way of reconnecting the specialized discussions happening in the heritage field with the broader architectural discourse. There is no better partner for that: ArchDaily is genuinely shaping and actively participating in the global architectural conversation.
CH: I'd add one more dimension: what World Monuments Fund and ArchDaily together make possible is not just ensuring that the architecture that matters survives physically, but that the knowledge around it also survives. That, for me, is the core of this partnership.
RB: One of the defining features of the partnership is the focus on modernist architecture, with a particular emphasis on the Global South. Javier, why do you think that is the right frame for this collaboration?
JOA: What initially drew me to the field of preservation and documentation of modernist architecture was the opportunity to tell a larger story about 20th-century architecture. In my experience as an architect, the established narrative around modern architecture heritage remains quite narrow, focused primarily on the United States and Europe.
 But modernism was not confined to those regions. It took different shapes in South America, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East, adapting to different climates, materials, and technologies. Since joining WMF, part of my mission has been to tell that larger story through our sites and projects.
To give concrete examples: we developed a conservation management plan for the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium in India, a brutalist structure designed by Charles Correa and Mahendra Raj during the post-independence period. The urgency was heightened after the demolition of modernist sites in India, but also because these buildings are aging and require expert conservation management. In Africa, we are currently working in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, in a remarkable and relatively unknown example of modernist architecture deeply grounded in the local climate and vernacular construction traditions, using earthen materials and natural ventilation. The partnership with ArchDaily is an opportunity to expand that global narrative while also addressing the real technical challenges these buildings face.
RB: Christele, you've mentioned ArchDaily's coverage on heritage throughout the years. How do you see WMF's work fitting into ArchDaily's agenda?
CH: Being global is foundational for ArchDaily, but what we've been working toward is becoming more intentional about what "global" actually means. It is not just about publishing projects from many countries. It is about understanding architecture in its full context: shaped by climate, culture, politics, materials, economies, communities, and histories. That applies directly to modernism. We have long questioned the idea that architectural movements radiated, unchanged, from one center outward. We know that they were transformed, became hybrid, were appropriated, and challenged. Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, Central Asia — all of these places produced distinct histories of modernism.
 When we choose what to publish and how to contextualize it, we are participating in the construction of architectural history. We are adjusting the narrative. That has been central to our work for at least a decade.
With WMF, we have the opportunity to take it further: to discover more places, more contexts, more projects, and to push forward the idea that preserving modernism also means shaping what becomes visible and what is taken as a reference.
RB: When we think about heritage, modernist buildings don't enjoy the same prestige as, for instance, a Gothic cathedral or a medieval town when it comes to preservation. Javier, how do you build the case for this kind of work? How do you approach governments, communities, and other stakeholders?
JOA: That is the fundamental challenge. A medieval building, a castle, a cathedral, a mosque, is automatically recognized as a place of historical value and significance. A building from the 1950s, 60s, or 70s has to constantly prove that it embodies heritage values, historical significance, and architectural innovation. That is frustrating for anyone working in this field, but it is also the central challenge we all contribute to overcoming.
 Our approach is grounded in interpretation and education. We work to show — to communities living near these sites, to governments, to the broader public — that the value of these places is not based solely on age, but on the political and historical context in which they were built and the architectural innovation they represent.
Take the United Nations' Africa Hall in Addis Ababa, recognized by WMF in 2026 for its restoration project. Its importance is not that it dates to a particular decade. It lies in what it represents: decolonization, institution-building in Africa, the creation of a continental platform for political discussion. The fact that it was built in Ethiopia — the only African country never colonized — is, itself, a layer of historical significance. There is also remarkable architectural innovation in its use of reinforced concrete. Much remains to be done in terms of interpretation and knowledge dissemination to overcome the perception that these buildings are too recent to be preserved. In fact, many of them are approaching a century of age. Interpretation, ultimately, is where the opportunity lies.
RB: Many of the cities where these buildings are located are facing rapid urban growth. How do conservation and urban development coexist? How do we balance civic interest, land value, and the preservation of buildings that, as you've said, are not measured by age alone?
CH: I don't see them as opposing forces. We tend to forget that cities are living systems, and that heritage, the buildings we're discussing, was always part of those systems and evolved alongside them. The question we should always be asking is how we allow our cities to change, to grow, to evolve, while also understanding what they already carry culturally, socially, and in terms of heritage value.
And not just what that value is, but who gets to define it. That question is crucial. WMF is doing important work in redefining which buildings can be considered to carry value, not necessarily because of specific construction techniques, but because of their place in the urban fabric, the stories they hold, and how they are embedded in the lives of the communities around them. In rapidly changing cities, the communities living in these places must be part of determining their future. Heritage cannot be defined only institutionally or architecturally, without understanding its collective and lived value. It is not a question of conservation or urban growth — it is a question of how our cities can evolve with a greater awareness of what already exists, what we need to preserve, and what we might lose in the process.
JOA: I agree entirely. People tend to see conservation and development as opposing forces, but they shouldn't. The question for me is: how can architecture and conservation serve as vehicles for informing the decisions we make about how our cities grow? Cities have always changed — and modernism itself was a force of urban transformation in the 20th century. So the question is not conservation versus growth, but rather how heritage preservation can provide the tools to ensure that when cities change, those decisions are informed by community needs, by the cultural and historical places embedded in the built environment.
 Conservation, rather than being imposed, should be one more tool in the toolkit — helping us make informed, sustainable decisions. I prefer to see it as a tool to manage change, not resist it.
This is also why I advocate for architects to be more actively involved in government, in institutions like WMF, in platforms like ArchDaily — because that is where these ideas need to be present to have real impact.
CH: That's something I say constantly: architects need to be in decision-making positions, especially in politics. Change happens faster, and with greater impact, when it comes from there.
RB: What will ArchDaily readers find on the platform that they wouldn't without this partnership?
CH: We're digitizing WMF's projects and creating an online library that will document them through project features, narratives, interviews, stories, and accounts of specific conservation processes. What we want to do is turn WMF's archive into active architectural knowledge and situate it within ArchDaily's ecosystem of architectural knowledge.
JOA: This is a genuine opportunity for WMF to present our work in a completely different way: to tell a comprehensive story about what we've been doing in modern architecture since the early 2000s, not just through completed projects but through new material we'll generate together. We will speak about projects currently underway and begin working on a new project next year, with ArchDaily as a partner. What excites me most is the idea that the editorial angle can be an integrated part of our work — not something that happens after the fact, but something that runs alongside the conservation process from the beginning.
RB: Could you tell us more about this new project for next year?
CH: This is the most exciting part. We always say architecture matters, and this is our chance to demonstrate that in practice. This will be the first ArchDaily-supported conservation project, and the financial commitment matters because it marks a shift from documenting value to actively supporting it.
 We'll follow the process from beginning to end, showcasing how the project evolves — the stages, the phases, the story behind it. It's an educational process in itself. It extends what ArchDaily is already doing; I see it as the next step, a natural continuation.
JOA: Absolutely. This is really an opportunity to go beyond a conventional communications partnership and put everything we've been discussing into real practice. WMF is constantly engaging new sites, and the scope varies enormously — from physical restoration to conservation planning, adaptive reuse, advocacy campaigns for sites under threat. We don't yet know exactly what shape this project will take with ArchDaily, but that's also part of the excitement: exploring how editorial and communications expertise can be integrated into a project from the very beginning. Knowledge sharing and visibility are also forms of advocacy — and many of these sites urgently need that.
CH: What I find most compelling is using an individual site as a reference point for larger questions. How has modernism been transformed across continents? How have political and social histories shaped architecture, and how do they continue to shape it today? How have communities changed these buildings, and what can those transformations teach us? How might all of this change our contemporary practice? Using this site to answer larger questions — about heritage, about modernism, about the world, about the narratives we tell — that is what this is really about.

Russia’s state arms giant claims a new drone-missile class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:59:51 UTC
16:59:51 KST

- Russian state conglomerate Rostec said its S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T jet-powered strike drones perform the role of cruise missiles at lower cost.
- Rostec said the weapons are already used in Ukraine and should become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec says three of its newest jet-powered strike drones, the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, can now do the job of cruise missiles at a fraction of the cost, and that all three are already being used against Ukraine.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda published on Sept. 30, describing the weapons as a new category that sits between attack drones and missiles. The company did not give prices, production numbers or performance figures for any of the three, and its claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
“In fact, a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle. However, not every UAV of this type is a cruise missile. Nevertheless, in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased,” Rostec said in its statement.
The company said the drones have the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles while being significantly cheaper than conventional missiles, and that the gap between the two kinds of weapon will keep shrinking as drone production matures. Rostec said it expects the new jet-powered drones to become a standard weapon for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside the glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023.
The S-71M and S-71K are designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Rostec told the state news agency TASS. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57’s internal weapons bay, which lets the jet carry them without spoiling its radar-evading shape, and Russia’s arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has examined debris from both. It says the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance, and that the S-71M, called Monokhrom, contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small U.S.-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board, Militarnyi reported. Some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets and can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones, which suggests the company is aiming it at export buyers. Accounts of where the Dan-T comes from differ: some analysts describe it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt, while Ukrainian experts have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T’s range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, citing Ukrainian intelligence officials who said Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025 and is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region. Ukraine’s military intelligence says the Banderol contains a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly U.S.-made electronics, Euronews reported.
Cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build, the same logic behind Russia’s mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons that includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group’s KUB loitering munitions.

Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT) has captured Omar al-Khatib, a Syrian suspect accused of helping plan the 2013 Reyhanli bombings near the Turkish-Syrian border that killed 53 people.
Al-Khatib, who was wanted under an Interpol Red Notice, was intercepted while attempting to flee to Europe by sea and brought to Türkiye, security sources said on Thursday.
The sources said he helped plan and organise the attack and coordinated contacts between its perpetrators and intelligence officers loyal to ousted regime leader Bashar al Assad.
MIT had been monitoring his activities in Syria as part of efforts to track down those responsible for the bombings in Türkiye’s southern Hatay province.
Planning and preparation
According to the sources, al-Khatib arranged meetings in 2013 between Yusuf Nazik, another planner of the attack, and Syrian intelligence official Kifah Melhem, during which details of the operation were decided.
Al-Khatib and Nazik entered Türkiye through Hatay in February that year to identify targets, subsequently obtaining approval from Melhem, who was based in Latakia, the sources said.
In May, before the attack, al-Khatib accompanied Temir Dukanci to the Latakia branch of Syrian military intelligence to collect materials for the explosive device, they added.
The sources said Dukanci and Nazik transported the bomb-laden vehicle to Reyhanli, where it was detonated remotely.
After the attack, the pair fled to Syria, where al-Khatib took them to the same military intelligence branch in Latakia. The sources alleged that the ousted Assad regime rewarded al-Khatib and the other perpetrators with money.
Efforts to track down suspects
MIT began tracking those responsible immediately after the bombings and closely monitored al-Khatib’s activities in Syria, the sources said.
His capture follows the arrests of Nazik in 2018, Cengiz Sertel in 2024, and Muhammed Dib Korali and Temir Dukanci in 2025.
Melhem, whom the sources identified as the major general who ordered the attack, was appointed head of the National Security Bureau by Assad in February 2024.
He fled abroad after the fall of the Assad regime, according to the sources.

Pentagon taps Musk and Luckey to map the future of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:39:42 UTC
16:39:42 KST

- Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced Project Meridian on Sept. 30, co-led by Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich.
- The 120-day study will identify future battlefields and the technologies U.S. forces need, with findings due in a public report.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has put Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich in charge of Project Meridian, a 120-day Pentagon study of where future wars will be fought and what weapons the U.S. military will need to win them.
Hegseth announced the project on Sept. 30 during his “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, after Pirate Wires first reported the plan. The three co-leads will work under Emil Michael, the Department of War’s chief technology officer, alongside a wider team drawn from industry, academia and the policy world, though the Pentagon has not said how many people will take part or whether the co-leads will be paid.
“Project Meridian will provide the transformative vision to secure American dominance across every future warfighting domain,” the Department of War’s chief technology office wrote on X.
In a letter launching the effort, Hegseth directed Michael to study the battlefields of the future, identify the weapons and technologies troops will need there, and propose concrete steps to start developing, testing and fielding them. The findings are due within 120 days, which puts the deadline in late January 2027, and are expected to be released in an unclassified report with a classified annex. Hegseth said the Joint Staff and all the military services should be ready to connect their own future-warfare research to the project.
Hegseth framed the effort as a look decades ahead, saying it would consider the wars the United States cannot afford to fight in 2030, 2050 and 2100. He also said the project was deliberately futuristic and was not meant to produce new strategies or policies, The Hill reported, and that the three co-leads would hold their first meeting immediately after the speech in a secure facility at the base.
The choice of leaders has drawn attention because two of them run companies that sell to the Pentagon. Musk’s SpaceX holds billions of dollars in U.S. military contracts for rocket launches and satellites, and Luckey’s Anduril builds drones, counter-drone systems and other autonomous weapons for the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy and other services, the kinds of technologies a study of future warfare is likely to examine. The Pentagon has not said how it will handle potential conflicts of interest.
The appointment is also Musk’s first official advisory role in the Trump administration since he left the Department of Government Efficiency and fell out publicly with President Donald Trump last year, Axios reported. Gingrich, who led the House from 1995 to 1999, has long written and spoken about defense reform and space policy.
Project Meridian was one of several changes Hegseth announced in the same speech, which also included a new Autonomous Warfare Command focused on robotic, drone and artificial intelligence warfare, and a plan to cut 20% of general and admiral positions by January.

ICEYE and Nokia team up on sovereign satellite internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:34:41 UTC
16:34:41 KST

- Finland's ICEYE and Nokia will jointly develop sovereign low Earth orbit broadband satellite communications systems that governments can own and control.
- The companies expect to launch the first communications satellites in 2028 and did not disclose customers, costs or satellite numbers.
Finnish satellite company ICEYE and telecommunications group Nokia will jointly develop broadband satellite communications systems that governments can own and run themselves, with the first satellites expected to launch in 2028, the two companies said on Oct. 1.
The systems will use satellites in low Earth orbit, a few hundred kilometers above the surface, to give defense forces, border guards, emergency services and disaster response teams fast, high-capacity connections over priority areas when ground networks are damaged or cut. Each customer country would own the satellites, the ground stations and the user terminals. Neither company disclosed how many satellites a national system would include, what it would cost, or whether any government has signed up.
“Nations must be able to fully own and control their communications, without dependency on a foreign commercial operator’s terms of service,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE.
The companies said the systems are meant to work alongside existing military and commercial networks, adding coverage and backup capacity. ICEYE will bring its experience building and delivering satellites, and Nokia its secure networking technology, with the two integrating the satellites, ground infrastructure and rugged terminals into one package.
ICEYE is best known for its radar imaging satellites, which can photograph the ground through cloud and darkness, and it has built a business selling countries their own satellites rather than only selling images. The new venture applies the same model to communications.
“We delivered Poland its own radar satellite system in under a year. Partnering with Nokia lets us move at a similar speed for satellite communications, on the timelines nations need,” Modrzewski said.
Poland bought its own constellation of ICEYE radar satellites in 2025, making it one of the first countries to own a dedicated fleet built on the company’s design.
Modrzewski’s comment about foreign operators touches on a debate that has run through European capitals since the war in Ukraine showed how much militaries can come to depend on SpaceX’s Starlink network, which is owned and controlled by a private American company. The European Union is building its own secure communications constellation, IRIS², but it is not expected to enter full service until around 2030.
Nokia, which sells mobile and fixed network equipment to telecom operators worldwide, has been expanding its defense business. Its CEO, Justin Hotard, said secure connectivity across land, sea, air and space would give nations the awareness and control they need in contested environments.
Modrzewski and Hotard are due to speak at the Helsinki Security Forum on Oct. 2 in a session on Europe’s technological sovereignty.

Beyond the Red Sea: Ethiopian-Eritrean conflict risks converging with Yemen crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:33:55 UTC
16:33:55 KST

Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia and worsening tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara are reopening one of the Horn of Africa’s most dangerous fault lines at a moment when the Red Sea itself is under growing pressure. 
The latest fighting in Ethiopia has already shaken the 2022 Pretoria agreement that ended the previous Tigray war. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive last week, seizing airports and advancing into neighboring areas before Ethiopian federal forces and allied militias began counterattacks. On Monday, pro-government forces claimed to have recaptured the strategic town of Alamata, south of Mekelle.
But the concern now extends beyond another internal Ethiopian conflict. 
Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, has publicly accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting forces fighting the federal government, adding a regional dimension to an already volatile confrontation. All three countries have denied involvement, while Sudan has in turn accused Ethiopia of supporting forces hostile to Khartoum—allegations Addis Ababa denies. 
At the same time, just across the Red Sea, the Houthis have dramatically expanded their position along Yemen’s western coast, taking Mokha and strategic islands near Bab el Mandeb in September. The advance has increased pressure on one of the world’s most important maritime passages and renewed fears that conflicts on the two shores of the Red Sea could increasingly intersect. 
For Dr. Gashaw Ayferam Endaylalu, Senior Researcher of Hydropolitics and Geopolitics in the Horn of Africa and Director General for African Affairs at the Institute of Foreign Affairs, the current Ethiopia–Eritrea tensions cannot be reduced to another temporary deterioration in bilateral relations. 
“It is serious, and it would be a mistake to treat it as a passing spike in tension,” Endaylalu told The Media Line. “The current escalation has several layers. On the surface, there is renewed fighting between the federal forces and TPLF [Tigray People’s Liberation Front]-affiliated elements in the north. Beneath that is a wider effort to build an anti-Ethiopia alignment, the so-called ‘Tsimdo’ alliance, in which Eritrea is a key organizer and driver.” 
“In my assessment, Asmara pushed for the early resumption of hostilities and provides political and logistical backing,” he further noted. 
Those claims reflect an Ethiopian assessment of Eritrea’s role and remain contested. Asmara has denied Ethiopian accusations of destabilization, while the precise extent of external support for the various armed groups remains difficult to establish independently. 
The deterioration is particularly striking because Ethiopia and Eritrea were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war. Their relationship worsened after the Pretoria peace agreement, from which Eritrea was excluded despite the participation of Eritrean forces in the conflict. Red Sea access has since emerged as another point of friction, with Addis Ababa repeatedly stressing the economic and strategic importance of obtaining reliable maritime access. 
Endaylalu, however, argued that the port question should not be viewed as the main cause of the present confrontation. 
“Ethiopia sees access to the sea as an existential and economic necessity,” he said. “A country of more than 120 million people cannot indefinitely depend on a single corridor, given that over 97 percent of its trade passes through Djibouti,” he added. 
But, he continued, “I would not describe the sea-access question as the likeliest cause of war. If confrontation comes, sea access will be a secondary cause, not the primary one.” 
For Endaylalu, the deeper disagreement concerns the political architecture of the Horn itself. 
“The primary driver is a deeper disagreement between Addis Ababa and Asmara over the regional order in the Horn of Africa,” he said. “Ethiopia envisions a Horn based on interdependence and shared economic opportunity, while Asmara’s approach depends on an Ethiopia that stays inward-looking and divided.”
He pointed to the earlier Ethiopia–Eritrea war as evidence that bilateral hostility predates the latest debate over Assab and Red Sea access. 
“Look at Asmara’s conduct during the EPRDF [Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratif Front] era, from 1991 to 2018. That government did not press any claim on Assab, and yet relations still deteriorated into a devastating war and years of hostility,” he said. 
“The risk is real, but it is not inevitable,” he added. 
The danger becomes more complicated when Ethiopia and Eritrea are placed within a much wider regional map. 
Mowlid Ali, a security intelligence analyst on the Red Sea at INGO Advisory, said the Horn can no longer be analyzed separately from the competition among regional and international actors for ports, military access and influence. 
“The situation in the Horn of Africa is deteriorating because of the dominance of powers trying to come to Africa and occupy the ports,” Ali said. “They are all in competition. So the violence in the Horn of Africa is going to get worse,” he added. 
That competition now overlaps with instability from Sudan to Yemen. 
Sudan has been at war since 2023, while Ethiopia and Sudan still have unresolved tensions along their border. At the same time, both governments have traded accusations of assisting hostile armed actors. Reuters reported this month that diplomats increasingly fear a renewed Ethiopian conflict would unfold not in isolation but alongside Sudan’s civil war, Nile tensions and the spillover of Middle Eastern rivalries into the Horn. 
Endaylalu called the Ethiopia-Sudan-Eritrea border area one of the most vulnerable points in that landscape. 
“The border triangle is the region’s most delicate fault line,” he said, citing “unresolved border issues between Ethiopia and Sudan” and “the convergence of three states at a single point, with overlapping security interests.”
“Any confrontation in this area would very likely make the conflict regional,” he further noted. 
He also alleged that Port Sudan and Eritrea are facilitating forces hostile to Addis Ababa. Such claims have not been independently established, and Sudan’s military has called Ethiopian accusations that it supports armed opposition groups “baseless.” 
Egypt adds another layer. 
Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa have for years been strained by the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and disagreements over the Nile. Eritrea, meanwhile, has developed closer relations with both Sudan and Egypt, creating a diplomatic geometry that Ethiopian officials increasingly view with suspicion. 
Endaylalu described Cairo as a major actor in the current regional competition. 
“Egypt is already deeply engaged. Cairo’s policy in the Horn is one of encirclement, aimed at limiting Ethiopia’s strategic reach and thereby sustaining its own dominance over the Nile and the Red Sea,” he said. 
“We see Egypt trying to assemble an anti-Ethiopia axis—Cairo, Port Sudan, Asmara and others—to pressure Ethiopia into accepting a Nile arrangement that reflects colonial-era assumptions,” he added. 
That is Endaylalu’s assessment, rather than an established description of Egyptian policy. Egypt on Tuesday rejected allegations that it was supporting Ethiopian opposition forces and said its foreign policy is based on respect for sovereignty and non-interference in other states’ internal affairs. 
For Cairo, however, developments farther north in the Red Sea create an additional security concern. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have already stressed the need to guarantee freedom of navigation through Bab el Mandeb and the Red Sea as Yemen’s conflict intensifies. 
That is where the Horn’s internal tensions risk intersecting with a second crisis. 
The Houthi advance through western Yemen has brought the group to strategically important territory overlooking Bab el Mandeb. Although commercial shipping has not been completely halted, the military shift has increased the Houthis’ capacity to threaten or influence navigation through the southern entrance to the Red Sea. 
Ali said the implications go far beyond Yemen. 
“If they get hold of Bab el Mandeb, it is going to become a chokehold for humanitarian access and for the shipping lines,” he said. 
He warned that deteriorating security on both shores of the waterway could turn separate crises into an interconnected regional security problem. 
“You have the situation in Somalia to the east, piracy, and you have the Houthis on the other side of the Red Sea attacking ships and cargo vessels,” Ali said. “There is also a humanitarian catastrophe in Sudan,” he added. 
“We have to keep an eye on the escalating security situation in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” he further noted. 
For both analysts, that intersection is what makes the present moment particularly difficult to contain. 
Endaylalu warned that the Horn already contains “overlapping alliances, including Gulf, Turkish, Egyptian and Israeli engagement,” and said that if Ethiopia’s internal conflict develops into “a proxy arena for these competing alignments, the consequences could extend well beyond Ethiopia’s borders.” 
Ali reached the same broader concern from the maritime-security side. 
“If Iran blocks the Strait of Hormuz and then you have the Houthis in Yemen blocking Bab el Mandeb entirely,” he said, “it is going to be catastrophic.”, he concluded. 
Neither an Ethiopia–Eritrea war nor a wider regional confrontation is inevitable. But the number of unresolved disputes is increasing at the same time: renewed war in northern Ethiopia, tensions with Eritrea, Sudan’s continuing conflict, the Nile dispute with Egypt and a rapidly changing military balance across the Red Sea in Yemen. 
The risk is therefore no longer limited to one border or one conflict. It lies in the possibility that crises that have so far remained partly separate begin to converge around the same strategic space— the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.

Beyond the Bunker: Lessons from Survivalist Architecture on Resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

"Let us take a hard look at the facts." With this direct and hardly reassuring sentence, the director of the Office of Civil and Defense Mobilization opened The Family Fallout Shelter, a 32-page manual published by the U.S. government in 1959 amid Cold War tensions. The document taught families how to build shelters capable of protecting them from radioactive fallout after a possible nuclear attack and, through technical drawings and sketches, outlined solutions using concrete blocks, walls filled with earth or sand, underground structures, and ventilation systems. It was a survival manual that, in many ways, also functioned as a construction manual.
The logic of preparedness did not disappear with the end of the Cold War. Instead, it began responding to threats that were more diffuse and often more familiar: economic and energy crises, natural disasters, pandemics, prolonged disruptions to supply networks and infrastructure, and even speculative fears surrounding artificial intelligence, including scenarios in which autonomous systems could escape human control or even turn against humanity. Contemporary survivalism emerged in response to this wider range of risks, encompassing practices that range from keeping several days' worth of supplies on hand to seeking remote properties, adapting homes for greater autonomy, or, at the more extreme end, building bunkers and other fortified shelters.
This differs from the off-grid architecture we have previously explored, where water collection, energy generation, and sewage treatment must be resolved by the building itself. While off-grid architecture assumes a reduced or permanent dependence on certain networks, survivalism introduces another possibility: that networks normally taken for granted may stop functioning altogether.
Related Article
A Guide to Off-Grid Architectures
For Raphael Cozzi, founder of the Preppers Brasil community, preparedness does not necessarily begin with the expectation of an apocalyptic scenario, but with a simple question: "How long could I keep my family functioning normally if what is outside stopped working?" This can include prolonged power outages, flooding, or interruptions to the water supply, alongside economic crises, difficulties accessing food, and family emergencies. The goal, he explains, is to anticipate consequences rather than predict exactly what the next disaster will be.
Preppers, however, are far from a homogeneous group. Geographer Kezia Barker notes that the figure of the prepper is often ridiculed by the media and framed in pathologizing or dismissive ways. Her research places prepping within vulnerabilities that are already familiar, especially our dependence on infrastructure networks and the inequalities that shape who can or cannot rely on protection during a crisis. Supplies, tools, skills, and equipment can therefore form a kind of "parallel infrastructure," capable of taking over certain functions when conventional systems stop responding.
Once this parallel infrastructure outgrows a backpack or closet and begins to require dedicated space, technical systems, and construction solutions, survivalism becomes an architectural question. Unlike an off-grid house, designed to operate continuously with less dependence on conventional networks, survivalist architecture generally considers two possible states: everyday operation and the eventual interruption of those networks. For Cozzi, this possibility could be anticipated from the design stage, including "the possibility of the residence operating partially without the electrical grid."
When the House Becomes Infrastructure
These priorities begin to reshape the house itself. Cozzi places water at the top of the hierarchy: "We can go some time without electricity or with limited food, but water is an immediate necessity." Energy comes next, not necessarily to keep the entire house operating as if nothing had happened, but to "ensure essential functions: lighting, communication, charging equipment, preserving certain foods, and operating important devices."
Preparedness often starts small. Many people begin by storing water, food, medication, flashlights, and batteries. Then other questions emerge: where to store these resources, how to filter water, how to cook without electricity or gas, how to maintain communication, and which functions should have alternatives in case one system fails.
Cozzi summarizes much of this logic in one word: "redundancy." As he explains, "if I have only one way of obtaining water, I have a single point of failure." The same logic applies to energy, communication, and other essential functions.
"The organization of the house itself changes," he observes. "You begin to see the residence not simply as a property, but as an infrastructure that needs to continue providing certain basic functions even when some external services temporarily cease to exist."
Even so, the bunker occupies a much larger place in the popular imagination than it does in everyday preparedness. "It represents a very small portion of the prepper universe," Cozzi says. For him, a resilient home is a more useful reference than an underground fortress: an apparently conventional house can incorporate water reserves, alternative energy, storage, communication, and emergency equipment. Preparedness can also involve mobility, since remaining in the building will not always be the appropriate response. "Preparedness does not necessarily mean building a fortress. It means creating options."
Survivalism also has an escapist dimension. If many speculative architectures of the 20th century imagined other worlds in which it might be possible to live, certain forms of preparedness make an almost inverse move: they attempt to create a relatively autonomous world within the one that already exists. In this case, the alternative world is not on Mars, at the bottom of the ocean, or in virtual reality. It may instead be underground, in the countryside, or behind the walls of an apparently ordinary house. A remote property, a residence capable of operating for long periods without conventional networks, or, at the extreme, a bunker can reduce exposure to external instability. The goal is not always to abandon society. Still, there is a clear tension between autonomy and isolation: to what extent does becoming less dependent on collective systems also mean withdrawing from them?
Many of the qualities associated with preparedness-oriented architecture are already familiar to the discipline: durability, thermal insulation, weather tightness, resource efficiency, energy independence, repairability, and redundancy. Under extreme conditions, these characteristics are pushed to their limits, but many are also becoming relevant in the face of more severe climate events, power outages, or buildings located in remote areas.
Repairability matters too. Cozzi points to our growing dependence on complex systems that users can rarely repair themselves. In his view, more resilient architecture should consider solutions that can remain operational, even at reduced capacity, during an emergency, while also providing alternatives for certain critical functions from the design stage onward.
The same questions apply well beyond bunkers. As materials and technologies expand what a building can produce, store, filter, and control on its own, autonomy and resilience are taking on a larger role in architectural design. Survivalism pushes this logic to an extreme, exposing dependencies that usually remain out of sight.
Cozzi reduces this principle to an almost banal question: "What if this stops working?" What if the power goes out? The water? Communications? What if the street becomes inaccessible? Asked during design, these are no longer exclusively prepper questions. They are also questions about whether a building can continue providing basic conditions when the systems around it fail.
If, in 1959, The Family Fallout Shelter asked readers to "take a hard look at the facts," it was responding to a threat that was easier to identify and name. Today, risk is more diffuse, shaped by forecasts, misinformation, alarmism, and competing interpretations of what may happen next. For architecture, predicting the next disruption may matter less than understanding how dependent buildings already are on systems beyond their walls. Water tanks, batteries, filters, stored supplies, backup systems, and other forms of redundancy make those dependencies visible. That may be the most useful architectural lesson of prepper culture.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Pentagon orders 14,000 attack drones from Neros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:29:27 UTC
16:29:27 KST

- Neros said the U.S. Department of War ordered 14,000 drones and explosive payloads, valued above $100 million, after Drone Dominance Gauntlet II.
- The company also received a bonus order for 800 Gauntlet I drones reallocated from competitors that missed production deadlines.
The U.S. Department of War has ordered 14,000 attack drones and explosive payloads from California drone maker Neros after the company finished near the top of both events in the Pentagon’s latest Drone Dominance competition, a deal Neros values at more than $100 million.
Neros announced the order on Sept. 30 and said it had also received a second bonus order for 800 more drones from the program’s first round, reassigned from competitors that could not meet their production deadlines. The Pentagon has not published the value of either order.
The Gauntlet II order is split between two versions of the company’s Archer drone. Archer AI is a 10-inch first-person-view attack drone, a size class named for its propellers, with terminal guidance that lets it fly itself to a target the operator has picked, which helps when jamming cuts the link to the pilot, while Archer 5 is a smaller variant built for close-quarters fighting in towns and inside buildings.
“We’re proud to be the only manufacturer to have placed top three in both Gauntlet II mission sets, and are already fulfilling this next tranche of orders,” Neros said in a post on X.
Gauntlet II, held in August at Fort Carson, Colorado, tested 23 drone designs from 19 companies across 1,858 sorties flown by military operators, and the program’s leaderboard now shows 60,000 drones ordered, split evenly between its two events. In deep strike, Perennial Autonomy, the drone company backed by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, won with 80.1 points and an 8,000-drone order, followed by Hyperscale with 7,000, Neros with 6,000, Skycutter with 5,000 and Swarm Defense Technologies with 4,000. In close-quarters battle, Neros won with 88.1 points and 8,000 drones, ahead of ORQA US with 7,000, XTEND Reality with 6,000, Vector with 5,000 and ModalAI with 4,000.
Neros’s combined 14,000 drones account for nearly a quarter of the 60,000 total, well ahead of the 8,000 ordered from Perennial Autonomy, the next-largest single order.
Neros’s figure of more than $100 million is higher than the program’s own prices suggest. At the Gauntlet II unit prices of $3,500 and $4,500, 14,000 drones would cost between $49 million and $63 million, DroneXL calculated, and Neros has not explained the difference, though its order also covers explosive payloads.
The 800-drone bonus comes from a problem that has dogged the program’s first round. Gauntlet I, held at Fort Benning, Georgia, earlier this year, produced orders for about 30,000 drones from 11 companies, which had to deliver half within two and a half months and the rest within four and a half. By August, only three of the 11 had finished, as most struggled to find motors, sensors, batteries and chips that meet U.S. rules barring certain foreign parts, Inside Unmanned Systems reported.
Neros was the first to finish, completing its 2,400-drone order in July and earning a 2,000-drone bonus, and the new 800-drone award brings its Gauntlet I total to 5,200 drones. The company was building about 1,200 Archers a week in August, the same month it raised $250 million at a $2.5 billion valuation.
Drone Dominance is a $1.1 billion, four-round Pentagon effort to buy cheap one-way attack drones in large numbers and push U.S. manufacturers to produce them at scale, with each round pairing field testing by troops with fixed-price orders and tight delivery deadlines.
The program opened its third round on Sept. 28 with $450 million for about 60,000 drones and an option for up to 40,000 more, and companies that want to compete must first deliver a 400-drone order within about two months.

When Israel pushed the limits — and Saudi Arabia drew the line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:26:50 UTC
16:26:50 KST

The attempted hijacking of Israelis aboard a Flydubai flight is not expected to affect relations between Jerusalem and Riyadh. The aircraft was not bound for Saudi Arabia and, as far as is known, the attacker did not intend to crash it on Saudi soil. He tried to take control of the plane only once it was over Jordan.
The nature of relations between the two countries can also be seen in the fact that throughout the incident, the Mossad remained in continuous contact with Saudi officials.
The Saudis played an important and positive role in escorting the aircraft and receiving it at their airport. They treated the Israeli passengers very well, providing them with food and medical care. Passengers said the treatment they received was excellent, something that should not be taken for granted.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia firmly refused to allow Israeli Air Force Hercules transport planes to land in the kingdom to evacuate the Israelis. That was considered a step too far and could have been seen as an act of normalization at this time.
Behind the scenes, however, the Mossad came close to persuading the Saudis to allow an unmarked white Israeli aircraft to land in Tabuk. In the end, the plane was not needed after all the passengers agreed to board Flydubai’s rescue flight.
A senior Israeli official said sending an Israeli aircraft, which would almost certainly have been photographed, was too much for Saudi Arabia.
“This also shows that Saudi Arabia, or at least Saudi public opinion, is still not ready for an overt Israeli presence or visible ties with Israel,” the official said. “The kingdom currently enjoys a security relationship in the form of a ‘mistress,’ paying no price for it and only benefiting. If Israel is smart, it will know how to leverage the security relationship and gain diplomatic benefits from it as well.”
Since October 7, Saudi Arabia has continued allowing Flydubai aircraft to cross its airspace on flights to Israel and from Israel to the Gulf.
A senior Israeli official said the incident had already strengthened ties by demonstrating that Saudi Arabia was willing to allow a plane carrying 180 Israelis to land there, adding that Riyadh deserved credit for the way it treated the Israeli passengers.
Beyond that, relations between the two countries depend in part on the continuation of the conflict with Iran.
Only recently, the Saudis asked Israel, through U.S. Central Command, for intelligence assistance in their fight against the Houthis, and Israel apparently did not turn them away. That came despite tensions in relations following the signing of the “Mecca alliance,” which includes Turkey and Pakistan.

The last general election in New Zealand took place in October 2023. The maximum term of the New Zealand Parliament is three years.

The last thing Albanese needed was free advice from his own side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:08:15 UTC
16:08:15 KST

analysis
After rate hikes and inflation woes, the last thing Albanese needed was advice from Minns
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Under pressure from opponents after another interest rate hike and more bad inflation news, the last thing Anthony Albanese needed was free advice from his own side.
But that's what the prime minister got this week when fellow a Labor leader, NSW Premier Chris Minns, weighed in on the impact of government spending on Australia's economic woes.
Albanese and Minns have been downplaying reports they've had something of a falling out recently.
First, there were reports that the relationship between the prime minister and the NSW premier had deteriorated after the Bondi terror attack in December last year. Then came Minns's frustration over the tobacco tax excise, GST carve-up and hospital bed funding — to name a few issues said to have caused tension.
But off the back of headline inflation jumping to 4 per cent and an interest rate hike this week, Minns seemed to add another gripe to his list: government spending.
"I'm not going to make a long commentary about other governments. It's up to them and their decisions, obviously," Minns said. "But we want to make it clear that we've been careful with public money, particularly the growth in public money, and that will continue if we're re-elected next March."
With an election of his own around the corner, Minns did not come to Treasurer Jim Chalmers's defence and again distanced himself from his federal Labor counterparts. He wants voters to blame them, not him, when they head to the polls next March.
It's the kind of jab more likely to come from the Coalition than a politically aligned leader; case in point was a speech from Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki. He used his address to the National Press Club on Wednesday to take a swing over the GST and cost-shifting.
Former RBA governor Philip Lowe also popped up. He reckons the government should be running surpluses off the back of a near record-high tax take. It's not — and the intergenerational report handed down last week predicted there are 40 years of deficits to come.
Nothing to see here?
Albanese and Chalmers had been on the defensive all week over the government's economic record, arguing the Middle East war, not government spending, is turbocharging inflation.
RBA Governor Michele Bullock didn't want to engage in the "blame game" when asked after the bank's board hiked the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent.
But she did say inflation had been too high before the war and "domestic capacity measures" only added to it. Sluggish productivity was "doing nothing" to help the matter.
Both the prime minister and treasurer rebuffed Minns's swipe when asked. Just like with the question of if they're at odds with Bullock, there is nothing to see here, they claim.
Chalmers spent the week arguing that the government has been responsible in its spending decisions. Asked if more drastic action was required, he accepted there was always more work to do.
A tough love approach to tackling inflation typically means cutting spending. But that won't necessarily sit well with a cohort of cash-strapped voters already looking elsewhere, including to One Nation, for the answers.
Perhaps that's why by Wednesday, Albanese was already flagging more cost-of-living relief in the mid-year budget update in December. What form it will take has yet to be revealed. Chalmers insists it won't be another cut to the fuel excise.
Coalition's make-or-break moment
The next three months could make or break Angus Taylor's leadership.
Momentum over government spending could provide him with an opportunity. The Coalition, or more specifically Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson, have long been trying to make "Jimflation" happen.
Taylor wrote to the prime minister back in February calling for a taskforce on spending restraint. He seized on this week's gloomy economic picture to prosecute the argument that Chalmers had lost control of the economy.
Complicating the Coalition's argument is that they have backed themselves into their own big spending corner. Their promise to combat bracket creep by indexing tax brackets to inflation would be enormously expensive.
Paired with their plan to slash the tobacco excise and cut the fuel excise every time the two week average global oil price jumps over US$100 ($140) a barrel, that would inject a lot of extra cash into the economy when inflation is already running hot.
The Coalition argues all that spending will be offset elsewhere: the fuel excise will be funded, for example, by people buying more legal cigarettes once the excise on tobacco drops. Further offsets will be revealed closer to the 2028 election.
If the opposition doesn't gain ground soon then Taylor's challengers will likely start jostling. In the meantime, Angus Taylor may hope to be like the bogong moth — currently swarming across the country after years of decline.
Loading
A new era for the Greens
Standing under the tree of knowledge, a sprawling fig outside the NSW parliament, a new era of the Greens began.
A three-cornered battle for the leadership took place. It's the first time the minor party's leadership has been contested.
David Shoebridge emerged as the leader with a pitch about the hip-pocket. He declared the Greens were coming to replace Labor. As he was talking, Mehreen Faruqi revealed her plan to freelance now she's not in the party's leadership.
Loading...
In the same statement, she attacked the manner in which Shoebridge was elected over her.
"Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party," she said. "I call on the leadership team to set a timeline for one member, one vote."
A timeline for the post-2028 election has been set for that grassroots vote. But circumstances overtook that timeline. While Larissa Waters stepped aside for health reasons, her lack of cut through was of concern.
Shoebridge is the third leader in 18 months (Adam Bandt was dumped by voters at the last election). Shoebridge has a tough task in front of him: to unite a divided party room (several of his colleagues were curiously silent about his appointment) and lift the primary vote from where it's currently stuck around 10 to 12 per cent.
As Patricia Karvealas wrote this morning, the Greens are looking to replicate the success of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's progressive campaign.
Shoebridge wants a harder line on Labor than Waters took, and he's vowing to play hardball. That includes when it comes to legislation in the Senate, where Labor needs the minor party's vote.
The approach sounds similar to the one Bandt and former MP Max Chandler-Mather (now head of the Green Institute) took last term — an argument the prime minister also made on Thursday.
Both ended up losing their seats. But perhaps in the time of Pauline Hanson's rise, the Greens have learned the lesson that sometimes you just need to wait and try again when the times suit you.
