Leaked Warrant List Reveals How Turkmenistan Targets Critics Abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

But Annayev and other activists soon discovered they were not safe in Turkey where authorities began detaining people who did not have valid documentation to stay in the country.
As Annayev documented dissent online, so did Farhat Meymankulyyev, a fellow Turkey-based YouTuber.
In August 2021, Meymankulyyev was lured into a car by men presumed to be working for Turkmenistan security services. He ended up inside the consulate building, where he was beaten before being released.
Then, in May 2023, Meymankulyyev was arrested at a friend’s house by Turkish police and immediately deported. Witnesses saw him later at the airport in the Turkmenistan capital of Ashgabat. He was sentenced to 18 to 22 years in prison on unknown charges, and has not been seen or heard from since.
The list obtained by reporters shows that Turkmenistan’s Ministry for National Security issued arrest warrants for both Meymankulyyev and Annayev in 2022. 
The previous year, Annayev had been beaten up on the streets of Istanbul. It was just days before he was scheduled to travel to Warsaw and speak at an event organized by the human rights office of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). He said he was convinced the attackers were working for the Turkmenistan security services. 
“I returned to Istanbul after the conference. I started to receive various phone calls, SMS messages, and death threats,” he told Turkmen.news in 2022. 
He then attended another OSCE event, and decided to seek asylum in Poland. His claim failed there, and he has tried also in Sweden and the Netherlands. 
Annayev was the victim of a knife attack a year ago in Amsterdam, which left him lightly injured. The assailants are unknown, but Annayev is suspicious they may have been working for Turkmenistan’s security services.
So far unsuccessful in his bid for political asylum, Annayev continues his bureaucratic battles in Europe, all the while unleashing a torrent of YouTube videos criticizing the Turkmenistan regime.
Turkmenistan prevents internet users inside the country from accessing platforms like YouTube and TikTok, although some people use VPN technology to get around the ban. 
But the government has come up with new tactics to block his broadcasts, Annayev alleges. He says bots are being used to file complaints to TikTok and YouTube about his account, or content. 
Given enough complaints, TikTok may automatically remove an account or content. YouTube may remove content upon receiving a complaint about it displaying a person’s image. As the platform’s guidelines state, third-party complaints are accepted when “the individual whose privacy is being violated does not have access to a computer or the internet.”  
Neither TikTok nor YouTube responded to requests for comment.
Annayev said the Turkmenistan regime wants to stop diaspora activists like him from getting their messages to people inside the country.
“They are afraid, and our livestreams are very important in Turkmenistan. Why? Because there is no one else who can do that like us,” he said.

Herzog recommends the Presidential Medal of Civilian Valor to the four Israelis who helped save Flydubai flight FZ1073 and its captain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:51:23 UTC
15:51:23 KST

Herzog recommends Presidential Medal of Civilian Valor for five Israelis who helped save Flydubai flight FZ1073
Herzog said, "At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness, and extraordinary mutual responsibility"
President Isaac Herzog spoke with five Israelis, Yaniv Hayun, Dr. Shota Musayev, Zvika Manes, Tali Manes, and Asaf Rajuan, who acted with what his office called extraordinary heroism during a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel. The incident occurred after one pilot stabbed the other and the aircraft began losing altitude.
According to the President's statement, after Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar fought the attacker and opened the cockpit door, Tali Manes, Zvika's wife, raised the alarm about the incident. Hayun, Manes and Rajuan rushed into the cockpit and 'put themselves at risk' to subdue the attacker, with Hayun helping stabilize the aircraft's controls.
After the assailant was subdued, Dr. Musayev provided life-saving medical treatment to the critically injured pilot, helping stabilize him until the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Herzog told the four men, "At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness, and extraordinary mutual responsibility. You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster. Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society. I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel."
The president said he intends to bring their story before the advisory committee for the President's Medal for Civilian Bravery and recommend that all four receive the award. Herzog also extended gratitude to Captain Machchhar, saying his "determination and actions enabled the neutralization of the threat and saved many lives."
Dr. Shota Musayev described the incident to the president, saying, "It was a very difficult incident, and we truly were saved." He added, It wasn't only my heroism. Everyone who was there and came near the cockpit was part of it. We were all heroes. All the passengers were heroes. We supported one another on the plane and also when we arrived in Saudi Arabia, and we took care of each other as we should. It shows our strength as a people."
Yaniv Hayun told the president, "Everyone was so moved and welcomed me with great emotion. I'm glad we're here, glad it's all behind us, and very grateful for the call and the warm embrace. It's truly moving."
Asaf Rajuan recalled the moment, saying, "It was an extraordinary incident. We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn't know who to turn to. But it was all instinct: to survive, to save the family, the people, and the children."
The President's Medal for Civilian Bravery was established by Herzog during the war to honor citizens who acted with extraordinary heroism, risking their own lives out of a sense of mutual responsibility to save others. The award is granted following a case review and recommendation by a presidential advisory committee and has previously been given to Israelis who distinguished themselves, including several who acted heroically on October 7 in the Gaza Envelope area.

He also accused Israel of ingratitude toward Britain, which he said has paid a heavy price for helping defend Israel physically. British pilots shot down about 100 drones during the war, he said, yet Israel did not even consult Britain before announcing sanctions against it.
The diplomat noted that Israel gave one month’s notice that it would close the British Consulate in Jerusalem, which employs about 30 diplomats, a move he said was inconsistent with accepted diplomatic practice.
“Russia, when it closed the British Consulate in St. Petersburg, gave the British four months to prepare,” he said. “Closing a diplomatic mission within a month is an unacceptable step and it will not pass without a response.”
That one-month period is due to end Oct. 8, after which Britain could respond to the move. So far, it has not announced what its response will be. Behind the scenes, the two countries are holding contacts aimed at lowering tensions.
The senior diplomat expressed concern that Israel was taking harsh punitive measures against European countries for domestic political reasons, in an effort to appeal to its political base rather than out of concern for its own security.
He concluded: “Israelis must wake up and understand how much damage the current government is causing you. [National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich are running wild and Netanyahu is not in control of the situation.”

Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:34:01 UTC
15:34:01 KST

Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - San Francisco
- Summary:
- People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.
- Share:
A small preliminary study from UC San Francisco adds to mounting evidence that eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help reduce symptoms of depression.
Published Sept. 23 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study was funded by the National Institutes of Health. Researchers believe it is the first study to compare depression symptoms in the same participants before and after they moved from their usual ultra-processed diet to healthier foods.
The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, said it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial."
Depression Symptoms Improved After a Major Diet Shift
Participants cut their intake of ultra-processed foods by more than 85%. After doing so, they showed moderate to large improvements across three different measures of depression. Anxiety scores also improved modestly.
Ultra-processed foods include products such as packaged snacks, fast food, sugary drinks, and other industrially manufactured foods. These products may contain ingredients including preservatives, artificial coloring, flavor enhancers, and emulsifiers.
"Reducing the amount of ultra-processed food in our diet can be challenging, because it's highly palatable, cheap, and convenient," said corresponding author Nyasha Chagwedera, MD, PhD, assistant professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. "Ultra-processed food triggers dopamine, the pleasure hormone, which promotes craving. Food companies work with scientists to find just the right amount of sugar, salt, and fat that make you want to eat more and more."
Testing the Gut-Brain Connection
The participants had an average age of 44, and 70% were female. Along with depression, 14 participants also had anxiety. Everyone in the study had a high BMI and at least one metabolic disorder -- such as hypertension, diabetes, or elevated LDL cholesterol.
Researchers divided the participants into two groups. One group stayed on its usual diet for four weeks, while the other switched to a diet low in ultra-processed foods. Participants selected and bought their own food with guidance from the research team. After four weeks, the groups switched diets.
Chagwedera, who founded the UCSF Metabolic and Mental Health Program, said one possible explanation for the connection between ultra-processed food and depression involves what she described as a "leaky, out-of-balance gut." According to this idea, ultra-processed foods may damage the protective lining of the gut.
"This gut damage can create low-grade, chronic inflammation throughout the body that either directly causes depression or makes people more vulnerable to it."
"In other words, junky processing may harm your gut in ways that ripple up to your brain."
Larger Depression Trial Planned
Because the study was small, the findings are still preliminary. The researchers now plan to investigate the effect in a larger group, with enrollment for phase 2 expected to begin in 2028.
Authors: Additional UCSF authors include Eliana Kim, MD, Dorothy T. Chiu, PhD, Chengshi Jin, PhD, Catherine Lee PhD. Other authors are Susannah Tye, PhD, of the University of Queensland, Australia, Mayo Clinic, and Emory University.
Funding: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, National Institutes of Health, through UCSF-CTSI Grant Number UL1 TR001872; NHLBI grant R38AG070171, NIMH grant R38AG070171, and the UCSF Weill Institute of Neurosciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - San Francisco. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- D. Nyasha Chagwedera, Eliana Kim, Dorothy T. Chiu, Chengshi Jin, Catherine Lee, Susannah Tye, Andrew Krystal. Reducing Ultraprocessed Foods From the Diets of Patients With Depression. JAMA Psychiatry, 2026; DOI: 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.2320

Fondation Beyeler’s Expansion and Safdie Architects’ Carnegie Library Restoration: This Week’s Review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Architecture this week reflects on how buildings and cities adapt to changing cultural, social, and environmental conditions. From the expansion of established institutions and the preservation of architectural archives to new approaches to housing and the use of domestic space, several stories consider how architecture negotiates between existing contexts and future needs. These questions extend beyond individual buildings, touching on the role of public space, infrastructure, energy, and collective memory in shaping the built environment. At the same time, new projects and cultural programs across different contexts demonstrate how architecture can respond to local histories, urban transformation, and resource constraints while establishing new relationships between buildings, landscapes, and the communities that use them.
Architecture, Landscape, and Cultural Memory
At the Fondation Beyeler in Riehen, Switzerland, Peter Zumthor's expansion extends Renzo Piano's existing museum with three new buildings, an enlarged park, and the adaptive reuse of historic structures. The ensemble includes the three-story Wyss Museum, which adds approximately 1,500 square meters of exhibition space and is organized around existing trees, the Ammann Pavilion, a public space for cultural events, and the Erlen Torhaus, which accommodates artwork handling facilities and workspaces. Almost 10,000 square meters of previously private parkland will also open to visitors, nearly doubling the size of Beyeler Park. The expansion will begin welcoming visitors during a preview period on September 26, 2026, ahead of its full opening on January 15, 2027, alongside a year-long cultural program.
Related Article
Citizen-Led Campaign Seeks UNESCO Status for Select Pre-Colonial Sites in Lima, Peru
Questions of preservation and cultural memory also shape the Sharjah Architecture Triennial's A Journey into Architecture Archives, which has released three documentary films focused on Baghdad, Damascus, and Tunis. Curated and directed by George Arbid, the project combines archival research, fieldwork, and oral histories with contributions from architects, archivists, residents, and historians. Building on earlier films focused on Beirut, Cairo, and Rabat, the 2026 iteration expands the initiative's geographic scope while continuing to examine how architectural histories are documented, preserved, and reinterpreted. The project approaches archives not simply as repositories of the past, but as active sites for research and the production of architectural knowledge.
Housing, Space, and the Pressures on Architecture
A fire severely damaged Jean Nouvel's La Querola d'Ordino residential development in Andorra during the early hours of September 22. Designed in collaboration with Ribas & Ribas Arquitectes and Jordi Sala, the seven-building complex had been completed but was not yet occupied. According to the Andorran government, approximately 10,000 square meters of residential space and 12,000 square meters of parking were affected, while no injuries were reported. Conceived as a low-density residential ensemble, La Querola distributes its buildings across the steep mountainous site, allowing them to follow the terrain and establish different relationships with the surrounding landscape. The cause of the fire has not yet been established, and authorities are continuing to assess the damage and future of the complex.
Meanwhile, looking ahead to the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale, the Luxembourg Pavilion will examine the consumption and distribution of domestic space through Excess! On the Overconsumption of Living Space. The selected proposal by housing expert Céline Zimmer and architects Bùi Quý Sơn and Paul-Antoine Lucas of Exutoire will place housing conditions in Luxembourg and Vietnam into dialogue, examining the relationship between living space, economic and demographic growth, and finite ecological resources. The exhibition will also consider housing affordability, cooperative models, and alternative approaches to how space is produced and inhabited. It will be presented at the Luxembourg Pavilion in the Arsenale when the Biennale opens on May 8, 2027.
On the Radar
Safdie Architects to Restore Brooklyn's First Carnegie Library
Safdie Architects is set to restore Pacific Library in downtown Brooklyn, the first Carnegie library built in the borough, which has served the community since 1904. Developed in collaboration with New York-based AYON Studio, the renovation will add approximately 1,500 square feet while restoring elements of the historic building and expanding its public spaces. The design introduces a new two-story glass solarium within gardens created around the building, providing dedicated spaces for children and teenagers while bringing additional daylight into the lower level. The original roof shape and skylight will also be restored, alongside a new interior skylight at the upper level. Accessibility and community programming will be supported through a new elevator, reconfigured circulation, classrooms, and upgraded building systems, with the project targeting LEED Gold certification.
Cocentaina Returns as Guest Municipality for Open House Valencia 2026
Cocentaina will participate in Open House Valencia for the third consecutive year as a Guest Municipality, opening six historic buildings and archaeological sites to the public on October 3 and 4, 2026. The program brings together guided visits and three urban routes exploring different aspects of the town's architectural and cultural heritage, including its medieval urban fabric, relationship with water, and local traditions. Featured sites include the Palau Comtal, a historic air-raid shelter, the Monestir de la Mare de Déu del Miracle, and the Casa-Museu Centre d'Estudis Contestans. The routes will explore the town's natural water sources, the Fraga neighborhood and its relationship with the landscape, and the architectural and urban context of the Moros i Cristians festival.
Park Associati Designs Mobility Hub Connecting Transport, Public Space, and Energy in Bolzano
Park Associati has designed La Casa della Mobilità in Bolzano, Italy, a new headquarters bringing together the city's Department of Infrastructure and Mobility, Mobility Division, and STA – Strutture di Trasporto Alto Adige. Selected through an international design competition, the project replaces an existing building and introduces approximately 6,000 square meters of above-ground space and 2,000 square meters below ground. Located between Bolzano's historic center and railway station, the compact eight-story volume establishes a new urban edge while creating a small public square at its entrance. Its aluminum façade draws on the pattern of traditional Alpine shingles, incorporating photovoltaic technology into the cladding.
This article is part of our new This Week in Architecture series, bringing together featured articles this week and emerging stories shaping the conversation right now. Explore more architecture news, projects, and insights on ArchDaily.

Plovdiv Bans Older Cars From City Center Starting October 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Plovdiv introduces its first low-emission zone today, October 1, 2026, restricting the oldest and most polluting cars from entering the city center during the colder months.
The zone, called "Maliyat ring" (Small Ring), covers the area enclosed by Ruski, Tsar Boris III Obedinitel, Hristo Botev and Shesti Septemvri boulevards. The restriction will apply every year from October 1 to April 30, the period when air pollution from traffic and household heating typically peaks.
The ban covers vehicles in the first and second environmental groups. In practice, this means petrol cars made before 1996 and diesel cars made before 2002 in the first group, and petrol cars first registered between 1996 and 1998 and diesel cars from 2002 to 2007 in the second group. Cars with LPG systems are also restricted if they fall into one of these groups. Vehicles from the third, fourth and fifth environmental groups can enter freely. A car's environmental group is determined at its annual technical inspection, and vehicles with no data on their environmental category are not considered violators.
Owners and tenants of homes inside the zone are exempt, along with members of their household, as long as their permanent address matches the property. Historic vehicles are exempt as well. To use the exemption, residents must apply to the municipal company "Parking and Repatriation" and be entered into the municipality's electronic database. The pass is valid for up to one year and covers one vehicle per home.
The municipality says the measure aims to improve air quality by reducing emissions of fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide. According to local media, there will be no postponement, and drivers who break the ban will be fined. Plovdiv Municipality urged residents to check their cars' environmental group and, if eligible, to submit the exemption documents before the zone takes effect.

Tennessee woman survives two lethal injection attempts in 'failed' execution: lawyers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:15:56 UTC
15:15:56 KST

Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, has survived two lethal injections intended to execute her, her lawyers said.
In a federal court filing seeking to halt the execution late on Wednesday, her lawyers said Pike was “still alive and snoring” at 0126 GMT on Thursday, adding that she had not lost consciousness and still had a heartbeat, NBC News reported.
Her legal team later said she had been taken to a nearby hospital, but her condition remained unclear.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” her attorneys said in a statement. “Christa is being treated at a nearby hospital. We have not been informed as to her condition.”
Pike had been scheduled for execution at 1500 GMT at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
Journalists were among the witnesses present when the injections were administered.
“It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go,” said John North, an investigative journalist with WBIR who witnessed the procedure.
“When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.”
An ambulance with its lights flashing was seen leaving the prison during a livestream, though it was unclear whether it was transporting Pike.
Supreme Court clears execution
The execution attempt went ahead hours after the US Supreme Court cleared the way for it to proceed, with liberal justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting.
“The Court’s decision... unnecessarily prevents that [lower] court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” the dissenting justices wrote.
“Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the State to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”
The Supreme Court had also rejected an application on Tuesday to stay the execution. That application argued that Pike’s history of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant lethal injection would cause “needless suffering”.
Clemency appeals
Pike’s case has fuelled debate over capital punishment for people who committed crimes at a young age and the treatment of prisoners with mental health conditions.
She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
Pike’s lawyers sought clemency on the grounds of her age and mental health at the time of the killing.
“She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill,” they wrote in a petition to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who declined to intervene.
Independent UN rights experts had also urged US and Tennessee authorities to “immediately halt” the execution and commute her death sentence.
“Pike’s execution would mark the culmination of a trajectory of severe physical and psychological suffering marked by childhood abuse and nearly three decades of solitary confinement on death row,” they said.
Only 18 women have been executed in the United States since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this october
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:15:07 UTC
15:15:07 KST

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this october
explore our monthly round up of must-see art, design, and architecture exhibitions to check out around the world.
October exhibitions from DESIGNBOOM RADAR
Porcelain bowls drift across pools in Athens, paintings change with the temperature in London, and dense webs of thread fill galleries in Montreal. October’s exhibitions radar takes us through spaces where the artwork changes how we move and what we notice, alongside shows that revisit the images and objects of everyday life. From the domestic futures once promised to American households to the creative exchanges behind 1990s British fashion, designboom rounds up exhibitions to visit around the world this month.
Some of the exhibitions highlighted in earlier radars and listings on our dedicated events guide remain on view, giving designboom readers more time to encounter them around the globe.
home of the future, 1925–1985: designing domestic utopias
Self-cleaning kitchens and houses assembled from plastic promised Americans a different domestic life during the twentieth century. At LACMA, Home of the Future, 1925–1985: Designing Domestic Utopias follows the ways these visions were imagined and sold, from the scale of a household appliance to an entire living environment.
Architectural models and films appear alongside domestic objects, showing how technology entered the image of tomorrow’s home. The exhibition also asks who these futures were intended to serve and who was excluded from their promises. Alternative visions widen the account beyond the versions of domestic progress promoted to consumers.
name: Home of the Future, 1925–1985: Designing Domestic Utopias
 museum: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
 location: Los Angeles, USA
 dates: September 27th, 2026 — March 14th, 2027
geoffrey bawa: architecture for the senses
Geoffrey Bawa’s buildings make room for the landscape around them. At the Vitra Design Museum, Architecture for the Senses traces the Sri Lankan architect’s work through projects in which existing trees and rocks become part of the plan, and gardens carry the experience beyond the walls. The exhibition spans a career of more than fifty years, with buildings ranging from private houses to Sri Lanka’s parliament.
Archival drawings and models sit alongside newly commissioned photographs and films that convey how these spaces feel today. The presentation also examines Bawa’s collaborations with artists and craftspeople, whose textiles and artworks became integral parts of his architecture. Exhibition design is by Lina Ghotmeh Architects.
name: Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses
 architect: Geoffrey Bawa
 museum: Vitra Design Museum
 location: Weil am Rhein, Germany
 dates: September 26th, 2026 — February 28th, 2027
krasner and pollock: past continuous
Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock met in New York in 1941, then moved to Springs, Long Island, after marrying four years later. At The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Past Continuous follows their careers together through more than 120 works, giving each artist’s practice space while examining the exchanges between them.
The exhibition takes its title from a 1976 painting by Krasner. Pollock’s poured and dripped compositions appear within a longer artistic trajectory, while Krasner’s changing approaches to abstraction reveal her sustained interest in nature and color. Their shared life runs through the exhibition, followed by the years in which Krasner continued working after Pollock’s death.
name: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
 artists: Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock
 museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
 location: New York, USA
 dates: October 4th, 2026 — January 31st, 2027
this is still not a pipe: the afterlife of magritte
Apples and bowler hats return at Gagosian’s Grosvenor Hill gallery, where René Magritte’s familiar images meet works by more than forty artists. Organized with the Fondation Magritte, This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte brings together paintings and sculpture alongside works on paper from across the Belgian artist’s career.
The exhibition follows the continuing reach of Magritte’s visual puzzles through different generations of artists. Several works were made specifically for the presentation, placing his questions about images and the things they represent within contemporary practice. The installation allows these exchanges to happen across the room, with Magritte’s paintings interspersed among later responses.
name: This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte
 artists: René Magritte and more than forty participating artists
 gallery: Gagosian
 location: London, UK
 dates: September 24th — December 12th, 2026
clinamen
White porcelain bowls drift across three circular pools at Onassis Mandra in Athens. As they meet, their edges produce delicate sounds, forming a changing composition within Céleste Boursier-Mougenot’s installation clinamen.
First developed in 1997, the work takes its title from the unpredictable deviation of atoms described in Epicurean philosophy. This outdoor presentation allows the surrounding weather to enter the composition, with rain adding another sound to the bowls’ movements. Set within a historic open-air theater, the installation gives visitors a place to pause and listen to a work whose arrangement changes from moment to moment.
name: clinamen
 artist: Céleste Boursier-Mougenot
 venue: Onassis Mandra
 location: Athens, Greece
 dates: September 26th — December 5th, 2026
chiharu shiota: the soul trembles
Thread stretches through the galleries of the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts in Chiharu Shiota’s The Soul Trembles. Making its North American debut, the touring exhibition covers more than thirty years of the Berlin-based Japanese artist’s career, including installations built by hand in response to the rooms they occupy.
The Montreal presentation includes Uncertain Journey and In Silence, with sculptures and performance documentation extending the account of her practice. Ordinary objects become caught within dense networks of thread, giving physical form to the memories and relationships they carry. Each installation is remade for its setting, continuing Shiota’s interest in the impermanence of both the work and the experiences behind it.
name: Chiharu Shiota: The Soul Trembles
 artist: Chiharu Shiota
 museum: Montreal Museum of Fine Arts
 location: Montreal, Canada
 dates: September 26th, 2026 — February 14th, 2027
chasing clouds
Early photographers could record a landscape yet struggle to capture the sky above it. Chasing Clouds at The Metropolitan Museum of Art follows the ways artists worked around this problem, from painting skies into photographs to combining separate negatives.
The exhibition begins with nineteenth-century oil sketches, made as painters studied changing weather outdoors and meteorologists developed systems for classifying clouds. Later photographic advances brought the sky within reach of the camera. The presentation ends with Alfred Stieglitz’s Equivalents from the 1920s, in which cloud formations become images capable of carrying feeling as well as recording nature.
name: Chasing Clouds
 museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art
 location: New York, USA
 dates: through February 28th, 2027
ann veronica janssens: 5 chome 4-1 ginza, tokyo
A pink star made from intersecting beams of light changes the atmosphere of Hermès Maison Ginza Le Forum in Ann Veronica Janssens’s first solo exhibition in Japan. Titled after the gallery’s street address, 5 Chome 4-1 Ginza, Tokyo brings together around a dozen works that respond to the space and the visitor’s perception of it.
The selection includes Rose, formed from seven spotlights, and Swing, whose seat is sensitive to temperature. Across the exhibition, Janssens introduces subtle changes in light and physical sensation, drawing attention to the conditions through which a room is experienced. Curated by Reiko Setsuda, the presentation takes a retrospective view of her practice.
name: 5 Chome 4-1 Ginza, Tokyo
 artist: Ann Veronica Janssens
 gallery: Hermès Maison Ginza Le Forum
 location: Tokyo, Japan
 dates: September 11th, 2026 — January 11th, 2027
broken: the power of the fragment
A broken sculpture carries traces of what happened to it. At Palazzo Strozzi, Broken: The Power of the Fragment examines how damaged and incomplete works have held viewers’ attention across cultures and centuries, inviting them to imagine the missing whole or consider the fragment on its own terms.
Organized with the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the exhibition follows the forces that alter sculpture, including war and iconoclasm. It also examines the artistic possibilities of incompleteness, extending to works conceived as fragments from the outset. Across this history, a surviving piece can preserve evidence of destruction while taking on a new life as an artwork.
name: Broken: The Power of the Fragment
 venue: Palazzo Strozzi
 location: Florence, Italy
 dates: September 25th, 2026 — January 24th, 2027
luciano fabro: abitare lo spazio. inhabiting space
Luciano Fabro’s sculptures ask viewers to consider the room around them. At Pirelli HangarBicocca, Abitare lo spazio. Inhabiting Space gathers around fifty sculptures and installations in the first museum retrospective dedicated to the artist in Italy since his death in 2007.
The exhibition follows his spatial experiments from early works with reflective surfaces to the architectural environments he called ‘habitats.’ Several are reconstructed in the Navate using his original plans and instructions. These environments house other works while shaping the routes and viewpoints through which visitors encounter them, extending sculpture into the experience of moving through a space.
name: Luciano Fabro: Abitare lo spazio. Inhabiting Space
 artist: Luciano Fabro
 venue: Pirelli HangarBicocca
 location: Milan, Italy
 dates: October 8th, 2026 — February 21st, 2027
arthur jafa: i am tony
Arthur Jafa occupies two floors of the expanded New Museum with I Am Tony, a survey spanning nearly forty years of his practice. Named after jazz drummer Tony Williams, the exhibition follows the development of a filmic language shaped by the rhythms and textures of Black music.
Celebrated works including Love is the Message, The Message is Death and The White Album appear alongside new work and recent paintings. Sculptural and photographic objects extend the presentation beyond the screen, while large-scale film installations examine how images carry the history and contemporary realities of Black life in America.
name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
 artist: Arthur Jafa
 museum: New Museum
 location: New York, USA
 dates: September 24th, 2026 — January 3rd, 2027
kenny scharf
Kenny Scharf’s brightly colored creatures arrive at Madrid’s Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in an exhibition presented through its program devoted to the Blanca and Borja Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection. The Los Angeles-born artist emerged within New York’s East Village scene during the 1980s, developing a visual language he calls ‘Pop Surrealism.’
His fantastical figures draw on popular culture while taking on human expressions and personalities. The exhibition introduces a practice that moves beyond painting into everyday and public settings, reflecting Scharf’s longstanding interest in bringing art into contact with a wider audience. His saturated palette carries the same energy across these different forms.
name: Kenny Scharf
 artist: Kenny Scharf
 museum: Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza
 location: Madrid, Spain
 dates: September 29th, 2026 — January 17th, 2027
trop mignon! l’art du bonheur
An ancient toy hedgehog and contemporary pink figures share the wider history examined in Trop mignon! L’art du bonheur at Louvre-Lens. Bringing together nearly 300 works, the exhibition asks how images and objects produce affection, and why certain forms make people feel comforted.
The presentation moves from antiquity to contemporary ideas of cute and kawaii, exploring the emotional pull of animals alongside the associations of pink. Works by artists including Rosa Bonheur and William Wegman reveal the place of animal companionship within art, while other pieces expose the more ambiguous feelings that can sit beneath an adorable surface.
name: Trop mignon! L’art du bonheur
museum: Louvre-Lens
 location: Lens, France
 dates: September 23rd, 2026 — January 18th, 2027
justin caguiat: change ringing
Paintings change with the temperature at Serpentine South, where Justin Caguiat uses heat-sensitive pigments in Change Ringing. As conditions shift, forms emerge and disappear across their surfaces, bringing the gallery’s atmosphere into the work.
Bronze bells cast in the shapes of flowers and plant seeds sound in changing sequences throughout the exhibition. Their score, composed by Lily Pickett, draws on English change ringing, while the gallery walls gather and amplify the chimes. Caguiat brings these elements together in an installation that considers buildings as places shaped by repeated actions and accumulated memory.
name: Justin Caguiat: Change Ringing
 artist: Justin Caguiat
 gallery: Serpentine South
 location: London, UK
 dates: October 8th, 2026 — January 10th, 2027
remember me
Around 700 works fill the Bourse de Commerce for Remember Me, an exhibition marking the bicentenary of photography’s invention. Drawn from the Pinault Collection, the presentation brings together more than seventy artists, moving between historical photographs and contemporary images.
Curators Matthieu Humery and Lola Regard arrange the works without a chronological sequence, allowing connections to form across different periods and photographic approaches. The title comes from a work by Barbara Kruger, who also presents an installation in the museum’s rotunda and display cases. Throughout the exhibition, photography’s ability to preserve a face or a passing moment provides a shared point of departure.
name: Remember Me
 artists: More than seventy participating artists
 museum: Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection
 location: Paris, France
 dates: From October 7th, 2026 (closing date unpublished)
myths and monsters: the art of fantasy in asia
Fantasy connects Japanese woodblock prints with the worlds of manga and anime at M+ in Hong Kong. Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia follows these connections from the nineteenth century to the present, examining how imagined characters and environments respond to the circumstances in which they are made.
The exhibition begins with earlier traditions, including Chinese shadow puppetry and Tibetan Buddhist scrolls, before tracing Surrealism’s circulation through Asia and the rise of Japanese manga. Its final chapter follows fantastical anime aesthetics into contemporary design and digital culture, revealing how these images travel between disciplines and across regions.
name: Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia
 museum: M+

Israeli airlines launch rescue flights for stranded passengers after Flydubai attempted hijacking
Israel will begin operating rescue flights to evacuate Israelis stranded in Dubai after Flydubai suspended flights for at least six days following an attempted hijacking aboard flight FZ1073
Rescue flights for Israelis stranded in Dubai will begin as early as tomorrow, operated by Israeli airlines under heavy security. Shin Bet security personnel are expected to arrive in Dubai to oversee security preparations for the return flights.
Emirates and Etihad are separately considering increasing flight capacity to boost service between Israel and the UAE. They are currently operating two daily flights from Abu Dhabi to Israel, while Flydubai has independently suspended service to Israel as it has initiated an internal investigation.
Israel is treating the incident aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073, which was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, as an attempted hijacking. According to Israeli officials, shortly after the flight entered Jordanian airspace, an Omani co-pilot stabbed the pilot, who was an Indian national, and attempted to forcibly take control of the aircraft. During the altercation, the pilot transmitted an emergency signal indicating a possible hijacking as the plane plunged 14,000 feet in a single minute and was diverted toward Saudi Arabia.
Israeli passengers and crew who heard the altercation managed to subdue the co-pilot, though his intent remains unclear. An Israeli official said it is unknown whether he intended to hijack the plane toward Israel, crash it, or carry out a 9/11-style attack, but added, "What is clear is that he wanted to hijack the plane and that a major disaster was averted."
Suggested articles
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised Indian Flydubai pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, calling him a "HERO" in a post on X. "In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Modi wrote. "His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy." Modi said he prayed for the captain's "speedy recovery, renewed strength and good health."
All passengers have since returned safely to Israel aboard a Flydubai rescue flight whose staff were vetted and approved by Mossad.

The Lingering Shadow of Rodrigo Duterte’s Drug War in the Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:57:00 UTC
14:57:00 KST

A few bags of chips and sweets line the modest storefront of Salvacion Ramos’ home in the Batasan neighborhood on the outskirts of Manila. At 68, she has turned the front of her house into a small convenience store to help pay for the education of her grandson, who has been in her care since her daughter’s death.
It was on that same doorstep one night in February 2017 that Cristeta Ramos was shot once in the back and three times in the head by four plainclothes police officers. “She died in my arms. I didn’t even get to say goodbye,” Salvacion recalls, tears in her eyes.
Beside her, her friend and neighbor Llore Pasco is also mourning her children. Her two sons, Cristanto and Juan Carlos, 34 and 31, were killed during a police operation as they were on their way to work in May 2017. “The police say they chased them because they thought they were thieves, but the bullet wounds were on the front of their bodies,” Llore says. She is now raising her five grandchildren.
“Cristeta was not a criminal” Salvacion says. “She did take drugs with the people she was with, but she wanted to get better. The barangay [neighborhood-level community] was offering a program for drug users to seek treatment, so I gave them her name.”
Llore’s sons had stopped using drugs well before Duterte’s election. After he took office, local officials insisted that former drug users register, presenting the process as a simple verification. Her sons initially refused. Llore eventually convinced them. They had been sober for more than a year. “Today I keep thinking that if they had not gone there, they might still be alive,” she says.
In neighborhoods across the country, barangays began compiling “watch lists” of current and former drug users. For some residents, getting off those lists came at a price. “At least five families I know paid 10,000 pesos (about $180) to the local government to get their names removed from the list, and their children are still alive,” Salvacion says.
Under Duterte, the war on drugs also became a source of income for some local actors. Along with the grief of losing their children and the guilt of having registered them with local authorities came the burden of paying to recover their bodies from the morgue. In Salvacion and Llore’s cases, authorities initially demanded 120,000 pesos and later 70,000 pesos, or about $1,350, after the intervention of the NGO Rise Up for Life and For Rights.
“Duterte destroyed these families, and now these mothers have to keep working to raise their orphaned grandchildren,” says Leah Valencia, a coordinator with the organization, which supports families in their search for justice.
Rise Up for Life and For Rights has also passed their testimonies to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, where Duterte has been held since his arrest in March 2025. The case accuses Duterte of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, during his time as mayor of Davao City and later as president. Prosecutors have identified 78 victims in the incidents specifically detailed in the case: 76 alleged murders and two attempted murders. The figure does not represent the total number of deaths attributed to Duterte’s drug war, but a selection of incidents presented by prosecutors to establish the alleged crimes against humanity.
The historic trial is scheduled to begin on November 30.
If Duterte is found guilty of crimes against humanity, he would become the first former president convicted by the ICC.
“The ICC is a very small ray of hope, but we are asking the government to turn Bato over and open an investigation to prosecute all those responsible,” Salvacion Ramos and Llore Pasco say together.
Duterte could soon be joined by his ally Senator Ronald dela Rosa, known as “Bato,” whom Duterte appointed chief of the Philippine National Police after he took office in 2016. In this capacity, dela Rosa oversaw the launch of “Double Barrel,” a cornerstone of the drug war that would leave about 30,000 people dead, according to estimates by several NGOs. (The official death toll of the police is around 6,000.)
On May 11, an attempt to arrest dela Rosa on a warrant for the ICC ended with him taking refuge inside the Philippine Senate as shots were fired in the building. The former police chief was placed under a form of protective custody inside the chamber before leaving the building a few days later. He is currently at large and wanted by Philippine authorities.
The fact that such chaos is possible reflects how politically sensitive the drug war remains at the highest levels of the Philippine state. In 2022, Duterte completed his single six-year term and was succeeded by Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the son of the former dictator who ruled the country from 1965 to 1986, who was elected through an alliance with the Duterte camp. But the alliance did not last.
As relations between the two political clans deteriorated, Marcos gradually shifted his position on the International Criminal Court. In March 2024, he said the ICC had no authority to investigate the Philippines’ drug war and that his government would not cooperate with the court. Months later, as his alliance with the Dutertes unraveled, he adopted a softer stance, saying his government would not block an ICC investigation and would comply with its obligations to Interpol. By early 2025, his administration had also signaled that it was open to limited cooperation with the court.
Duterte was arrested by Philippine authorities, based on an Interpol Red Notice, at Manila’s airport on March 11, 2025.
While Marcos allowed police to enforce the ICC arrest warrant and accepted the presence of ICC investigators, he never openly opposed the drug war waged by his predecessor. He largely avoided the issue during the 2022 presidential campaign, particularly to preserve his alliance with the Duterte camp and its supporters.
He distanced himself from it only after taking office, when he promised a “bloodless” war on drugs. Joel Ariate, a social sciences researcher at the University of the Philippines and founder of the DAHAS project, which has tracked drug-war deaths since 2017, called the term “pure propaganda.”
“The Marcos government says there is no more blood being spilled. That is absurd. The drug war continues. The number of victims has dropped sharply, but there are still 200 to 300 deaths every year,” Ariate says. One-third of the victims are killed in police operations, he says, while the rest are mainly linked to private militias or hit men hired for less than $100 per killing.
The decline in violence against drug users could be a sign of progress under the Marcos government, but Ariate remains pessimistic. “Those responsible for thousands of killings, particularly low-ranking police officers, are still in their jobs. The police know the details and who took part,” the researcher says.
So far, only five cases have resulted in the conviction of nine police officers for crimes linked to Duterte’s drug war, according to a report from Human Rights Watch published in June this year. Yet DAHAS has documented many other cases in which police officers themselves filmed killings and posted the footage online as trophies.
Sitting in the university library where he works, Ariate shares his main concern. “In reality, the institutions that failed during the drug war have not changed,” he says. “In two years, there will be another presidential election, and if a politician like Duterte wins, it could all start again because the mentality has not changed either.”
In May 2025, two months after his arrest and transfer to The Hague, 63 percent of registered voters surveyed by Pulse Asia said they still trusted Duterte.
“Populist leaders present themselves as defenders of order and the fight against crime,” says Christopher Magno, a criminologist specializing in political violence and co-founder of the Truth Commission. “To justify their policies, they identify a group as responsible for insecurity: immigrants in the United States under Trump, and poor people and those accused of using or trafficking drugs in the Philippines under Duterte. By identifying an ‘enemy,’ they can legitimize a repressive policy and strengthen their popularity. Duterte therefore left office with very high levels of public support.”
The Truth Commission, established in 2026, is an independent body that brings together civilian experts from different fields, including law, forensic medicine, journalism, trauma-informed care, and education. Its work centers on collecting testimonies from victims and their families, preserving their stories, and examining the institutions and practices behind the drug war.
“Our goal is to document the facts and establish a truthful account, but above all to humanize the victims and begin a process of healing through a change in mentality,” Magno says.
The commission’s work is expected to last two years and be completed before the next elections, with findings released every six months. It offers new hope to victims’ families, though they remain cautious.
“We are still observing what will happen with the Truth Commission,” Salvacion Ramos and Llore Pasco say, as if protecting themselves from another disappointment in their quest for justice in the Philippines.
Magno says that some police officers are “beginning to open up” during interviews conducted by the Truth Commission. He adds, “The national police have also supported us and say they will follow the conclusions of our commission.”
The criminologist knows the heavy responsibility facing his team: a process of truth and remembrance aimed at putting people and victims back at the center of this tragedy. There is also the challenge of having the commission’s findings recognized by everyone – from institutions to victims’ families, but above all by a divided society – so that the wound left by Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war can finally begin to heal.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survives lethal execution attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:44:02 UTC
14:44:02 KST

Tennessee officials failed to execute Christa Gail Pike by lethal injection Wednesday after administering two doses of pentobarbital, an unprecedented outcome that prompted Gov. Bill Lee to halt the state’s remaining executions for the year and order an independent review.
Pike, 50, remained alive after the attempted execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and was taken by ambulance to an outside hospital. Her attorneys said she had been loudly snoring after the drugs were administered and that they had not been informed of her condition.
Pike had been sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at a Knoxville job training program. Had the execution succeeded, Pike would have become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement announcing a “comprehensive, third-party review” of what happened.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it had “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”
The state’s protocol calls for a second set of drug syringes to be administered if the prisoner remains alive after the first. It does not specify what officials should do if the prisoner remains alive after the second dose.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, described the failed execution as “singular and unparalleled.” She said seven other people had survived execution attempts because teams were unable to establish intravenous access, but no one was known to have survived after receiving the drugs intended to cause death.
Pike’s attorneys said the outcome validated concerns they had raised about the execution process, including difficult vein access, damaged veins, the condition of the pentobarbital and the availability of emergency medical care.
Execution stretches for more than an hour
Media witnesses said the curtains to the execution chamber were raised at 7:27 p.m., revealing Pike strapped to a gurney.
“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” Pike said in what were intended to be her final words. She said she was at peace.
But Pike remained awake. At one point, she raised her head and asked prison officials whether her arm was supposed to feel the way it did, though it was unclear what she was experiencing.
By 8:26 p.m., witnesses were told that a second dose of pentobarbital had been administered. Pike could later be heard snoring after the curtains were closed. The microphone from the execution chamber was cut off at 8:53 p.m. and media witnesses were escorted from the area.
Pike’s lawyers filed emergency motions seeking to halt the execution, arguing that she was experiencing “unnecessary agony” in violation of the constitutional prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment. They also called on prison officials to begin lifesaving treatment.
The failed attempt was Tennessee’s second aborted execution this year. In May, officials called off the execution of Tony Carruthers, convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after spending more than an hour unsuccessfully trying to establish an IV line.
Execution delayed by last-minute court battle
Pike had initially been scheduled to die at 10 a.m. Wednesday, but the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals voted 2-1 about an hour beforehand to stay the execution while considering whether allegations that Pike suffered sexual abuse as a child had been adequately considered during sentencing.
Tennessee’s attorney general appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing that another last-minute delay would traumatize Slemmer’s family and reward what the state described as “abusive delay tactics.”
Hours later, the Supreme Court cleared the way for the execution. The court’s conservative majority did not explain the decision, while its three liberal justices dissented and said Pike’s claims warranted further examination.
Pike has not denied killing Slemmer. Her lawyers and supporters, however, have argued that her age at the time of the crime, mental illness and allegations of severe childhood sexual abuse should have been given greater consideration.
Pike was 18 at the time of the killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she had intended to fight Slemmer but lost control during the attack.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid,” Pike said in a statement. “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done.”
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell has called Pike’s death sentence an outlier, noting that other defendants who were 18 when they committed crimes in Tennessee have had their death sentences overturned.
A killing that shocked Knoxville
Prosecutors said Pike believed Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend and lured her into a wooded area in Knoxville on Jan. 12, 1995.
Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large piece of asphalt. Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, admitted carving a pentagram into Slemmer’s body. The details of the killing attracted national attention amid widespread fears about Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.
Pike received a death sentence, while her boyfriend was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, traveled to Nashville hoping to witness the execution after waiting more than three decades for Pike’s sentence to be carried out.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez told The Associated Press before the scheduled execution.
Martinez said her daughter remained constantly on her mind and would have turned 51 in September.
Women rarely executed in US
Only 18 women have been executed in the United States since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, accounting for about 1% of executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the United States this year.
Tennessee switched in 2024 from a three-drug lethal injection protocol to a single dose of pentobarbital. The change came more than two years after the state abruptly halted another execution and acknowledged that it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were properly tested.
Lee’s order means Tennessee will conduct no further executions this year while officials investigate why Pike survived Wednesday’s attempt.

Keogh says he can still work with veterans after health cap backdown

Unknown Publisher

Matt Keogh says he can work 'collaboratively' with veterans after health cap backdown
In short:
Minister for Veterans' Affairs Matt Keogh plans to keep working with veterans, saying he has no plans to step down.
Mr Keogh has faced pressure from the Coalition and veterans to resign after a plan to cap allied health care for veterans at $5,000 a year, which has since been axed.
What's next?
The government is "on track" to deliver two-thirds of the recommendations made by the Royal Commission in Defence and Veteran Suicide.
Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh says he will keep working with veterans, rebuffing calls to resign as minister after the government backed down on its proposed cap on allied health services for veterans.
Facing several questions about scrapping the limit on veteran supports two weeks ago, Mr Keogh said he had listened to veterans and could still "work collaboratively" with them.
"We engaged with the veteran community. We heard, and we responded. And I think that's what people actually want from good, effective government," he told reporters today.
"What's really important about how I do my job is the commitment to engage, to listen, to bring forward good ideas and to make sure that we're delivering good outcomes for our veteran community."
The proposed cap would have imposed a $5,000 annual limit on services such as physiotherapy and dentistry unless veterans could demonstrate "clinical need".
The policy announced in the May budget would have saved the federal government $750 million over three years. Still, critics argued it would create barriers for ex-servicemen and women, particularly those with complex, ongoing medical needs.
Senator Jacquie Lambie, who is a veteran, made an impassioned plea on the floor of the Senate not to restrict health services for veterans, describing her own health issues after service.
The backdown also came days after Mr Keogh conceded he had made a mistake when he initially refused to meet with a veterans group who had pleaded for the veteran cap to be axed.
Before the policy shift, frustrated veterans who had travelled to Canberra for the meeting said they had lost faith in the minister, urging he be sacked.
Several opposition members, including Liberal leader Angus Taylor, also called for Mr Keogh's resignation, saying the veteran community had "lost faith" and it was untenable for him to remain in the position.
Today, Mr Keogh rebuffed calls for him to step down, arguing "there's still more to do".
Asked who made the call to scrap the cap, he said it was a government decision.
"That's how governments work. We listen and we responded,"
"We've worked collaboratively with the sector the whole way through, making once-in-a-century reform to improve the veteran entitlement system as well the legislative system."
Department figures suggest that only about 10 per cent of veteran cardholders spend more than $5,000 on allied health services each year.
Advocacy group Fair Care for Veterans spokesman John Armfield, a former Navy clearance diver, thanked Mr Keogh for ditching the health service cap.
"Nobody had to lose for this to happen. The minister made the right call, and he deserves credit for it," he said.
Mr Keogh said the government was "on track" to deliver two-thirds of the recommendations made by the Royal Commission into Defence and Veterans suicide.
That includes increasing fees paid to providers to encourage more to take on veterans as clients and removing requirements for referral.
"We've maintained the fee increase. We dropped the threshold proposal, and we'll continue to work closely with the sector on the further implementation of recommendations as we go forward," he said.

The Copenhagen Architecture Biennial Announces Theme and Dates for Its Second Edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The origins of the Copenhagen Architecture Biennial trace back to the establishment of the CAFx yearly festival in 2014, which was renamed Copenhagen Architecture Forum in 2024 to lead new projects focused on architecture and urbanism, such as the shift from festival to biennial, with a first edition in 2025. Today, the details of the second edition are being announced: it will take place from September 9 to October 15, 2027, under the theme "Elements." After the Biennial's inaugural call to Slow Down, the event is turning its attention to the planetary elemental forces that architecture has sought to master and prepare to inhabit, questioning one of modernity's most persistent promises: control over the environment. Activities will be dedicated to and organized around each of the four elements: fire, earth, air, and water, including an open call for pavilions, exhibitions, and a symposium.
The curatorial approach begins with a critique of the modern promise of unlimited technological development, beyond climate, geographical, biological, and material constraints. Architecture has been a tool for fulfilling this promise, managing temperature, humidity, and contact. The organization's diagnosis is that this foundational modern promise is increasingly unattainable in a world marked by rising temperatures, polluted air, rising sea levels, dead soils, and growing pressure on natural resources needed to sustain life. The promise has become an undesirable future. This year's theme for the Copenhagen Architecture Biennial is grounded in this double disenchantment, leading to the question of how architecture can live, build, and plan with "elements" rather than against them, in protection of human life. The Biennial poses the questions: Who is protected and who is exposed? What is maintained and what is allowed to fail? And what kinds of common life might emerge: habit, happiness, ritual, and care?
 For decades, architecture has promised us mastery over heat, earth, air and water. With 'Elements', we ask what happens when we stop pretending we ever had that mastery, and start designing from dependence instead? The buildings that will serve us best aren't the ones that shut the world out, they're the ones that let us feel it. - Josephine Michau, part of the Curatorial Collective & Director of the Copenhagen Architecture Biennial
Related Article
Copenhagen Architecture City Guide: 44 Projects Defining the Capital of Human-Scale Design
The program will take place across Copenhagen's Cultural District and more than 60 venues across the city. Event highlights include four exhibitions exploring architecture's relationship with elemental forces, held at the newly built Vandkulturhuset Papirøen by Kengo Kuma, as well as at Simian, Kunsthal Nord, and Halmtorvet 27. The Biennial's professional symposium, Assemble!, will focus on policy, the regulatory structures that govern how cities build, extract, and consume, following the inaugural edition's call for new legislation. After the success of the Biennial's Slow Pavilions, there will be a second open call inviting architects, designers, and researchers to propose new pavilions responding to the Elements theme. Details of the call will be available on the website. Further program details, including exhibiting practices, pavilion winners, Assemble! speakers, and the full public events schedule, will be announced ahead of the Biennial's opening.
 With four exhibitions built around fire, earth, air and water, an open call for new public pavilions, and Assemble! Returning with a sharper focus on policy, the 2027 Biennial is our most ambitious attempt yet to make the elemental legible as the very ground of architecture itself. - Josephine Michau, Founder and Chief Curator, CAFx & Copenhagen Architecture Biennial
For the second year running, Copenhagen was named the world's most livable city in the 2026 Economist Intelligence Unit's Global Liveability Index. According to the Danish Architecture Center, part of this progress in urban quality of life is due to the work of Danish architect and urban planner Jan Gehl, whose 90th birthday is being celebrated at DAC with a calendar of activities and an exhibition. Around the world, other architectural events are sharing content to advance the architectural discipline. In the UAE, the Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT) has released the full documentary film series A Journey into Architecture Archives: Baghdad, Damascus, Tunis online. In Chile, a new gathering in Valparaíso is bringing together master builders to safeguard traditional trades. In Estonia, the 8th Tallinn Architecture Biennale (TAB 2026) brings the question "How Much?" to the center of its program, examining how cost, scarcity, and constraint shape architectural production.

AI agents attempted to hack US, Canadian gov't websites: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:29:18 UTC
14:29:18 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents have attempted to hack US and Canadian government websites, according to a report by the San Francisco-based nonprofit research lab Transluce.
Released on Wednesday, the report said that researchers found "two rudimentary and failed hacking attempts, one against the US Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection, and one against Library and Archives Canada, a Canadian federal agency."
The researchers said the failed attempts were linked to other activity in which agents "used an array of aggressive tactics short of hacking to probe US government websites, often using sites in unintended ways and sometimes violating explicit usage policies."
The activity targeted websites of the White House, the Departments of War, Justice and Commerce, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Securities and Exchange Commission and state agencies in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York, the report said.
"We have so far identified no instances in these datasets where agents gained access to any information that is not publicly available," the researchers said.
The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said in a statement on Tuesday that it was aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity.
"There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time," Canadian officials said.

“The concepts of order which [the culture industry] hammers into human beings are always those of the status quo. They remain unquestioned, unanalyzed and undialectically presupposed, even if they no longer have any substance for those who accept them. In contrast to the Kantian, the categorical imperative of the culture industry no longer has anything in common with freedom. It proclaims: you shall conform, without instruction as to what; conform to that which exists anyway, and to that which everyone thinks anyway as a reflex of its power and omnipresence.”
— Theodor W. Adorno, “Culture Industry Reconsidered”
