Six US House Democrats have prepared legislation to be formally introduced that would impose targeted sanctions on individuals and entities involved in constructing or expanding illegal Israeli settlements and outposts across the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Representatives Joaquin Castro, Madeleine Dean, Don Beyer, Greg Casar, Sara Jacobs, and Veronica Escobar are co-sponsoring the draft measure, titled the Stop the Settlements Act.
The proposed legislation seeks to halt the construction of new illegal settlements alongside the physical expansion of existing illegal Israeli outposts.
It aims to achieve this through punitive financial sanctions and a strict ban on the importation of commercial goods produced within illegal Israeli settlements and outposts located in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Countering 'land grab'
Backers of the bill argue that the proposed economic measures are essential to halt the continuing displacement of Palestinians and protect an enduring diplomatic pathway towards a negotiated political resolution where both Israelis and Palestinians can exercise self-determination.
Castro, one of the primary sponsors, issued sharp criticism against the current Israeli administration and its accelerating expansion policies across the occupied West Bank.
"Under [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's government, settlers are engaged in a violent land grab that's ripping Palestinians from their land," Castro said in an official statement.
The Texas Democrat characterised the relentless expansion of settlement infrastructure as one of the primary obstacles to regional peace, urging the US Congress to deploy legislative sanctions directly against those facilitating settlement growth.
"Democrats must face this with urgency—act now or watch the prospect of Palestinian self-determination slip away forever," Castro warned.

Chokehold, headphone cables and first aid: How 4 Israelis helped save 174 aboard Flydubai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:12:56 UTC
08:12:56 KST

There were 174 passengers aboard the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when screams about a stabbing suddenly spread through the cabin. Four Israeli passengers rushed toward the cockpit, each playing a different role in the struggle that followed.
Yaniv Hayun says he choked the suspected attacker and later pulled back on the aircraft’s controls. Zvika Manes and Assaf Rajuan helped overpower and restrain the suspect. Dentist Shota Musaev treated the badly wounded captain and stopped his bleeding. And passengers believe Indian captain Smit Machchhar, despite being stabbed, managed to leave them a way into the cockpit before collapsing.
Together, their accounts describe a frantic fight aboard a plunging aircraft after the Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain, apparently using a crash axe found in the cockpit.
‘I watch Air Crash Investigation’
Hayun, one of the four Israelis who intervened, spent much of the day speaking with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He landed in Israel with his shirt stained with blood but said he had not been injured.
Hayun said the cockpit door was not locked when passengers reached it, something he believes may have been the wounded captain’s doing.
“The captain was very close to the door, and that made it difficult for us to open it,” Hayun said. “My conclusion is that he managed to open it for us before he collapsed, with tremendous presence of mind.”
Once inside, Hayun said he saw the Omani co-pilot between the seats.
“He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the aircraft. I grabbed the attacker, choked him and pulled him out. I called the Israelis and told them. We pinned him down,” he said.
Then Hayun went back into the cockpit.
“I jumped back into the cockpit. I watch ‘Air Crash Investigation,’ so I pulled the controls and the plane began to level out. After that, a pilot who was traveling on the plane told me he was taking control,” Hayun said.
Two pilots who were aboard then took over the cockpit and eventually landed the aircraft safely.
“I think because of my children, I behaved the way I did,” Hayun said.
‘The plane was 90 degrees down’
Assaf Rajuan, an insurance agency owner and tennis enthusiast, had been returning from a vacation in Thailand when the flight turned into what he described as a “horror movie.”
“We heard screams from near the restroom. A girl’s mother came out screaming, and we understood something had happened to the plane,” he said. “It lost control, went down at a 90-degree angle, and we understood there was no control over the aircraft and something had happened.”
Rajuan was among those who helped overpower the suspected attacker.
“The cockpit door was open and we started seeing the cockpit fill with blood,” he said. “People went in. There was a guy who got there before me named Zvika Manes. I went in with two other guys and we tried to overpower the attacker, and we succeeded.”
“We also had help from some of the crew. We managed to keep the attacker neutralized for 50 minutes and land in Saudi Arabia,” he said.
Rajuan said he was still struggling to process what happened.
“I was in Thailand a few hours earlier, and after that I was in a horror movie,” he said. “Of course, it wasn’t just me. Bigger and stronger guys than me helped, blocked the doors and decided to go all the way, because life is stronger than anything and we wanted to fight for it. For our families, our children, the crew.”
“It’s hard to believe it ended this way, but it did,” he added. “I saw all the bursts of blood, the cuts, the Indian pilot. I know the plane lost control and plunged. Luckily, the right people were there at the right time.”
Headphone cables used to restrain suspect
Zvika Manes, CEO of Bank Leumi’s underwriting company, also rushed the suspected attacker and helped restrain him using cables from the multimedia headphones distributed on the flight.
The incident began for Manes when his wife went to the restroom with their daughter and heard a confrontation in the cockpit.
“There was a lot of blood. The plane plunged rapidly like you see in horror movies. There were screams. It was a very difficult event until the pilot stabilized the plane,” Manes said.
“We lost our angles. He was really trying to fly the aircraft toward the ground, and people were thrown around and screaming,” he said of the co-pilot.
“We later tied him up and neutralized him. It took quite a bit of physical force. He was a strong man, probably full of adrenaline,” Manes said.
He said a doctor and nurse aboard the flight then worked to stabilize the wounded captain, who had suffered stab wounds across his body.
Manes, like Hayun, said he believed the stabbed captain managed to open the cockpit door, giving passengers the chance to intervene.
The dentist who treated the captain
Dentist Shota Musaev initially rushed forward to help fight the suspected attacker. After the man was restrained, Musaev turned his attention to the badly wounded captain.
“The pilot was in very serious condition, with heavy bleeding from his head and hands,” Musaev told ynet. “I was the only doctor on the plane. I managed to stop the bleeding, and the pilot was in fairly stable condition until close to the landing, when his condition deteriorated somewhat.”
Musaev said the captain remained able to communicate while lying on the floor and told those around him that he was 39 and had two children.
“The attacker stabbed him and cursed him,” Musaev said. “At that moment you don’t think, you just act. There were four of us who took control of the entire situation, and if we hadn’t, we wouldn’t be talking to you.”
“I saw something was wrong and ran forward. I didn’t wait for someone to call me,” he said. “I came to fight the attacker when I heard the screams. I didn’t come to provide medical treatment. But after we tied him up, I treated the stabbed pilot.”
Musaev said the suspect continued struggling and trying to break free.
“We tied him several times, both his legs and his hands. He was thrashing around, so we tied him even more tightly. Then he calmed down and understood that he was in our hands,” he said.
He said Saudi medical teams later treated the captain and that he was told the pilot had survived and was no longer in immediate danger.
The wounded captain who may have left a way in
Captain Smit Machchhar remains hospitalized in Saudi Arabia in serious condition, although reports Wednesday evening said he was out of immediate danger.
He has not yet publicly given his version of events.
But according to passengers, his actions may have been decisive. They believe that despite being wounded in the confrontation with the Omani co-pilot, Machchhar managed to leave the cockpit accessible before collapsing.
That opening allowed the Israeli passengers to get inside, overpower the suspected attacker and make way for another flight crew to take control of the aircraft.
Each person aboard the flight played a different part in those minutes: restraining the suspect, pulling back on the controls, stopping the bleeding or, passengers believe, leaving the cockpit door open long enough for help to get through.

Measuring the Skills That Travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:07:15 UTC
08:07:15 KST

Ratnesh Jha discusses English proficiency and workforce mobility
Adaptability has become one of the most valued qualities in today’s workforce. Employers want people who can adjust to new technologies, move between roles, work across cultures, and respond to challenges that may not have existed when they were first trained.
Workers feel that pressure too. In the 2026 ETS Human Progress Report, 77% of employees globally said job security no longer exists without continuous adaptation. The challenge is that adaptability is difficult to define and even harder to measure well. We talk about it constantly, but it is not a quality that lends itself easily to a single score.
For those of us in assessment, that should give us pause. The answer is not necessarily to create a new measure for every quality employers say they value, whether that is adaptability, resilience, or agility. Some human capabilities are simply too complex to reduce in that way. A more useful question is what adaptability looks like when someone actually has to perform. Language offers an interesting way to think about that.
A language assessment cannot tell us whether someone is an adaptable person, and it should not try to. What it can help us understand is whether someone can take what they know and apply it as the situation changes. That is something we do constantly when we communicate. We listen, interpret meaning, read the context, choose language that fits the audience, and adjust when a conversation moves in an unexpected direction or when we are misunderstood.
“Competence is not only about what someone knows. It is also about what they can do with that knowledge when the context changes.”
For multilingual people, there may be another layer of complexity. They often move between languages, cultural expectations, levels of formality, and different ways of expressing the same idea. That does not mean multilingualism automatically makes someone more adaptable in every aspect of life or work. It does, however, illustrate an important principle. Competence is not only about what someone knows. It is also about what they can do with that knowledge when the context changes.
That distinction matters more as the world of work becomes less predictable. We cannot prepare people for every task they will encounter over the course of a career. We cannot know exactly which technologies they will use, what industries they may enter, or what responsibilities they may eventually take on. What we can do is help people build capabilities that transfer across situations and become better at recognizing when those capabilities are genuinely there.
Language assessment has been grappling with this question for years. A meaningful assessment of communication should do more than determine whether someone recognizes vocabulary or understands a grammatical rule. It should also show whether that person can understand information, interpret meaning, and communicate effectively for a particular purpose.
The question is not simply whether someone knows something, but whether they can use what they know. That distinction has implications well beyond language.
If the skills employers increasingly need involve judgment, communication, and the ability to respond to unfamiliar situations, assessments that primarily reward the reproduction of familiar answers can only tell us so much. We need to understand how knowledge holds up when circumstances shift.
Workplace language assessment provides one example of how that role is already expanding. Research conducted for the TOEIC Global English Skills Report found that employers are using English assessments at several points in an employee’s journey. They may use them during recruitment, before training, or when considering employees for advancement.
These are very different moments. During hiring, an assessment may help determine whether someone is prepared for a particular role. Before training, it can help identify where development is needed. Later in a career, it can help make progress and newly acquired capability more visible.
In each case, the assessment does not predict the person’s future. It provides a clearer picture of what that individual can do now and where further development may create additional opportunities. That is an important shift in how we think about the role of assessment.
Assessment has often been viewed primarily as a gateway. A person reaches a certain score and gains access to a program, role, or opportunity. That function will always matter, but assessment can also help guide development. It can give learners a clearer understanding of where they stand, help employers identify areas for growth, and provide individuals with a way to demonstrate progress over time.
As the role of assessment changes, assessment itself also has to become more responsive to how skills are actually used. A single, uniform approach makes less sense when organizations are hiring and developing people for very different roles, industries, and communication needs.
We have seen this firsthand in the development of TOEIC Link, which allows organizations to assess listening, reading, speaking, and writing skills individually or in combination depending on their needs. The point is not that every assessment should become modular. It is that the way we measure skills should continue to evolve alongside the environments in which those skills are used.
As work becomes more dynamic, assessment should become more flexible too, while preserving the rigor, reliability, and comparability that make the results meaningful.
The same principle applies after an assessment is complete. A score is most useful when it helps someone understand what to do next. Measurement can identify a strength or a gap, but its value grows when learners can act on that information through targeted practice, feedback, and continued development.
That creates a more useful relationship between assessment and learning. Instead of measurement being the end of the process, it can become part of an ongoing cycle of understanding, development, and progress.
Language is particularly relevant because proficiency can expand the number of environments in which someone is able to participate. An engineer may be able to contribute to an international project. A frontline employee may become eligible for a regional role. A researcher may gain access to a wider professional community. A manager may be better equipped to lead colleagues across countries. In that sense, language proficiency can create greater optionality.
Learning English does not guarantee career mobility, and no language score should ever be treated as a proxy for intelligence, talent, or potential. It can, however, expand the range of settings in which someone is able to communicate effectively and contribute with confidence.
In an unpredictable labor market, having more options matters. The career someone begins in their 20s may look very different from the work they are doing in their 40s. Industries change. Technology changes. People retrain, relocate, and take on responsibilities they never anticipated.
Do our assessments require people to apply knowledge rather than simply recall it? Do the tasks reflect the situations in which those skills will actually be used? Do the results help people develop as well as demonstrate what they can already do? Can those results remain meaningful as people move between institutions, jobs, and countries?
Most importantly, we should ask whether we are only measuring what a person knows or whether we are getting closer to understanding what that person can actually do. Language assessment has been wrestling with these questions for decades. As education and work become more dynamic, they are becoming relevant far beyond language.
The future of assessment should not be about pretending we can predict exactly who will thrive in an uncertain world. It should be about giving people better ways to demonstrate capabilities that remain useful even as the world around them changes.
Language is one of those capabilities. Its value is not merely that it helps someone communicate today. It can also expand where they can contribute, how they can grow, and the opportunities they may be able to pursue next.
If adaptability is what we increasingly expect of workers, then assessment should be willing to adapt as well.
Ratnesh Jha is Global General Manager, Institutional Products, at ETS.

aston martin DBX GT wraps 717 horsepower in a quieter, softer-riding SUV
aston martin retunes its fastest SUV around comfort, with memory foam seats, revised dampers, and a quieter V8.
aston martin gives its 717-hp DBX a softer side with new GT
Aston Martin has added a second personality to its fastest SUV. The new DBX GT arrives alongside the more overtly performance-focused DBX S, using essentially the same mechanical package while tuning the experience around comfort, reduced cabin noise, and a more restrained exterior. Under the hood is the familiar 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 producing 717 bhp, enough to send the large SUV from 0 to 60 mph in 3.1 seconds and on to 193 mph.
The interesting part is what Aston Martin has done around that engine. The GT keeps the speed, carbon-ceramic brakes, and quicker steering ratio of the DBX S, then changes how much of all that activity reaches the people inside.
Suspension calibration has been revised, including new internal damper valves designed to absorb the small, rapid movements produced by coarse pavement and rumble strips before they travel through the cabin. The standard wheels are 22 inches rather than the available 23-inch setup, paired with all-season tires chosen partly for ride quality and road noise.
the DBX turns down its visual aggression
The difference begins at the front, as the team at Aston Martin has replaced some of the DBX’s harder-edged detailing with a double-vaned metal grille that stretches visually toward the outer vents and daytime running lights. Lower sections of the front bumper, side sills, and rear diffuser come painted in the body color, while a two-piece metal side strake mixes polished and satin surfaces. A new set of horizontal quad exhaust tips finishes the rear.
It is a subtle shift in emphasis for a car that still has the proportions of a high-performance SUV. The standard 22-inch forged wheels leave a little more tire visible around the rim, and the body-colored lower sections reduce some of the contrast usually used to make performance cars appear lower and sharper.
Marek Reichman, Aston Martin’s chief creative officer, describes the GT as a more discreet interpretation of the DBX, with its outright performance receding visually even as the underlying hardware remains close to the DBX S.
more attention goes to the people inside
A larger part of the GT treatment happens where the changes are easiest to feel. Aston Martin has redesigned the front and rear seats with additional cushioning and reshaped bolsters, adding a 10 mm layer of memory foam to the seat base. The rear bench also gains two more deeply sculpted outer seating positions with taller headrests, while retaining space for a fifth passenger in the center. A panoramic glass roof comes standard.
There is plenty of labor buried in the upholstery. Aston Martin says each front seat uses 691 meters of thread and 3,297 perforations, requiring more than four and a half hours of work. Semi-aniline leather and deep-pile carpeting are joined by additional sound-deadening in the doors, wheel arches, and cargo area, along with acoustic laminated rear side glass.
The company reports a 13% improvement in its Articulation Index, a measurement concerned with how easily occupants can understand conversation while the vehicle is moving.
717 horsepower stays in the background until you ask for it
The 4.0-liter V8 uses turbocharger technology shared with Aston Martin’s mid-engine Valhalla and produces 664 lb-ft of torque. The nine-speed automatic has received revised calibration for smoother gear changes, while the throttle mapping has been adjusted to make smaller pedal inputs easier to control.
Engineers also added a stiffer transmission mount and dampers between the body and rear subframe, aimed at reducing movement through larger bumps and compressions.
Even the exhaust has been retuned around that idea. Gas flow is mixed twice inside the rear muffler to remove some harsher metallic frequencies, with GT mode keeping the sound subdued and Sport modes opening things up when the driver wants the V8 to come forward. First deliveries of the Aston Martin DBX GT are scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026.

 top speed: 193 mph / 310 km/h

Why Serbia’s Election Matters to Israel’s Arsenal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Why Serbia’s Election Matters to Israel’s Arsenal
Israel’s next defence headache may have little to do with Iran, Gaza or Hezbollah. It could begin in Belgrade.
The upcoming snap elections in Serbia on 25 October mark a critical juncture in the country’s political landscape. Called amid heightened political polarisation, prolonged public protests and intense institutional pressure, the vote is widely seen as a major test for President Aleksandar Vučić and the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The decision to head to the polls prematurely follows months of societal tension, rising economic demands and an increasingly vocal opposition seeking to capitalise on growing public discontent.
Locally, the ramifications of this vote extend far beyond a mere allocation of parliamentary seats. A shift in the political balance could trigger policy re-evaluations, administrative turnover and shifting legislative priorities across key state industries. In a country where central authority heavily influences economic and industrial planning, domestic political friction directly affects governance, regulatory predictability and institutional continuity.
Yet, while the immediate focus remains on Belgrade’s political future, the consequences of this domestic contest extend far beyond the Balkans.
Serbia’s election matters to Israel because political continuity in the country, or a lack thereof, could be a test for a European defence-industrial partnership of ever greater strategic significance. Serbia is not just a friendly government or another arms customer. It is a potential production hub within a wider network that could give Israel a broader production base during a prolonged conflict.
The vote is, therefore, a strategic question for Jerusalem, not just another political episode in the Balkans.
An Emerging Defence-Industrial Link
At first glance, the strategic logic is not exactly obvious – Serbia is a small, landlocked country on the edge of Europe, whereas Israel’s security concerns are overwhelmingly concentrated in the Middle East. Yet the two countries are forging a defence-industrial relationship of mounting consequence.
Having the cleverest weapons is not the way to win a modern war. They are won by having enough of them. Ukraine has revealed the brutal arithmetic of industrial warfare: artillery shells, drones, missiles and spare parts are consumed at extraordinary speed. That being the case, sophisticated armies need something less glamorous than cutting-edge technology – factories capable of producing more.
Industrial capacity is military power.
Serbia matters because it has that capacity.
Serbia’s defence industry is an asset that can translate diplomatic relations into tangible economic and strategic leverage. Its ability to manufacture ammunition, weapons and military equipment increases its strategic weight beyond that of a small European state
According to official sources, Serbia has a sizeable defence industry, with nearly 200 public and private companies producing weapons, ammunition, and military. Serbia's defence sector comprises around 200 companies and remains central to both national defence capabilities and export performance. The sector is central to Serbia’s defence capability and a major source of export revenue. Israel, meanwhile, has established itself as an important supplier of advanced defence technologies to Serbia, reflecting the increasingly strategic nature of the bilateral relationship. Cooperation, however, has moved beyond the procurement of military equipment. In April 2026, President Aleksandar Vučić revealed plans for a Serbian-Israeli combat drone production programme, signaling a new phase in defence-industrial cooperation between the two countries. Furthermore, the launch of the Serbia-Israel Strategic Dialogue in April 2026 formalised cooperation across strategic sectors including technology, innovation, and economic cooperation, entrenching a commitment to a deeper long-term partnership. The trend culminated in September 2026 with the opening of a joint assembly facility for Israeli-designed combat drones in Serbia, suggesting a deeper stage of defence-industrial integration and the localisation of advanced defence production capabilities.
This potentially carries far greater weight than a conventional arms contract.
It creates a defence-industrial partnership bringing together a state with advanced military technology and a European country that can offer well-developed manufacturing capacity, a skilled workforce and an established defence sector.
Belgrade’s Balancing Act
Which brings us back to the Serbian election.
President Vučić, who resigned on 27 September, had spent years practising a distinctly Balkan form of geopolitical balancing. Serbia aspires to membership of the European Union (EU), maintaining close relations with the West along the way. It has also preserved the relationship with Russia and deepened its ties with China. More recently, Belgrade has added another dimension to that balancing act by forging increasingly strong defence ties with Israel.
Critics tend to point out that Serbia remains unintegrated into the EU, lagging behind in foreign policy alignment and adherence to institutional norms. Paradoxically, it is precisely the lack of full EU institutional embeddedness that lends exceptional agility to Belgrade’s foreign policy. Unencumbered by collective EU consensus mechanisms, restrictive bloc-wide export vetoes or strict normative mandates, Serbia retains the autonomy to conclude pragmatic defence-industrial deals, export military equipment across geopolitical lines and forge dynamic partnerships with non-EU powers like Israel.
This strategic flexibility has served Serbia well, but it is also highly dependent on political continuity.
A change of government – or even substantial political instability in the wake of the vote – would not necessarily turn Serbia against Israel, or threaten existing defence contracts.
The danger is more mundane – and therefore more plausible.
Governments do change contracts, reconsider export policies or scrutinise procurement decisions. Coalition partners often demand different priorities, and government officials do not hesitate to review arrangements made by their predecessors.
In peacetime, these processes are irritating.
During a war, they can be strategic.
A delayed export licence or a contract review may sound like bureaucratic trivia. But defence supply chains are only as reliable as their weakest political link. A production line disrupted for six months cannot be easily mended by a press release saying that the relationship is as good as ever.
For Israel, this is the central risk of political discontinuity in Serbia: not an abrupt diplomatic rupture, but uncertainty over a defence-industrial partnership that Jerusalem may regard as an increasingly important strategic asset.
Israel has learnt this lesson before. Its extraordinary military capabilities cannot shield it from the vulnerabilities embedded in international supply chains. Indeed, the more intensive the fighting, the more vital the capacity to replace depleted stocks.
This is why Jerusalem should not think of Serbia simply as another friendly government.
Instead, it should see it as an emerging fixture in a wider defence-industrial network, treating the stability of that network as a strategic concern.
Diversification and its Limits
Diversification should be the obvious answer. Israel would want to expand domestic production, maintain multiple suppliers and avoid dependence on any single foreign partner. Serbia should be regarded as an additional source of industrial capacity, not as a replacement for Israel’s own defence industry.
But diversification only works as long as each partner remains politically reliable enough to deliver.
An opportunity for Belgrade lies in this logic, too.
Serbia’s defence industry is an asset that can translate diplomatic relations into tangible economic and strategic leverage. Its ability to manufacture ammunition, weapons and military equipment increases its strategic weight beyond that of a small European state. It may give Serbia a role in strengthening the resilience of Israel’s defence supply chains, as well as in Europe’s broader military-industrial recovery.
But that advantage depends on credibility.
International defence companies may appreciate a charming president, but they build long-term production partnerships because they expect contracts to be honoured, political stability to last and institutions to survive elections.
This is where the Serbian vote becomes consequential.
Vučić has built his political system around an extraordinary ability to simultaneously maintain relationships with several competing powers. A potential successor may attempt to draw Serbia closer to Brussels. Another might put greater emphasis on relations with Moscow or Beijing. An opposition coalition might seek to distance itself from Vučić by reviewing some of his most controversial policies.
None of these outcomes necessarily threatens Israel, but all of them create uncertainty around the industrial relationship Israel needs more and more.
Israel should therefore resist the temptation to personalise its relationship with Serbia. The safest strategy is to make defence cooperation sufficiently institutionalised that a change of government does not automatically become a change of strategic direction.
That means durable contracts, transparent procedures, multiple political channels and production arrangements designed to withstand electoral change. If Serbia is to become part of Israel’s defence-industrial network, the relationship will benefit from a stable, long-term framework that can support continued cooperation.
The Industrial Base as Strategy
There is a broader lesson here as well. The war in Ukraine has reinforced the importance of industrial capacity as a core element of national security. Israel, mindful of the prospect of a prolonged and multidimensional conflict, is reckoning with similar strategic imperatives. Defence production often takes place away from active theatres of conflict, but its contribution to military effectiveness can be decisive. Recent conflicts have made it clear that the ability to sustain production, maintain supply chains, and replenish military stock is a vital component of long-term operational resilience. This makes Serbia's election more than another episode in the Balkan politics. For Belgrade, the stakes have risen well above electoral politics, involving the more pressing matters now - the country's long-term strategic orientation and domestic stability. For Israel, the question the polls have triggered is whether an emerging defence-industrial partnership in Europe can prove dependable and resilient in the long run. Obviously, political continuity in Serbia cannot guarantee Israel's security, but a major political shift may disrupt the regulatory framework and production, licencing and supply arrangements underpinning the bilateral ties in the defence sector. In the larger strategic context, domestic political developments in partner states can test stability, predictability, and long-term viability of strategic defence partnerships.

Trump 'thinking about' diesel export ban, but says it could have 'negative impact' on gasoline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:43:53 UTC
07:43:53 KST

President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he is still "thinking about" banning diesel exports in an attempt to get a handle on high energy prices, but noted that doing so may have a "negative impact on gasoline."
Trump, asked in the Oval Office if he has decided on a ban, said his aides think it would help diesel "but it might raise the price of other things."
"And I think we're in a good place because oil prices are going to start to come down," Trump added.
Just three days earlier, Trump said he was "very seriously" considering the move, despite warnings from the U.S. oil industry that it would force refineries to cut production and ultimately raise domestic energy prices.
But his latest comments appeared to show him cooling to the idea of an export ban, even as he declined to rule it out entirely.
"We're in a very good place," Trump said, highlighting a recent resurgence in crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
The strait is a major throughway for the global oil trade that saw ship traffic stifled after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. But this week it saw daily exports return to prewar levels.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright, standing next to Trump at the Resolute Desk, said, "You've seen diesel prices come down the last week. I think you'll see them move meaningfully down in the coming weeks and days."
But Wright acknowledged that diesel supplies are "tight" because of export loss related to conflicts in Russia and the Middle East, as well as from China.
"So that's a lot of interruptions. But American refiners are running at record highs," Wright said, "and you will hear announcements from our our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that'll come to the market. That'll meaningfully push diesel prices down."
When a reporter asked if Wright has advised against a diesel export ban, Trump interjected, saying, "No, I think it's something that we think about and we talk about every day."
"But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline," he said. "That would go up a little bit and diesel would come down a little bit."
Trump also repeated his claim that Russia's war against Ukraine was "really the biggest problem for diesel."
Diesel prices have soared to record highs amid the continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, which have caused major disruptions to global energy flows. Oil prices rose on Wednesday as the prospect of U.S. talks with Iran appeared to stall out once again.

Wallaby who overcame cystic fibrosis to play rugby diagnosed with MND

Wallaby Nathan Charles diagnosed with motor neurone disease aged 37
In short:
Nathan Charles, who played four Test matches for the Wallabies, has revealed he has motor neurone disease (MND).
Charles revealed the diagnosis during an interview with Stan Sport.
MND has dominated sporting headlines in 2026, with the death of 2025 Australian of the Year Neale Daniher and the diagnosis for Qld State of Origin representative Jai Arrow.
Former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who defied cystic fibrosis to play international rugby, has been diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).
The 37-year-old, who played four Test matches for Australia in 2014, publicly announced his diagnosis during an interview with Stan Sport.
During the interview, Charles, who retired from professional rugby in 2018, said he had been experiencing challenges for eight months.
"For a long period there I just didn't know what it was," Charles told interviewer and former Wallaby Justin Harrison.
"I've had that many tests, seen that many doctors and it just wasn't getting any outcome. But my health just kept declining.
"And then recently, in the last few weeks, I was actually diagnosed with motor neurone disease, which has been extremely challenging and overwhelming. And, yeah, just at times quite cruel."
In the interview with Stan Sport, Charles said his first thoughts after being told the MND diagnosis were of his family.
"I felt as though this would impact them greater than it would me. So, yeah, that was my first thought," he said.
"I had a bad feeling going into that appointment and my fears were realised. It was the people around me that I felt worse for."
MND has dominated sporting headlines in 2026, with the death of 2025 Australian of the Year Neale Daniher, and the diagnosis for Queensland State of Origin representative Jai Arrow.
Loading...
"My first question was, 'How long have I got?' Charles said.
"I know that every person with MND has a different journey, a different path and it affects everyone differently.
"I know there's no cure and … your physicality, your body deteriorates and, yeah, your life cuts short."
Charles was a hooker who played Super Rugby for the Western Force and Melbourne Rebels, and also had short stints in England and France.
His career in contact sport was remarkable considering Charles had been diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, a genetic disorder which impairs the lungs and can also affect the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine.
Prior to his first Test match in 2014, then Wallabies coach Ewen McKenzie described Charles as someone who had "defied science".
"If you look at the symptoms and classic outcomes of cystic fibrosis, it's not a great scenario from a sporting point of view, but he seems to have defied science and defied logic," McKenzie said at the time, as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald.
Speaking to Stan Sport, Charles said MND was affecting him.
"I'm already greatly impacted by it," he said.
"I'm getting around with mobility aids. I struggle to do a lot of daily tasks, and putting on shoes and socks and stuff like that is a bit of a challenge.
"So it's already impacted me, and I'm going to have my ups and downs."

A buyer's market without buyers: Housing downturn deepens with nationwide falls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:21:13 UTC
07:21:13 KST

in brief
- House prices have fallen 1.1 per cent in September, marking their sixth monthly decline.
- The latest data from Cotality suggests widespread national downturn, rather than isolated declining regional markets.
Australian property values fell 1.1 per cent in September, dropping for the sixth consecutive month as the national housing downturn continues to pick up speed.
Cotality's latest home value index report shows overall property values are now 5.2 per cent lower than their March peak, with clearance rates faltering. Houses are sitting on the market for an average of 39 days across capital cities, up from 23 days a year ago.
The property market analysis firm's executive research director, Tim Lawless, said the downturn reflects a "combination of affordability constraints," including higher interest rates, elevated living costs, and weaker consumer sentiment. All of these have "reduced purchasing capacity and dampened buyer demand", Lawless said.
On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to their highest level in 15 years, bringing the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, in a bid to tackle persistent inflation. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows that borrowers are now spending an average of roughly $4,500 per month to service a standard 30-year loan.
"Borrowers are not only facing higher mortgage costs, but also an extended period of elevated living expenses and negative real income growth," Lawless said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Together, these pressures are narrowing the pool of buyers able to qualify for a mortgage and reducing the amount they can afford to pay."
Total advertised housing stock increased 23.1 per cent year-on-year, despite fresh listings entering the market, which dropped 9.2 per cent, as sales velocity declined.
"The lift in available stock is improving choice for buyers, but ironically, many prospective buyers don't have the confidence or financial capacity to buy at the moment," Lawless said.
A national downturn
While the market first showed signs of a downturn in the capital cities of Melbourne and Sydney, the scope and scale of the shift has widened to include virtually every market in the country.
In capital city suburbs, 97 per cent recorded a drop in dwelling values over the three months to the end of September. Every capital city recorded a monthly value fall in September, except Darwin, which rose 0.4 per cent.
In Sydney, housing values fell 1.4 per cent last month, and have dropped 8.6 per cent from their peak in February. The current pace of the decline is slightly faster than what was seen during the equivalent phase of the 2022-23 downturn.
"Sydney continues to lead the housing correction ... highlighting how rapid demand has weakened across the nation's largest housing market," Lawless said.
Melbourne property values dropped 0.7 per cent in September and are down 7.2 per cent below their November 2025 peak.
In regional areas, 71 per cent of local sub-markets dropped over the last month, falling 0.7 per cent. However, regional values remain 5.6 per cent higher annually.
Conditions shift in Brisbane
Brisbane saw the sharpest fall of all capital cities in September, dropping 1.5 per cent, outpacing Sydney's decline.
"The result highlights how sharply conditions have shifted in what had previously been one of the strongest performing housing markets," Lawless said.
Sales volumes have fallen the fastest in major cities which were previously growth leaders in the market. Brisbane is down 27.2 per cent, with Sydney just behind on 26.5 per cent and Perth at 24.2 per cent.
In mid-sized cities, the decline was less pronounced. Perth's home values have dropped 1.2 per cent over the past month while Adelaide fell 1.3 per cent.
Decline still has further to go
While the market is largely being driven by economic conditions, the Cotality report identifies changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax arrangements as having added "another layer of downside risk".
However, high construction costs, driven by inflationary pressures and labour force tightness, continue to suppress new housing supply, stabilising the market. Low unemployment rates are also preventing widespread selling, the report finds.
Speaking to ABC News on Thursday morning, Lawless said the property market is a buyer's market without buyers.
"Seller numbers are right down and I think that this really reflects the confidence in the housing market and the broader economy and cost of living pressures and high interest rates," he said. "So for now, even though it is a buyer's market, the missing piece of the puzzle is actually buyers."
Lawless pointed to the federal budget as having sent "a shudder" through the housing market, something Labor has frequently denied, and said that even bargain-hunters are staying away out of expectation that the market will continue to decline until interest rates drop.
The country's four largest trading banks all predict that interest rates will remain at their current level, if not higher, with the cycle starting to come down well into next year.
"It's pretty clear that headwinds facing demand are outweighing those supply-side challenges," Lawless said.
"That will be the case, I think, for at least going into 2027 — probably around the middle of next year."

‘I started talking to God’: Children recount terror aboard Flydubai flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:09:46 UTC
07:09:46 KST

“The plane started going wild. Two heroes jumped forward toward the pilot and stopped the attacker,” 16-year-old Peleg Itali recalled after surviving Wednesday’s suspected terror attack aboard a Flydubai flight.
Peleg was traveling through Dubai with his parents and sister when, according to Israeli accounts of the incident, one pilot stabbed the other and allegedly tried to crash the aircraft with 174 passengers aboard.
“I was sitting right near the front rows, and suddenly the plane started going wild,” Peleg told ynet. “I heard a woman shouting, ‘He was stabbed, he was stabbed.’ Two heroes jumped forward toward the pilot, and it turns out they managed to stop the attacker who stabbed one of the pilots.”
He described the fear and confusion as passengers struggled to understand what was happening.
“You don’t know what’s going on. Nobody explains to you that there’s an attacker or that someone was actually stabbed,” he said.
“I started talking to God. I told him, ‘I’m sorry for everything I’ve done. Please, heaven.’ That’s what I was thinking, because you see the ground, you feel yourself falling. You feel like you’re just a touch away from God. I almost started writing my eulogy.”
Peleg said the presence of young children made the situation even harder.
“There were families there, mothers with children. One woman was trying to calm two girls, not very old, maybe 4 and 6,” he said. “It’s hard. How do you explain to them that there’s an attacker, that someone attacked the pilot and that there’s a chance we’re going to die? You can’t. It was frightening. Everyone was screaming.”
Eight-year-old Omer Shalom, who was traveling with her parents and two sisters, said she was terrified.
“I was really scared because I thought we were going to crash,” she said.
Omer said her mother later told her, after the suspect had been subdued, that the aircraft would land in Saudi Arabia and that they still faced several more hours before reaching home.
Her father said a passenger near the cockpit played a crucial role in alerting others.
“The great miracle was that a woman got up to go to the bathroom near the cockpit, heard screams from inside and shouted to her husband,” he said. “Yaniv Hayun was the hero of the flight who overpowered the attacker.”
He described the aircraft plunging violently.
“From the speed of the fall, the rear wing was damaged. We dived downward. It went on for a long time, with jolts up and down, the plane at unbelievable angles,” he said. “Everything goes through your head, all the things I can’t say again in front of the girls.”
A preliminary investigation has raised the possibility that the co-pilot stabbed the Indian captain with an emergency crash axe kept inside the cockpit and intended for breaking aircraft windows.
Investigators have ruled out an earlier theory that the co-pilot boarded the aircraft carrying an axe, according to the report, because flight crews undergo security screening before boarding.
One possibility under examination is whether the co-pilot was directed by Iran. At this stage, however, there is no evidence supporting that theory.

Who wins your vote for the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:31:46 UTC
06:31:46 KST

Scutter or flutter? Who wins your vote for the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year?
Two very different butterflies, a pair of cute beetles, the iconic Otway glow-worm and a super-fly guy with eyes on stalks.
These are the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year finalists selected by experts ahead of a national vote to choose the nation's favourite small wonder.
The Australian Insect of the Year is an annual online poll run by the ABC in partnership with insect conservation organisations.
This year's top six were nominated by the CSIRO, Invertebrates Australia, Australian Entomological Society and Zoos Victoria, along with Gardening Australia magazine and A Naturalist's Guide to the Insects of Australia.
Their finalists:
- Gold Christmas beetle (Anoplognathus aureus)
- Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly (Ogyris subterrestris)
- Orchard swallowtail butterfly (Papilio aegeus)
- Otway glow-worm (Arachnocampa otwayensis)
- Stalk-eyed signal fly (Achias australis)
- Tortoise-shelled ladybird (Harmonia testudinaria)
Eminent entomologist Ken Walker, who nominated last year's champion, the graphic flutterer dragonfly, said each of this year's finalists represented an important story about insects.
He said that through charismatic creatures like butterflies and beetles, Australians could learn about insects, most of which remained unnamed and unknown.
"A review by the Academy of Science in 2018 looked at the state of our understanding of the Australian fauna of insects and estimated only 30 per cent of our insect fauna is named, which means 70 per cent of our insect fauna is unnamed," Dr Walker said.
"When you're used to things going along quite nicely, you don't notice something until it goes wrong. So much of that is due to insects doing things like pollination. It's easy to forget 90 per cent of crops rely on insect pollination.
"On the other hand, only 1 per cent of known insects are pest species, but we tend to know those quite well."
Dr Walker said it was vital that people protect insects for our environment.
"Through Insect of the Year, we can highlight the importance of conservation. Insects play an essential role in nature and agriculture," Dr Walker said.
"We need to protect them and to mitigate the things that reduce insect populations, because without them we are all stuffed."
This year's ABC Insect of the Year expert panellists were:
- CSIRO entomologist Keith Bayless
- Australian Entomological Society president Mark Schutze
- Invertebrates Australia founding managing director Kate Umbers
- Gardening Australia magazine horticultural editor AB Bishop
- Zoos Victoria invertebrate conservation coordinator Jessie Sinclair
- Author and nature photographer Peter Rowland
The blue-banded bee (Amegilla cingulata) was the inaugural ABC Insect of the Year, with the graphic flutterer dragonfly (Rhyothemis graphiptera) winning last year's popular vote.
You can cast your vote for the 2026 Australian Insect of the Year until the end of October.
Dr Walker said much of the public awareness of insects centred on the adult life stage, which included familiar butterflies, beetles, flies and ants.
He said the nomination of the Otway glow-worm, the larval stage of a gnat, highlighted the complex life cycle of many insects.
"People might only think about the adult stage, but they've got eggs, larvae and pupae," Dr Walker said.
"So much of their life we don't notice them because they're out of sight.
"It's great then, with the Otway glow-worm, we have one of the contenders as the grub or larval stage."
Two finalists, the Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly and the gold Christmas beetle, are currently subjects of conservation programs at Zoos Victoria and Invertebrates Australia, respectively.
Dr Walker said countless insect species could be subjects of conservation programs if more was known about their plight.
"There are myriads of other insects that deserve similar conservation but they just haven't been studied,"
"They do need our conservation and protection."
You can cast your vote for the 2026 Australian Insect of the Year until the end of October.
The 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year will be announced on November 9, coinciding with the start of Australian Pollinator Week.
Your 2026 Australian Insect of the Year finalists
Gold Christmas beetle (Anoplognathus aureus)
"These iconic and much-loved beetles emerge over the festive season and were once a common fixture of summer nights.
"However, sightings of this species, and many others, have become rare.
"That's why scientists are gathering data via the Christmas Beetle Count to learn more about these beetles to help protect them."
– Dr Kate Umbers, Invertebrates Australia
Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly (Ogyris subterrestris)
"The critically endangered Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly embodies everything that makes Australian insects extraordinary — striking in appearance and ecologically remarkable.
"By celebrating this insect, we celebrate the importance of protecting entire ecosystems and the overlooked invertebrates that keep them functioning."
– Jessie Sinclair, Zoos Victoria
Orchard swallowtail butterfly (Papilio aegeus)
"The orchard swallowtail, also known as the Australian citrus butterfly, is one of our largest and most spectacular butterflies.
"While the larvae occasionally nibble the leaves of backyard citrus, they rarely cause lasting damage and are well worth accommodating because the adult butterflies are important pollinators."
– AB Bishop, horticulture editor, Gardening Australia Magazine
Otway glow-worm (Arachnocampa otwayensis)
"Glow-worms are mysterious, ethereal, and beautiful … and they're not worms at all! They are juvenile flies: fungus gnat 'maggots', to be precise, which become bioluminescent to attract prey.
"This species (otwayensis) is unique to south-west Victoria and a magnificent tourist drawcard yet is highly susceptible to ecological disturbance."
– Mark Schutze, Australian Entomological Society
Stalk-eyed signal fly (Achias australis)
"It's weird but beautiful. As its name suggests, it has eyes on stalks. Their purpose is to attract females and compete with rival males. The females have much smaller heads.
"This species is largest stalk-eyed fly in Australia, and is found in north Queensland, where it feeds on rotting fruit and animal faeces, helping to clean up the environment."
– Keith Bayless, CSIRO
Tortoise-shelled ladybird (Harmonia testudinaria)
"Beyond their spectacular appearance, these striking but tiny (about 6 millimetres) ladybirds are the mighty unsung heroes of our backyards and ecosystems.
"Both the adults and their larvae are voracious predators, eating soft-bodied pests like aphids. The tortoise-shelled ladybird proves Australia's most beautiful insects are often its hardest workers."
– Peter Rowland, nature writer and photographer

Carlton continues push for AFLW top four in win over Hawks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:31:20 UTC
06:31:20 KST

Carlton have weathered wet and wild conditions to leap into the AFLW's top four with a 12-point win over Hawthorn.
On a day when profiting from key moments defined the Princes Park clash, four minutes of first-quarter magic set the Blues up for a 5.6 (36) to 3.6 (24) victory on Thursday.
Carlton fired three scintillating goals in unrelenting rain while keeping the Hawks scoreless until midway through the second term.
But the visitors suddenly found themselves firmly in the contest when forward Poppy Stockwell and midfielder Kaitlyn Ashmore kicked back-to-back third-quarter majors to level the scores.
Carlton slotted two goals either side of three-quarter time to put themselves in the box seat for victory.
Midfielder Abbie McKay (33 disposals, six clearances) was typically inspirational for Carlton while Irish star Erone Fitzpatrick posted 26 disposals and two goals to help last season's preliminary finalists (6-2) go third on the ladder.
"[It was] great Irish weather, so the Irish are used to this," Fitzpatrick told Channel 7.
"It was just the kind of game that you just need to keep getting the ball forward, whether it's a handball, a kick on the ground, or just a surge kick."
For the Hawks (4-4), the loss keeps them out of the congested top eight with four games remaining as they struggled to capitalise on their 52 inside 50s.
Regardless, star ruck Lucy Wales shone with 20 disposals and nine hitouts, while midfielder Eliza West registered 22 disposals.
Hawthorn had the first seven inside-50s of the match, but it was Carlton who drew first blood when Sophie McKay scooped up a loose ball and kicked a goal.
Moments later, Blues midfielder Dayna Finn capitalised on a rogue handball from defender Lavinia Cox before Fitzpatrick added another major.
Trailing 19-0 at the first break, the Hawks were finally rewarded when Stockwell kicked a goal to close the deficit to 12 points at halftime.
Hawthorn upped the ante again, giving the Blues barely any attacking ball as they scored two majors before Fitzpatrick grabbed her second of the evening to re-establish the home team's advantage.
With the game in the balance, Carlton's Keeley Sherar poked the ball through the centre sticks and the home team emerged victorious.

Childhood trauma is linked to suicidal thoughts and attempts in adults with depression and anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
22:00:06 UTC
07:00:06 KST

An analysis of data from the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety found that among adults with depressive or anxiety disorders, those who experienced more childhood trauma were more likely to report recent suicidal thoughts and past suicide attempts. Personality traits, insomnia, and low social support statistically accounted for part of this link. The paper was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Suicide is a major global health problem, and people living with depression or anxiety are among those at the greatest risk. Experiencing abuse or other serious trauma during childhood can increase this risk further, sometimes many years after the original events. One explanation (called the diathesis-stress model) is that childhood trauma creates a lasting vulnerability that can interact with later stresses, such as mental illness, difficult life events, or lack of social support.
Childhood trauma may shape personality in ways that increase vulnerability, for example by contributing to hopelessness, aggression, neuroticism, or a reduced sense of control over one’s life. It may also affect a person’s social world, increasing the likelihood of loneliness, poor support, and repeated negative life experiences. Additionally, childhood trauma is associated with problems such as disturbed sleep, alcohol use, smoking, physical inactivity, and higher body weight. It may also alter biological stress systems, including inflammatory processes and the hormonal system, further affecting how the body responds to stress.
Study author Jasper X.M. Wiebenga and his colleagues set out to examine the association between childhood trauma and suicidal outcomes (suicidal ideation and suicide attempts), as well as various factors that might mediate this association. In other words, they were interested in identifying factors that may be affected by childhood trauma and that may, in turn, affect the risk that a person will start thinking about suicide or attempt suicide.
The researchers analyzed data from the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety (NESDA), a large, ongoing study designed to investigate depressive and anxiety disorders. They hypothesized that more severe childhood trauma would be associated both with a higher likelihood of having suicidal thoughts without having attempted suicide and with a higher likelihood of having attempted suicide.
The analysis used data collected between 2004 and 2007 from 1,572 individuals between 18 and 65 years of age who had been diagnosed with a depressive or anxiety disorder in the 12 months before enrolling in the study. Participants were recruited from across the Netherlands. Of these individuals, 24% had a depressive disorder without an anxiety disorder, 30% had an anxiety disorder without a depressive disorder, and 46% had both. Just over half (55%) reported experiencing childhood trauma. Participants’ average age was 41 years, and 67% were women.
To assess childhood trauma, the researchers used the Childhood Trauma Index, a structured interview about emotional neglect, emotional abuse, physical abuse, and sexual abuse before age 16, scored from 0 to 8 based on the number of trauma types and how often they occurred. Suicidal ideation in the past week was assessed with a shortened version of the Scale for Suicide Ideation, and lifetime suicide attempts were assessed with the question “Have you ever made a serious attempt to end your life, for instance by harming or poisoning yourself or by getting into an accident?”
Based on their answers, participants were divided into three groups: those with neither recent suicidal thoughts nor a past attempt (1,248 people), those with recent suicidal thoughts but no past attempt (231 people), and those with recent suicidal thoughts and a past attempt (93 people). People who had attempted suicide in the past but had no recent suicidal thoughts were left out of the analysis.
The researchers also used data on participants’ personality traits (the Leiden Index of Depression Sensitivity-Revised, the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and the Pearlin Mastery Scale), negative life events (the Recent Life Events Questionnaire), social support, loneliness, lifestyle (alcohol consumption, smoking, sleep quality, physical activity, and body mass index), markers of systemic inflammation (C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, measured from blood samples), and levels of the stress hormone cortisol (from saliva samples).
After controlling for age and sex, each one-point increase in childhood trauma score was associated with 51% higher odds of having recent suicidal thoughts without a past attempt, and 2.68 times higher odds of having recent suicidal thoughts along with a past suicide attempt. When the researchers compared participants with severe childhood trauma (a score of 4 or more) to those with no childhood trauma, the odds of recent suicidal thoughts without an attempt were 2.63 times higher. The odds of having recent suicidal thoughts and a past attempt were almost 10 times higher.
Further analyses tested each potential mediator separately. For both suicide outcomes, a number of factors showed significant indirect associations consistent with mediation: aggression, insomnia, lower social support, loneliness, neuroticism, lower extraversion, hopelessness, and a weaker sense of control over one’s life (people who feel that events in their life are outside their control were more likely to report suicidal thoughts).
Interestingly, higher levels of interleukin-6, a marker of systemic inflammation, also emerged as a potential mediator of the link between childhood trauma and suicide attempts, although it accounted for only about 3% of the association and was no longer significant once other factors were considered together. Other biological markers, including C-reactive protein and cortisol, were not significant mediators. Among lifestyle factors, only insomnia played a role; alcohol use, smoking, physical activity, and body weight were not significant mediators.
The researchers then entered the significant mediators into combined models, which test how much each factor contributes after accounting for the overlap among them. For recent suicidal thoughts without an attempt, neuroticism, lower extraversion, aggression, hopelessness, insomnia, and social support together accounted for about 66% of the association with childhood trauma. For suicidal thoughts with a past attempt, a weaker sense of control, aggression, insomnia, and social support accounted for about 39% of the association. In both cases, childhood trauma remained significantly linked to the suicide outcomes even after accounting for these factors.
“Altogether, CT [childhood trauma] was associated with both suicide outcomes, but SI+SA+ in particular. These associations were substantially attenuated in multiple-mediator models in which multiple personality traits, insomnia, and perceived social support showed significant indirect associations consistent with mediation after accounting for shared variance among variables,” the study authors concluded.
“Aggression, insomnia and social support statistically accounted for the link between CT and the outcomes SI+SA- and SI+SA+. Neuroticism, introversion, and hopelessness linked CT to SI+SA- in particular, whilst locus of control showed a significant indirect association consistent with mediation of the association between CT and SI+SA+. The findings point to potentially modifiable factors relevant for suicide prevention, especially aggression, insomnia and social support, that require further investigation in longitudinal studies.” (In the authors’ shorthand, SI+SA- refers to suicidal ideation without a suicide attempt, and SI+SA+ refers to suicidal ideation with a suicide attempt.)
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of factors associated with suicide attempts and suicidal ideation. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be drawn from the results. The potential mediators were measured at the same time as suicidal thoughts, so the study cannot show whether they came before or after them. Additionally, childhood trauma was reported by participants as adults, leaving room for recall bias, although the authors note that research suggests such retrospective reports are generally reliable.
Many of the potential mediators were also correlated with one another, so the combined models capture each factor’s unique contribution rather than its full role. Finally, all participants had depressive or anxiety disorders, and the sample was predominantly Dutch and female, so the findings may not apply to the general population, to men, or to other cultures.
The paper, “Childhood trauma and suicide ideation and attempts: Examining the mediating role of psychosocial, personality, lifestyle and biological factors,” was authored by Jasper X.M. Wiebenga, Lili Lokhorst, Adriaan W. Hoogendoorn, Henriette D. Heering, Merijn Eikelenboom, Erik J. Giltay, Patricia van Oppen, and Brenda W.J.H. Penninx.
